design_detail: Opportunistic longitudinal follow-up of people first tested in two earlier studies from the same unit (Curran & Morgan, 2000; Curran & Monaghan, 2001), which the authors call an independent group longitudinal design (p. 1452). Baseline is the drug-free session those studies held 3 days after a night on which the ketamine participants had taken ketamine; the follow-up, 3–4 years later, repeats the same battery with alternate test versions. Analysed: 18 people from the original ketamine groups, all of whom had cut their use, and 10 polydrug controls. Group (ketamine, control) × time (baseline, follow-up) repeated-measures ANOVAs, Mann–Whitney tests and correlations of change scores (pp. 1452–1454). There is no group that continued using ketamine.
can_establish: In this small re-contacted sample, whether group differences present 3 days after ketamine use were still present 3–4 years later, after a self-reported fall in frequency of use, relative to polydrug controls retested on the same tasks over the same interval.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the baseline or the persisting differences (there is no measurement before use, and the persisting differences were present at baseline and did not change, which fits pre-existing differences as well as lasting effects, as the authors concede for episodic memory, p. 1458); that cutting down caused the improvement in category fluency (no group continued using, and the baseline, taken 3 days after use, may include after-effects of that use); or anything about the 38 original ketamine participants who could not be contacted (p. 1459).

sample.recruitment: Originally recruited at nightclubs and parties by snowball sampling for the two earlier studies. 33 of the 76 original participants could be contacted and all but 2 agreed, 19 of them from the original ketamine groups (p. 1452).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participation in one of the two earlier studies. Excluded: one member of the original ketamine group who had since developed schizophrenia, and two polydrug controls who had started using ketamine (p. 1452). No other criteria are stated. No abstinence requirement before the follow-up session and no ethics committee approval are reported; participants gave written, witnessed informed consent (p. 1452).
sample.demographics: Ketamine group: 18 (4 women); mean age 28.1; spot-the-word score 48.38 (SD 3.46). Controls: 10 (6 women); mean age 26.5; spot-the-word 50.12 (3.16). The dispersions printed for age (0.81 and 0.70) are too small to be standard deviations (see reporting issues). HADS anxiety 7.89 (4.96) vs 6.63 (3.74); HADS depression 5.27 (4.32) vs 2.00 (2.45) (Table 1 and Results › Demographics, p. 1454). Education and occupation are not reported for this sample.
sample.attrition: 33 of the 76 original participants could be contacted (p. 1452), and 38 members of the original ketamine group could not be (p. 1459). The two earlier papers report 20 + 37 ketamine participants and 19 controls (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 577; Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 751), so 18 of 57 (32%) of the ketamine participants and 10 of 19 (53%) of the controls were analysed, which also implies that the 2 who declined were controls (editors' calculation). Completers are not compared with those lost on their baseline scores.
sample.selection_effects: Strongly selected. About a third of the original ketamine participants were analysed, all of whom had reduced their use; the authors note that many could not be contacted because of transient lifestyles and that those lost may have continued using (p. 1459). The one participant with the most severe outcome (schizophrenia) was excluded, and so were the two controls who had started using ketamine. The ketamine group combines participants from both earlier studies, one of which compared frequent with infrequent use, in proportions that are not reported; all controls came from Curran & Morgan (2000), whose controls had little or no prior ketamine use (p. 577 of that paper). The sex ratio differs (22% vs 60% women; Fisher's exact P = 0.10, editors' calculation) and is not adjusted for.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at follow-up: current drug use and questions on patterns of ketamine use such as craving and periods of abstinence (p. 1452); the baseline frequency comes from the original studies. No hair or urine analysis at follow-up; the authors state that retrospective estimates are inevitably inaccurate and could not be checked objectively (p. 1459).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported. Frequency of ketamine use fell from a mean of 6.45 (SD 8.13) days per month at baseline to 1.61 (3.19) at follow-up, reported as an average reduction of 88.3%; 8 of 18 had not used ketamine for more than 6 months; the reported amount per occasion rose from 0.31 (0.25) g at baseline to 0.44 (0.97) g at follow-up (Results › Drug use, p. 1454). Duration of use, route and purity are not reported. None had escalated or kept the same level of use (p. 1459).
exposure.polysubstance: Both groups used other drugs (Table 2, p. 1454): regular cannabis use 77.8% vs 80%, alcohol 94.4% vs 100%, MDMA 72.2% vs 60%, cocaine 61.1% vs 50%, with no significant differences in these proportions or in days per month of use; amounts were not analysed because the estimates could not be standardized; there was a trend for longer cannabis use in the ketamine group (U = 46.5, P = 0.052). Other current use: amphetamines (4 in the ketamine group, 1 control), benzodiazepines (1 and 1), LSD or psilocybin (2 and 1) (p. 1454). No other drug was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported for the follow-up session: no required interval since last use and no urine screen are described, and 10 of the 18 in the ketamine group had used ketamine within the previous 6 months (p. 1454). The baseline session was held 3 days after a night of drug use (p. 1452).

comparison.controls: 10 polydrug controls from the control group of Curran & Morgan (2000), recruited in the same party and club settings and retested on the same schedule (p. 1452).
comparison.matching: Not matched by design. The authors describe the groups as well matched on drug use, IQ and age (p. 1457) and on other drug use and demographic variables (p. 1459). The sex ratio differs, education is not reported for this sample, and HADS depression was higher in the ketamine group at follow-up.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before ketamine use: the baseline itself followed recent use in people with a history of use. Premorbid ability only as a current reading-based estimate (spot-the-word). Family psychiatric history and childhood adversity are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls used cannabis, alcohol, MDMA and cocaine at rates similar to the ketamine group (Table 2, p. 1454); their lifetime ketamine use is not reported in this paper.

outcomes.instruments: All measured in drug-free sessions; nothing was measured during intoxication. Semantic memory: speed of comprehension (sentences marked as sensible or not within 2 minutes; number judged correctly and errors; described here as 200 sentences, see reporting issues) and category fluency (members of a category named in 90 seconds; correct exemplars, perseverative and semantic errors). Episodic memory: prose recall from the Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test, immediately and after a filled delay of about 20 minutes (idea units, maximum 21). Executive and attentional tasks: digit cancellation (time to cross out every 4 among 400 digits; omission and commission errors), serial sevens (subtractions in 90 seconds; errors) and letter fluency (words in 90 seconds; perseverative and alphabetical errors). Self-ratings: the Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire (state schizotypal symptoms); a dissociative states scale (introduced as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale, analysed as an adapted scale total); Bond–Lader mood visual analogue scales (three factors); a 14-item visual analogue scale of bodily, perceptual and cognitive symptoms associated with ketamine; the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale for the past week. Spot-the-word as an estimate of premorbid verbal IQ (pp. 1452–1453).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published tests (Rivermead prose recall, speed of comprehension, HADS, spot-the-word) alongside two of the authors' own state scales (the schizotypal questionnaire and the subjective-effects scale, from Curran & Morgan, 2000), which have no norms. Scores are compared only with the 10 controls, never with norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or deficit means a lower score than the 10 polydrug controls (a main effect of group across both sessions); recovery means a group × time interaction with no group difference at follow-up; persisting means a main effect of group without an interaction. No clinical threshold is applied.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 23 scores were tested at P < 0.05 (13 cognitive scores and 10 self-rating scores); correlations were limited to measures with significant group effects or interactions, which the authors present as a guard against Type 1 errors (p. 1454).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The first author interviewed participants (epigraph, p. 1451), and group membership was known from the earlier studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Test statistics without confidence intervals; means for the main measures (category fluency, sentences judged, prose recall) appear only as bars with standard errors (Figures 1–3). Category fluency: group × time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032; baseline difference t = 2.42, P = 0.023; no difference at follow-up (p. 1454). Speed of comprehension: group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007; errors group × time F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047 (p. 1455). Prose recall: group F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047 (immediate) and 4.43, P = 0.045 (delayed) (p. 1456). Digit cancellation: group F(1,26) = 7.09, P = 0.013; ketamine group 66.01 (14.12) and 65.32 (11.34) s against controls 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74) s (p. 1456). Schizotypal symptoms: group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001; time F(1,26) = 59.25, P < 0.001 (p. 1456). Subjective-effects factors at follow-up: U = 34, 21 and 39.5 (P = 0.007, 0.001 and 0.014) (p. 1456). Change in category fluency correlated with change in ketamine use (r = 0.712) and with time since last use (r = 0.723), both P < 0.002 (p. 1457). Editors' calculation (pooled SD; 95% CI by the large-sample approximation): digit cancellation d ≈ 0.93 (0.12 to 1.74) at baseline and 0.89 (0.08 to 1.70) at follow-up; schizotypal score d ≈ 1.49 at baseline and 1.05 (0.23 to 1.87) at follow-up; HADS depression d ≈ 0.87 (0.06 to 1.67); for r = 0.712 with n = 18 (Fisher z), 95% CI 0.37 to 0.88.
analysis.covariates: None, apart from a re-analysis of digit cancellation time adjusting for errors, which did not change the result (p. 1456).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No group × time test is reported for prose recall or for the number of sentences judged correctly, although the abstract describes improved semantic memory and persisting episodic deficits; the improvement in sentences judged rests on inspection of Figure 2 (p. 1455). Means and standard deviations for these measures are not printed. Correlations with cannabis and alcohol use were planned (p. 1454) but are not reported, and the number of correlations run is not stated. The four dissociation factors named in the Method are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 18 and 10 participants only large differences can be detected; the absence of differences on dissociation, mood, serial sevens and letter fluency is uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 28 of the 76 original participants, the ketamine group's lower category fluency 3 days after use was no longer different from the controls' 3–4 years later, after a self-reported fall in frequency of use, and the gain in category fluency correlated with the reduction in use and with time since last use. Prose recall, digit cancellation time and the number of sentences judged were lower in the ketamine group across both sessions, without a reported change over time; the controls' delayed recall fell at follow-up, leaving a gap of under one idea unit (editors' reading of Figure 3). State schizotypy was higher in the ketamine group at both sessions and fell in both groups. At follow-up the ketamine group rated more perceptual, bodily and cognitive symptoms and more depressive symptoms than the controls.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that semantic memory impairments are reversible on marked reduction of use, that episodic and possibly attentional impairments appear long-lasting, that schizotypal symptoms and perceptual distortions may persist after cessation, and that people who use or might use ketamine should be aware of its “enduring effects” on memory and experience (p. 1450). The Discussion attributes the baseline semantic differences to ketamine because the groups were matched on drug use, IQ and age (p. 1457), yet concedes that the persisting episodic deficit could be pre-existing (p. 1458) and that it is unclear whether the schizotypal elevation is pre-existing or a chronic effect (p. 1459). Differences present at the drug-free baseline that did not change cannot separate a lasting drug effect from a pre-existing difference, and since 10 of the 18 had used ketamine within the previous 6 months the data cannot show persistence after cessation. The attentional claim rests on slower digit cancellation without more errors, which the authors themselves say may be general slowing (p. 1458). The semantic recovery rests on one interaction in 28 people, with no group that continued using and a baseline taken 3 days after use, and the improvement in sentences judged is read from a figure. The inference of a “low potential for dependence” (p. 1459) is drawn from people who were selected by having cut down and could still be contacted.

timeline.event: Baseline source for 20 of the original ketamine participants and all controls: 3 days after use, the ketamine group scored lower than polydrug controls on semantic memory tasks and higher on dissociation and schizotypy

Baseline source for the other 37 original ketamine participants (18 frequent, 19 infrequent; no control group): 3 days after use, the frequent group was more impaired than the infrequent group on episodic and semantic memory tasks

Cross-sectional study of 150 people from the same unit: no group differences in prose recall or category fluency, including the ex-ketamine group; the authors suggest the prose recall deficits of the earlier day-0 and day-3 designs may have reflected a lack of practice effects (pp. 82–85)
One-year follow-up of the 2009 sample: no group differences in prose recall, and no cognitive deficits in the abstinent group at either session

replication.where_it_stands: This follow-up remains a single, small and highly selected sample, and no independent longitudinal replication appears among the sources read for this card (later studies were not searched by this reader). In the same unit's larger studies, prose recall and category fluency did not differ between people with frequent, infrequent or past ketamine use and controls (Morgan et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2010b), so the persisting episodic memory deficit reported here is not supported by the same group's later data. The absence of deficits in the 2009 ex-ketamine group is consistent with, but does not test, the recovery of category fluency reported here.

funding.funder: Medical Research Council (UK) studentship to C.J.A.M. (Acknowledgements, p. 1460).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors were at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London, which ran both baseline studies; the second author was second author of one of them (Curran & Monaghan, 2001).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before they start using ketamine and at intervals afterwards, with a comparison group matched on other drug use and tested at the same intervals, ketamine use and abstinence verified by hair and urine analysis, enough people who continue, reduce and stop to compare them, assessors blind to group, and means reported for every measure.

domains.note: No adjustment for any variable. The sex ratio differs, education is not reported, HADS depression differs at follow-up and ability before use is unknown; the claimed matching on age and other drug use cannot be checked, because the printed dispersions appear to be standard errors.

Ketamine use and its change over 3–4 years rest entirely on self-report, retrospective at both sessions, with no biological verification; the authors call such estimates inevitably inaccurate (p. 1459). The method behind the reported 88.3% reduction is not stated.

Only 33 of 76 could be contacted, and 18 of 57 original ketamine participants were analysed (editors' calculation), all of whom had cut down; those lost may have kept using (p. 1459), and the participant who developed schizophrenia was excluded. Selection is related to the exposure (change in use) and plausibly to the outcomes.

Whether anyone received treatment for drug use between the sessions, and what else changed in their lives, is not reported; the authors attribute the fall in schizotypy and dissociation in both groups to age and lifestyle (p. 1459).
About two thirds of the original participants are missing at follow-up, with no comparison of their baseline scores against those of completers.

Standard tasks with alternate versions, but testers were not blind to group, two self-rating scales are the authors' own, and some error scores were at floor; the descriptions of two tasks differ from the baseline study's (see reporting issues).

Means not printed for the main outcomes; interaction tests not reported for prose recall and sentences judged; planned correlations with cannabis and alcohol use not reported; dissociation factors not reported; several table cells appear duplicated or contradict the text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design cannot answer its own question: with no group that continued using, and with about a third of the original ketamine participants retained, selected by having cut down, neither recovery nor persistence can be attributed to the change in ketamine use. The persisting differences were already present at the drug-free baseline and did not change, which fits pre-existing differences as well as lasting drug effects, and practice, regression toward the mean and after-effects at the 3-day baseline are uncontrolled. The source may be cited as a description of what this follow-up observed (category fluency no longer different after reduced use; lower prose recall and slower digit cancellation at both sessions; higher state schizotypy and subjective symptoms), with its limits stated; it should not be cited for reversibility, for lasting effects of ketamine, or for a low potential for dependence.

key_findings.finding: Of the 76 participants of the two earlier studies, 33 could be contacted and all but 2 agreed, 19 of them from the original ketamine groups; after excluding one person who had developed schizophrenia and two controls who had started using ketamine, 18 from the ketamine groups and 10 polydrug controls were retested 3–4 years after their first testing.
key_findings.locator: Method, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Discussion adds that 38 members of the original ketamine group could not be contacted (p. 1459, Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph). With 57 original ketamine participants and 19 controls in the two earlier papers, 18 of 57 (32%) and 10 of 19 (53%) were analysed (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The ketamine group reported using ketamine on 1.61 (SD 3.19) days per month at follow-up against 6.45 (SD 8.13) at baseline, described as an average reduction in frequency of 88.3%; 8 of 18 had not used ketamine for more than 6 months, and the reported amount per occasion had risen from 0.31 (0.25) g to 0.44 (0.97) g.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug use (Table 2), 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Self-report only. The group means imply a 75% fall in mean frequency; the method behind 88.3% (perhaps the mean of individual reductions) is not stated (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Category fluency showed a group × time interaction (F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032) and a main effect of time (F(1,26) = 7.50, P = 0.011): the ketamine group generated fewer category members than controls at baseline (t = 2.42, P = 0.023) but not at follow-up. Perseverative errors were more frequent in the ketamine group at both sessions (group F(1,26) = 6.13, P = 0.02): 1.94 (2.36) vs 0.5 (0.71) at baseline and 1.29 (2.29) vs 0.4 (0.68) at follow-up; semantic errors were at floor at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Semantic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1454, continuing on p. 1455); Table 3 and Figure 1 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: Group means appear only as bars with standard errors (Figure 1). Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi: about 16 vs 21 category members at baseline and about 20 vs 21 at follow-up. The t statistic is printed with df 1,27 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: On speed of comprehension the ketamine group judged fewer sentences correctly than controls across both sessions (group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007); no interaction is reported for this score, and the authors describe an apparent increase in the ketamine group from Figure 2. Errors showed a group × time interaction (F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047): more errors in the ketamine group at baseline (1.06 (1.12) vs 0.2 (0.42)) but not at follow-up (0.38 (0.46) vs 0.4 (0.52)), when errors were at floor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Speed of comprehension task, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi: about 62 vs 86 sentences judged correctly at baseline and about 73 vs 83 at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Prose recall showed a main effect of group (immediate F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047; delayed F(1,26) = 4.43, P = 0.045), the ketamine group recalling less across both sessions; no group × time result is reported, and the authors note that the controls' delayed recall fell at follow-up (Figure 3b).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Means appear only as bars on axes that start at 4 idea units. Editors' reading of Figure 3 at 300 dpi: immediate recall about 7.9 vs 10.3 idea units at baseline and 7.4 vs 8.9 at follow-up; delayed recall about 7.2 vs 9.7 and 7.4 vs 8.2. The follow-up gap in delayed recall is under one idea unit (maximum score 21), so the main effect rests largely on the baseline difference; no test of the follow-up difference is reported.

key_findings.finding: Digit cancellation was slower in the ketamine group at both sessions (group F(1,26) = 7.09, P = 0.013; no interaction or effect of time): 66.01 (14.12) s at baseline and 65.32 (11.34) s at follow-up, against 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74) s in controls; errors did not differ, and adjusting for errors did not change the result (editors' calculation: d ≈ 0.93 at baseline and 0.89 at follow-up).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Digit cancellation, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say the slower time may reflect general psychomotor slowing rather than an attentional impairment (p. 1458, Discussion › Attention and working memory, 1st paragraph). The ketamine group mixes participants of the two earlier studies in proportions that are not reported, and the authors note that those from Curran & Monaghan (2001) already had poorer attentional functioning at the first session than those from Curran & Morgan (2000), whose ketamine group had shown no attentional difference from its controls 3 days after use (p. 1458); the 10 controls came from the original polydrug control group (p. 1452). The slower times at both sessions may therefore partly reflect who came from which study.

key_findings.finding: There were no group differences at either session on letter fluency (baseline 19.8 (6.23) vs 21 (5.94) words; follow-up 21 (5.62) vs 20.4 (4.01)) or serial sevens (baseline 24.8 (8.16) vs 20.78 (10.17) subtractions; follow-up 22 (9.33) vs 23 (7.97)); perseverative errors in letter fluency showed a trend towards more in the ketamine group (F(1,26) = 3.30, P = 0.081).
key_findings.locator: Results › Executive functioning › Serial sevens and verbal fluency, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The ketamine group's baseline serial sevens value, 24.8 (8.16), is identical to the controls' baseline schizotypal total in Table 4 (p. 1455); one of the two may be a transcription error.

key_findings.finding: State schizotypal symptoms (Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire) were higher in the ketamine group than in controls across both sessions (group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001) and fell in both groups (time F(1,26) = 59.25, P < 0.001), without an interaction: totals 51.5 (21.28) vs 24.8 (8.16) at baseline and 18.67 (17.05) vs 4.0 (4.06) at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures (Table 4) › Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire, 1st paragraph (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The scale indexes state rather than trait schizotypy, and schizotypal scores did not correlate with ketamine use (p. 1459, Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph). Editors' calculation: d ≈ 1.49 at baseline and 1.05 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.87) at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Dissociative-states scores fell in both groups (time F(1,26) = 5.93, P = 0.022) with no group difference (totals 10.11 (15.38) vs 5.44 (5.85) at baseline and 3.24 (4.53) vs 0.80 (1.54) at follow-up); the text reports no group differences on any of the three mood factors at either session.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures › Adapted Dissociative States Scale and Mood Rating Scale paragraphs (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The dissociation measure is introduced in the Method as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (p. 1453) but analysed as an adapted scale total, and Table 4 marks baseline mood differences that the text denies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: At follow-up the ketamine group rated more perceptual (U = 34, P = 0.007), bodily (U = 21, P = 0.001) and cognitive or mental-state symptoms (U = 39.5, P = 0.014) than controls on the 14-item visual analogue subjective-effects scale: perceptual 8.4 (7.71) vs 1.18 (1.45), somatic 9.33 (7.14) vs 1.14 (1.25), cognitive 14.47 (14.89) vs 3.75 (3.95).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective measures › Subjective Effects Scale, 1st paragraph (p. 1456); Table 4 (p. 1455)
key_findings.note: The perceptual difference was at least as large at baseline (13.43 (9.20) vs 1.12 (1.56); editors' calculation, Welch t ≈ 5.5), although Table 4 marks no baseline significance; the follow-up difference therefore does not show a change over time, and 10 of the 18 had used ketamine in the previous 6 months.

key_findings.finding: At follow-up the ketamine group scored higher than controls on HADS depression (5.27 (4.32) vs 2.00 (2.45); U = 55.5, P < 0.031) but not on HADS anxiety (7.89 (4.96) vs 6.63 (3.74)); change in depression cannot be assessed because one of the two earlier studies did not use the HADS.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics (Table 1), 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 1454); Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
key_findings.note: The authors state that the ketamine group was not within a clinical range of depression (p. 1459) but give no cut-off or individual scores. Editors' calculation: d ≈ 0.87 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.67). The printed test does not reproduce: U = 55.5 with 18 and 10 participants gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10 (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Change in category fluency (follow-up minus baseline) correlated with change in ketamine use (r = 0.712, P < 0.002) and with time since last ketamine use (r = 0.723, P < 0.002); the sample used and the sign convention for change in use are not stated. Digit cancellation did not correlate with immediate or delayed recall.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlations, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Method says correlations were also run within the ketamine group (p. 1454). Editors' calculation for n = 18: 95% CI 0.37 to 0.88 for r = 0.712. Those who used most at baseline had the most room both to cut down and to improve, so regression toward the mean is not excluded.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the persisting episodic memory deficit could be due either to pre-existing differences or to ketamine use (p. 1458), that it is unclear whether the higher schizotypal scores reflect pre-existing differences or chronic effects of ketamine (p. 1459), and that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out without prospective studies (p. 1459).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph (p. 1458); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph, and Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)

key_findings.finding: None of the 18 had escalated or kept the same level of ketamine use, and all reported few problems in cutting down, which the authors read as a low potential for dependence; they acknowledge that the 38 uncontacted members of the original ketamine group may have continued using and that a group continuing ketamine use would have been the right comparison.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: One member of the original ketamine group had developed schizophrenia by the time of follow-up and was excluded (p. 1452); the Discussion presents this case as anecdotal evidence (p. 1459).
key_findings.locator: Method, 1st paragraph (p. 1452); Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1459)
key_findings.note: The Discussion places this person within the sample of 18, although the Method excluded them before the 18 were counted (see reporting issues). A single excluded case gives no estimate of risk.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is headed as giving standard deviations, but its age dispersions (0.81 and 0.70 years, for means of 28.1 and 26.5) are too small to be standard deviations if, as the text says, the groups did not differ in age; the text also reports no group differences in days per month of alcohol use (16.67 (2.69) vs 13.70 (3.23)) or cocaine use (2.28 (0.94) vs 1.00 (0.44)) in Table 2. Editors' calculation: read as SDs, these give Welch t ≈ 5.5 (P < 0.001) for age, 2.5 (P ≈ 0.03) for alcohol and 4.9 (P < 0.001) for cocaine; read as standard errors, the age difference gives t ≈ 1.5 (P ≈ 0.15). Other rows, such as years since first cannabis use (9.94 (5.94)), behave like SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell which dispersions are standard deviations and which standard errors, so the matching on age and other drug use on which the authors rest their attribution to ketamine cannot be checked; if the printed values are SDs, the groups were not matched on age, alcohol or cocaine use.

reporting_issues.issue: The baseline category fluency comparison is printed as t(1,27) = 2.42; an independent t-test with 18 and 10 participants has 26 degrees of freedom (the printed P = 0.023 fits either).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the F tests correctly use df 1,26.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline reduction in frequency of ketamine use (88.3%, in the abstract and Results) does not follow from the printed group means of 6.45 and 1.61 days per month, and the method of calculation is not stated (editors' calculation: the means imply a 75% fall).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 88.3% figure should be cited, if at all, as the authors' average of a reduction computed in an unstated way; individual changes in use are not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The dissociation measure is introduced as the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale with four factors (p. 1453) but reported as an adapted scale total, labelled ADSS in Table 4 and ADDS in the text (pp. 1455–1456); one of the baseline studies describes the adapted version as the 19 self-rated items of that scale (Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 752). The three mood factors are named alertness, calmness and discontentedness in the Method (p. 1453), sedation, discontentedness and calm in Table 4, and drowsiness, discontentedness and anxiety in the Results (p. 1456).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dissociation results come from a self-rated adaptation, not from the clinician-administered scale, and should not be cited as CADSS scores; the mood factors cannot be identified with certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports no group differences on any mood factor at either session (p. 1456), but Table 4 marks baseline differences in discontentedness (21.47 vs 37.92, P < 0.01) and calm (24.54 vs 37.9, P < 0.05); Table 4 also marks the baseline schizotypal difference but not the larger baseline perceptual-symptom difference (13.43 (9.20) vs 1.12 (1.56); editors' calculation, Welch t ≈ 5.5), although the Method says post hoc tests were run only after significant interactions (p. 1453).
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance markers in Table 4 cannot be relied on; baseline mood and subjective-symptom differences should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Identical values appear in unrelated cells: the ketamine group's baseline serial sevens score (24.8 (8.16), p. 1456) equals the controls' baseline schizotypal total (24.8 (8.16), Table 4, p. 1455); the controls' baseline discontentedness and calm scores are 37.92 (9.59) and 37.9 (9.59); and both groups' baseline cognitive-symptom SDs are 20.08 (Table 4). Table 4 also leaves a parenthesis unclosed (12.12 (12.61).
reporting_issues.consequence: Suggests transcription errors in the tables; these cells should not be cited without the authors' data.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that one of the ketamine participants from the sample of 18 had developed schizophrenia (p. 1459), but the Method states that this person was excluded, leaving 18 from the original ketamine group (p. 1452).
reporting_issues.consequence: The person was not in the analysed sample; no statement about schizophrenia among people who use ketamine can rest on this study beyond the existence of one excluded case.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says the same battery was used at both sessions, but describes the speed of comprehension test as 200 sentences and the delayed prose recall as following a delay of about 20 minutes (p. 1453), whereas both baseline studies describe 100 sentences and a delay of 15 minutes or about 15 minutes (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 578; Curran & Monaghan, 2001, p. 752).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the description is wrong or the follow-up tasks differed from the baseline ones; a changed task would confound the time and group × time effects on these two measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The follow-up depression difference is printed as U = 55.5, P < 0.031 (p. 1454; Table 1 marks P < 0.05), but U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10 (one-tailed about 0.05; normal approximation and exact null distribution, editors' calculation); a t-test on the printed means and SDs gives about 0.04 (Welch about 0.02). The trend printed for years of cannabis use (U = 46.5, P = 0.052) gives about 0.04 with the same group sizes, while the three subjective-effects tests on p. 1456 (U = 34, 21 and 39.5) reproduce their printed P values.
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up depression difference is less secure than printed and should be cited with the recalculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the participants of Curran & Morgan (2000) did not differ from controls on depression at baseline (p. 1459), but that paper reports higher HADS depression scores in its ketamine group on both test days, including the drug-free session 3 days after use that this paper uses as baseline (4.30 against 1.68; group F(1,32) = 19.4, p<0.001; Curran & Morgan, 2000, pp. 581, 585).
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up depression difference cannot be read as new since the first testing: for the participants of the 2000 study a difference was already present at baseline.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper cites Morgan et al. (2004a), which its reference list gives as the team's Neuropsychopharmacology laboratory study (29, 208–218), for the finding that healthy volunteers showed no residual effects 3 days after a single dose (pp. 1451, 1457), and in the same paragraph on p. 1451 for volunteers liking ketamine and wanting more of it, which is the subject of the Psychopharmacology paper listed as 2004b (172, 298–308); Morgan et al. (2009, p. 78) cites the Psychopharmacology paper for the 3-day finding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which laboratory study showed no residual effect 3 days after a dose cannot be established from the team's papers; the finding should be cited only as the team's second-hand statement.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Morgan_2004a_BeyondTheKHole3Year.pdf, printed pp. 1450–1461 (all 12 pages; Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–3 checked on the rendered pages at 150 and 300 dpi); the participant and task descriptions of the two baseline studies were checked in PDFs/Ketamine/Curran_2000_RecreationalUsersNightAnd3Days.pdf (pp. 575–578) and PDFs/Ketamine/Curran_2001_InAndOutOfTheKHole.pdf (pp. 749–752)

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives two-tailed p of about 0.10 (one-tailed about 0.05), not the printed P < 0.031; a t-test on the printed means and SDs gives about 0.04 (Welch about 0.02); the cannabis-years test (U = 46.5, printed P = 0.052) gives about 0.04; the three subjective-effects U tests reproduce.
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed with the normal approximation and the exact null distribution for groups of 18 and 10: U = 55.5 gives p = 0.098 to 0.103; U = 46.5 gives 0.035 to 0.039; U = 34, 21 and 39.5 give about 0.007, 0.001 and 0.015, as printed. Added as reporting issue 8; key finding 10's note cross-refers.

design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of five groups of 30 recruited from the unit's participant database and by snowball sampling: frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (less than four times a week but at least once a month), ex-ketamine (abstinent at least 1 month), polydrug controls matched to the current-use groups on other drugs, and controls who did not use illicit drugs. One drug-free session, at least 24 hours after any psychotropic drug, with CANTAB tasks, a source memory task, prose recall, fluency, the Hayling test and self-report symptom scales; hair analysis (3 cm, about 3 months) for ketamine. One-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni post hoc tests (p. 80).
can_establish: Whether, at one time point, people with frequent, infrequent or past ketamine use differed from each other and from polydrug and non-drug controls on the tasks and symptom scales used, within this convenience sample.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine caused any difference (there are no data from before use, and the frequent group had about 3 fewer years of education, a lower premorbid IQ estimate and more family history of mental illness, none of them adjusted for in the group comparisons); whether the frequent group's differences are lasting or short-lived after-effects (it was tested a mean of 1.6 days after last use); or whether deficits reverse after stopping, because the ex-ketamine group is a different set of people, most of whom had used less.

sample.recruitment: The unit's existing database of participants and snowball sampling (p. 78). All participants were paid; the institutional ethics committee approved the study (p. 78).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Groups defined by self-reported frequency (p. 78): frequent, more than four times a week; infrequent, less than four times a week but at least once a month; ex-ketamine, abstinent for at least 1 month (12 previously frequent, 8 formerly daily); polydrug controls matched with the current-use groups for other drugs; non-drug controls taking no illicit drugs. Drug-using participants had to abstain from psychotropic drugs for at least 24 hours before testing, and all had to have no history of head injury or organic brain damage and English as native language (p. 78). How many people were screened or excluded is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a single session; all 150 completed (p. 80).
sample.selection_effects: Convenience sample drawn from the research unit's own database and participants' networks, with group membership by self-reported frequency, checked against hair ketamine but without stated criteria for exclusion. The frequent group differs from the others in education, premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness; the polydrug group had the highest premorbid IQ estimate and the non-drug group one of the lowest. The current-use groups are people still using; people who stopped because of problems could appear in the ex-ketamine group or not be recruited at all. Group sizes were fixed at 30, so the sample says nothing about how common these patterns of use are.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history; urine samples analysed (Medscreen) but results not reported; hair samples (3 cm, about the previous 3 months; Trichotech) analysed for ketamine and said to confirm self-reported other drug use (pp. 78, 80–81). Correlations used self-reported amount per session because hair indices were considered somewhat unreliable (p. 80).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 81). Frequent group: 3.80 (2.36) g per session on 20.13 (2.36) days per month, last use 1.6 (1.27) days before testing (range 1–7), 6.07 (4.89) years of use; 19 reported using ketamine daily (p. 80). Infrequent group: 1.28 (1.13) g on 3.25 (2.55) days per month, last use 11.3 (9.36) days before testing, 4.20 (2.20) years. Ex-ketamine group: 1.49 (2.00) g on 2.55 (3.90) days per month just before stopping, abstinent 344.43 (624.72) days (range 120–2980), 7.63 (2.63) years of use; 8 had used daily, and the group's peak frequency was 11.21 (9.34) days per month (p. 80). In the first 2 months of use all three groups reported 0.50 to 0.62 g per session; age at first use 19.83 (8.21), 21.17 (6.01) and 20.03 (5.03) years. Hair ketamine 282.14 (566.53), 18.01 (41.06) and 3.55 (13.63) ng/mm; none detected in either control group. Route and purity not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Regular use (more than 10 times a year; Table 3, p. 81) of cannabis by 21, 21, 21 and 29 of 30 in the frequent, infrequent, ex-ketamine and polydrug groups; ecstasy 20, 28, 19, 22; cocaine 21, 26, 19, 22; amphetamine 13, 16, 4, 9; alcohol 29, 29, 25, 26 and 29 (including the non-drug group). The authors report no differences between the four drug-using groups in self-reported amounts or frequencies (p. 81), but the proportions of people with regular use differ (editors' calculation: χ²(3) = 8.9, P = 0.03 for cannabis; 8.5, P = 0.04 for ecstasy; 11.9, P = 0.008 for amphetamine). Table 4 (p. 82) shows that more people in the ketamine groups than in the polydrug group had used or tried 2CB, 2C-I, DMT, GHB or nitrous oxide (for example, 2CB tried by 16 in the frequent group and none of the polydrug controls). No drug other than ketamine was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 24 hours from psychotropic drugs for drug-using participants, by self-report; urine results are not reported, and the follow-up paper on the same participants states that the 24 hours could not be verified biologically (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132). Cigarettes were allowed in the hourly 10-minute breaks (p. 79). The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days (mean 1.6) after last ketamine use (Table 2, p. 81); the follow-up paper gives 2 (SD 2.60) days for the same session (reporting issue 8).

comparison.controls: 30 polydrug controls (no ketamine detected in hair) matched to the current-use groups on other drug use, and 30 controls who did not use illicit drugs (29 of them regular drinkers), recruited in the same way (pp. 78, 80–81).
comparison.matching: Matched on other drugs by design (self-reported amounts and frequencies did not differ, but the proportions of people with regular use did; see polysubstance); age and sex similar; education, premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness differ and are not adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No cognitive or psychiatric measurement before use; premorbid ability only as a current reading-based estimate, which was lowest in the frequent group. Childhood trauma was not measured; the authors note it as a risk factor for dissociation (p. 86).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The polydrug controls used cannabis (29 regular), ecstasy, cocaine, alcohol and amphetamine at rates similar to or higher than the ketamine groups but had less experience of other hallucinogens and dissociatives (Table 4); the non-drug controls used alcohol only.

outcomes.instruments: All measured in a drug-free session; nothing was measured during intoxication. CANTAB pattern recognition memory (percentage correct), spatial working memory (errors and strategy score) and Stockings of Cambridge (problems solved in the minimum number of moves); a source memory task (80 low-frequency words heard in a male or female voice, recognition after a filled 6-minute delay; recognition d′, bias C and source accuracy); Rivermead prose recall, immediately and after about 10 minutes; category (fruit or vegetables) and letter (M or B) fluency in 90 seconds; the Hayling test of response initiation and inhibition; spot-the-word as a premorbid IQ estimate. Self-reports: the short Oxford–Liverpool Inventory of Feelings and Experiences (unusual experiences, cognitive disorganization, introvertive anhedonia, impulsive non-conformity, rated for daily life when not under the influence of drugs), the Peters et al. Delusions Inventory (total, distress, preoccupation, conviction), the Dissociative Experiences Scale, the Beck Depression Inventory and the Spielberger trait anxiety scale (pp. 79–80).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard published tasks and scales, but no comparison with norms: impairment means a lower score than other groups in this sample. The scoring of the Dissociative Experiences Scale is not described (group means 321 to 784).
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or elevation means a significant one-way ANOVA followed by a Bonferroni post hoc difference from other groups (p. 80). No clinical threshold is applied, except that the Discussion calls the frequent group's mean depression score mild to moderate (p. 85) without giving cut-offs.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni within each ANOVA's post hoc comparisons only; no correction across the 25 outcome scores (14 cognitive and 11 self-report) or across the correlations, whose number is not stated.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the drug history was taken at the start of each session (p. 78), so testers knew group membership.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means and SDs for most measures (Tables 5–6, pp. 83–84); spatial working memory errors, pattern recognition and the O-LIFE subscales appear only as bar charts (Figures 1–3). Omnibus F(4, 145): SWM errors 8.05 and strategy 5.00; Stockings 6.58; pattern recognition 6.37 (all P < 0.001); d′ 2.74 (P = 0.031); PDI total 8.40 and DES 6.60 (P < 0.001); BDI 3.04 (P = 0.019); unusual experiences 6.12, cognitive disorganization 4.81 and impulsive non-conformity 3.96 (pp. 81–84). Correlations in the frequent group: PDI total with current amount per session r = 0.433 (P = 0.019); d′ with spot-the-word r = 0.474 (P = 0.009) (p. 84). Editors' calculation, frequent group against polydrug controls (pooled SD, n = 30 each; 95% CI by the large-sample approximation): Stockings d ≈ −1.18 (−1.73 to −0.63); SWM strategy 0.66 (0.14 to 1.18); d′ −0.65 (−1.17 to −0.13); PDI total 0.81 (0.29 to 1.34); DES 0.75 (0.23 to 1.28); BDI 0.62 (0.10 to 1.14); category fluency 0.10 (−0.41 to 0.60). Fisher z 95% CI for r = 0.433 with n = 30: 0.09 to 0.69.
analysis.covariates: None in the group comparisons. Spot-the-word and years of education were examined only by correlation within the frequent group (p. 84).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract lists a simple vigilance task that appears in neither the Method nor the Results. Spatial working memory errors, pattern recognition and the O-LIFE subscales are shown only in figures. The number of correlations run is not stated, and one significant correlation with ketamine use is reported. Urine results and hair results for drugs other than ketamine are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. Thirty per group gives reasonable power for large differences between two groups, but little for the pattern across five groups on which the conclusions about infrequent and past use rely.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one session, the frequent ketamine group, tested about 1.6 days after last use and with fewer years of education and a lower premorbid IQ estimate, made more spatial working memory errors, had a poorer search strategy, solved fewer Stockings problems, recognised fewer patterns and had lower word-recognition d′ than the other groups; prose recall, letter and category fluency, the Hayling test and source memory did not differ. The infrequent and ex-ketamine groups did not differ from controls on any cognitive measure. The frequent group scored highest on delusional ideation, dissociation, unusual experiences and depression; the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups scored above the non-drug controls on some of these, but are not reported to differ from the polydrug controls.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the frequent group was impaired on category fluency, which the Results contradict (p. 82; Table 5, p. 83). It concludes that frequent use is associated with impairments and reduced wellbeing, and that the cognitive impairments may be reversible on stopping because the ex-ketamine group showed none, whereas “delusional symptoms persist” (p. 77). Reversibility is inferred from different people: the ex-ketamine group had used less before stopping (2.55 days per month, peak 11.21) than the frequent group (20.13), and the authors themselves state that only retesting the frequent group after abstinence could show it (p. 86). The persistence of delusions rests on the ex-ketamine group's PDI total exceeding the non-drug controls' (P < 0.01 as printed), a difference that cannot be reproduced from Table 6 (editors' calculation) and was not shown against the polydrug controls, whose mean was close (13.03 vs 15.79). The argument that symptoms rising with ketamine use tell against pre-existing differences (p. 85) relies on a gradient across groups that also differ in education and family history and on one correlation (r = 0.433) out of an unstated number. The Discussion's statement that groups were matched for other drug use objectively by hair analysis (p. 85) is not backed by reported hair data for other drugs. The Summary's “broad-ranging cognitive impairments” (p. 86) overstates differences found on four of the tasks, and the authors' own suggestion that these might reflect withdrawal (p. 86) cannot be excluded with testing 1 to 7 days after last use.

timeline.event: Frequent and infrequent ketamine groups tested on the night of use and 3 days later: on day 3 the frequent group was more impaired on episodic and semantic memory tasks

Three-year follow-up of 18 people who had cut down their ketamine use: category fluency no longer different from polydrug controls, but prose recall lower and digit cancellation slower at both sessions; prose recall did not differ in the present study

One-year follow-up of 119 of these 150 participants: the frequent group's spatial working memory errors and pattern recognition differed from other groups averaged over both sessions, but its follow-up means approached the controls'; its Stockings and strategy scores improved to control levels; delusional ideation and dissociation remained highest in the frequent group; depression scores rose in the frequent and abstinent groups

replication.where_it_stands: The only later data read for this card come from the same participants' 1-year follow-up (Morgan et al., 2010b), which tests the stability of these differences rather than replicating them in an independent sample; there, some differences persisted (delusional ideation, dissociation, averaged cognitive differences) and others resolved (planning and strategy). Earlier studies from the same unit reported prose recall deficits that this study did not find, which the authors attribute to the earlier testing designs (p. 85). Later independent studies were not searched by this reader, so the status is provisional.

funding.funder: Grant to H.V.C. and C.J.A.M. from the UK Economic and Social Research Council (RES-000-23-0945) (Acknowledgements, p. 86).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: None (p. 86).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London; participants were recruited partly from the unit's own database (p. 78).

what_would_settle_it: Repeated testing of the same people before and after they stop using ketamine, with abstinence verified biologically, alongside people who continue, with education, premorbid ability, family history and other hallucinogen use adjusted for, testers blind to group, and an interval since last use long enough to separate lasting effects from after-effects of recent use or withdrawal.

domains.note: Education (12.27 vs about 15 years), premorbid IQ estimate and family history of mental illness differ, and none is adjusted for; other hallucinogens and dissociatives were used more in the ketamine groups; the polydrug matching holds for self-reported amounts but not for the proportions of people with regular use.

Self-reported use, checked against hair ketamine but with no stated thresholds or exclusions; ketamine was found in the ex-ketamine group's hair despite reported abstinence of at least 120 days; urine results not reported; the frequent group's frequency figures are internally inconsistent (see reporting issues).

Convenience sample from the unit's database and participants' networks; current-use groups are people still using, and people who stopped because of problems may be under- or over-represented in the ex-ketamine group.

The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days after last use, so after-effects or withdrawal may contribute, as the authors note (p. 86); whether the ex-ketamine group stopped with treatment is not reported.
All 150 completed the session; no missing data are reported.
Standard tasks and scales, but testers were not blind to group, the symptom measures are self-reports, and the scoring of the Dissociative Experiences Scale is not described.

The abstract contradicts the Results on category fluency and names a vigilance task that is never reported; several post hoc differences on which the conclusions rest cannot be reproduced from the printed tables, and two recomputed F values differ from those printed; several measures appear only in figures; the number of correlations is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The frequent group's lower scores on the CANTAB tasks and d′ and its higher symptom scores are sizeable and measured with standard instruments, but uncorrected differences in education, premorbid ability and family history, and testing only 1 to 7 days after last use, prevent attributing them to lasting effects of ketamine; and the pattern of post hoc differences on which the claims about infrequent and past use rest is not reproducible from the printed tables. The source may be cited for the frequent group's lower performance on spatial working memory, planning, pattern recognition and word recognition, and higher delusional ideation, dissociation and depression scores, relative to this sample's other groups, with the confounders named, and for the absence of cognitive differences in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups; it should not be cited for reversibility, for delusions persisting after stopping, for a category fluency deficit, or for causation.

key_findings.finding: Groups did not differ in age or sex, but the frequent ketamine group had fewer years of education (12.27 (4.84) vs 15.33 (2.56) in the infrequent and 15.10 (2.47) in the non-drug group; F(4, 145) = 4.07, P = 0.004; post hoc P = 0.018 and 0.04), a lower premorbid IQ estimate (spot-the-word 45.67 (6.13) vs 50.90 (4.09) infrequent, P = 0.04, and 51.53 (4.22) polydrug, P = 0.01; F(4, 145) = 7.29, P < 0.001) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 vs 1 to 3 of 30 in the other groups; χ²(4) = 12.59, P = 0.013).
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: No first-degree relative with schizophrenia was reported in any group (p. 78). The polydrug group also scored higher than the non-drug group on spot-the-word (P = 0.028). Table 1 gives 22 men and 10 women in the polydrug group, 32 for a group of 30 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Self-reported ketamine use: the frequent group used 3.80 (2.36) g per session on 20.13 (2.36) days per month, last 1.6 (1.27) days before testing (range 1–7), and 19 of 30 reported daily use; the infrequent group 1.28 (1.13) g on 3.25 (2.55) days, last 11.3 (9.36) days before testing; the ex-ketamine group 1.49 (2.00) g on 2.55 (3.90) days per month just before stopping, abstinent for 344.43 (624.72) days (range 120–2980), 8 of whom had once used daily, with a group peak of 11.21 (9.34) days per month. All three groups reported 0.50 to 0.62 g per session in their first 2 months of use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 2nd paragraph (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
key_findings.note: A mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 cannot be reconciled with daily use by 19 of 30 (see reporting issues). Amount, frequency and days since last use differed between the frequent and infrequent groups (Z = 1.81, 3.87 and 2.84), with two Z–P pairs inconsistent (see reporting issues). The follow-up paper gives 2 (SD 2.60) days since last use for the frequent group at this same session (reporting issue 8).

key_findings.finding: Hair analysis (3 cm, about the previous 3 months) showed ketamine at 282.14 (566.53) ng/mm in the frequent, 18.01 (41.06) in the infrequent and 3.55 (13.63) in the ex-ketamine group (group difference F(4, 149) = 6.70, P < 0.001), and none in the hair of any participant in either control group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 1st paragraph (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
key_findings.note: The ex-ketamine group's shortest reported abstinence (120 days) exceeds the window of a 3-cm sample, yet its mean is above zero; the paper does not comment and gives no thresholds for classifying participants by hair. With 150 participants in five groups the df should be 4,145.

key_findings.finding: Groups differed in spatial working memory errors (F(4, 145) = 8.05, P < 0.001) and strategy score (F(4, 145) = 5.00, P < 0.001): the frequent ketamine group made more errors than the others (P < 0.01) and had a poorer, that is higher, strategy score than all other groups (32.73 (5.77) against 26.53 to 28.93; P < 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Spatial working memory (Fig. 1) (p. 81, continuing on p. 82); Figure 1 (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Error means appear only in Figure 1 (editors' reading: about 32 errors in the frequent group against about 11 to 19 in the others). Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): the strategy difference from the polydrug controls (32.73 vs 28.93) gives P ≈ 0.11.

key_findings.finding: The frequent group solved fewer Stockings of Cambridge problems in the minimum number of moves than every other group (7.66 (1.61) against 8.89 to 9.53; F(4, 145) = 6.58; post hoc P < 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Stockings of Cambridge (Table 5) (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: The omnibus P is printed as < 0.00. Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): P ≈ 0.03 against the ex-ketamine group and below 0.002 against the others; d ≈ −1.18 (95% CI −1.73 to −0.63) against the polydrug controls.

key_findings.finding: The frequent group recognised fewer patterns on the pattern recognition memory task than all other groups (F(4, 145) = 6.37, P < 0.001; post hoc P < 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Pattern recognition memory (Fig. 2) (p. 82); Figure 2 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Means appear only in Figure 2, whose axis starts at 75% (editors' reading: about 83% correct in the frequent group against about 90 to 95% in the others).

key_findings.finding: Word-recognition discriminability (d′) on the source memory task differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 2.74, P = 0.031): frequent 2.36 (0.74), infrequent 2.74 (0.73), ex-ketamine 2.97 (0.63), polydrug 2.85 (0.76) and non-drug 2.67 (0.82); the paper reports the frequent group as lower than all other groups (P < 0.05). Bias (C) and the proportion of source errors did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Source memory task (Table 5) (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reaches P < 0.05 (P ≈ 0.02); against the non-drug controls P ≈ 0.11 even without correction. Within the frequent group d′ correlated with spot-the-word (r = 0.474, P = 0.009; p. 84).

key_findings.finding: There were no group differences in prose recall (only a main effect of delay, F(1, 145) = 34.37, P < 0.001; group means 8.11 to 8.32 idea units immediately and 7.20 to 7.83 after the delay), letter fluency (15.14 to 17.53 words), category fluency (14.73 to 17.27; frequent group 16.84 (4.80), non-drug controls 14.73 (3.99)) or the Hayling test (overall scores 6.76 to 7.31, and no difference on the response-inhibition part); fluency error rates were at floor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Prose recall, Fluency and Hayling test paragraphs (pp. 82–83); Table 5 (p. 83)
key_findings.note: The abstract nevertheless lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: On the O-LIFE, unusual experiences differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 6.12, P < 0.001), higher in the frequent group than in all others (P < 0.05); cognitive disorganization (F(4, 145) = 4.81, P = 0.001) was higher in the frequent and infrequent groups than in the non-drug controls (P < 0.001); impulsive non-conformity (F(4, 145) = 3.96, P = 0.005) was higher in all four drug-using groups than in the non-drug controls (P < 0.01); introvertive anhedonia did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-report measures › O-LIFE (p. 83); Figure 3 (p. 84)
key_findings.note: Means appear only in Figure 3, whose axis starts at 1 (editors' reading: unusual experiences about 6.1 in the frequent group, about 4.3 in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups, 3.3 in the polydrug and 2.4 in the non-drug controls).

key_findings.finding: Delusional ideation (PDI total) differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 8.40, P < 0.001): frequent 22.72 (14.10), infrequent 15.1 (10.33), ex-ketamine 15.79 (11.47), polydrug 13.03 (9.17), non-drug 9.43 (9.21); the paper reports the frequent group higher than all others (P < 0.05) and the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups higher than the non-drug controls (P < 0.01). Conviction (F(4, 145) = 2.73, P = 0.031) and preoccupation (F(4, 145) = 3.71, P = 0.007) were highest in the frequent group; distress did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-report measures › PDI (p. 83); Table 6 (p. 84)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 6 (one-way ANOVA, pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): F ≈ 5.9 rather than 8.40; P ≈ 0.27 (ex-ketamine) and 0.48 (infrequent) against the non-drug controls, and about 0.08 and 0.16 for the frequent group against the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups. The ex-ketamine and polydrug means were close (15.79 vs 13.03).

key_findings.finding: Dissociative experiences differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 6.60, P < 0.001): frequent 784 (451), infrequent 630 (408), ex-ketamine 401 (264), polydrug 488 (325), non-drug 321 (267); the frequent group was higher than all groups except the infrequent group (P < 0.01), and the infrequent group higher than the non-drug controls (P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-report measures › Dissociative experiences scale (p. 83); Table 6 (p. 84)
key_findings.note: How the scale was scored is not described. Editors' calculation from Table 6: F ≈ 8.3 rather than 6.60.

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (Beck Depression Inventory) differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 3.04, P = 0.019): frequent 11.48 (8.17), infrequent 9.03 (6.10), ex-ketamine 6.00 (5.11), polydrug 7.17 (5.38), non-drug 7.23 (7.00); the paper reports the frequent group higher than all others (P < 0.05). Trait anxiety did not differ (group means 31.17 to 36.03).
key_findings.locator: Results › Beck Depression Inventory (Table 6) and Speilberger Trait Anxiety scale (Table 6); Table 6
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 6 (pooled SD): frequent against infrequent P ≈ 0.14 without correction; against the polydrug and non-drug controls P ≈ 0.11 and 0.12 after Bonferroni correction; only the difference from the ex-ketamine group (P ≈ 0.01) is reproduced. The Discussion calls the frequent group's mean mild to moderate depression (p. 85) without giving cut-offs.

key_findings.finding: Within the frequent group, PDI total correlated with the current amount of ketamine per session (r = 0.433, P = 0.019); no other correlation between self-reported ketamine use and the key cognitive and symptom measures was significant, and amounts of cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine did not correlate with them. d′ correlated with spot-the-word (r = 0.474, P = 0.009), while years of education correlated with none of the cognitive measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 30): 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69 for r = 0.433. The number of correlations run is not stated.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that the prose recall deficits found in their earlier studies, which tested people on the night of use and 3 days later, may simply reflect a lack of practice effects in the ketamine groups, and state that recreational use, on average 3 days per month here, was not associated with impaired cognitive function.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: From the absence of deficits in the ex-ketamine group the authors infer that cognitive impairments may be reversible on stopping, noting that 8 of that group had used daily and that the group had used ketamine for longer than the others.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The ex-ketamine group's frequency just before stopping (2.55 days per month) and its peak (11.21) were far below the frequent group's current 20.13 days (Table 2, p. 81).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that a study of this kind cannot rule out pre-existing group differences (p. 85), that the frequent group's greater family history of mental illness may have contributed to the findings, that only retesting the frequent group after a sufficient period of abstinence could show that deficits are reversible, and that the frequent group's cognitive impairments might reflect a withdrawal state (p. 86).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 1st paragraph (p. 85); Neurocognitive function, 5th paragraph, and Limitations (p. 86)

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that the 19 people reporting daily use, some reporting up to 6 g per day, meet criteria for dependence, citing an earlier qualitative paper; the Method describes no measure of dependence.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Claims about dependence in this sample cannot rest on this paper's own data.

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states, citing reference 9, that 3 days after taking part in a laboratory study, healthy volunteers who had received ketamine did not differ from those who had received placebo, and sets out three explanations for poorer memory in people who use ketamine when tested drug free: after-effects of taking the drug a few days earlier, differences that predate use, and long-lasting effects. It describes the less frequent group of Curran and Monaghan (2001) as using ketamine once a month.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the laboratory study was not read for this card, and the team's papers cite two different laboratory reports for this finding (reporting issue 9). Curran and Monaghan (2001) give their less frequent group 0.45 days a month, about once every 2 months (that paper, pp. 753–754).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments (p. 77), but the Results report no group differences in category or letter fluency (p. 82), Table 5 shows the frequent group's category fluency (16.84) above the non-drug controls' (14.73) (p. 83), and the Discussion lists retrieval from semantic memory as unimpaired in this group (p. 85).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract cannot be cited for a category fluency deficit; the Results show none.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists a simple vigilance task among the cognitive tasks (p. 77), but no such task is described in the Method (p. 79) or reported in the Results (pp. 81–84).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either an outcome was measured and not reported, or the abstract is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the polydrug group as 22 men and 10 women, in a group the text and the other tables give as 30 (editors' calculation: the counts sum to 32).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the sex distribution of the polydrug controls cannot be stated with certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Degrees of freedom do not match the sample: the hair comparison across five groups of 30 is printed as F(4, 149), and the comparison of years of use across three groups of 30 as F(2, 89) (editors' calculation: expected denominator df 145 and 87).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; suggests typing errors or different numbers analysed than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of the frequent and infrequent groups gives Z = 1.81 with P = 0.003 for amount used and Z = 2.84 with P < 0.001 for days since last use (editors' calculation: two-tailed P for these Z values is about 0.07 and 0.005).
reporting_issues.consequence: The difference in amount per session between the frequent and infrequent groups may not be statistically significant as printed; at least one of each pair of numbers is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is internally inconsistent for the frequent group: a mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 is incompatible with daily use by 19 of 30 (if the 19 used ketamine on at least 28 days and the others on just over 4 days a week, the mean would be at least about 24 days; editors' calculation), and the same SD (2.36) is printed for the amount per session in the adjacent row. The frequent group's mean age at the start of regular use (25.90) exceeds its mean age (25.87, Table 1) although regular use is said to have lasted 5.03 years; in the ex-ketamine group, mean years of use (7.63) exceed the mean time since first use (27.3 minus 20.03, about 7.3 years) although the group had stopped a mean of 344 days earlier.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures for frequency and duration of use cannot all be right; claims should not rest on the frequent group's mean frequency or on durations of use from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: Several post hoc results cannot be reproduced from the printed means and SDs under the stated analysis (one-way ANOVA, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons; editors' calculation with the pooled within-group SD): d′ lower in the frequent group than in all others (only the ex-ketamine comparison reproduces); BDI higher in the frequent group than in all others (only the ex-ketamine comparison reproduces; against the infrequent group P ≈ 0.14 uncorrected); PDI total higher in the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups than in the non-drug controls at P < 0.01 (P ≈ 0.48 and 0.27); and the frequent group's SWM strategy against the polydrug controls (P ≈ 0.11). The omnibus F recomputed from Table 6 is about 5.9 for the PDI total (printed 8.40) and about 8.3 for the DES (printed 6.60).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims that delusional ideation is elevated in infrequent and ex-ketamine use, and that the frequent group is worse than every other group on word recognition and depression, are not supported by the printed tables; either the tables or the tests are in error.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites reference 9 for an opportunistic study of 18 people who used ketamine (p. 85), but reference 9 is a laboratory study in healthy volunteers; the 18-person follow-up is reference 35 (Morgan et al., 2004) (p. 87).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error; the 2004 follow-up is the study meant.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same first session, Morgan et al. (2010b) prints figures that differ from this paper's: the frequent group's days since last ketamine use, 2 (SD 2.60) against 1.6 (SD 1.27), range 1–7, here (2010b, Table 2, p. 125; here Table 2, p. 81); its Beck Depression Inventory score, 7.08 for the 25 retested against 11.48 for all 30 here, which can both hold only if the 5 not retested averaged about 33.5 (editors' calculation; 2010b, Table 4, p. 128; here Table 6, p. 84); and its amount per session (2.77 against 3.80 g) and the SD of its frequency of use (7.41 against 2.36 days a month), both for n = 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline values cannot be taken interchangeably from the two papers; claims that cite this paper's 1 to 7 days since last use or its depression score of 11.48 should note the other report (card sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issue 9).

reporting_issues.issue: The laboratory finding of no difference from placebo 3 days after a dose is cited to reference 9, the team's Psychopharmacology paper of 2004 (172, 298–308) (pp. 78, 87), whereas the team's 3-year follow-up attributes the same finding to its Neuropsychopharmacology paper of 2004 (29, 208–218), listed here as reference 3 (Morgan et al., 2004a, pp. 1451, 1457). Reference 9 is also cited on p. 85 for the 18-person follow-up (reporting issue 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which laboratory study shows no residual effect 3 days after a dose is unclear; claims should cite it only as the team's second-hand statement.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Morgan_2009_FrequentInfrequentExUsers.pdf, printed pp. 77–87 (all 11 pages; Tables 1–6 and Figures 1–3 checked on the rendered pages at 110–150 dpi)

disagreements.first_pass: At least 24 hours from psychotropic drugs for drug-using participants, by self-report; urine results are not reported. The frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days (mean 1.6) after last ketamine use (Table 2, p. 81).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: cigarettes were allowed during hourly breaks, the 24-hour abstinence from psychotropic drugs was self-reported, and the follow-up paper says it could not be verified biologically for this same session (Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 132).
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 79 (Procedure: 10-minute hourly breaks with a cigarette allowed) and in Morgan et al. (2010b), p. 132 (Discussion › Methodological considerations). Field extended.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed (cross-paper): for this same baseline session, Morgan et al. (2010b, Table 2, p. 125) gives the frequent group's days since last use as 2 (SD 2.60), range 1–14 (here 1.6 (1.27), range 1–7), and its BDI for the 25 retested as 7.08 (here 11.48 for all 30, which would need a mean of about 33.5 in the 5 not retested); a cross-reference would help, since claims cite the 1–7 days and the 11.48 from this paper.
disagreements.resolution: Verified here (Table 2, p. 81; Table 6, p. 84) and in Morgan et al. (2010b), Table 2 (p. 125, rendered at 220 dpi and rotated) and Table 4 (p. 128); arithmetic recomputed (33.48). Added as reporting issue 8, with the amount and frequency-SD differences that the 2010b card records; the bracketed (1–14) is not called a range, because that table's bracketed values are often not ranges (sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issue 5). Key finding 1 cross-refers.

disagreements.first_pass: A mean of 20.13 days per month with an SD of 2.36 cannot be reconciled with daily use by 19 of 30 (see reporting issues). Amount, frequency and days since last use differed between the frequent and infrequent groups (Z = 1.81, 3.87 and 2.84), with two Z–P pairs inconsistent (see reporting issues).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228 (the cross-paper point above).
disagreements.resolution: Cross-reference to reporting issue 8 added.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: the laboratory statement on p. 78 (Introduction, 3rd paragraph) matters for the night-of-use claim, which cites it second-hand from this paper; the paper also describes the less frequent group of Curran & Monaghan (2001) as using once a month.
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 78. The statement, which a claim anchor cites, had no key finding: added as key finding 17, with the description of the 2001 group checked against Curran & Monaghan (2001), pp. 753–754 (0.45 days a month).

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: the p. 78 statement cites reference 9 (Psychopharmacology 2004; 172: 298–308), whereas Morgan et al. (2004a, Addiction, p. 1451) attributes the same finding to the Neuropsychopharmacology paper (29: 208–218); which laboratory study shows it is unclear.
disagreements.resolution: Verified at p. 78, in this paper's reference list (p. 87: reference 3 Neuropsychopharmacology, reference 9 Psychopharmacology) and in Morgan et al. (2004a), pp. 1451, 1457 and 1461. Added as reporting issue 9; the same point is on sc_morgan_2004a (reporting issue 10).

verification.checked_by: AI reader 228 (blind second reading) and AI reader 232 (adjudication)

design_detail: One-year follow-up of the 150 participants of Morgan et al.
