design_detail: Narrative review of the clinical pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of ketamine in anaesthesia and pain therapy, written by four anaesthesiologists and clinical pharmacologists for a pharmacokinetics journal. One database (PubMed Medline) was searched to 2 February 2016 with eight listed keywords, limited to English-language papers in peer-reviewed journals; further papers were taken from review articles and from the bibliographies of relevant papers, titles were screened for relevance by the authors, and data were extracted after what the authors call critical examination. No eligibility criteria, no counts of records found, screened or included, no duplicate screening, no appraisal of the included studies and no quantitative synthesis. The review has 159 references, one large table collecting pharmacokinetic parameters by route and formulation from fourteen primary studies, two figures redrawing the drug-interaction results of five studies by the authors' own group, and sections on mechanism, perioperative and chronic-pain use, depression, formulations by route, and side effects.
can_establish: What the anaesthesia and pain literature to February 2016 reported about ketamine's absorption by route, its metabolism by cytochrome P450 enzymes, its interactions with inhibitors and inducers of those enzymes, the plasma concentrations associated with loss of consciousness and with experimental analgesia, and the state of the clinical evidence in perioperative care, chronic pain, cancer pain and depression, with the primary studies named so that each figure can be traced.
cannot_establish: Whether the evidence summarized is complete or representative (one database, English only, no eligibility criteria and no record counts); the quality of any cited study, none of which is appraised; any pooled estimate or interval; the frequency of any adverse effect; and anything about the harms of non-medical ketamine use or about deaths, which the review covers in a single short section.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence base is whatever the authors retrieved from PubMed Medline up to 2 February 2016, plus papers found in review articles and in the bibliographies of retrieved papers; no number of records found, screened, excluded or included is given (p. 3 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: English-language papers in peer-reviewed journals; beyond that, relevance to the aim of the review as judged by the authors, with no stated criteria and no second screener (p. 3 of the online-first PDF).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: One database, one language and selection by the authors' own judgement, so what was left out cannot be seen. The review's frame is anaesthesia and pain therapy, and the human pharmacokinetic table is built from small studies, several with three to eight participants, including six from the authors' own group on oral S-ketamine and its interactions. The sections on perioperative and chronic-pain use cite systematic reviews, while the section on long-term harm rests on four sources.

exposure.measurement: Varies across the cited studies and is not described: Table 1 gives route, nominal amount, sample size and the parameters, but not the analytical method, and the review does not say which rows come from stereoselective assays, although it reports separate values for S-ketamine and the racemate throughout.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported as study conditions in Table 1: single intravenous, intramuscular, oral, sublingual, rectal and intranasal administration and short infusions of racemic ketamine or S-ketamine, in healthy volunteers and in patients with neuropathic pain, with sample sizes of 3 to 12 per row (pp. 4-5 of the online-first PDF). The review also prints clinical anaesthetic and analgesic dosing schemes and definitions of low-dose use; these are the review's clinical recommendations for practitioners and are not reproduced in this card.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited pharmacokinetic studies. Combinations are covered only as pharmacokinetic interactions with cytochrome P450 inhibitors and inducers (clarithromycin, grapefruit juice, ticlopidine, itraconazole, rifampicin, St John's wort) and as the clinical co-administration of sedatives to attenuate psychotomimetic effects; combinations used outside medicine are not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable: the review compares routes and formulations with intravenous administration as each cited study did, and compares S-ketamine with racemic ketamine and with R-ketamine.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review reports no primary data of its own.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Pharmacokinetic parameters as the cited studies reported them (peak concentration, area under the curve, time to peak, elimination half-life, bioavailability), collected in Table 1; cytochrome P450 interaction effects as the mean percentage change in area and peak concentration with 95% confidence intervals, redrawn in Figures 3 and 4 from five studies by the authors' group, with no numerical values printed; effective concentrations for loss and return of consciousness and for experimental analgesia taken from cited studies; clinical outcomes as the cited trials and systematic reviews reported them.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review does not say how it chose which figures to carry forward, and the footnotes to Table 1 show that the entries mix means with standard errors, means with standard deviations, medians with ranges and medians with interquartile ranges, and areas integrated over different windows, within the same columns (pp. 4-5 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.operationalization: Bioavailability is reported as each cited study computed it, against that study's own intravenous reference. Harm is not operationalized: the side-effects section lists reported adverse effects without frequencies, denominators or exposure durations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no synthesis, no pooling and no statistical testing of the review's own.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported as cited, with no synthesis. Disposition: alpha half-life 2-4 minutes and beta half-life 2-4 hours; plasma protein binding 10-30%; steady-state volume of distribution 160-550 L per 70 kg; systemic clearance 60-147 L/h per 70 kg; about 80% of ketamine N-demethylated to norketamine, measurable in plasma 2-3 minutes after an intravenous bolus with a peak at 30-60 minutes (pp. 3, 7 of the online-first PDF). Bioavailability by route: 8-24% by mouth overall, with 17-24% for racemic ketamine and 8-11% for S-ketamine; 24-30% sublingual; about 30% rectal; about 45% nasal; about 93% intramuscular (pp. 2, 12-14 of the online-first PDF). Concentration-effect: effective concentrations for loss of consciousness 241 ng/mL (SD 90) for the racemate and 111 (SD 30) for S-ketamine, and for return of consciousness 148 (SD 46) and 75 (SD 21), taken from a textbook chapter; psychedelic effects reported from about 50 ng/mL with intensity increasing linearly between 50 and 200 ng/mL; experimental analgesia above 100-160 ng/mL after intravenous racemate and at about 40 ng/mL after oral dosing (p. 9 of the online-first PDF). Enantiomers: clearance of S-ketamine given alone 26.3 mL/min/kg against 14.8 for racemic ketamine, and 18.5 for the S-enantiomer within the racemate, in ten healthy men (p. 7 of the online-first PDF). Clinical: perioperative low-dose ketamine reported to reduce opioid consumption by 40%; two systematic reviews found no reduction in chronic postsurgical pain overall, but restricting to intravenous administration the relative risk fell by 25% (number needed to treat 12) at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; subcutaneous ketamine added to opioids in 185 patients with cancer pain did not reduce pain scores against placebo; an anaesthetic amount of S-ketamine raised whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic amount by 13% (pp. 10-12 of the online-first PDF). Interaction magnitudes appear only as figures without numbers.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the review is not described as systematic and follows no reporting guideline.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 leaves the bioavailability column empty for every row taken from the three-person formulation study (Yanagihara et al., 2003), although the text cites that same study for the rectal figure of about 30% and the nasal figure of about 45%, which the source does print. The interaction results are shown only as figures, so the magnitudes and intervals cannot be read. Sample sizes appear in Table 1 but are never carried into the text, the Key Points or the abstract, where the bioavailability figures are stated as properties of the drug. The side-effects section runs to one short section with five references and gives no frequency for any adverse effect.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative summary in which the primary studies are named and tabulated: oral bioavailability of ketamine is low and highly variable because of first-pass metabolism by CYP3A and CYP2B6; inhibitors and inducers of those enzymes change exposure to oral S-ketamine substantially; sublingual, rectal and especially nasal administration give higher systemic availability and less norketamine than swallowing; concentrations associated with loss of consciousness, psychedelic effects and experimental analgesia differ by about an order of magnitude; and in clinical use the evidence is strongest for perioperative opioid sparing and weakest for long-term analgesia in chronic pain and for cancer pain. The table shows that most of the route figures come from studies of three to twelve people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The route figures are stated without their sample sizes or sources wherever they are given as numbers (the Introduction on p. 2, Sections 7.2 and 7.5 on pp. 12-13 and the Summary on p. 14), so that oral bioavailability of 8-24% and nasal bioavailability of about 45% read as constants of the drug rather than as results from small studies, the nasal figure resting on three people; the Abstract and the Key Points make the same point without a figure. Section 7.3 attaches the intramuscular bioavailability of about 93% to an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, whereas the study cited for it that I have read gave 0.5 mg/kg and computed 93% from four participants. The Summary states that S-ketamine is a two times more effective anaesthetic and analgesic than the racemate, where the abstract says this has been postulated. The side-effects section states that because ketamine raises blood pressure and heart rate and preserves respiratory activity a lethal overdose is unlikely, with no citation and no mortality data, in a review whose sources on long-term harm are a survey of urinary symptoms, a review of cystitis, a diffusion-imaging study and a pharmacy update; the same section calls the long-term safety profile unclear.

timeline.event: Bioavailability and kinetics of intravenous, intramuscular and oral ketamine in healthy volunteers; the source of the intramuscular figure of about 93% and the oral figure of about 17% that this review carries, from four people per route
Plasma profiles after five racemic preparations in three healthy Japanese men; the source of this review's sublingual, rectal and nasal figures
Review of ketamine use for the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs, covering the non-medical-use, bladder and cognitive literature that this review treats in one short section
Absolute bioavailability of racemic ketamine from a sublingual formulation in eight healthy volunteers (Rolan et al.), tabulated here at 29%

Population pharmacokinetics of S-ketamine and norketamine after intravenous and oral dosing (Fanta et al.), cited here for steady state after the third dose and for the estimate that a 2.4 times larger oral amount is needed to match intravenous exposure

replication.where_it_stands: The review is a pointer to primary studies, not an independent source of data. For every route-by-route figure the encyclopedia should cite the primary study that Table 1 names, with its sample size; the review's own contribution is the collection, the account of cytochrome P450 interactions from its authors' trials, and its judgements about where the clinical evidence was insufficient as of February 2016. Its treatment of long-term harm was already thin relative to the urological and cohort literature published between 2007 and 2014 and says nothing about deaths.

funding.funder: No funding was received for the conduct of this study (Compliance with Ethical Standards, p. 14 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The four authors state that they have no conflicts of interest directly relevant to the content of this study (p. 14 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Turku and Turku University Hospital, and University of Helsinki and Helsinki University Hospital. Five of the drug-interaction studies that the review summarizes in Table 1 and redraws in Figures 3 and 4 are the authors' own, and the review's conclusions about the metabolism and interactions of oral S-ketamine follow from them. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol, several databases, no language limit, duplicate screening and extraction, and formal appraisal of the pharmacokinetic studies, reporting every bioavailability figure with its sample size, its assay and an interval; and, separately, a systematic review of the harms of repeated and long-term ketamine exposure that includes the bladder, cognitive, dependence and mortality literature, which this review's frame excludes.

domains.note: More than most narrative reviews: one named database, a stated last-search date (2 February 2016) and eight listed keywords, with papers added from reviews and bibliographies. But one database only, English only, no eligibility criteria, no counts of records found or included, no second screener, and selection by the authors' judgement of relevance, so what was omitted cannot be seen.

No formal appraisal of any study, and Table 1's rows carry no caveat about their sample sizes in the text. Methodological weakness is nevertheless named in several places: the pharmacometric models are called preliminary and to be interpreted cautiously, the evidence on intracranial pressure is reported as graded C with severe methodological limitations, both complex regional pain syndrome trials are said to have methodological shortcomings, and one of them is noted as stopped halfway.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The section on cytochrome P450 interactions and both of its figures rest on five studies by this group, and the review's conclusions about oral S-ketamine follow from them. The rest of the review draws on a wide literature.

The review generally marks uncertainty, saying that the optimal route and duration are yet to be established, that preliminary results should be interpreted carefully, and that the long-term safety profile is unclear. Against that, it states without any citation that ketamine's cardiovascular and respiratory profile makes a lethal overdose unlikely, and prints clinical dosing schemes without the dose-finding evidence behind them.

domains.domain: Balance of clinical benefits against harms (non-medical use, deaths and long-term bladder and cognitive damage under-represented)
domains.note: Eleven sections cover mechanism, anaesthesia, analgesia, special patient groups, chronic pain, depression and formulations; harm is one short section with five references, which names cystitis, bladder changes, cognitive disturbances, psychological dependence, hepatic dysfunction and hypersalivation without a single frequency, and the review states that a lethal overdose is unlikely without engaging any mortality literature. The frame is the clinical use of ketamine by anaesthetists, and the harms of repeated use are outside it.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The search is better documented than in most narrative reviews and the clinical sections are explicit about where the evidence is insufficient, but the selection is unsystematic and single-database, nothing is appraised, the interaction evidence is the authors' own, and the treatment of harm is minimal to the point of a stated safety conclusion with no supporting data. The source can be cited for the review's own summary statements about ketamine's clinical pharmacology, for its collection of pharmacokinetic parameters by route with the primary studies named, for the cytochrome P450 interaction findings, and for its judgements about the state of the clinical evidence in February 2016. It cannot be cited as the evidence for any bioavailability figure (cite the primary study, with its sample size), for the frequency or severity of any adverse effect, or for anything about the risk of death.

key_findings.finding: Oral bioavailability of ketamine is low: the review states that 17-24% of oral racemic ketamine and 8-11% of oral S-ketamine reach the systemic circulation, citing six studies, and gives the combined range as 8-24% in the Introduction and in the Summary. The Abstract and the Key Points make the point without a number, calling oral bioavailability poor and low.
key_findings.locator: Section 1 Introduction (p. 2); Section 7.2 Oral Ketamine, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Section 9 Summary, 2nd paragraph (p. 14); Abstract (p. 1) and Key Points, 1st box (p. 2), which carry no figure
key_findings.note: The sample sizes behind these figures (3 to 12 people per study) appear only in Table 1 and never in the text.

key_findings.finding: Intramuscular bioavailability is given as approximately 93%, with the terminal plasma half-life not significantly different from that after intravenous administration, ketamine detectable in plasma after 4 minutes and peak concentrations within 5-30 minutes of injection.
key_findings.locator: Section 7.3 Intramuscular Ketamine
key_findings.note: The figure is attached here to an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, but the study cited for it that I read (Clements et al., 1982) gave 0.5 mg/kg and computed 93% from four participants.

key_findings.finding: Sublingual and oral ketamine are said to share poor bioavailability of 24-30%, with less norketamine formed after sublingual intake; sublingual wafer formulations are reported to vary less between people than lozenges and tablets.
key_findings.locator: Section 7.4 Sublingual Ketamine

key_findings.finding: Nasal bioavailability is given as approximately 45%, higher than sublingual, rectal and especially oral administration, with peak concentrations reached in 10-17 minutes and low norketamine exposure because first-pass metabolism is largely bypassed; the review adds that the amount delivered nasally is difficult to control.
key_findings.locator: Section 7.5 Nasal Ketamine
key_findings.note: Cited to two studies, one of them the three-person formulation study (Yanagihara et al., 2003) whose nasal row this card's companion appraisal shows cannot rest on exactly three determinations.

key_findings.finding: Rectal bioavailability is given as approximately 30%, with a norketamine area very similar to that after a sublingual tablet, citing the same three-person study.
key_findings.locator: Section 7.6 Rectal Ketamine

key_findings.finding: Disposition: a short distribution half-life of 2-4 minutes and a longer elimination half-life of 2-4 hours; plasma protein binding 10-30%; steady-state volume of distribution 160-550 L per 70 kg; systemic clearance 60-147 L/h per 70 kg, which the review describes as equalling liver blood flow and uses to explain the low oral bioavailability. The elimination half-life of S-ketamine is given as slightly longer (4-7 hours) than that of the racemate.
key_findings.locator: Section 4 Pharmacokinetics of Ketamine, 1st paragraph (p. 3), continuing on p. 6

key_findings.finding: Metabolism: ketamine is N-demethylated to norketamine, mainly by CYP3A and CYP2B6, with CYP2C9 also contributing in vitro; about 80% of ketamine is converted to norketamine, which is measurable in plasma 2-3 minutes after an intravenous bolus and peaks at 30-60 minutes; metabolites are excreted in bile and urine after glucuronidation and only traces of the parent drug appear in urine; recent work indicates norketamine is itself rapidly metabolized and may not be the main circulating metabolite.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.1 Biotransformation and Pharmacokinetic Drug-Drug Interactions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Interactions: inhibition of CYP3A by clarithromycin or grapefruit juice greatly increased exposure to oral S-ketamine; the CYP3A inducers rifampicin and St John's wort substantially reduced plasma concentrations of oral S-ketamine, with a smaller effect after intravenous administration; the CYP2B6 inhibitor ticlopidine impaired the metabolism of oral S-ketamine; itraconazole, a CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor, had no significant interaction, which the authors attribute to concurrent action of other transporters.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.1, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 6, ends at the top of p. 7); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Figures 3 and 4 show mean percentage change in area and peak concentration with 95% confidence intervals but print no numbers, so no magnitude can be anchored to this review; the five underlying studies are the authors' own.

key_findings.finding: Concentration-effect relations as cited: effective concentrations for loss of consciousness 241 ng/mL (SD 90) for racemic ketamine and 111 (SD 30) for S-ketamine, and for return of consciousness 148 (SD 46) and 75 (SD 21); psychedelic effects reported from about 50 ng/mL, with intensity increasing linearly over 50-200 ng/mL; analgesia in experimental pain models above 100-160 ng/mL after intravenous racemic ketamine, and at about 40 ng/mL after oral dosing.
key_findings.locator: Section 6 Pharmacodynamics and Clinical Use of Ketamine, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The loss- and return-of-consciousness values are taken from a textbook chapter rather than a primary study.

key_findings.finding: Enantiomers: S-ketamine is described as having about four times the affinity of R-ketamine for the NMDA receptor, and is said to be postulated as about four times more potent than R-ketamine and about twice as potent as the racemate; there is no interconversion, and R-ketamine inhibits the elimination of S-ketamine, with clearance of 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine given alone, 14.8 for racemic ketamine and 18.5 for the S-enantiomer within the racemate, in ten healthy men.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Section 4.1, 1st paragraph (p. 6, for the absence of interconversion); Section 4.2, 2nd paragraph (p. 7, for the clearance figures); Section 6, 2nd paragraph (p. 9)
key_findings.note: The fourfold figure is the review's explanation of an analgesic potency difference and is attributed to a single 1992 source. It should not be confused with the separate statement in Section 5.2 (p. 8) that S-ketamine has 2 to 3 times higher affinity for opioid receptors than R-ketamine.

key_findings.finding: Oral S-ketamine produces much more metabolite than parent drug: the review reports that the S-norketamine area was 16.5 times greater than that of S-ketamine after oral dosing, that steady state is reached after the third dose without accumulation on twice-daily dosing, and that about 2.4 times more S-ketamine is needed by mouth than intravenously for the same exposure, because S-norketamine is a weaker analgesic than S-ketamine in animals.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.2, 8th paragraph (p. 8); Section 7.2 Oral Ketamine (p. 12), continuing on p. 13

key_findings.finding: Chronic postsurgical pain: two systematic reviews found that perioperative low-dose intravenous or epidural ketamine did not reduce the risk of chronic postsurgical pain, but when only intravenous studies were analysed the relative risk fell by 25% (number needed to treat 12) at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; two later randomized trials found no reduction in chronic post-thoracotomy pain.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.4.1 Ketamine in the Prevention of Chronic Pain, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic and cancer pain: ketamine is reported to reduce chronic pain in several conditions in the short term, with long-term analgesic effects less well documented; in cancer pain the review states that the current evidence is insufficient to recommend ketamine as add-on therapy, citing a Cochrane review and a placebo-controlled trial of subcutaneous ketamine in 185 patients in which pain scores did not fall.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.4.2 Ketamine and Chronic Pain, 1st paragraph (p. 11); Section 6.4.3 Ketamine and Cancer Pain (p. 12); Section 9 Summary (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Side effects and long-term safety: the review states that the safety profile of ketamine in long-term use is unclear; that chronic administration is linked to severe and persistent urinary disease including cystitis, contracted bladder and bladder wall thickening; that cognitive disturbances may affect colour perception, memory, attention, reaction time and the sense of time, with psychological dependence, in people who use ketamine long-term; and that hepatic dysfunction and hypersalivation have been reported. No frequency is given for any of these.
key_findings.locator: Section 8 Side Effects and Limitations

key_findings.finding: In the same paragraph the review states that because ketamine raises blood pressure and heart rate through sympathetic activation and preserves respiratory activity, a lethal overdose is unlikely.
key_findings.locator: Section 8 Side Effects and Limitations, 1st sentence
key_findings.note: No citation is attached to this statement and no mortality data appear anywhere in the review; it should not be used to support any claim about the risk of death.

key_findings.finding: Brain imaging as cited: an anaesthetic amount of S-ketamine increased whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic amount by 13%, with the metabolic rate of oxygen and glucose virtually unaffected, so that perfusion rose most in the insula and anterior cingulate; the review also reports that monitors of anaesthetic depth do not give a reliable estimate under ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Section 6.3.2 Effects on Neurotoxicity, Neuroprotection, and Intracranial Pressure, 5th paragraph (begins p. 11); Section 6.2, last paragraph (p. 10)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 has no row attributed to reference 11, the 1982 bioavailability study, yet its first three rows reproduce exactly the values printed in Table II of that paper, which I read. The first row is attributed to reference 87 (Clements & Nimmo, 1981) and prints an area of 27.5 (1.2), a half-life of 3.1 h and norketamine values of 40 (6), 63 (23) and 35.4 (3.8); the intramuscular and oral rows are attributed to reference 10 (Grant et al., 1981) and print peaks of 243 (49) and 44 (10), times to peak of 22 (4) and 30 (5), half-lives of 2.6 and 2.9 h, an oral area of 4.8 (0.8), an oral bioavailability of 17% and norketamine values of 92 (10), 31.3 (3.8), 78 (14) and 200 (44), 36.7 (3.9), 60 (13). Every one of these is the corresponding entry of the 1982 table, with half-lives converted from minutes to hours. I have not read the two 1981 papers and cannot say whether they print the same values.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim citing this review for the intravenous, intramuscular or oral figures would be following citations to papers other than the one that prints them. Claims should cite Clements et al. (1982), where the sample sizes and the four-person bioavailability denominators are visible (see sc_clements_1982).

reporting_issues.issue: In converting those half-lives from minutes to hours, Table 1 prints the intramuscular value as 2.6 h with a standard error of 0.1. Editors' calculation against the source read for sc_clements_1982 (Table II, p. 541 of that paper, which gives 155 minutes with a standard error of 12 minutes): the standard error should be 0.2 h. The intravenous and oral conversions, 3.1 (0.1) and 2.9 (0.8), are correct.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dispersion of the intramuscular half-life is halved in the table; small, but it makes that estimate look more precise than its source does.

reporting_issues.issue: The bioavailability column of Table 1 is empty for the intramuscular row and for every row taken from the five-preparation study (reference 12), although the text gives about 93% for the intramuscular route, about 30% for the rectal and about 45% for the nasal route, and the formulation study prints bioavailability for all four of its non-injected preparations. The column is filled only for the oral row (17%), two rows from a sublingual and oral formulation study (24% each), one oral S-ketamine row (11%) and one sublingual row (29%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table does not support the three route figures the text states most prominently; a reader checking them against Table 1 would find blanks.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the time to peak for the sublingual row from reference 151 as 45 minutes with a range of 15 to 1, which cannot be a range.
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing error in one cell; that row's time to peak cannot be quoted from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.3 states that bioavailability is approximately 93% following an intramuscular dose of 2-4 mg/kg, citing two studies; the one I read gave 0.5 mg/kg, and the review's own Table 1 prints the intramuscular row as 0.5 mg/kg.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's text attaches a measured figure to an amount roughly five to eight times larger than the one at which it was measured, and contradicts its own table; a claim about intramuscular bioavailability should state the amount studied.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.4 states that the time to peak is shorter after sublingual than after oral administration (0.5 against 2 hours), citing one study; the other sublingual study in Table 1 (reference 12) gives a sublingual time to peak slightly later than its oral one (40.0 against 33.3 minutes for the (R)-enantiomer). The disagreement is not mentioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: A general statement about sublingual absorption rests on one of the two cited sources, and the review's own table contains the counter-example.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 7.2 states that peak concentrations of ketamine are reached about 40-55 minutes after ingestion, citing three sources; Table 1's oral rows give median times to peak of 42-54 minutes for oral S-ketamine but 30-33 minutes for oral racemic ketamine in one study and 120 minutes in another.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated range describes the oral S-ketamine studies, five of them by the authors' own group, and not the oral racemic studies in the same table.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4 states that systemic clearance of 60-147 L/h per 70 kg equals liver blood flow. Editors' calculation: the hepatic blood flow of 1.53 L/min used by Clements et al. (1982) is about 92 L/h, so the cited clearance range brackets that figure rather than equalling it, its lower bound about a third below it and its upper bound about 60% above it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument from clearance to low oral bioavailability is sound in direction, but the range as printed includes values both well below and well above hepatic blood flow and should not be quoted as an equality.

reporting_issues.issue: The first row of Table 1 prints the amount with a comma as the decimal separator, and two later rows split the unit across lines so that a dose reads as 0.1 mg/k g.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only, but it makes the table's amounts harder to read correctly.

reporting_issues.issue: The saved PDF is the online-first version, which carries no printed page numbers at all; the reference record gives the printed article as volume 55, issue 9, pages 1059-1077.
reporting_issues.consequence: Every anchor on this card cites the PDF's own sequential pages and says so; a reader with the printed issue will need to locate the named section rather than the page.

reporting_issues.issue: The review contradicts itself on which enantiomer produces more of the psychosis-like effects. Section 6 (p. 9) says the S(+)-enantiomer produces more auditory and visual disturbances than the R(-)-isomer, while the Abstract (p. 1) and the Summary (p. 14) say that fewer psychomimetic adverse effects have been reported with S-ketamine than with the racemate and than with R-ketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim about how the two forms differ in subjective or psychosis-like effects may rest on a single sentence of this review; where it is cited, both statements have to be carried.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4.1's first paragraph calls norketamine the major metabolite in humans and, three sentences later, reports that recent studies indicate it is rapidly further metabolized and is not the major metabolite in the circulation, without resolving the two.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim using this review for what the body turns ketamine into has to carry the tension rather than either half of it; the review gives no sample size or interval for either statement.

design_detail: Within-person laboratory study in 10 healthy volunteers, described by the authors as placebo-controlled and counterbalanced, with brain imaging. Each person had three [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose PET scans a month apart: a baseline (placebo) scan, an (S)-ketamine scan and an (R)-ketamine scan. In each drug scan an induction amount of 15 mg of the enantiomer in 20 ml saline was given intravenously over 5 min, followed by 5 min with no further supply and then a continuous intravenous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min; the (R)-ketamine condition was equimolar to the (S)-ketamine condition (pp. 26-27). Psychopathology was rated with the APZ, AMDP, EPI and EWL scales, cerebral glucose metabolism (CMRglu) was measured in 18 regions of interest per hemisphere placed on Talairach coordinates, and arterial plasma ketamine was measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry at five time points. All comparisons used Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests and Spearman correlations with no correction for multiplicity.
can_establish: Whether, in 10 healthy volunteers acting as their own controls, a subanesthetic intravenous infusion of (S)-ketamine changes psychopathology ratings and regional brain glucose metabolism relative to a placebo scan, and whether an equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion does the same; and how the two enantiomer conditions compare within the same people.
cannot_establish: Which specific brain change produces which symptom (correlations with n=10 and no multiplicity correction, as the authors say); whether the effects were observed under maintained blinding (every participant had already received (S)-ketamine in a preliminary session and the authors state that all of them recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect, pp. 28, 36); anything about repeated or longer-term use, about people who use ketamine outside the laboratory, about racemic ketamine as sold, or about people with psychiatric illness; and whether any change outlasts the session, since all measurements were made during or immediately after the infusion.

sample.recruitment: Not stated beyond the setting: volunteers examined at the Research Department of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich, the MRI Center of the University Hospital of Zurich and the PET Department of the Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen. No advertisement, register or referral route is described (p. 26).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers screened by psychiatric interview for absence of personal and first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder; anyone with a history of non-medical use of illicit drugs was excluded (the paper uses the older term); the openness and neuroticism scales of the Freiburg Personality Inventory were also used as exclusion criteria; physical examination, electrocardiogram, blood and urine analysis normal, and a normal MRI (p. 26).
sample.demographics: 10 volunteers, 6 men and 4 women, mean age 30.4 years (Table 1 ages 24-42). Table 1 gives each person's FPI openness (mean 7.9, SD 3.1) and neuroticism (mean 3.5, SD 2.2) against sex- and age-matched normative means printed in the table footnote (openness 6.79 +/- 2.79 men, 6.05 +/- 2.87 women; neuroticism 5.52 +/- 3.52 men, 6.73 +/- 3.65 women). No education, occupation, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine data (pp. 26-27).
sample.attrition: None reported: all 10 are listed in Table 1 with scores in all conditions, and no withdrawal is mentioned although participants were free to withdraw at any time (pp. 26-27).
sample.selection_effects: A small, screened, psychiatrically and physically healthy volunteer sample at a university hospital, deliberately selected for low openness and neuroticism scores and for absence of non-medical drug use, and prepared by a preliminary (S)-ketamine session. Effects in such a group need not transfer to people who use ketamine outside the laboratory, to people with psychiatric illness, or to people taking other drugs; and a sample conditioned by a prior drug exposure session will have different expectations from a drug-naive one.

exposure.measurement: Drug given and measured in the laboratory: arterial plasma ketamine by a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method with a stated sensitivity of 10 ng/ml, sampled through the radial artery cannula at 0, 10, 30, 48 and 54 min; samples stored at -20 degrees C (p. 29). The enantiomers were prepared by the Department of Pharmacology, University of Oslo and dissolved in 0.9% sterile NaCl at 1 mg/ml each (p. 27).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as printed: intravenously, 15 mg of (S)- or (R)-ketamine in 20 ml saline over 5 min as an induction step, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min, by infusion pump; the (R)-ketamine condition was equimolar to the (S)-ketamine condition, and the (S)-ketamine condition was described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study. One exposure per condition, three conditions a month apart (pp. 26-27).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: no concurrent medication, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine use is reported, and nothing is said about what participants consumed on scan days. The only other drug exposure described is the preliminary (S)-ketamine session before the PET phase (p. 28).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. No pre-scan toxicology or abstinence requirement is described; scans were a month apart, and arrival at the PET department was at 1100 h (p. 28).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own baseline (placebo) PET scan, and the other enantiomer condition in the same person. No separate control group and no group of people with psychiatric illness.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the three scans were counterbalanced at monthly intervals. No randomisation method, sequence generation or allocation concealment is described, and no period or carryover effect is modelled (p. 26).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense, because each person is their own baseline. What is unmeasured is expectancy: every participant had already experienced (S)-ketamine in the preliminary session, no measure of what participants believed they had received is reported, and the placebo scan is a single occasion with no test of whether people could tell it apart from the drug scans.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group). Participants' own use of other substances is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Psychopathology, rated for the phase during the PET scan: the Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (APZ), a self-report giving a global score and three subscale scores, oceanic boundlessness (OSE, derealisation and depersonalisation with positive mood), dread of ego-dissolution (AIA, ego-disintegration, loss of autonomy, anxiety, paranoid feelings) and visionary restructuralization (VUS, illusions, pseudo-hallucinations and hallucinations, changes in the meaning of percepts); the Ego Pathology Inventory (EPI), rated by a psychiatrist, giving a global score and five subscales (ego identity, demarcation, consistency, activity, vitality); the AMDP inventory, giving syndrome scores for schizophrenia and manic-depression and 12 subscales including apathy, hallucinatory-disintegration and thought disorder; and the EWL self-rated mood scale with seven scales (efficiency, deactivation, extroversion, introversion, well-being, irritability, anxiety). Imaging: [18F]FDG PET on a CTI Siemens 933/04-16 tomograph, 8 mm in-plane resolution, 12 planes, mean administered FDG dose 177.6 MBq (min 107.3, max 244.2), 23 arterial samples, autoradiographic method of Rhodes et al., images transformed to Talairach space, standardised regions of interest (5.6-10.4 mm) drawn symmetrically in both hemispheres; absolute CMRglu in micromol per 100 g per min, relative CMRglu (region divided by whole-brain mean) and metabolic gradients (ratios between two regions in the same hemisphere) (pp. 27-29).
outcomes.validity_norms: The APZ dimensions are said to have been derived and validated in an international study of altered states and to be independent of what induced the state; the EPI is cited as a validated measure of ego pathology; FPI normative means for healthy controls are printed in the Table 1 footnote. No norms are given for the AMDP or EWL, and no reliability figures for any rating in this study. The PET method is standard for its time but regional values are hand-placed standardised regions of interest, not voxelwise statistics.
outcomes.operationalization: No outcome is operationalised as harm or impairment. The psychosis-like state is operationalised as changes from the baseline scan in self-rated and psychiatrist-rated scale scores; hyperfrontality is operationalised as an increase in absolute and relative frontal CMRglu and an increase in fronto-occipital and fronto-temporal ratios, the ratio method being taken from published work on people with schizophrenia.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, and the authors say so: with no correction for the number of comparisons the results should be regarded as exploratory rather than confirmatory (p. 29). The count of about 180 is the editors' tally of the comparisons actually displayed or reported: 32 regional absolute CMRglu tests per enantiomer condition (Figs. 4 and 5), whole-brain tests, the relative CMRglu values reported in the text, 32 metabolic-ratio tests (Table 2, 8 ratios by 2 hemispheres by 2 conditions), about 34 psychopathology comparisons (Figs. 1 and 2) and about 45 correlations. The true number of comparisons made is larger, because 18 regions per hemisphere were measured and only 16 are plotted.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants are stated to have been blind to the drug conditions (p. 26); no blinding of the examining psychiatrist, of the person placing the regions of interest or of the analysts is reported. The Discussion states that participants could tell the (R)-ketamine condition from the placebo condition and that all of them correctly identified it as a drug effect, so blinding did not hold (pp. 34, 36).

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported: results are percentage changes from baseline with Wilcoxon P-levels, and correlations given only as P-levels with a sign. No confidence intervals, no standardised effect sizes, no test statistics. Dispersion is shown only in figures (mean and standard error bars in Figs. 1, 2, 4 and 5) and in Table 1 for the global scores. Editors' calculations from the per-person values in Table 1 (p. 27): the within-person difference between the (S)- and (R)-ketamine conditions in APZ global score is 22.6 points (SD 6.3; 95% CI 18.1 to 27.1; standardised paired difference about 3.6) and in EPI global score 23.3 points (SD 10.9; 95% CI 15.5 to 31.1; standardised paired difference about 2.1), with every one of the 10 participants higher under (S)-ketamine (exact two-sided sign test P = 0.002).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted within-person comparisons; relative CMRglu and ratios are used instead of covariate adjustment to handle global and between-person variation in metabolism (pp. 28-29).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome. One a priori hypothesis is named, that (S)-ketamine would increase frontal CMRglu; everything else is described by the authors as exploratory (p. 29).
analysis.selective_reporting: Substantial. Of 18 regions per hemisphere, 16 are plotted and only some are given numerically in the text. Relative CMRglu values are reported for the regions that changed and not for the rest. Correlations are reported selectively: Table 2 shows only 8 of the many possible ratios, correlations with absolute CMRglu appear only in the text, and one result is given as data not shown (p. 36). Several values appear only in figures, from which exact numbers cannot be read.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 10 participants and paired non-parametric tests the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.002, so single P-values below 0.01 carry little information about size; the authors attribute several null correlations to the small sample (pp. 35-36).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 10 healthy volunteers, an (S)-ketamine infusion at the stated rates produced a short-lived psychosis-like state (higher APZ, AMDP and EPI scores than the baseline scan) together with higher glucose metabolism across most of the brain, largest in frontal and cingulate cortex and smallest in posterior and subcortical regions, so that fronto-temporal and fronto-occipital ratios rose. An equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion in the same people produced no psychotic symptoms but a state of relaxation, with a general tendency to lower metabolism that reached significance only in the temporomedial cortex bilaterally and the left insula. The correlations between symptom scores and regional metabolism are exploratory, uncorrected, and based on 10 people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the metabolic changes in frontal and left temporal cortex correlated with ego-disintegration and hallucinatory phenomena, and that the (S)-ketamine-induced hyperfrontality appears to parallel findings in people with acute schizophrenic psychosis (p. 25). Two steps go beyond the data. First, the correlation claims rest on uncorrected tests in 10 people, reported as P-levels only, so neither their size nor their robustness can be judged; the authors themselves call the analysis exploratory (p. 29) and attribute non-significant correlations to the small sample (pp. 35-36). Second, the comparison with schizophrenia is made against published studies, not against patients studied here; the discussion is explicit that ego-pathology scores were about two-thirds of those reported for people with first-episode schizophrenia and that ego-activity and ego-vitality were clearly less affected (p. 34). The conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetically active agent in racemic ketamine (p. 34) rests on a comparison with a different sample in the companion paper, not on a racemic condition tested here.

timeline.event: Krystal et al. report dose-related perceptual, cognitive and psychotomimetic effects of subanesthetic ketamine in healthy volunteers; cited here as the comparison for the symptom profile

Lahti et al. report that ketamine given to people with schizophrenia stabilized on haloperidol raised frontomedial and anterior cingulate blood flow with an exacerbation of positive symptoms (as cited in this paper, p. 36; not appraised here)
Companion paper from the same laboratory, in a different sample of 10 healthy volunteers, finds the same hyperfrontal pattern with racemic ketamine and larger whole-brain increases
The same group reports a [11C]raclopride PET study of striatal dopamine under (S)-ketamine (listed in the project source list as Vollenweider et al. 2000, J Psychiatr Res; not read here)

A meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies of ketamine in healthy volunteers is listed in the project source list (Ait Bentaleb et al.) and has not yet been appraised; it is the place to check whether the hyperfrontality finding holds across methods

replication.where_it_stands: The psychopathological contrast between the two enantiomer conditions is the paper's most robust result: it is within-person, in the same direction in all 10 participants, and large. The metabolic findings for (S)-ketamine agree with the same laboratory's racemic study in a different sample, which is consistency within one group rather than independent replication. The enantiomer comparison of cerebral glucose metabolism itself has not, as far as this reading shows, been repeated anywhere; later imaging work used different tracers and methods, and whether the hyperfrontality finding holds up across methods is a question for the neuroimaging meta-analysis on the project list, not yet appraised.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: University and national-laboratory setting (Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich; Paul Scherrer Institute; University of Oslo, which prepared the enantiomers). what_would_settle_it: A larger within-person study with a maintained and tested blind (participants and raters asked what they believed they received, with guessing reported), randomised order with period effects modelled, a pre-specified primary outcome and a correction for multiplicity, ideally with a racemic condition included in the same people so that the enantiomer comparison does not depend on a different sample, and with the imaging analysed voxelwise so that regional claims do not rest on hand-placed regions of interest.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three conditions)
domains.note: Order is described only as counterbalanced at monthly intervals; no sequence generation, no allocation concealment and no statement of who assigned the order (p. 26).

Scans were a month apart, which makes pharmacological carryover unlikely, but no period or order effect is modelled or reported, and every participant had had a preliminary (S)-ketamine session before the PET phase (p. 28), so psychological carryover into the placebo and (R)-ketamine conditions cannot be excluded.

Participants are said to have been blind to the conditions, but the Discussion reports that they could distinguish the (R)-ketamine condition from placebo and that all of them correctly identified it as a drug effect (pp. 34, 36); with a prior drug-exposure session the (S)-ketamine condition cannot have been blind either. The self-rated APZ and EWL scores and the psychiatrist's ratings were therefore made in an effectively unblinded condition.
All 10 participants appear in Table 1 with scores in every condition and in the PET analyses; no missing data are reported.

PET quantification is objective, but regions of interest were placed by hand on standardised coordinates with no stated blinding and no reliability data. The psychopathology ratings are partly retrospective: the APZ and EWL were completed after drug effects had completely subsided and refer to the scan period, while the AMDP and EPI were rated immediately after the scan (p. 28).

No protocol and one named a priori hypothesis, with about 180 displayed comparisons and no multiplicity correction; regions, relative values, ratios and correlations are reported selectively, one correlation is given as data not shown (p. 36), and several values exist only in figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a within-person comparison of two enantiomer conditions against a placebo scan the design is strong, and the psychopathological contrast between (S)- and (R)-ketamine is large, consistent across all 10 participants and unlikely to be an artefact of the ratings alone. The overall judgment is set by the failure of blinding, which the authors themselves describe, and by the selective reporting of a large number of uncorrected comparisons. The source can be cited for: the psychopathological and metabolic profile of a subanesthetic (S)-ketamine infusion at the stated rates in healthy volunteers; the contrast with an equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion; plasma concentrations during such an infusion; and the pattern of regional glucose-metabolic change. It cannot be cited for the size of any symptom-metabolism association, for a causal statement about which brain region produces which symptom, for any claim about racemic ketamine as sold, or for any equivalence between this state and schizophrenia.

key_findings.finding: Ten healthy volunteers (male=6, female=4), mean age 30.4 years, each had three FDG-PET scans a month apart in counterbalanced order: a baseline (placebo) scan, an (S)-ketamine scan and an equimolar (R)-ketamine scan, with participants described as blind to the conditions.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Subjects (2.1) and Experimental design (2.2)

key_findings.finding: In each drug scan the enantiomer was given intravenously as 15 mg in 20 ml saline over 5 min, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min; the (S)-ketamine amount is described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study, and the (R)-ketamine condition as equimolar to it.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Experimental design (2.2), last paragraph (p. 26) continuing on p. 27

key_findings.finding: Plasma levels ranged from 269 to 523 ng/ml (mean 379, SD 71) in the (S)-ketamine condition and from 280 to 508 ng/ml (mean 389, SD 74) in the (R)-ketamine condition; psychotic symptoms appeared about 5 min after the start of the (S)-ketamine infusion at a mean plasma level of 539 ng/ml.
key_findings.locator: Results, Plasma ketamine levels (3.1)
key_findings.note: The 539 ng/ml at symptom onset lies above the top of the stated (S)-ketamine range of 269-523 ng/ml; the paper does not reconcile the two, and does not say whether the range refers to per-person means of the five samples. The two conditions are described as equimolar, but no molar calculation, salt form or concentration check is printed beyond 1 mg/ml in 0.9% NaCl (p. 27), so these measured plasma levels are the only evidence that the two conditions were comparable.

key_findings.finding: (S)-ketamine produced depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances from pseudohallucinations to complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy; auditory changes were illusions rather than true hallucinations. Reported emotional reactions were heightened feelings or euphoria in 30%, indifference in 30% and heightened anxiety in 40%. EWL mood scores rose for deactivation (P<0.01), introversion (P<0.05), emotional irritability (P<0.05) and anxiety (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology (3.2.1)

key_findings.finding: Equimolar (R)-ketamine produced no psychotic symptoms in the same people but a state of relaxation: the APZ oceanic-boundlessness score rose only at trend level (P<0.06), EWL well-being at P<0.09 and emotional irritation fell at P<0.08.
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology (3.2.2)

key_findings.finding: Per-person global scores (Table 1): under (S)-ketamine the APZ global score ran from 25 to 55 and the EPI global score from 10 to 48, against 8 to 33 and 0 to 5 under (R)-ketamine. Editors' calculation from those 10 pairs: the within-person (S) minus (R) difference is 22.6 points (SD 6.3) for APZ global and 23.3 points (SD 10.9) for EPI global, higher under (S)-ketamine in every participant (exact two-sided sign test P = 0.002).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns S-Ketamine APZ/EPI global and R-Ketamine APZ/EPI global
key_findings.note: The printed mean and SD for the S-ketamine APZ global column (37.0, 12.6) do not match the 10 values above them, which give 38.2 and 10.3 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: (S)-ketamine increased absolute CMRglu across most regions, with a front-to-back gradient: frontomedial 19.6%, frontolateral 20.1%, cingulate anterior 23.5%, cingulate posterior 24.0% and parietal 27.35% bilaterally; somatosensory 21.1% and motor 23.0% significantly in the left hemisphere only; the thalamus was the only subcortical region with a bilateral increase, at trend level (17%, P<0.07); whole-brain metabolism rose 12% but not significantly (P<0.09). Cortical regions were about 2-3 times more stimulated than subcortical regions and frontal regions about twice as much as posterior ones.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 1st paragraph (p. 29) continuing on p. 31; Fig. 4 (p. 32)

key_findings.finding: Relative CMRglu (region divided by whole brain) rose bilaterally in the frontomedial (7.7%), frontolateral (8.4%) and cingulate posterior (12.5%) cortex and in the left parietal cortex (18.2%), and fell in the left temporomedial cortex (4.8%), all at P<0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: (R)-ketamine tended to lower CMRglu across regions: whole-brain -9.8% (P<0.07, not significant); significant absolute decreases bilaterally in the temporomedial cortex (-13.4%) and in the left insula (-14%); relative decreases in the right temporal cortex (-4.0%, P<0.05) and bilaterally in the cerebellum (-5.0% and -4.0%, P<0.05). Decreases in the cerebellum and left caudate-putamen reached only P<0.07.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 2nd paragraph (p. 31); Fig. 5 (p. 33)

key_findings.finding: Metabolic gradients under (S)-ketamine (Table 2): fronto-temporal ratios rose between 6.8% and 14.0% and fronto-occipital ratios between 9.1% and 11.7%, with the left frontolateral-caudate ratio up 16.0%, the right frontomedial-putamen ratio up 12.3% and the right frontolateral-putamen ratio up 13.2%. Under (R)-ketamine the same ratios rose only 0.1% to 7.4%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, columns Change of gradients (%) for S-Ketamine and R-Ketamine
key_findings.note: Significance varies by row and hemisphere: of the fronto-occipital ratios only the left frontolateral-occipitolateral change is marked P<0.05, the left frontomedial-occipitomedial change is trend level and both right-hemisphere changes are marked not significant.

key_findings.finding: Correlations with absolute CMRglu under (S)-ketamine, all uncorrected and in the whole sample of ten: APZ oceanic boundlessness with frontomedial cortex (left P<0.05, right P<0.07) and right temporomedial cortex (P<0.05); EPI ego-identity impairment with frontomedial (P<0.04/P<0.04), frontolateral (P<0.05/P<0.04), cingulate anterior (P<0.01/P<0.004) and right cingulate posterior (P<0.04) cortex; APZ visionary restructuralization and AMDP hallucinatory-disintegration with occipitomedial (P<0.07/P<0.06) and occipitolateral (P<0.06/P<0.05) cortex; AMDP apathy with both parietal cortices (P<0.01/P<0.04) and the left insula (P<0.04).
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology and correlations with metabolism (3.5.1)

key_findings.finding: The AMDP hallucinatory-disintegration subscale and schizophrenic syndrome score correlated negatively with the fronto-temporal and fronto-occipital ratio increases; the frontolateral-putamen ratio was the only cortical-subcortical ratio with a significant negative correlation with hallucinatory-disintegration in both hemispheres (left P<0.02, right P<0.001). The authors call this surprising and suggest that illusions and hallucinations relate more to occipital than to frontal change.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 33); Results (p. 34, 1st paragraph); Discussion, Hyperfrontality and psychopathology (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: Compared with published ego-pathology scores in people with first-episode schizophrenia, the (S)-ketamine scores for ego-consistency, ego-identity and ego-demarcation were about two-thirds of the patients' values, and the ego-activity and ego-vitality scores were clearly less affected; no patients were studied in this paper.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, Psychopathology (4.1), 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All participants recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect and could tell it from the baseline (placebo) condition; the authors note that each had already received (S)-ketamine in a preliminary session held so that they could get used to lying still under the drug.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Phase I (2.5) (p. 28); Discussion, Psychopathology (p. 34); Discussion, Hyperfrontality and psychopathology (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: No correction was made for the number of comparisons, and the authors state that the results should be regarded as "exploratory rather than confirmatory".
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Statistical analysis (2.8)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a mean of 37.0 and an SD of 12.6 for the (S)-ketamine APZ global column, above which stand the ten per-person values 25, 47, 27, 37, 46, 27, 38, 33, 47 and 55. The editors' calculation from those ten values gives a mean of 38.2 and an SD of 10.3, and the printed pair is instead exactly the mean and SD of the racemic-ketamine APZ global column in Table 1 of the companion paper (p. 11 of Vollenweider et al. 1997b: 37.00 and 12.63), which lists a different set of ten people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary row for the paper's main psychopathological outcome appears to have been carried over from the companion study rather than computed from this study's data. The per-person values, not the summary row, should be used; all other columns of Table 1 reproduce correctly.

reporting_issues.issue: The column headed r(sp) in Table 2 holds P-levels with the sign of the correlation, not Spearman correlation coefficients, although the heading and the footnote both call them Spearman rho. The text confirms this: the frontolateral-putamen correlations with hallucinatory-disintegration are given there as P<0.02 (left) and P<0.001 (right), the same numbers printed in Table 2 as -0.02 and -0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the table at face value would record correlations of about -0.001 to -0.08, that is essentially zero, where the authors mean significance levels with a direction. No correlation coefficient is printed anywhere in the paper, so the size of every symptom-metabolism association in this study is unknown and cannot be used in a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean plasma level at the appearance of psychotic symptoms, 539 ng/ml, lies above the stated (S)-ketamine range of 269 to 523 ng/ml on the same page.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the range describes per-person means of the five scan-period samples while 539 is an early induction-phase value, or one of the two is wrong; the paper does not say, so neither figure should be quoted as the concentration at which these effects occur.

reporting_issues.issue: The (S)-ketamine condition is described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study, following a pilot potency ratio of about 1:0.6 mg/kg that is reported in one sentence with no sample size, no method and no reference. Editors' calculation from the two Methods sections (p. 26 here against p. 11 of Vollenweider et al. 1997b): the induction step is 75% of the companion study's (15 mg against 20 mg) and the maintenance rate 67-70% (0.014-0.02 against 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min), but the maintenance phase here ran 53 min against 60 min, so the total amount over a session works out at about 61-64% for a person of 70 kg, close to the stated 60%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated ratio is consistent with the printed conditions once the shorter infusion is counted, so the objection to the conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic component of racemic ketamine (p. 34) is not arithmetic: it is that no racemic condition was given to these ten people, so the comparison is with a different sample in the companion paper, and that the pilot study behind the ratio is undescribed.

reporting_issues.issue: The third APZ subscale is labelled OSE where it should be VUS: the first subscale is introduced as OSE (oceanic boundlessness) and the third as OSE (visionary restructuralization), while the next sentence names the three dimensions OSE, AIA and VUS.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical slip, but it means the abbreviation OSE appears in the methods for two different subscales; all later uses of OSE in the results and discussion refer to oceanic boundlessness.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that (S)-ketamine significantly increased the fronto-occipital ratios about 10% in both hemispheres, indicating a hyperfrontal pattern, but Table 2 marks both right-hemisphere fronto-occipital changes as not significant and the left frontomedial-occipitomedial change as trend level only; of the four, only the left frontolateral-occipitolateral change carries P<0.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The hyperfrontality conclusion as drawn from the fronto-occipital ratios is weaker than the text states; the fronto-temporal ratios, which the table does mark significant in both hemispheres, carry most of the evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that (S)-ketamine binds with a 3-4 times higher affinity to the PCP binding site than (R)-ketamine, while the Introduction gives 4 to 5 times, both citing the same source.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the affinity ratio is the stated rationale for the dose choice and for the interpretation; neither figure should be quoted from this paper without going to the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a mean age of 30.4 years and the text repeats it, above the ten ages 30, 40, 30, 42, 26, 24, 25, 34, 24 and 28, whose editors' calculation gives 30.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for interpretation; recorded because it is the second arithmetic slip in the same table.

reporting_issues.issue: The dispersion shown in the psychopathology figures is stated two ways at once: the titles printed inside Figs. 1 and 2 give mean and standard deviation, and the captions of the same two figures open by saying mean and standard deviation and then state that the boxes indicate mean and standard error.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures carry the only dispersion information for the AMDP, EWL and subscale scores, since no table prints them; with the two readings differing by a factor of about three for ten participants, nothing quantitative should be read off them.

reporting_issues.issue: The R-ketamine left frontomedial-temporolateral row of Table 2 carries a capital A as its P-level marker, where the footnote defines lower-case a as P<0.05 and lower-case b as P<0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; read as P<0.05 by analogy with the rest of the table, but the paper does not define it.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Fig. 2 (p. 30) says that (S)-ketamine significantly increased the scores for 'emotional irritability' and 'anxiety', while the Results on p. 29 report four significant EWL scales: deactivation (P<0.01), introversion (P<0.05), emotional irritability (P<0.05) and anxiety (P<0.01).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is the only place the scale-by-scale mood data appear, and it disagrees with the text about how many mood scales changed; the Results' four scales should be used, with the disagreement stated.

Tables 1 and 2 and the figures were checked on pages rendered at 150-400 dpi; no supplementary material exists.
