design_detail: Qualitative interview study (Addiction Research & Theory 2008;16(3):231–244), part of a larger study of drug use in British electronic dance music (EDM) club settings that also included two online surveys, surveys and observation in clubs (not reported here). 12 people who described their ketamine use as current and regular (all had used in the past 3 months), recruited by peer referral starting from clubbers known to the authors, were interviewed in 10 in-depth semi-structured interviews of 60–90 minutes (two were joint interviews). The schedule, co-developed with people who used ketamine regularly, covered eight areas: music and club attendance; legal and illegal drug use; typical and last occasion of ketamine use, including how it was obtained; experiences before, during and after use; the K-hole; ketamine and the law; ketamine and health; and the interview process. Interviews were transcribed and organised by these areas, and accounts were analysed around two emergent themes, 'intensity' and 'sociability'. The study began in summer 2005, six months before ketamine became a Class C drug on 1 January 2006; interview dates are not given. Setting: north-west England. Findings are presented as themes with quoted extracts attributed to pseudonyms with age and occupation; there are no tables or figures.
can_establish: How these 12 people who regularly used ketamine in north-west England's club scene explained, in their own words, why they used it (fun and pleasure, judged by how intense and how sociable the experience was), how they accounted for bad experiences, and how they set themselves apart from negative portrayals of ketamine and from forms of use they considered problematic.
cannot_establish: How common any motive or experience is (no counts are reported beyond statements that all interviewees shared a view), whether these accounts hold for people who use ketamine outside employed or student club-going networks (for example people who inject, use daily or have health problems from ketamine), or anything about effects and harms beyond what participants said.

sample.recruitment: Peer referral: initial contact with clubbers known to the authors, each participant then asked to suggest another; access depended on the authors' 'partial insider status' in EDM club cultures (p. 233). Recruitment inside clubs was tried several times, but interest shown in clubs did not always carry over outside them (p. 234). Payment, ethics approval and consent are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Self-defined current regular ketamine use; all had used ketamine within the past 3 months (note 4, p. 243). 'Regular' is not defined and no exclusion criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: Aged 18–32; 4 women and 8 men; all employed or university students (p. 234). Ethnicity, sexuality, education, social class, length of ketamine use and frequency of use are not reported. All took ketamine intranasally (p. 240).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). The number approached or declining is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A peer-referral chain starting from the authors' own club networks selects people who are comfortable talking about their use with researchers who share their scene. All were employed or students, all used intranasally, and all described themselves as sensible, recreational and in control; people who inject, use outside club times, or have dependence or health problems from ketamine are not represented, and these were exactly the forms of use participants described as problematic. The authors stress that EDM cultures differ by music genre, region, class, age, gender, ethnicity and sexuality, that their insider status is only partial, and that accounts in other studies in the same journal issue differ from theirs (p. 233); they refer to known problems of snowball sampling (p. 234). There is no limitations section.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview; no biological verification. The interviews collected quantitative information on drug use and on typical and last occasions of ketamine use (p. 233), but none is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported (no frequency, duration or amount data). All interviewees took ketamine intranasally (p. 240).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants described ketamine as one part of polydrug use on club nights, mostly at post-club 'chill-out' gatherings, as people came down from ecstasy (some still taking ecstasy alongside) and before moving on to cannabis or alcohol (pp. 238–239); other drug use was asked about but is not reported. Effects described cannot be separated from those of other drugs taken on the same occasions.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; intoxication at interview is not reported.

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Comparisons are internal: participants contrasted ketamine with psychedelics (shorter, more controllable) and with ecstasy (more sociable in clubs), and contrasted their own use with injecting or 'habitual' use outside club times.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No information on mental or physical health history, problems with other drugs, or how long participants had used ketamine.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Semi-structured interview schedule co-developed with people who used ketamine regularly (not published), covering eight areas (p. 233). The interviews were transcribed and organised by these areas (p. 234); the analytic approach (thematic, discourse or other), coding procedure, number of coders, software and any saturation criterion are not described.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. Credibility rests on the authors' partial insider status and on quoted extracts; the authors state that the levels of intensity and sociability were not objectively measured but produced through interaction between people using together and between interviewer and interviewee (p. 241).
outcomes.operationalization: Motives, consequences and meanings were left to participants' own accounts and interpreted by the authors through two emergent themes, 'intensity' and 'sociability', combined in a proposed 'pleasure nexus' (pp. 234, 242).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis testing).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Who conducted the interviews is not stated; the authors describe themselves as partial insiders in the scene studied.

analysis.effect_sizes: None, and none would be appropriate. The only quantifiers are statements that something applied to all interviewees (12 of 12): the wish to control ketamine's effects shaped their efforts to increase pleasure and reduce harm (p. 236); all spoke at length about regulating how much they took (p. 237); all highlighted ketamine's place alongside ecstasy (p. 239); all were aware of conflicting, mostly negative representations of ketamine (p. 239); all took it intranasally (p. 240).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration, protocol or ethics approval is mentioned; interviewees' names were changed (note 5, p. 243).
analysis.selective_reporting: The interviews covered eight areas and produced quantitative as well as qualitative data (p. 233), but no quantitative data are reported, and the areas on the law and on health are not reported in this paper (the authors refer to a separate chapter on criminalisation, Measham and Moore 2008). How many participants held each view is not given except where the text says 'all'; quoted extracts come from 9 named participants.
analysis.power: Not applicable; no saturation criterion is stated for 12 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Participants described fun and the pleasure of intoxication as the main reason for using ketamine, valuing its 'playful' effects, its short duration and, for some, a sense that it could be controlled, in contrast with psychedelics. Preferences differed: some sought mild, sociable intoxication, some intense, inward experiences, and some moved between the two; more intense states were generally described as less sociable. Bad experiences (unwanted intensity, failed interactions, an unintended K-hole described as frightening, being stuck in loops, regret) were often accounted for as the person's own error of judgement about amount, setting or other drugs, not by ketamine alone; the unpleasant sensation of snorting it was also often mentioned. Some self-described experienced participants sought the K-hole as a 'journey'. Participants described injecting and use outside club times as problematic, and countered negative media and peer images of ketamine with accounts of sensible, controlled use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion stay mostly within these accounts, and the authors say that intensity and sociability were not measured but produced in interaction (p. 241). Stretches: the abstract says participants controlled the quantity, quality and frequency of dose (p. 231), whereas the text reports how they talked about controlling amount and setting, not frequency; the statement that ketamine pharmacologically supports young people's wish to extend their leisure time (p. 239) generalizes from participants' reports of distorted time; the 'growing role' of ketamine in chill-out settings (p. 239) is not measured in this study; and the suggestion that the 'pleasure nexus' could apply to alcohol, ecstasy and polydrug use (p. 242) is offered without data on those drugs. The introduction's view that criminalising ketamine was not justified by the evidence then available (p. 232) is the authors' policy argument, based on cited reports, not a finding of this study.

timeline.event: Dillon, Copeland & Jansen: interview survey of 100 people in Sydney with any lifetime non-medical ketamine use (1998–1999); the drug's effect (62%), friends (25%) and curiosity (11%) as main reasons for first use, and 'to party' (61%) among reasons for continuing
Copeland & Dillon, The health and psycho-social consequences of ketamine use (Int J Drug Policy 16:122–131), cited here as survey evidence of growing leisure use (p. 232); not read for this card

Muetzelfeldt et al.: structured interviews with 90 people in the UK (frequent, infrequent and former use); effects most often rated appealing were 'melting into the surroundings', visual hallucinations, out-of-body experience and 'giggliness'

This study (study begun summer 2005; interview dates not given). Other interview studies of ketamine use appeared in the same journal issue, including Newcombe on 'psychonauts' (cited p. 238; not read)

replication.where_it_stands: A small interview study from British club culture and the usual source for pleasure, and the intensity–sociability framing, as an answer to why people take ketamine. Its picture of fun and of the drug's own effects as the main draw agrees with the larger UK interview study of Muetzelfeldt et al. (2008) and the Sydney survey of Dillon et al. (2003), which used different samples and methods, but it adds no frequencies. Cite it for how these participants made sense of their use, not for how common any motive or experience is.

funding.funder: Lancaster University (note 1, p. 242).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest and state that they alone are responsible for the content and writing (p. 242).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Applied Social Science, Lancaster University (p. 231). The authors describe 'partial insider status' in EDM club cultures, which gave them access to participants (p. 233); their framing is sociological (pleasure, normalisation, a critique of 'pathology' accounts of drug use), and the introduction argues that the evidence available did not justify criminalising ketamine (p. 232). Recorded as context for interpretation, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Interviews with a purposive sample spanning club and non-club settings, occasional and daily use, and people with and without problems from ketamine (including people who inject or are in treatment), analysed with a described method, double coding and counts of how many participants expressed each theme; together with a survey that measures how common each motive is.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: The question is how people understand and talk about their motives and experiences; in-depth semi-structured interviews suit it.

Peer referral seeded by the authors' acquaintances; 12 people, all employed or students and all using intranasally; no account of how many were approached or declined, of efforts to include different kinds of use, or of saturation.

60–90 minute semi-structured interviews, transcribed, with a schedule co-developed with people who used ketamine; but the schedule is not published, the interviewer(s) and interview settings are not described, and two joint interviews may have produced shared rather than individual accounts (visible in the extracts from the joint interview of two women).
Unusually explicit discussion of the authors' partial insider status and of knowledge as co-produced (p. 233), but no account of how this shaped the interviews or the interpretation.
No ethics approval or informed consent is reported; names were changed (note 5, p. 243); research ethics are mentioned only as one concern of insider research (p. 233).

No analytic method is described beyond transcription, organisation by interview area and two 'emergent' themes: no coding procedure, second coder, negative-case analysis, audit trail or reporting checklist.

Themes are illustrated with attributed extracts from 9 of the 12 participants, including contrasting views; some statements go beyond the accounts (pharmacological effects on leisure time, a 'growing role' of ketamine).
The authors stress the diversity of club cultures and the partiality of their position, but extend the 'pleasure nexus' to other drugs and to young people's leisure in general.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a qualitative study with the editors' checklist. The design suits the question, and the authors are reflexive about their insider position, but the analysis is not described at all, the sample is 12 people reached through the authors' own networks, and no ethics approval or consent is reported. Under the checklist's rule the overall judgment follows the worst domain (rigour of analysis). The accounts are credible as illustrations of how people who regularly use ketamine in one club scene describe pleasure, control and bad experiences, and can be cited for the vocabulary and the range of motives (fun, mild and sociable versus intense and inward states, sensible use), never for how common anything is.

key_findings.finding: 12 people (4 women and 8 men, aged 18–32, all employed or university students) were interviewed in 10 in-depth semi-structured interviews of 60–90 minutes, two of them joint interviews; they were recruited by peer referral starting from clubbers known to the authors (recruitment inside clubs was also tried, but interest did not always carry over outside them). All described their ketamine use as current and regular and had used ketamine in the past 3 months.
key_findings.locator: Researching clubbers' ketamine use, 2nd paragraph (p. 233; self-defined current regular use), 5th paragraph (p. 233, continues on p. 234) and 6th paragraph (p. 234); note 4 (p. 243)
key_findings.note: The counts of women, men and interviews are partly printed in words ('four were female and eight were male', 'Ten in-depth'); the total of 12 and the 10 interview occasions are printed in figures on p. 234.

key_findings.finding: The study began in summer 2005, six months before ketamine became a Class C drug in the UK on 1 January 2006, so as to study use at the moment it was criminalised; the interviews were part of a larger study that also included two online surveys and surveys and observation in clubs. Interview dates are not given.
key_findings.locator: Researching clubbers' ketamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; British ketamine use: prevalence and criminalisation, 3rd paragraph (ends on p. 233)

key_findings.finding: The interview schedule, co-developed with people who used ketamine regularly, covered eight areas (music and club attendance; legal and illegal drug use; typical and last occasion of use, including how ketamine was obtained; experiences before, during and after use; the K-hole; ketamine and the law; ketamine and health; the interview process). Interviews were transcribed and organised by these areas, and accounts were analysed around two emergent themes, 'intensity' and 'sociability'.
key_findings.locator: Researching clubbers' ketamine use, 4th paragraph (p. 233) and 6th paragraph (p. 234)

key_findings.finding: Having fun and the pleasure of intoxication were the main motives in participants' accounts. They stressed ketamine's 'playful' effects (feeling happy and 'bouncy', often childlike); two participants valued its short duration and the sense that it could be controlled, in contrast with psychedelics that last for hours.
key_findings.locator: Accounting for clubbers' ketamine use, 1st paragraph (p. 234); Ketamine intoxication: 'intensity' and 'sociability' of experience, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (quoted extracts not counted)

key_findings.finding: Preferences differed: some participants enjoyed being only mildly intoxicated, some sought intense experiences (one described sometimes taking it intending to have an out-of-body experience), and some enjoyed moving between the two; more intense states were generally described as less sociable. Some preferred less intense intoxication when other people were around, and one now chose to take it at home rather than in clubs; another found ketamine in a club too intense, with no proper conversation possible, and contrasted it with the sociability of ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Accounting for clubbers' ketamine use, 1st paragraph (p. 234); Ketamine intoxication: 'intensity' and 'sociability' of experience, 2nd–5th paragraphs (p. 235)

key_findings.finding: Apart from the often-mentioned unpleasant sensation of taking ketamine intranasally, negative experiences were described mostly as overly intense, unsociable states, such as frustration at failed interactions or being too far gone to chat, and were often accounted for not by ketamine alone but by errors of judgement about intake and the setting at that moment.
key_findings.locator: Ketamine intoxication and control: context, dose and the K-hole experience, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: For all interviewees, wanting to control ketamine's effects shaped what they did to increase pleasure and reduce harm: they described managing the setting (where and with whom they used, music and lighting) and regulating how much they took, and all spoke at length about making the amount taken more predictable, which the authors frame as lay harm reduction. Some said music could sound unpleasant on ketamine. Unpleasant episodes (being sick) after ketamine had been taken with alcohol were described as one-off events that taught them a lesson.
key_findings.locator: Ketamine intoxication and control: context, dose and the K-hole experience, 3rd paragraph (p. 236) and 4th–5th paragraphs (p. 237)

key_findings.finding: Asked to describe the K-hole, participants talked about regulating intake: taking too much was framed mainly as entering a K-hole involuntarily, or one more intense than wanted. Some described it as a loss of control, being stuck in a loop of repeated images, ideas or conversation, or sinking into blackness with fear and no way out; for some it was too intense and asocial, bringing anxiety, embarrassment and regret when entered unwittingly. Participants who called themselves experienced described it as a 'journey' or 'place' they sometimes sought, while still valuing control over going in and coming out and the more sociable state afterwards.
key_findings.locator: Ketamine intoxication and control: context, dose and the K-hole experience, 6th–9th paragraphs (quoted extracts not counted)

key_findings.finding: The appeal of ketamine was tied to post-club chill-out gatherings, as a 'bonus stage' that extended the night within polydrug use: ketamine sessions were described as the stage when people were coming down from ecstasy (some still taking ecstasy alongside) and before moving on to depressants such as cannabis or alcohol. One participant described time seeming to slow down or disappear, and the authors suggest the drug supports the wish to extend leisure time. From their own visits, the authors add that ketamine use was far more visible and open at after-hours clubs than at dance clubs.
key_findings.locator: Ketamine intoxication and control: context, dose and the K-hole experience, 10th paragraph (continues on p. 239) and 11th–12th paragraphs (p. 239); note 6 (p. 243)

key_findings.finding: All interviewees knew of conflicting, mostly negative portrayals of ketamine by other clubbers, the media and official responses, and countered them by describing ketamine as relatively safe and themselves as sensible, recreational and knowledgeable; those who managed this less well were typically participants who had used for a shorter time and whose friends were not, for the most part, people who used ketamine regularly, and some hid their use even from friends who used club drugs. Some accounts framed ketamine as unfit for humans because of its veterinary use; other participants saw it as safer than ecstasy or cocaine because of its use in children's medicine.
key_findings.locator: Contested meanings of ketamine, 3rd paragraph (continues on p. 240) and 4th paragraph (p. 240)

key_findings.finding: Injecting ketamine and 'habitual' use outside club times and places were described as clearly problematic; all interviewees took ketamine intranasally. Stories of bad experiences when the usual pattern was not followed (for example one midweek occasion) were used to distance themselves from problematic use.
key_findings.locator: Contested meanings of ketamine, 5th paragraph (p. 240) and 6th–7th paragraphs (p. 241)

key_findings.finding: The authors propose a 'pleasure nexus' of two axes, intensity and sociability, on which each person seeks their own point of greatest pleasure through dose and setting, and suggest that it could apply to other drugs; they note that intensity and sociability were not objectively measured but produced in interaction between people using together and between interviewer and interviewee.
key_findings.locator: Discussion – the pleasure nexus, 1st paragraph (p. 241) and 3rd–4th paragraphs (p. 242)

reporting_issues.issue: The interviews are said to have produced detailed quantitative as well as qualitative data, including legal and illegal drug use and the typical and last occasion of ketamine use (p. 233), but no quantitative data are reported; the sample is described only by age range, sex and occupation (p. 234).
reporting_issues.consequence: How often and for how long participants had used ketamine, and what else they used, cannot be known; 'regular' use is undefined.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis is described only as transcription and organisation by the eight interview areas, with accounts considered in relation to two emergent themes; no analytic method, coding procedure or check on coding is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rigour of the analysis cannot be assessed; the themes rest on the authors' reading alone.

reporting_issues.issue: No ethics approval or informed-consent statement appears anywhere in the article; the only protection reported is that names were changed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Ethical conduct cannot be verified from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Two joint interviews are said to have been held because two female participants asked to be interviewed together; 12 people in 10 interviews does require two joint interviews of two people each, but only one pair is described, and who formed the second pair is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the composition of the joint interviews, which may produce shared rather than individual accounts, is partly unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical inconsistencies: the same participant is 21 years old on p. 234 and 22 on p. 236; 'The Guardian 2005a' is cited on p. 239, but the reference list has The Guardian 2005 and 2005b (p. 243).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the findings; quote attributions should be cited by pseudonym only.

design_detail: Cross-sectional structured-interview study with mixed methods (Drug Alcohol Depend 2008;95:219–229), University College London. 90 people who used ketamine recreationally, recruited through advertisements on dance-scene websites and by snowballing (about half had taken part in the team's earlier studies or knew a current participant), in three quota groups of 30: frequent use (more than 4 times a week), infrequent use (from 2 times a month to fewer than 4 times a week) and former use (abstinent at least 84 days). Interviews were typed onto a laptop by two researchers rather than audio-recorded. Part 1 (structured): initiation, liked and disliked effects at first use and now (or before stopping), medical attention, pattern and context of use, each narrative followed by statements rated on 1–5 Likert scales, true/false setting items and a forced choice among three styles of use. Part 2 (open): perceived long-term effects and concerns. Quantitative part: frequency counts of coded themes and of endorsed statements, and chi-squared comparisons between the three groups. Qualitative part: content analysis at a descriptive level with an a-priori and emergent coding frame (Table 1), one coder (LM) coding every narrative, a second (SK) independently checking four random interviews, then the two discussing the coding of each narrative together. Dates of data collection are not reported; the paper places its 'follow-up' stage after the UK's 2006 reclassification of ketamine.
can_establish: What these 90 people, recruited through dance-scene websites and the research team's own network in the UK, reported about how they started using ketamine, which effects they liked and disliked, how and where they used it and what worried them, and how these reports differed between people using frequently, infrequently or no longer.
cannot_establish: How common any reason, effect or concern is among people who use ketamine (quota convenience sample); whether frequent use caused the differences between groups (the design is cross-sectional and the groups also differed in education, premorbid-IQ estimate, employment and mental-health and family histories); or whether the 'dependence' described meets any diagnostic definition (no dependence instrument was used).

sample.recruitment: Advertisements on popular dance-scene websites and snowballing; approximately half of the participants had taken part in the team's earlier studies or contacted the team through someone currently participating. Screened by a brief telephone interview (p. 220). Most interviews took place at the UCL psychopharmacology laboratories, a few at participants' homes, with interview sites evenly spread across the groups (p. 220). Payment, ethics approval and consent are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Only the group definitions are given: frequent use more than 4 times a week; infrequent use from 2 times a month to fewer than 4 times a week; former use with at least 84 days without ketamine (the abstract says at least 3 months) (pp. 219–220). The 15 pilot interviewees were not included. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: Frequent / infrequent / former-use groups (Table 2, p. 224): men/women 19/11, 24/6, 20/10; mean age 25.87 (SD 9.23), 27.37 (6.73), 27.3 (5.31); white 86.7%, 70.0%, 70.0%; years in education 12.27 (4.84), 15.33 (2.56), 14.95 (3.83); currently employed 13, 27, 21; Spot-the-Word score (premorbid-IQ estimate) 45.67 (6.13), 50.90 (4.09), 49.79 (3.89); personal history of mental illness 7, 2, 8; family history of mental illness 8, 2, 3; family histories of drug and of alcohol problems (rows labelled 'abuse') 9, 0, 3 and 9, 5, 9. Age at first use 19.83 (range 11–52), 21.17 (16–38), 19.97 (13–36).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). Numbers screened, eligible or declining are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Quota convenience sample: about half came through the team's earlier studies or their contacts and the rest through dance-scene websites, so people connected with the London dance scene and with this research programme are over-represented. Everyone reported snorting as the main route and only one person reported occasional injecting, so people who inject are essentially absent. Despite the stated matching, the frequent group had less education, a lower premorbid-IQ estimate, fewer people in work and more family history of drug problems than the other groups (Table 2, p. 224). The former-use group reported on use that had ended a mean of about 1.5 years earlier (days since last use 555.90, range 84–2980; editors' conversion), so their accounts are retrospective. The authors acknowledge that the sample was for the most part a convenience sample, which makes generalization across ketamine experiences difficult, and note that most people who use ketamine use several drugs, so the effects reported could come from combinations of drugs (p. 228); for the sample itself, urinalysis is said to have verified recent use of several drugs, with no figures (p. 220).

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview, with urine and hair analysis: urinalysis is said to have verified recent use of several drugs (no figures), and hair ketamine averaged 282.14 (SD 566.53) ng/mg in the frequent group, 18.01 (41.06) in the infrequent group and 3.56 (13.63) in the former-use group (p. 220). No hair segment length, cut-off or individual-level verification rule is reported; the non-zero mean in the former-use group means that ketamine was found in the hair of at least some people classed as no longer using.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 224): current frequency 20.13 (SD 2.36) days a month in the frequent group and 3.25 (2.55) in the infrequent group; total years of ketamine use 6.07 (4.89), 4.20 (2.20) and 7.63 (2.63) in the three groups. Self-reported amounts per session in the first 2 months of use were similar across the three groups; in the frequent group the current mean was 7.6 times the initial mean (editors' calculation from Table 2). All 90 reported snorting powder as their main route; 5 had unknowingly taken tablets containing ketamine; one person in the frequent group reported occasional injecting (pp. 220, 225).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants are described as already using several drugs when they started ketamine, and urinalysis is said to have confirmed recent use of several drugs, but no data on other drug use are reported. The authors note that the effects reported could result from combinations of drugs (p. 228).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not required of people still using ketamine: days since last ketamine use 1.6 (SD 1.27; range 1–7) in the frequent group and 11.3 (9.36; 1–28) in the infrequent group; former-use group 555.90 (632.89; 84–2980) (Table 2, p. 224). Intoxication or after-effects at interview were not assessed.

comparison.controls: No people without ketamine use. The comparison is between three self-selected groups defined by current frequency of ketamine use (frequent, infrequent, former).
comparison.matching: Said to be matched for age, estimated verbal premorbid IQ and gender (p. 220), but Table 2 shows the frequent group with a lower Spot-the-Word score (45.67 vs 50.90 and 49.79) and fewer years of education (12.27 vs 15.33 and 14.95), and a different sex ratio (11 of 30 women vs 6 and 10); no tests of these differences are reported. Editors' calculation (Welch t-test from Table 2, frequent vs infrequent): Spot-the-Word t≈3.9 (df≈50), standardized difference ≈1.0; education standardized difference ≈0.8.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measures. Personal and family histories of mental illness and family histories of drug and alcohol problems were recorded and differ between the groups (Table 2) but were not used in any analysis; other drug use, personality and sensation-seeking were not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no group without ketamine use); other drug use not quantified in any group.

outcomes.instruments: Investigator-designed structured interview, developed from an unpublished interview with people who had stopped using ketamine in the team's earlier longitudinal study, piloted with 15 people (5 per group) and revised (p. 220). Effects were rated 'liked' or 'disliked' on a Likert scale from 1 (very unappealing) to 5 (very appealing); the four effects most often rated quite or very appealing, and the four most often disliked, are reported (pp. 223–224). Setting items answered true or false; style of use chosen from three statements; initiation statements endorsed (Table 3, p. 225). Narratives coded by content analysis at a descriptive level: one researcher (LM) built the coding frames and coded every narrative; a second (SK) checked a random four interviews, with agreement reported as over 95%, and LM and SK then discussed the coding of each narrative together (agreement again reported as over 95%); disagreements resolved by discussion or coded 'ambiguous' (printed as under 0.02% of items); 27 codes under five headings for part 2 (p. 221; Table 1, pp. 222–223).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated instruments. The full list of Likert-rated effects is said to be in an Appendix 1 that is not printed in the article. Independent inter-rater agreement is a raw percentage on 4 of 90 interviews, not a chance-corrected statistic; the joint discussion of every narrative is a consensus review, not independent double coding. Interviews were typed during the interview, not recorded, because pilot participants were reluctant to be taped (p. 220).
outcomes.operationalization: Reasons, liked and disliked effects and concerns are the share of the 90 participants (or of each group of 30) whose narratives were coded to a theme, who rated an effect quite or very appealing (or disliked), or who endorsed a statement. 'Addiction/dependence' is a narrative code (concern about compulsive use; cravings, tolerance or drug seeking; ketamine as an important part of social relationships) plus endorsement of the statement 'I use K without stopping, until it is all gone'; no diagnostic or severity instrument was used. 'K-cramps' and cystitis are spontaneous mentions of an experience or a concern, not clinical diagnoses.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The number of tests is not stated; the text implies about 36 chi-squared comparisons (style of use; 7 settings; 9 initiation statements; 5 themes; 6 mental-health and 7 physical-health sub-themes; addiction narratives), several with expected cell counts below 5 (for example K-cramps, 13 of 90 overall).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the coders knew each participant's group (group letters are part of the participant identifiers).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages and chi-squared tests only; no effect sizes or confidence intervals. Group differences reported: style of use χ²(4)=16.81, p=.002; 'I wanted to explore my consciousness further' χ²(2)=10.36, printed p=.035; decline in mental health χ²(2)=6.53, p=0.038; decline in physical health χ²(2)=10.20, p=0.006; positive psychotic symptoms χ²(2)=5.84, p=0.054; K-cramps χ²(2)=12.29, p=0.002 (pp. 225–226). Editors' recomputation from the printed shares: style of use Pearson χ²(4) ≈ 15.5 (likelihood-ratio 16.7) and K-cramps (10, 1 and 2 of 30) χ²(2) ≈ 13.1 (12.7), close to the printed values; only the consciousness test does not reproduce (reporting issues). Editors' calculation of precision: a share in a group of 30 is imprecise, for example K-cramps in the frequent group, 10 of 30 (33.3%), 95% CI about 19% to 51% (Wilson); a share of the whole sample, for example 65 of 90 (72.2%) rating 'melting into the surroundings' appealing, 95% CI about 62% to 80%.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted chi-squared tests.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned; ethics approval and consent are not reported in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the top four liked and disliked Likert items are reported, and the full list (Appendix 1) is not printed. Group tests are reported mainly where significant or near-significant; the Methods say group differences in medical treatment sought warranted between-group analysis (p. 221), but no statistic is given for it (p. 226). Other drug use, said to be confirmed by urinalysis, is not reported. Dates of data collection are not given.
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 30 set by design.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 90 people recruited in the UK through dance-scene websites and the team's network, ketamine was typically started through a friend or acquaintance, with some prior knowledge of the drug (88%) and an interest in trying new drugs; 88% described their first experience as positive. The effects most often rated quite or very appealing were 'melting into the surroundings' (72.2%), visual hallucinations (71.1%), out-of-body experience (64.4%) and 'giggliness' (64.4%); the most often disliked were impaired memory (50%), decreased sociability (50%), nausea (42.2%) and impaired concentration (32.2%). The most endorsed initiation statements were being offered a line and enjoying it (80.9%), enjoying psychedelic drugs (77.7%) and friends doing it (75.3%). 51.1% (80.0% of the frequent group) chose 'I use K without stopping, until it is all gone' as their style of use, and 28% voiced concern about compulsive use. In the frequent group, 33.3% mentioned K-cramps, 20.0% cystitis or bladder problems, and 46.7% had sought medical help because of ketamine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says reported drug use was verified by hair analysis (p. 219), but only group means are reported, with no individual criterion (p. 220). It reports a six-fold mean increase in amount per session in the frequent group, while the Discussion reports a 760% increase (pp. 227–228); the Table 2 means give 7.6-fold, a 660% increase (editors' calculation). The Discussion states that ketamine is unique among hallucinogens in its dependence-forming properties (p. 228), although no other hallucinogen was studied and no dependence measure was used; the dependence that the abstract says participants frequently reported rests on narrative codes and one style-of-use statement. The abstract's statement that the authors identified specific health issues that seem uniquely related to ketamine use (p. 219) likewise rests on spontaneous mentions in three groups who had all used ketamine, with no comparison group of people who had not. The Discussion speaks of tracking the narrative from initiation to dependence, and of settings becoming more general as use escalated (p. 227); these are inferences about change drawn from a one-time comparison of groups that also differ in education, premorbid-IQ estimate and mental-health histories. It infers from one participant's report that reclassification is unlikely to change the behaviour of people currently using ketamine (p. 228), without saying how many were asked. The authors do state the convenience sample, the possibility of alternative interpretations and polydrug use as limitations (p. 228).

timeline.event: Curran & Monaghan: acute and residual effects in people using ketamine frequently and infrequently; summarized here as showing marked dissociation and schizophrenia-like symptoms after use in both groups and greater cognitive impairment in the frequent group when drug-free (p. 220)

Dillon, Copeland & Jansen: interview survey of 100 people in Sydney with any lifetime non-medical ketamine use (1998–1999); the drug's effect, partying and friends as the main reasons; altered senses and out-of-body experience as the most valued effects

Morgan, Monaghan & Curran: 3-year longitudinal study of people who had substantially reduced their ketamine use; an unpublished interview from this study was the starting point for the present interview and its a-priori codes (p. 220)
This study (data-collection dates not reported)
Moore & Measham: 10 in-depth interviews with 12 people (two joint interviews) in north-west England's club scene; fun and pleasure, judged by intensity and sociability, as the main motive; no counts

Morgan, Muetzelfeldt & Curran: comparison of frequent, infrequent and former ketamine use with polydrug and non-using controls (title from the reference record; not read for this card). Same team and same three groups by design; whether the participants overlap with this study is not stated in this paper

Morgan, Muetzelfeldt & Curran: 1-year longitudinal study of chronic ketamine self-administration (title from the reference record; not read for this card); this paper mentions a follow-up stage without describing it

replication.where_it_stands: The largest of the early UK interview studies of what people who use ketamine recreationally like and dislike about it. Its ranking of liked effects (dissociative and perceptual effects, laughter) and of reasons for starting (friends, interest in psychedelic drugs, wanting to try something new) agrees with the Sydney survey of Dillon et al. (2003) and with Moore & Measham (2008), though none of the three has a sampling frame. Its picture of compulsive use, K-cramps and medical help-seeking in frequent use comes from a confounded comparison of self-selected groups. Cite it for what this sample reported, with denominators, and treat the group differences as descriptive, not as effects of frequency of use; check for overlap with the same team's 2009–2010 cohorts before counting them as independent.

funding.funder: ESRC Grant RES-000-23-0945; the ESRC had no further role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (p. 228).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest (p. 228).
funding.affiliations_note: Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London (p. 219). Morgan and Curran designed the study and wrote the protocol; Taylor and Rees did the literature searches; Muetzelfeldt and Kamboj analysed the data and wrote the first draft (p. 228); the interviews were done by HR and CM (p. 220).

what_would_settle_it: A survey of people who use ketamine drawn from a defined frame with a known response rate, with published items asking reasons and effects, a validated dependence measure and recorded other drug use; and a cohort that follows the same people over time, so that changes in frequency, settings and problems such as K-cramps can be seen within people instead of inferred from self-selected groups compared at one time.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: dance-scene website advertisements and the team's own previous participants and their contacts.
Quota convenience and snowball sampling to 30 per group; about half from earlier studies of the same team (p. 220).
No rationale; shares of the whole sample of 90 are moderately precise, but shares within groups of 30 have intervals of about ±16 to ±18 percentage points (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 2 describes the groups in detail; dates of data collection, recruitment period, payment and other drug use are not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Most shares use all 90 (or 30 per group); the initiation statements imply 29 in the former-use group (for example 75.9% = 22 of 29), a missing answer that is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Unvalidated interview; themes from content analysis; no dependence instrument; hair results not used to verify individuals.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same structured interview for all, but answers were typed during the interview rather than recorded, and one coder coded everything, with only 4 of 90 interviews independently checked by a second, after which the two discussed the coding of every narrative together (p. 221).

Percentages suit the descriptive aim; the group comparisons are about 36 uncorrected chi-squared tests, some with small expected counts, one with an impossible combination of statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value, and no intervals.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: Response rate not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a mixed-methods study: the quantitative part (shares reporting each reason, effect or concern) with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias), the qualitative part described above. The sample has no frame, half of it came from the team's own earlier studies, the interview is unvalidated, the coding rests on one coder, independently checked on only 4 of 90 interviews before a joint review of every narrative, and several printed statistics and table entries are internally inconsistent. The shares describe this London-based, dance-scene-connected sample and must be cited as such. The comparisons between frequent, infrequent and former use were not appraised as exposure effects: the groups were self-selected and differed in education, premorbid-IQ estimate, employment and mental-health and family histories, none of which was adjusted for.

key_findings.finding: 90 people were recruited by advertisement on dance-scene websites and by snowballing (about half had taken part in the team's earlier studies or knew a current participant) into three groups of 30: frequent use (more than 4 times a week), infrequent use (2 times a month to fewer than 4 a week) and former use (at least 84 days without ketamine). All reported snorting powder as their main route; 5 had unknowingly taken tablets containing ketamine; one person in the frequent group reported occasional injecting.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Participants and procedures (single paragraph)
key_findings.note: The total is printed in words ('Ninety participants'); all 90 are also named on p. 225.

key_findings.finding: Group characteristics, frequent / infrequent / former use: years in education 12.27 / 15.33 / 14.95; currently employed 13 / 27 / 21 of 30; Spot-the-Word score 45.67 / 50.90 / 49.79; personal history of mental illness 7 / 2 / 8; family history of drug problems (row labelled 'abuse') 9 / 0 / 3; age at first ketamine use 19.83 (range 11–52) / 21.17 (16–38) / 19.97 (13–36); days since last use 1.6 / 11.3 / 555.90.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: No tests of group differences are reported, although the groups are said to be matched for age, premorbid IQ and gender (p. 220).

key_findings.finding: Participants were typically introduced to ketamine by a friend or acquaintance and already used several drugs; 88% (n=80) had some knowledge of the drug before first use and only 5 thought at first that it was another drug; a theme of peer pressure of some degree appeared in 23% (n=21) of responses.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Initiation into ketamine use, 1st–3rd paragraphs (quoted extracts not counted)

key_findings.finding: 88% (n=79) described their first experience as positive. Effects liked at first use: dissociation 34 (37.8%), contentedness 16 (17.8%), intense merriment 10 (11.1%), the intensity 9 (10.0%). Compared with other drugs: ketamine was 'different' 13 (14.4%), the short duration 9 (10.0%), less of a comedown 5 (5.6%); 10 (11.1%) compared the experience with other drugs, especially alcohol and LSD.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Effects compared to other drugs, 1st paragraph; 3.4 Effects that were liked, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Liked now (or before stopping): the general 'high' 20 (22.2%), the relaxing effect 14 (15.6%), the same effects as at first use 15 (16.7%); 6 (6.7%) described liking it for relief from cravings or filling a gap. Effects most often rated quite or very appealing on the 1–5 scale: 'melting into the surroundings' 72.2% (n=65), visual hallucinations 71.1% (n=64), out-of-body experience 64.4% (n=58), 'giggliness' 64.4% (n=58).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Effects that were liked, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (quoted extracts not counted)

key_findings.finding: Disliked at first use: nausea or vomiting 19 (21.1%), the intensity 22 (24.4%), loss of control 15 (16.7%), the dissociation 9 (10%). Effects most often rated disliked: impaired memory 50% (n=45), decreased sociability 50% (n=45), nausea 42.2% (n=38), impaired concentration 32.2% (n=29). 8 participants did not enjoy their first experience but went on using.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Effects that were disliked, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 224) and 2nd paragraph (p. 224)

key_findings.finding: Disliked about current use (or use just before stopping): reduced effect through tolerance or poorer quality 13 (14.4%), cognitive disorganization 9 (10.0%); 30 references (33.3%) to negative psychological effects: negative sociability 9, blunted affect 5, depression 4, dissociation 4, paranoia 4, and anxiety, aggression, restlessness and decreased sex drive 1 each.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Effects that were disliked, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 28% (n=25) voiced concern about the apparently compulsive nature of ketamine use; 8 participants (7 frequent, 1 infrequent) said they liked ketamine for reasons the authors associate with dependence (relieving boredom, filling a gap, satisfying cravings, escapism). Some who had stopped described leaving the social settings of their use to do so.
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Ketamine and addiction/dependence, 1st–3rd paragraphs (quoted extracts not counted)

key_findings.finding: Style of use: 51.1% (n=46) chose 'I use K without stopping, until it is all gone' (frequent 80.0%, n=24; infrequent 33.3%; former 40.0%), 46.7% (n=42) 'a little, wait, then use some more', and few 'some, then stop'; the group difference was χ²(4)=16.81, p=.002.
key_findings.locator: 3.7 Style and setting of use, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Settings ever used (true/false; several allowed): friend's house 84.5%, home 71.1%, squat parties 58.9%, outdoor parties 56.7%, clubs 52.2%, pubs 34.4%, dinner parties 22.2%. The text says the frequent group were much more likely than the other groups to endorse every setting except a friend's house (Table 3 marks every other setting p ≤ 0.001, without test statistics); the frequent group's shares are the highest of the three groups in every setting, a friend's house included (home 96.7%, friend's house 96.7%, squat and outdoor parties 93.3%, clubs 76.7%, pubs 66.7%, dinner parties 46.7%).
key_findings.locator: 3.7 Style and setting of use, 2nd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Statements endorsed about starting ketamine (several allowed): offered a line and enjoyed it 80.9%; enjoy psychedelic drugs and it sounded interesting 77.7%; friends were doing it 75.3%; wanted to explore my consciousness further 63.1% (frequent 56.7%, infrequent 56.7%, former 75.9%; printed χ²(2)=10.36, p=.035); saw people doing it at a party 57.4%; helped me get into music 37.1%; bored of other drugs 35.9%; wanted to forget my troubles 16.9%; did not know what it was 10.1%.
key_findings.locator: 3.7 Style and setting of use, 3rd paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: The consciousness statement's test does not match its own shares (see reporting issues). The music statement is printed 'I helped me get into music'.

key_findings.finding: Asked openly about long-term effects and concerns, participants' accounts fell under five themes: impaired cognitive functioning, decline in mental health and well-being, decline in physical health, awareness of addiction/dependence, and induction of a positive mental state. Groups differed on decline in mental health (χ²(2)=6.53, p=0.038) and decline in physical health (χ²(2)=10.20, p=0.006).
key_findings.locator: 3.8 Phenomenological ratings from spontaneous self-report, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Fig. 1 at 300 dpi, approximate (frequent / infrequent / former): decline in physical health about 77 / 40 / 43%; decline in mental health about 60 / 43 / 73%; impaired cognitive functioning about 40 / 63 / 50%; positive mental state about 13 / 10 / 23%. Values are not printed.

key_findings.finding: K-cramps (severe gastric cramps) were mentioned as an experience or concern by 33.3% of the frequent group, 3.3% of the infrequent group and 6.7% of the former-use group (χ²(2)=12.29, p=0.002); cystitis or bladder problems by 20.0%, 6.7% and 13.3% (no test reported).
key_findings.locator: 3.10 Decline in physical health (single paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Asked whether they had ever sought medical help because of ketamine use, 46.7% of the frequent group, 20.0% of the infrequent group and 10.0% of the former-use group said yes; the commonest reason was stomach problems including K-cramps (30.0%, 3.3% and 6.7%).
key_findings.locator: 3.11 Medical treatment sought due to ketamine use (single paragraph)
key_findings.note: No test of the group difference is reported.

key_findings.finding: Experiences of or concerns about addiction/dependence or drug seeking, or ketamine having become important in social relationships, came up in 56.7% of the frequent, 43.3% of the infrequent and 60.0% of the former-use group, with no significant group difference.
key_findings.locator: 3.12 Narratives of addiction/dependence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The former-use group showed a trend towards reporting more positive psychotic symptoms (paranoia, anxiety, depression, violent behaviour) as a long-term concern (χ²(2)=5.84, p=0.054).
key_findings.locator: 3.9 Decline in mental health (single paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Only one participant said that the change of ketamine to a Class C drug, which happened during the study's follow-up period, had affected their use, and only because they thought quality had fallen.
key_findings.locator: 3.12, 2nd paragraph (p. 226); 4. Discussion, 11th paragraph (p. 228)
key_findings.note: How many participants were asked, and when, is not reported.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: the reliability and validity of the verbal reports could be explored further in future studies with a more comprehensive clinical interview, the narratives allow other interpretations, the sample was for the most part a convenience sample that is hard to generalize from, and most people who use ketamine also use other drugs, so the effects reported could come from combinations of drugs.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The initiation statement 'I wanted to explore my consciousness further' is reported with χ²(2)=10.36, p=.035 and starred in Table 3 (shares 56.7%, 56.7%, 75.9%). Editors' calculation: χ² 10.36 on 2 degrees of freedom gives p≈0.006, and p=.035 corresponds to 4 degrees of freedom; the printed shares (17 of 30, 17 of 30, 22 of 29) give χ²(2)≈3.1, p≈0.21.
reporting_issues.consequence: The test must have used a different categorization from the one shown, or contains an error; the printed shares do show the former-use group endorsing the statement most often (75.9% against 56.7% and 56.7%), but they do not support a statistically significant group difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, Pubs row: 29.0% in the infrequent group is not a possible share of 30 people, and the total of 34.4% (31 of 90) implies 20.0% in that group.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is misprinted; cite the frequent and former-use shares only, or the total with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, style of use: the total printed for 'I use(d) some K, then stop' is 3.3%, although the group shares are 0.0, 3.3 and 3.3% (2 of 90). Editors' calculation: the correct total is 2.2%, the three printed style totals add up to 101.1%, and several initiation totals differ from the group shares by 0.1 to 0.2 points (for example 77.7% printed, 77.5% recomputed); the initiation totals are the unweighted means of the three group percentages (77.7 is the mean of 80.0, 63.3 and 89.7), which, with 29 answering in the former-use group, explains these small differences.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic errors; the group shares are the more reliable figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The escalation figure differs between places: the abstract gives a six-fold mean increase in amount per session in the frequent group (p. 219) and the Discussion a 760% increase (pp. 227–228). Editors' calculation from the Table 2 means (p. 224): 7.6-fold, which is a 660% increase; how either printed figure was computed is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither summary figure should be cited; if escalation is cited, use the Table 2 means with the method stated (ratio of group means of self-reports).

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 marks decline in mental health with two stars and decline in physical health with three, but the text gives p=0.038 and p=0.006, which correspond to one and two stars under the legend's own thresholds. Editors' reading of Fig. 1 (approximate): the bars for awareness of addiction (about 60, 47 and 63%) look one participant higher in each group than the 56.7%, 43.3% and 60.0% given in section 3.12.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure overstates significance; the text values should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's age and duration rows do not reconcile. In the frequent group the mean age at which regular use began (25.90) is higher than the mean current age (25.87), although the group reports 5.03 years of regular use; in the infrequent group, age at first use (21.17) plus total years of use (4.20) falls about 2 years short of the mean age (27.37), while the regular-use rows do reconcile. In the former-use group, age at first use (19.97) plus total years of use (7.63) plus the mean time since last use (555.90 days, about 1.5 years) gives about 29.1, and the regular-use rows (21.28 plus 6.13 plus 1.5) about 28.9, against a mean age of 27.3 (calculated by the editors, assuming total years run from first to last use). The frequent group's current amount per session and current frequency have the same SD (2.36). Editors' calculation: a mean age at regular use near 20.8 would fit the frequent group's other rows.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one value is probably misprinted in each of these rows; ages at first or regular use and years of use should be cited with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The groups are said to be matched for age, estimated verbal premorbid IQ and gender (p. 220), but Table 2 shows the frequent group with a lower Spot-the-Word score (45.67 vs 50.90 and 49.79) and less education (12.27 vs 15.33 and 14.95 years), with no test reported. Editors' calculation: frequent vs infrequent Spot-the-Word, Welch t≈3.9, standardized difference ≈1.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: The matching claim does not hold for premorbid IQ; differences between groups in reported effects and concerns may reflect these differences rather than frequency of use.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that reported drug use was verified by hair analysis (p. 219), but the Methods give only group means of hair ketamine (282.14, 18.01 and 3.56 ng/mg, with SDs larger than the means) without segment length, cut-off or individual checks (p. 220); the non-zero mean in the former-use group shows ketamine in some of their hair.
reporting_issues.consequence: Individual group membership is not shown to be biologically verified; 'verified' overstates what is reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Material referred to but not provided: Appendix 1, with the full list of rated effects, is cited (p. 224) but not printed; a 'follow-up period' or 'follow-up stage' during which ketamine was reclassified is mentioned (pp. 226, 228) but never described in the Methods; dates of data collection are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the top four rated effects can be cited; the reclassification finding has no denominator or timing; the study cannot be placed in time except relative to the 2006 reclassification.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor counting details: 88% is given both for n=80 (prior knowledge) and for n=79 (positive first experience) (p. 221); 6 participants are said to have liked ketamine for relief from cravings or filling a gap (p. 223) and 8 for dependence-type reasons including these (p. 225), without the relation between the counts being explained. Editors' calculation: 80 of 90 is 88.9% and 79 of 90 is 87.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the counts (n) rather than the percentages.

design_detail: Letter to the editors (Journal of Clinical Psychopharmacology 2008;28(1), printed pp. 114–116; read in the PDF of the journal's whole Letters to the Editors section, printed pp. 101–122, where this letter is PDF pp. 14–16). It counts UK deaths in which ketamine was mentioned, from two sources: the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD) database at St George's, University of London, which receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths (July 1997 to December 2006; 18 cases), and the drug-poisoning mortality statistics of the General Register Offices (GROs) for England and Wales and for Scotland, with GRO data for Northern Ireland supplied to np-SAD (January 1993 to December 2006; 5 further cases) (p. 114). A case was a death in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report, or with ketamine mentioned on the death certificate; deaths with ketamine given for medical reasons were excluded (p. 114). Table 1 (p. 115) summarizes the 18 np-SAD cases one characteristic per row (year, sex and age, drug history, prescribed medicines, incident site, recorded causes, drugs found at postmortem, circumstances, verdicts), without linking the rows to individual deaths, and the 5 GRO cases in brief. No denominator, rates or comparison.
can_establish: That at least 23 deaths in the UK in 1993–2006 had ketamine mentioned in a coroner's report notified to np-SAD or on a death certificate in GRO statistics, what was recorded about them (sex, age, other drugs found, recorded causes, circumstances and verdicts), and that ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of them.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused or contributed to these deaths (mention is the case definition; most also had alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA or other drugs, and some died by drowning or a stab wound); the risk of death from ketamine or how it compares with other drugs (no denominator); a trend over time (1 to 4 np-SAD deaths a year, with testing and reporting that may have changed); or that the count is complete (toxicology in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths, and ketamine screened routinely only in some laboratories, p. 116).

sample.recruitment: Registry: np-SAD, which receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK among people with and without drug dependence; a death enters np-SAD if one or more psychoactive substances were directly implicated, the person had a history of dependence or abuse of psychoactive drugs, or controlled drugs were found at postmortem; the coroners' response rate has been estimated to have been as high as about 90% to 95% (citing the authors' own annual report). Plus GRO drug-poisoning mortality statistics for England and Wales and for Scotland, and GRO data for Northern Ireland (p. 114).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: deaths in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report (other illegal drugs could also be written), or with ketamine mentioned on the death certificate; np-SAD July 1997 to December 2006, GRO January 1993 to December 2006 (p. 114), although Table 1 gives England and Wales 1993–2002, Scotland 1994–2006 and Northern Ireland 1997–2005 (p. 115). Excluded: deaths in which ketamine was present because it had been given for medical reasons (p. 114). The authors state that np-SAD cases were kept out of the count derived from the other records (p. 114); how duplicates were found is not described.
sample.demographics: All 23: 19 male; most aged 25 to 44; 21 recorded in England and Wales (pp. 114, 116). The 18 np-SAD cases: 16 male, 2 female; average age 32.74 years, range 19.8–49.4; drug history (Table 1 row 'Drug abuse history') yes 13, no 2, not known 3; prescribed medicines yes 6 (including methadone in 1 and diazepam in 2), no 6, not known 6 (Table 1, p. 115). The 5 GRO cases: in England and Wales 2 men and 1 woman aged 20–49; in Scotland a woman of 26; in Northern Ireland a man of 35 (Table 1, p. 115).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Only deaths in which ketamine was tested for, found and written down are counted: postmortem toxicology was done in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths, and ketamine was routinely screened for only in some highly specialized laboratories or on specific request (p. 116), so deaths with undetected ketamine are missing and the count is a minimum. np-SAD's entry criteria favour deaths of people with drug histories, its coverage starts in July 1997, and the GRO periods differ by country. Which deaths are included also depends on who was tested, which may have changed over time. By the editors' arithmetic, the 21 deaths recorded in England and Wales (pp. 114, 116) are the 18 np-SAD cases plus the 3 ONS cases, so every np-SAD case was from England and Wales, and Scotland and Northern Ireland are represented only by one GRO case each (Table 1, p. 115).

exposure.measurement: Postmortem toxicology as recorded in coroners' reports (np-SAD) and drugs mentioned on death certificates (GRO), found by text search for ketamine (p. 114). Laboratory methods, specimens and concentrations are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no concentrations, amounts or patterns of use. A route appears in two of the recorded circumstances (injecting with a partner; snorted while with others) (Table 1, p. 115).
exposure.polysubstance: Common. Ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of the 23 (2 np-SAD, 2 England and Wales GRO); in the others, alcohol (8), opiates/opioids (10), benzodiazepines (7) and cocaine (6) were found with ketamine, by the text (p. 116). Table 1 also lists MDMA or ecstasy, amphetamines including methylamphetamine, GHB, cannabis, ephedrine, codeine, lignocaine and co-proxamol (p. 115). How much each drug contributed is not analysed; the authors ask whether interaction or synergy explains the polydrug deaths (p. 116).

Recorded cause in the 18 np-SAD deaths (editors' count from Table 1): ketamine named in 8 (as the only drug in 1, 'ketamine toxicity'; with other drugs in 7); drug toxicity without the drugs named in 4; another drug named without ketamine in 3 (opiate poisoning, heroin poisoning, cocaine intoxication); drug abuse with bronchial asthma 1; drowning 1; stab wound to the chest 1. Verdicts in the 18: accident or misadventure 11, open 2, suicide 1, and one each of 'dependent abuse of drugs', 'abuse of drugs', 'nondependent abuse of drugs' and 'self-administered overdose of drugs'. Incident site: home or other residence 10, industrial site 1, place of recreation 1, river 1, not known 5. Ketamine alone in 4 of the 23, all with poisoning as the cause and verdicts of accident in 3 and suicide in 1 (p. 116).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Twenty-three UK deaths in 1993–2006 had ketamine mentioned in coroners' or death-certificate records (18 np-SAD, 5 GRO), with 1 to 4 np-SAD deaths a year from 1999 to 2006; 19 were male. Ketamine was the only drug found in 4. Of the 18 np-SAD deaths, the recorded cause named ketamine in 8 (alone in 1), named only other drugs in 3, gave drug toxicity without naming drugs in 4, and was not a poisoning in at least 2 (drowning, stab wound) (editors' count from Table 1). Most deaths involved alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA or other drugs as well.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title calls the 23 deaths 'associated with ketamine misuse' and places them in the K-hole, the out-of-body state described in the letter's first paragraph (p. 114); the text says they mostly occurred in 1999–2006 'with numbers increasing over time' (p. 114); the Discussion calls the series 'the largest available collection of ketamine misuse mortality data' from the UK and elsewhere and says the 4 deaths with ketamine alone somewhat question the high-safety profile suggested elsewhere (p. 116). The case definition is any mention of ketamine, which takes in a drowning, a stab wound and poisonings recorded as due to other drugs; 1 to 4 deaths a year, with testing and reporting that may have changed, cannot show a trend, as the authors partly acknowledge (p. 116); and the letter itself cites 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, 12 of them non-hospital polydrug intoxications (p. 114), so 'largest' holds only against the 12. The letter has no data on anyone's state at death, so the K-hole framing rests only on the Discussion's speculation that misjudged risk linked to ketamine's dissociative effects may explain the 4 ketamine-only deaths, which the text records as poisonings (p. 116). The Discussion is otherwise candid that presence is not cause and that ketamine was not routinely screened for (p. 116).

timeline.event: Gill and Stajic: 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, of which 12 were non-hospital deaths from acute polydrug intoxication and none was caused by ketamine alone (as cited, p. 114; not read).
Breitmeier et al.: 17 accidental autoerotic deaths examined in Hanover in 1978–1997, with ketamine among the compounds found; the letter does not say in how many (as cited, p. 114; not read).
This letter: 23 UK deaths in 1993–2006 with ketamine mentioned, 4 with ketamine as the only drug found.
Corkery et al., Journal of Psychopharmacology: recreational ketamine-related deaths notified to np-SAD, England, 1997–2019 (Tier A list; to be appraised).
Darke et al., Addiction: characteristics and circumstances of deaths related to self-administered ketamine (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: A first count from the authors' own national register; descriptive and not designed to be replicated. The same programme's later analysis to 2019 (Corkery et al., 2021) should supersede this letter for counts once appraised; this card does not use its content.

funding.funder: 'Research was supported by internal funds' (Acknowledgments, p. 116). The General Register Offices for England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland provided mortality data, and two named toxicologists (Guy's and St Thomas' Medical Toxicology Unit; Forensic Toxicology Service, St George's) gave general information on ketamine screening in unexpected deaths (p. 116).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the letter has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are with np-SAD, International Centre for Drug Policy, St George's University of London, which holds the database analysed; the first author is also at the School of Pharmacy, University of Hertfordshire (p. 116). The sources cited for the coroners' response rate and for toxicology coverage include the authors' own np-SAD annual report and an earlier paper by the same group (references 2 and 9, p. 116).

what_would_settle_it: A national series in which every unexpected death is screened for ketamine by a standard method, concentrations are recorded, each death is assessed for ketamine's contribution by a rule set in advance, and the counts are related to yearly estimates of how many people use ketamine, so that rates and trends can be compared with those for other drugs.

domains.note: Depends on whether ketamine was tested for (routinely only in some specialized laboratories or on request; toxicology in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths) and on coroners' notifications (a response rate estimated as high as about 90% to 95%); deaths with undetected ketamine are missing, so 23 is a minimum.

Any mention of ketamine in a coroner's report or on a death certificate, including a drowning, a stab wound and poisonings recorded as due to other drugs; the authors say presence does not imply contribution.
Toxicology as recorded, without methods, specimens or concentrations; some entries are unspecific ('opiate-type, and substance'; 'ecstasy').

No count of people who use ketamine and no comparison with deaths involving other drugs; statements about change over time rest on 1 to 4 deaths a year.
Limitations are stated plainly, but 'largest available collection', 'numbers increasing over time' and the questioning of ketamine's safety profile go beyond 23 unlinked cases.
Cocaine in 6 deaths in the text but 5 in Table 1; the data periods in the text (1993–2006) differ from those in Table 1; the 25 to 44 age statement cannot be checked.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a description of registry cases (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The letter is a short, transparent count from a national register run by the authors and may be cited for the 23 deaths in 1993–2006 with ketamine mentioned, their sex and age, the other drugs found, the recorded causes and verdicts as listed, and the 4 deaths in which ketamine was the only drug found. It may not be cited for the number of deaths caused by ketamine, for a death rate or trend, for ketamine's risk compared with other drugs, or for any combination being especially dangerous. A claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Background as cited: a self-selected readers' survey of a magazine for clubbers found lifetime ketamine use among respondents rising from 25.5% to 39.8%, and current use from 3.9% to 16.0%, between 1999 and 2003 (the letter calls these UK prevalence figures); Gill and Stajic reviewed 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, of which only 12 were non-hospital deaths from acute polydrug intoxication, and in none was the fatal intoxication caused by ketamine alone.

key_findings.finding: Sources and case definition: np-SAD data for July 1997 to December 2006, and GRO drug-poisoning statistics for England and Wales and for Scotland with GRO Northern Ireland data, January 1993 to December 2006. np-SAD records a death if a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, the person had a history of dependence or abuse of psychoactive drugs, or controlled drugs were found at postmortem; the coroners' response rate has been estimated to have been as high as about 90% to 95%. A ketamine-related death was one in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report (other illegal drugs could also be written); deaths with ketamine given for medical reasons were excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says cocaine was found with ketamine in 6 deaths; Table 1 lists cocaine in 5 of the 18 np-SAD drug entries and in none of the 5 GRO cases (editors' count). The other counts in the same sentence (alcohol 8, opiates/opioids 10, benzodiazepines 7) match Table 1 only when the GRO cases are included, and the opioid count only if co-proxamol is counted. The same sentence does not name MDMA or ecstasy, which Table 1 lists in 7 of the 18 np-SAD drug entries (editors' count), as many deaths as benzodiazepines and more than cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small for cocaine; cite it as 5 in Table 1 or 6 by the text, with the discrepancy noted. The four drugs the text names are not shown to be those most often found with ketamine; a list that follows the text alone leaves out MDMA or ecstasy (7 np-SAD deaths).

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the GRO data as January 1993 to December 2006 and the np-SAD data as July 1997 to December 2006; Table 1 gives England and Wales (ONS) 1993–2002, Scotland 1994–2006 and Northern Ireland 1997–2005, without saying whether these are the periods searched or the years in which cases were found.
reporting_issues.consequence: Coverage differs by source and by year, so the distribution of deaths over 1993–2006 is not comparable from year to year.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists each characteristic of the 18 np-SAD deaths separately, so causes, drugs, circumstances and verdicts cannot be linked to individual deaths. The text's statement that all 4 ketamine-only deaths were poisonings, 3 accidental and 1 suicide, cannot be checked: only one np-SAD cause names ketamine alone, and the 2 England and Wales ketamine-only deaths were accidental poisonings, so, if the text is right, the single np-SAD suicide verdict belongs to one of the 2 np-SAD ketamine-only deaths and the man who killed himself with a knife received another verdict.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ketamine-only figures are the authors' statement and cannot be verified from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter describes the readers' survey figures (lifetime use 25.5% to 39.8%, current use 3.9% to 16.0%, 1999–2003) as UK prevalence, although the same sentence says they come from a self-selected readers' survey of a magazine for clubbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures describe survey respondents, not the UK population; they should not be cited as prevalence.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says that, apart from ketamine, alcohol, chloroform and a propane-butane mixture were found in 17 autoerotic deaths examined in Hanover in 1978–1997, without saying in how many of them ketamine was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence cannot be cited as a count of deaths involving ketamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says most of the 23 were aged 25 to 44; Table 1 gives only the np-SAD average (32.74 years) and range (19.8–49.4) and the GRO ages (20–49 for 3; 26; 35).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the age-group statement cannot be checked.
