design_detail: Case series of 9 patients with lower urinary tract symptoms and chronic recreational ketamine use, from the Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto (Urology 2007;69:810–812; read as the published PDF, printed pp. 810–812). Every patient had a history and physical examination, cystoscopy, urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology; 4 had bladder biopsies, all read by one pathologist; computed tomography and other tests were done 'as indicated', without saying in how many (p. 810). Three patients are described one by one (the index case, a 28-year-old man; a 25-year-old woman; a 17-year-old boy); the other 6 share one paragraph (p. 811). The course after stopping ketamine, with or without pentosan polysulfate, is described in words, without symptom scores, bladder measurements, repeat cystoscopy or a follow-up period. The Comment adds the analysis of one small sample of illicit ketamine obtained with the help of the Toronto police narcotics division, not said to come from these patients (p. 812). No comparison group. Submitted June 2006 (p. 810).
can_establish: That 9 people with chronic recreational ketamine use seen by one Toronto hospital service had irritative lower urinary tract symptoms with sterile urine cultures (and, in the index case, negative cytology), an inflamed and ulcerated bladder at cystoscopy and, in the 4 biopsied, denuded urothelium with granulation tissue, fibrosis and eosinophils, and that the authors saw symptoms ease after ketamine was stopped in some of them: the first published description of what the authors named ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis, and a signal for later studies.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the cystitis (no comparison group, no testing for ketamine or other drugs, no amounts or duration of use, other causes not excluded patient by patient); how often bladder damage occurs in people who use ketamine (no denominator); what amount, frequency, duration or route carries risk (none reported); whether stopping ketamine or taking pentosan polysulfate helps, or how far symptoms recover (no measured outcome, no follow-up period, and the two were given together in 6 patients); or the long-term course, which the authors say remains to be defined (p. 812).

sample.recruitment: Clinic: patients who presented with lower urinary tract symptoms to the authors' service (Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto; corresponding author in the Division of Urology) (p. 810). How the patients were identified, whether they were consecutive, the period over which they were seen and how they were referred are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond chronic recreational ketamine use with genitourinary symptoms (Material and Methods, p. 810). The abstract adds that all 9 used ketamine daily and presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria (p. 810), which the Results do not bear out for every patient (see reporting issues).
sample.demographics: Given for 3 of the 9: the index case, a 28-year-old man who smoked one pack of cigarettes a day and had a history of juvenile diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and peptic ulcer disease (pp. 810–811); a 25-year-old woman; and a 17-year-old boy (p. 811). Age and sex of the other 6 are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable; no follow-up period is reported for any patient.
sample.selection_effects: Only people whose symptoms brought them to a hospital urology service are included; people who use ketamine with milder or no symptoms, or who were not referred, are absent, so the series shows the severe end of whatever range exists. How these 9 came to be reported is not stated. The authors' remark that people who use ketamine already know this as a complication rests on personal reports and is not quantified (p. 811).

exposure.measurement: The patients' own accounts in the clinical history (p. 810). No urine or blood testing for ketamine or other drugs is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported for any patient: no amounts, duration of use or route. The abstract and the index case describe daily use (p. 810); the second patient's symptoms began soon after she started 'experimenting with ketamine' (p. 811); the remaining 6 are said to have had similar patterns of use (p. 811).
exposure.polysubstance: The authors state that none of the 9 was using other illicit drugs (Comment, p. 811), without saying how this was established. The index case smoked a pack of cigarettes a day (p. 810); alcohol and tobacco use of the others are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at presentation. Stopping ketamine afterwards rests on the patients' accounts; how stopping was confirmed and for how long patients were followed are not reported.

comparison.controls: None: no people who use ketamine without symptoms, and no patients with other forms of ulcerative or eosinophilic cystitis examined in the same way.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Urinary history before ketamine use is reported only as the timing of onset (after daily use began in the index case; soon after first use in the second patient). The index case's diabetes and smoking are recorded but not discussed as possible contributors; for the other 8, past medical history and medicines (some medicines cause eosinophilic cystitis, p. 812) are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: History and physical examination; urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology (and microscopy, per the abstract) in all 9; cystoscopy in all 9; bladder biopsy in 4, stained with hematoxylin-eosin, with immunohistochemistry for c-kit to identify mast cells, all read by a single pathologist; computed tomography and other tests as indicated (pp. 810–811). Computed tomography is described only for the index case (Fig. 1), as are the tests for vasculitis (p. 811). Symptoms and their course are described from the history, in words. All findings concern lasting bladder disease seen in clinic, not effects during intoxication.
outcomes.validity_norms: No symptom score, voiding diary, bladder capacity measurement or urodynamic test, and no grading of the cystoscopic or histological findings, are reported.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Ulcerative cystitis' is the cystoscopic appearance, with the histology described for the 4 biopsied; 'improvement' and 'benefit' after stopping ketamine are the authors' descriptions, without a measure or a time frame.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the treating clinicians and the one pathologist knew the patients used ketamine.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only; no statistics. Of 9: urine cultures sterile in all (abstract, p. 810); ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy in all, called severe in the abstract, with the second patient's appearance described as mild squamous metaplasia with reddened flat ulcerated patches (p. 811); eosinophils in all 4 biopsies, to a variable degree (p. 812). Course after stopping ketamine, described in words: the index case noted that his hematuria had settled, but disabling urgency and frequency continued; the second patient herself observed a significant improvement; the third did not recover completely and was helped by pentosan polysulfate; the other 6 are said to have benefited from stopping ketamine plus pentosan polysulfate (p. 811).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a case series; no ethics approval or patient-consent statement is printed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 3 of the 9 patients are described individually; for the other 6 there are no ages, sexes, symptoms, findings or follow-up beyond 'similar' and 'benefited' (p. 811). The abstract presents computed-tomography findings and severe ulcerative cystitis as findings of the whole series, although CT is described for one patient and the Results grade no patient's cystitis as severe (pp. 810–811).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Nine people with chronic recreational ketamine use at one Toronto hospital had irritative lower urinary tract symptoms, sterile urine cultures and inflamed, ulcerated bladders at cystoscopy (cytology is reported as negative for the index case; results for the others are not given); the 4 biopsies showed denuded urothelium, granulation tissue, fibrosis and eosinophils. After stopping ketamine some improved (for the index case and the second patient, by their own observation), but in two of the three patients described individually symptoms did not resolve fully; the other six are said to have benefited from stopping plus pentosan polysulfate, without any measurement.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the series describes 'severe ulcerative cystitis as a result of chronic ketamine use' and that the condition may become more prevalent (p. 810). The Comment says the temporal association between onset and cessation of use in all 9 'implicates ketamine as a causal factor', and takes one police-obtained sample of pure ketamine hydrochloride to suggest that nothing else in recreational ketamine explains the presentation (pp. 811–812); the Conclusions call it a growing public health issue (p. 812). Nine uncontrolled cases without exposure testing or measured outcomes can raise the hypothesis but cannot show cause; the cessation half of the argument is borne out only in part: the index case reported that his hematuria settled and the second patient reported a significant improvement, but the index case's disabling urgency and frequency persisted and the third patient did not recover completely (p. 811); one sample obtained through the police, not said to come from these patients, says nothing about what they took; and the paper contains no data on prevalence or trend.

timeline.event: This series: 9 patients in Toronto, presented by the authors as the first report of what they name ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis (submitted June 2006).
Chu et al., BJU International: a series on destruction of the lower urinary tract in people who use ketamine (Tier A list; to be appraised from the full text).

Cottrell and Gillatt: survey of UK urologists reporting that about one-third of cases resolve after stopping ketamine, one-third stay the same and one-third may progress (as cited by Winstock et al., 2012, p. 4 of the online-first PDF; not read).
Mason et al., Clinical Radiology: radiological series on ketamine-associated lower urinary tract destruction (as cited by Winstock et al., 2012; not read).

Winstock et al.: online survey in which 26.6% of 1285 people who had used ketamine in the last year reported at least one urinary symptom they associated with ketamine; the authors describe the pathological picture (mucosal irritation, reactive atypia, eosinophilic inflammation of the lamina propria) as well recognized.
Chan et al., Hong Kong Medical Journal: systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-associated uropathy (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The clinical and pathological picture described here has since been reported by other groups (summarized by Winstock et al., 2012, pp. 1 and 4 of the online-first PDF; primary papers to be appraised), so the description is not isolated. Its causal reading, how often the condition occurs among people who use ketamine and the course after stopping rest on later work, not on this series; the systematic review of Chan et al. (2022) is to be appraised.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement or acknowledgments (pp. 810–812).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Surgery and Pathology, St. Michael's Hospital and University of Toronto; the corresponding author is in the Division of Urology (p. 810). The ketamine sample was obtained with the help of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department, Narcotics Division, and analysed at an unnamed national laboratory (p. 812).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use ketamine regularly, with use confirmed by testing, standard urinary symptom scores, voiding diaries and bladder capacity measured at entry and repeatedly, compared with people who use other drugs but not ketamine and followed after some stop; for the pathology, biopsies graded blind against other forms of cystitis; and, for treatment, a randomized placebo-controlled trial of pentosan polysulfate in people who have stopped ketamine.

domains.note: Nine patients from one hospital service; how they were identified, over what period and whether they were consecutive is not stated; only people with symptoms severe enough to reach urology are included.
Ketamine use, its daily frequency and the absence of other illicit drugs rest on the patients' accounts; no toxicology, and no amounts, duration or route for anyone.

Cystoscopy, culture, cytology and (in 4) histology read by one pathologist are objective findings, but CT was done only as indicated, there is no symptom score, bladder-capacity measure or grading, and improvement after stopping is described in words without a follow-up period.

Infection was addressed by sterile cultures in all 9; malignancy by cytology, reported negative for the index case only; and vasculitis by tests in the index case only. The absence of other illicit drugs is asserted without any testing; the index case's diabetes and smoking are not discussed; medicines and allergic disease linked with eosinophilic cystitis are not reported as excluded for any of the other 8; and the only contaminant check was one sample of illicit ketamine obtained through the police, not said to come from these patients.
Six of the 9 patients are summarized in one paragraph without age, sex, findings or follow-up; no amounts or duration of use for anyone.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: Causal wording ('as a result of'; 'implicates ketamine as a causal factor') and a public-health conclusion from 9 uncontrolled cases; the association with cessation is asserted for all 9, although two of the three patients described did not fully recover.

The abstract describes all 9 as having gross hematuria and severe cystitis and reports CT findings as if for the series, while the Results describe hematuria and CT for the index case only and do not grade any patient's cystitis as severe (reporting issues 1 to 5).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a case series (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The series is the first published description and may be cited for what was found in these 9 patients: the irritative symptoms, sterile urine cultures, the cystoscopic and histological appearance, and the authors' description of partial improvement after stopping ketamine, with persisting symptoms in at least two. It may not be cited for ketamine as the proven cause, for how often bladder damage occurs in people who use ketamine, for any amount or duration of use that carries risk, or for the effect of stopping ketamine or of pentosan polysulfate. A claim resting only on this series stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 9 patients, all described as using ketamine daily, presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria; urine cultures were sterile in all; computed tomography showed marked thickening of the bladder wall, a small capacity and perivesicular stranding; at cystoscopy all had severe ulcerative cystitis; biopsies in 4 showed epithelial denudation and inflammation with a mild eosinophilic infiltrate; stopping ketamine, with pentosan polysulfate added, appeared to give some relief of symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results)
key_findings.note: The Results bear out these statements only in part: hematuria and CT are described for the index case only, no patient's cystitis is graded as severe, and the Comment says the degree of eosinophilic infiltration varied across the 4 biopsies (reporting issues 1 to 4).

key_findings.finding: Methods: a detailed history and physical examination, cystoscopy, urine culture, urinalysis and urine cytology in all 9 patients; bladder biopsy in 4, all reviewed by a single pathologist; computed tomography and other tests as indicated.
key_findings.locator: Material and Methods (right column)

key_findings.finding: Index case: a 28-year-old man with a 6-month history of painful hematuria, dysuria, urgency and pain after passing urine, which began only after he started using ketamine daily; he smoked one pack of cigarettes a day and had a history of juvenile diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and peptic ulcer disease.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 810, right column, continuing on p. 811, left column)

key_findings.finding: Index case investigations: urine culture, urinalysis and cytology negative; computed tomography showed marked inflammatory change and a very small bladder capacity; cystoscopy showed multiple erythematous patches consistent with active cystitis; biopsy showed a substantially denuded urothelium with a thin layer of reactive and regenerating epithelial cells, an edematous superficial lamina propria with dilated vessels and scattered inflammatory cells (the appearance of granulation tissue), a dense fibrotic deeper lamina propria, and scattered lymphocytes and mast cells (c-kit immunohistochemistry) with eosinophils predominating; overall, the changes of chronic cystitis; investigations for vasculitis negative.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column); Figures 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Index case course: antibiotic and steroid treatment did not control his symptoms; after he stopped ketamine he noted that his hematuria had settled, but disabling urgency and frequency of urination continued.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Second patient: a 25-year-old woman with a 2-year history of frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort that, she noted, had started soon after she began experimenting with ketamine; cystoscopy showed mild squamous metaplasia and reddened flat ulcerated patches; she herself observed a significant improvement in her symptoms after she stopped ketamine. Third patient: a 17-year-old boy with recurrent dysuria and irritative voiding symptoms over several months and cystoscopic findings similar to the index case; his symptoms did not resolve completely after he stopped ketamine, other treatments had limited success, and pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) helped relieve his irritative symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Remaining 6 patients: similar patterns of ketamine use, symptoms and cystoscopic findings; 3 had biopsies with findings similar to the index case but a variable degree of eosinophilic infiltrate; all 6 are said to have benefited from stopping ketamine with pentosan polysulfate added.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: No ages, sexes, durations, measurements or follow-up periods are given for these 6; stopping ketamine and pentosan polysulfate were given together, so their effects cannot be separated.

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretation: this is the first report of the condition they name ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis; personal reports from people who use ketamine indicate it is a well-recognized complication among them; the mechanism is unclear, possibly an active metabolite; the temporal association of onset and cessation of ketamine use with the irritative symptoms in all 9 is taken to implicate ketamine as a cause; none of the 9 was using other illicit drugs.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Police-obtained sample: a small amount of illicit synthetic ketamine obtained with the help of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Department, Narcotics Division, was analysed at a national laboratory and found to be pure ketamine hydrochloride with only a trace of dimethyl sulfoxide; the authors take this to suggest that nothing else in recreational ketamine accounts for the presentation. They suggest that ketamine and its metabolites, which can be measured in high amounts in urine, may accumulate there and irritate the bladder.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd paragraph (p. 811, right column, continuing on p. 812, left column)
key_findings.note: One sample, not said to come from these patients; the analytical method is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Histology compared with eosinophilic cystitis: eosinophilic infiltrates were seen in all four biopsies, to a variable degree; whether they result directly from the drug or are a nonspecific inflammatory response is unclear; the authors judge that the features (marked changes in the epithelium and lamina propria with granulation tissue and fibrosis) appear distinct from classic eosinophilic cystitis, which has been described in association with bladder cancer, asthma and rhinitis, bladder outlet obstruction and medicines such as sulfonamides, warfarin and cyclophosphamide.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: many agents tried for the irritative symptoms failed in these patients; pentosan polysulfate appeared to relieve them partially and is put forward as a possible treatment; the long-term sequelae, including the potential development of fibrotic, small-capacity, noncompliant bladders, remain to be defined; the authors write that management should include stopping ketamine, possibly with pentosan polysulfate.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions (left and right columns)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all 9 patients presented with severe dysuria, frequency, urgency and gross hematuria. In the Results, hematuria is described only for the index case; the second patient had frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort and the third dysuria and irritative voiding symptoms; the other 6 are only called similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's symptom list cannot be taken as describing every patient; hematuria is documented in 1 of the 3 patients described individually.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all patients had severe ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy, but the Results grade severity for no one: the index case had multiple erythematous patches consistent with active cystitis, the second patient mild squamous metaplasia with reddened flat ulcerated patches, the third findings similar to the index case, and the other 6 'similar' findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Severe for all is the abstract's summary, not documented case by case; the word mild in the second patient's description qualifies the squamous metaplasia, not the ulceration, so it does not show a mild cystitis.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports computed-tomography findings (marked wall thickening, small capacity, perivesicular stranding) as findings of the series; the Methods say CT was done as indicated, and the Results describe CT only for the index case (Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: How many patients had CT, and how many had these findings, is unknown; cite the CT findings for the index case only.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the eosinophilic infiltrate in the 4 biopsies mild, while the Comment says its degree varied across the four (p. 812). That eosinophils predominated in the index case (p. 811) concerns the mix of inflammatory cells, not their density, and does not by itself conflict with the abstract's word mild.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; density was not graded, so the infiltrate cannot be characterized beyond present and variable.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes all 9 as using ketamine daily, but the second patient's symptoms began soon after she started experimenting with ketamine, and no frequency is given for the other 6 beyond similar patterns.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency, amount and duration of use behind these cases cannot be described from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment bases the causal inference on a temporal association with both onset and cessation of ketamine use in all 9 patients, but the Results report that the index case kept disabling urgency and frequency and that the third patient's symptoms did not resolve completely after stopping.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cessation part of the argument holds only in part (the index case's hematuria; the second patient); persisting symptoms after stopping are also part of what this series shows.

disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 812, Comment, 3rd paragraph (left column): the sample was secured with police help and its origin is not stated. The card stated an inference as fact, so the wording is corrected in all four fields; the conclusion that one sample says nothing about what these patients took stands.

disagreements.first_pass: Only 3 of the 9 patients are described individually; for the other 6 there are no ages, sexes, symptoms, findings or follow-up beyond 'similar' and 'benefited' (p. 811). The abstract presents computed-tomography findings and severe ulcerative cystitis as findings of the whole series, although CT is described for one patient and one cystoscopy was mild (pp. 810–811).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 481 (round-2 check): missed: the statement that one cystoscopy was mild recurs in key finding 0's note and analysis.selective_reporting; the source's mild qualifies squamous metaplasia (p. 811).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 811, Results, 4th paragraph (right column): mild qualifies squamous metaplasia. It matters because a reader would otherwise take one patient's cystitis to be mild; selective_reporting now says the Results grade no patient's cystitis as severe.

design_detail: Anonymous online cross-sectional survey: the research group's annual survey of drug use among people associated with the dance-music scene, promoted through a collaboration with the dance-music magazine Mixmag on the website dontstayin.com (BJU International 2012; read as the online-first PDF, pages numbered 1–5; the reference record gives the issue pages 110(11):1762–1766). Field period November 2009 to January 2010 by the abstract (the Results print 17 November 2010 to 4 January 2010). Of 3806 completed surveys, the 1285 respondents who reported ketamine use in the last 12 months answered further questions: typical and maximum amounts per session, maximum consecutive days of use, days of use in the last month, a proxy for dependence built from the seven DSM-IV criteria, five urinary symptoms they associated with ketamine in the last 12 months, how the symptoms changed in relation to their use, and help-seeking. Analysis by univariate chi-squared tests against three groups of typical amount and three groups of days of use in the last month. The first page labels the study 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)', level of evidence 1b, but nobody was followed up: the Methods call it a cross-sectional survey (p. 2).
can_establish: What share of a large, self-selected, mostly British online sample of people in the dance-music scene who had used ketamine in the past year reported urinary symptoms they attributed to ketamine in late 2009 (26.6% at least one), which symptoms, whether these reports differed across groups of self-reported typical amount and frequency of use, what respondents recalled about the course of their symptoms after stopping, and how many had sought medical help.
cannot_establish: How common urinary symptoms are among people who use ketamine in general (no sampling frame, no response rate); whether ketamine caused them (no comparison group, symptoms attributed by the respondents themselves, near-universal alcohol and polydrug use, no adjustment); whether symptoms rise steadily with amount or frequency (three-group chi-squared tests, no rates per group, no test for trend); whether the symptoms were brief episodes after a session or persistent (no duration, frequency or severity asked); natural history in the cohort sense (one survey, recalled course, no follow-up despite the 'prospective cohort' label); or any clinical diagnosis (no examination, urine test or validated symptom score).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement (self-selected online survey): through a collaboration with Mixmag, a dance-music publication, the questionnaire was heavily promoted on the website dontstayin.com (the abstract: by a national dance music magazine and website), as part of the group's larger annual survey of drug use and harms among people associated with the dance-music scene (Introduction and Methods, p. 2). Of the 1285 analysed, 80.3% (1032) were from the UK, 11.8% (151) from the USA and 7.9% (102) elsewhere (Results, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All completed surveys; the ketamine and urinary questions were asked only of respondents who reported ketamine use in the last 12 months (Results, p. 2). No other criteria and no checks for repeat responses are reported.
sample.demographics: Of the 1285: mean age 23.5 years (SD 5.8); mean age at first ketamine use 20.42 years (SD 4.3); 70.3% (869) male; 92.6% (1144) white; 73.2% (873) working; 86.7% (1065) heterosexual, 8.5% (105) bisexual, 4.6% (59) homosexual (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). The percentages imply denominators of about 1190 to 1240 rather than 1285 (for example, 869 men at 70.3% implies about 1236; editors' calculation), so some answers were missing; item non-response is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey); item non-response not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Readers of a dance-music magazine's website who chose to respond: no sampling frame, no response rate and no weighting; the authors call the population self-nominating and relatively poorly characterized (Discussion, p. 4). People with urinary problems may have been more or less likely to respond. Last-year use of other drugs and alcohol was almost universal (p. 3). Proportions describe this sample only.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the online questionnaire: lifetime, last-year and last-month use; typical amount per session chosen from fixed amounts; maximum amount in a session; maximum consecutive days of use; days of use in the last month (last-month respondents only); route only for the 307 for whom ketamine was the most recent drug they had tried for the first time (pp. 2–3). No biological verification; the content and purity of what was taken are unknown (p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, grouped by the authors after seeing the distribution of answers. Typical amount per session: 0.125 g or less, 31% (373), called low; 0.25 or 0.5 g, 35%, medium; 1 g or more, 34% (404), high; 4.9% (63) did not know; 5.2% (67) reported regularly taking 3 g or more in a session. Maximum ever in one session: 1 g or more 54.2% (674); 3 g or more 24.6% (307); 5 g or more 6.6% (74). Maximum consecutive days of use: mean 3.5 (mode 2); 11.6% (143) on 7 or more consecutive days. Last-month respondents (792): mean 4.2 days of use in the month (SD 4.87, mode 1), grouped as 1–4 days (70%), 5–8 days (15.6%) and 9 or more days (13.4%). Route (n = 307): 95% intranasal (pp. 2–3). Years of use were not asked; mean age minus mean age at first use is about 3 years (editors' calculation), which is time since first use, not duration of regular use.
exposure.polysubstance: Almost universal and not adjusted for. Last-year use: MDMA 95.5%, cannabis 91.7%, cocaine 78.7%, tobacco 77.5%, mephedrone 66.5%, amphetamine 32%, 'isopropyl nitrate' (poppers, as printed) 27.5%, alcohol 98%. AUDIT-C above the safe-drinking threshold in 87.7% (323) of women and 93.4% (812) of men, and at 8 or more in 35.3% (118) of women and 53.25% (463) of men. Drinking alcohol when taking ketamine: always 31.2% (313), 75% of the time 13.4% (135), 50% 16.3% (165), 25% 20.4% (205), never 18.6% (187) (p. 3). The authors list confounding by other substances and alcohol among the limitations (p. 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. In the question on the course of symptoms, stopping ketamine is self-reported; how long people had stopped for was not asked or is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Urinary symptoms were asked only of respondents who had used ketamine in the last 12 months, and only as symptoms associated with ketamine, so there is no rate among the 2521 respondents who had not used ketamine in the last year (editors' calculation from 3806 and 1285) or among people using the same other drugs. The only contrasts are within the ketamine sample: by typical amount per session, by days of use in the last month and by sex.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Urinary symptoms before ketamine use, urinary tract and sexually transmitted infections, and other conditions that cause the same symptoms were not asked about; the authors say pre-existing pathologies and misattribution cannot be excluded (p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no control group); within the sample, other drug and alcohol use was not compared between people with and without symptoms.

outcomes.instruments: Urinary symptoms: five yes/no items, each a problem the respondent had ever experienced in association with ketamine in the last 12 months: pain in the lower abdomen; burning or stinging when passing urine; needing to pass urine frequently; leakage of urine (incontinence); blood in the urine (Results, 7th paragraph, and Table 1, p. 3). Course of symptoms in relation to ketamine use (improved on stopping; stayed the same while continuing; worse after stopping) and help-seeking (general practitioner; referral to specialist services; accident and emergency) (p. 3). Dependence proxy: the seven DSM-IV dependence criteria, operationalized for the survey, with 3 or more together at some time in the last 12 months counted as dependence, plus markers of problem use (own concern, concern of family or friends, persistent desire or strong urge to use, wish to use less, wish for help to cut down) (p. 3). AUDIT-C, a three-item alcohol screen scored 0–12 (thresholds 3 for women and 4 for men; 8 or more taken to call for assessment for alcohol dependence) (p. 3). All measures are recalled at one time; none was taken during or just after a session.
outcomes.validity_norms: The urinary items and the dependence proxy are not validated, and their exact wording is not printed (the questionnaire is said to be viewable online, p. 2; not read). No validated urinary or bladder-pain symptom score was used, and the duration, frequency and severity of symptoms were not asked, so a single episode after a session counts the same as persistent symptoms. AUDIT-C is a published screen (reference 20).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Urinary symptoms' means a yes to at least one of the five self-attributed items for the last 12 months; 'dependence' means 3 or more of the seven operationalized DSM-IV criteria; 'natural history' means respondents' account, at the one survey, of how their symptoms changed with their use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 15 univariate tests are reported or mentioned (5 symptoms by typical amount, 5 by days of use, the dependence proxy by amount and by days of use, sex by two drinking patterns, sex by symptoms), plus unspecified comparisons of the course of symptoms between high-use and low-use groups (p. 3); no correction and no multivariable model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed anonymous questionnaire).

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without intervals, and chi-squared statistics without degrees of freedom or rates per group. Table 1 (n = 1285): needing to pass urine frequently 17.4% (224); pain in the lower abdomen 11.3% (145); burning or stinging 8.1% (104); leakage 3.3% (43); blood in the urine 1.5% (19); at least one symptom 26.6% (340) (p. 3). Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% interval, n = 1285): at least one symptom about 24.1% to 28.9%; blood in the urine about 0.9% to 2.3%. Typical amount (three groups): burning chi-squared 37.95, frequency 78.29, lower abdominal pain 39.0 (all P < 0.001), blood 6.52 (P = 0.038), leakage 7.44 (P = 0.024). Days of use in the last month (three groups, last-month respondents): lower abdominal pain 52.0 and frequency 39.56 (both P < 0.001), burning 9.8 (P = 0.007); blood 0.62 (P = 0.74) and leakage 5.66 (P = 0.06) not significant (p. 3). The printed P values match 2 degrees of freedom (editors' check), so each test compares three groups without testing a trend. Course of symptoms (n = 251): improved on stopping 51% (128), unchanged while continuing 43% (108), worse after stopping 3.8% (8); help-seeking among the 340 with symptoms: general practitioner 10% (35), specialist referral 2.9% (10), accident and emergency 1.8% (6) (p. 3). Dependence proxy 17% (218), associated with typical amount (chi-squared 170.9) and with days of use (122.3), both P < 0.001 (p. 3).
analysis.covariates: None; all comparisons univariate (Methods, p. 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported. Ethical approval from the Joint South London and Maudsley and Institute of Psychiatry NHS Research Ethics Committee (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: The symptom rates in each amount and frequency group, on which the dose-response conclusion rests, are not shown; the percentages for the dependence proxy by amount and by frequency are left blank in print; no symptom rate by dependence status is reported, although the Discussion says symptoms are particularly common among respondents with dependence; the Methods name t-tests and Mann-Whitney tests whose results do not appear; the sex comparison of symptoms is reported only as not significant (pp. 2–3). The Methods also say respondents were asked whether their symptoms had persisted after stopping (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2), but the Results give only improvement on stopping (128), no change while still using (108) and worsening after stopping (8) (Results, 10th paragraph, p. 3): how many had symptoms that persisted after stopping is not reported (perhaps among the 7 of the 251 not accounted for), so the share of those who stopped who improved cannot be worked out.
analysis.power: Not reported. The overall sample is large; the course and help-seeking figures rest on 251 and 340 respondents, and the rarest symptom (blood in the urine) on 19.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1285 self-selected respondents who had used ketamine in the last year, 26.6% (340) said they had had at least one of five urinary symptoms they associated with ketamine in that year, most often needing to pass urine frequently (17.4%) or lower abdominal pain (11.3%); 1.5% (19) reported blood in the urine. Reports differed across three groups of self-reported typical amount for all five symptoms, and across three groups of days of use for three of the five, in univariate tests with no group rates shown. Of 251 who described the course of their symptoms, 128 said they improved when they stopped and 8 that they got worse after stopping; of the 340 with symptoms, 35 had consulted a general practitioner, 10 had been referred to specialist services and 6 had attended an emergency department.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The first page labels the design a prospective cohort with level of evidence 1b; the abstract says a dose and frequency response relationship 'has been shown' and that symptoms are reported in over a quarter of people who use ketamine regularly (p. 1); the summary box says the symptoms may place a considerable demand on primary, secondary and emergency care and may improve once use is decreased (p. 1). The Discussion says the study 'clearly highlights' that urinary harms are dose related and particularly common among respondents with dependence, and that it 'shows the link between ketamine and urinary symptoms' (pp. 3–4). The data are one cross-sectional survey without follow-up; 26.6% is among anyone who used in the past year (70% of last-month respondents used on 1–4 days), not among people who use regularly; no group rates or trend tests are shown, so a graded dose-response is not demonstrated; no symptom rates by dependence status are reported; the recalled course concerns stopping, not reducing, and the Discussion's statement that in most individuals stopping goes with cessation or improvement of symptoms (p. 4) rests on 128 of 251, a denominator that includes the 108 still using, while the number whose symptoms persisted after stopping is not reported and complete cessation of symptoms was not a reported category (p. 3); and 'considerable demand' rests on 35, 10 and 6 people. With no comparison group and symptoms attributed by the respondents, the survey shows that respondents linked these symptoms to ketamine, not that ketamine caused them. The Limitations acknowledge self-selection, unknown content, polydrug and alcohol use and possible misattribution (p. 4).

timeline.event: Shahani et al.: first case series naming ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis (9 patients, Toronto).

Muetzelfeldt et al.: 90 people who used ketamine (frequent, infrequent and former); cystitis-like symptoms in 20% of the frequent and 6.7% of the infrequent group, and urinary symptoms in 13.3% of the former group (as cited, p. 4 of the online-first PDF; not read).
Cottrell and Gillatt: survey of UK urologists; about one-third of cases resolved after stopping, one-third stayed the same and one-third may progress (as cited, p. 4; not read).
Ng et al.: 233 emergency-department presentations after ketamine use in Hong Kong, 12% with urinary symptoms (as cited, p. 4; not read).
This survey: 26.6% of 1285 respondents who had used ketamine in the last year reported at least one urinary symptom they associated with ketamine.
Chan et al., Hong Kong Medical Journal: systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-associated uropathy (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The authors place their figure beside a smaller UK study whose frequent group reported cystitis-like symptoms at a similar rate (20%) and beside a urologists' survey of outcomes after stopping (p. 4); both are cited, not read. Later surveys and the systematic review of Chan et al. (2022) are to be appraised. Prevalence figures from self-selected online samples are not comparable with population estimates.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement or acknowledgments (pp. 1–5 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: 'None declared' (Conflict of interest, p. 4 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Addiction CAG, South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and St George's Hospital Medical School, London; Bristol Urological Institute, Southmead Hospital, Bristol (p. 1). The survey is the group's annual dance-music drug survey run with Mixmag, with the questionnaires hosted at globaldrugsurvey.com/mixmag (p. 2). The two urologist authors had earlier published on ketamine-associated urinary tract pathology (references 11 and 22, p. 5). In a later Global Drug Survey paper the first author declared that he founded and directs Global Drug Survey (Winstock et al., 2013, p. 6; card sc_winstock_2013); no such statement appears here. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who use ketamine, recruited from a known sampling frame, with validated urinary symptom scores, the duration and severity of symptoms, testing to confirm use, and a comparison group who use the same other drugs and alcohol but not ketamine, reassessed over time and after people stop, with symptom rates reported by amount and frequency and adjusted for alcohol and other drugs.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No sampling frame: readers of a dance-music magazine's website who chose to respond.
Self-nominating convenience sample, described in the abstract as purposeful sampling (p. 1).
1285 respondents; the any-symptom proportion has a 95% interval of about 24% to 29% (editors' calculation). The course-of-symptoms and help-seeking figures rest on 251 and 340.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Countries, demographics and other drug use are given, but denominators vary without explanation, the survey dates conflict between abstract and Results, and the question wording is not printed.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Item non-response is not reported; who the 251 describing their course were is not stated; the frequency comparisons can include only the 792 last-month respondents.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Five unvalidated self-report items in which respondents attributed symptoms to ketamine, without duration, severity, examination or urine testing; dependence by an unvalidated proxy.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same online questions for all, but recall over 12 months and self-attribution may differ between people, and route was asked of only 307.

No intervals; three-group chi-squared tests without group rates or trend tests; no adjustment for alcohol or other drugs; no correction for multiple tests; several sets of figures do not add up (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Open online survey: the number of people reached, the number who started but did not finish (only the 3806 completed surveys are counted, p. 2) and item non-response are not reported, and no weighting is reported, so neither the response nor its handling can be judged; self-selection itself is rated under items 1 and 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of what a large self-selected sample of people in the dance-music scene who had used ketamine reported in late 2009, the survey is informative and was one of the first to count ketamine-attributed urinary symptoms outside clinics. Its figures cannot be generalized (no frame, no response rate), the symptoms are self-attributed, unvalidated and of unknown duration, and the dose and frequency associations are univariate three-group tests with no rates shown and no allowance for near-universal alcohol and polydrug use. It may be cited for the proportions in this sample (26.6% with at least one symptom, and the five items), for the self-reported course in 251 respondents and for help-seeking among 340, each labelled as self-report in a self-selected online sample. It may not be cited for a population prevalence, for ketamine as the cause, for a demonstrated graded dose-response, for symptom rates among people meeting the dependence proxy, or for natural history followed over time.

key_findings.finding: Survey and sample: 3806 surveys were completed; 1947 (51.1%) respondents had ever used ketamine and 1285 (33.8%) had used it in the last 12 months; only the 1285 were asked the ketamine and urinary questions. The abstract dates the survey November 2009 to January 2010; the Results give 17 November 2010 to 4 January 2010.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Patients and methods and Results (p. 1); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2, right column)
key_findings.note: The Results' start date falls after its end date; the abstract's November 2009 start is probably right, but the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: The 1285: 80.3% (1032) from the UK, 11.8% (151) from the USA, 7.9% (102) elsewhere; mean age 23.5 years (SD 5.8); mean age at first ketamine use 20.42 years (SD 4.3); 70.3% (869) male; 92.6% (1144) white; 73.2% (873) working.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Self-reported typical amount per session, grouped by the authors: 0.125 g or less 31% (373); 0.25 or 0.5 g 35%; 1 g or more 34% (404); 4.9% (63) could not say; 5.2% (67) regularly took 3 g or more in a session. Maximum ever in one session: 1 g or more 54.2% (674), 3 g or more 24.6% (307), 5 g or more 6.6% (74).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, right column, continuing on p. 3, left column)
key_findings.note: Respondents' reports, measured by the study; not doses given. 74 is 6.6% only of about 1120; against the roughly 1245 implied by the other two maximum-amount figures it is about 5.9% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Frequency: maximum consecutive days of use mean 3.5 (mode 2), with 11.6% (143) having used on 7 or more consecutive days; the 792 who had used in the last month did so on a mean of 4.2 days (SD 4.87, mode 1), grouped as 1–4 days (70%), 5–8 days (15.6%) and 9 or more days (13.4%). Route was asked only of the 307 for whom ketamine was the most recent drug they had tried for the first time: 95% intranasal.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Dependence proxy: 17% (218) reported 3 or more of the seven operationalized DSM-IV dependence criteria together in the last 12 months; of the 792 who had used in the last month, 22.7% (180) wanted to use less and 5.9% (47) wanted help; the proxy was associated with typical amount (chi-squared 170.9, P < 0.001) and with days of use per month (chi-squared 122.3, P < 0.001), with the percentages left blank in print.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (left column, continuing in the middle column)
key_findings.note: The authors say the self-report proxy may overestimate dependence (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 4).

key_findings.finding: Other drugs and alcohol in the last year: MDMA 95.5%, cannabis 91.7%, cocaine 78.7%, tobacco 77.5%, mephedrone 66.5%, amphetamine 32%, 'isopropyl nitrate' (poppers, as printed) 27.5%, alcohol 98%. AUDIT-C above the safe-drinking threshold: women 87.7% (323), men 93.4% (812); 8 or more: women 35.3% (118), men 53.25% (463). Alcohol with ketamine: always 31.2% (313), 75% of the time 13.4% (135), 50% 16.3% (165), 25% 20.4% (205), never 18.6% (187).
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (middle column)
key_findings.note: The sex-specific figures for drinking with ketamine (44.6% of men against 31.6% of women always or 75% of the time; 30.8% of women against 21.0% of men never) cannot be reconciled with these totals (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 1, urinary symptoms respondents associated with ketamine in the last 12 months (n = 1285): needing to pass urine frequently 17.4% (224); pain in the lower abdomen 11.3% (145); burning or stinging when passing urine 8.1% (104); leakage of urine (incontinence) 3.3% (43); blood in the urine 1.5% (19). At least one symptom: 340 (26.6%). No significant difference between men and women in any symptom (chi-squared; no figures given).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 7th paragraph (middle column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: 340 of 1285 is 26.5% (editors' calculation). The items ask whether a problem was ever experienced in the year, not its duration or severity.

key_findings.finding: By self-reported typical amount (three groups), higher amounts went with higher rates of burning or stinging (chi-squared 37.95, P < 0.001), needing to pass urine frequently (78.29, P < 0.001), lower abdominal pain (39.0, P < 0.001), blood in the urine (6.52, P = 0.038) and leakage of urine (7.44, P = 0.024).
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Symptom rates per amount group are not given; the P values match 2 degrees of freedom (editors' check), a three-group comparison rather than a test for trend.

key_findings.finding: By days of use in the last month (three groups), more frequent use went with higher rates of lower abdominal pain (chi-squared 52.0, P < 0.001), needing to pass urine frequently (39.56, P < 0.001) and burning or stinging (9.8, P = 0.007), but not with blood in the urine (0.62, P = 0.74) or leakage of urine (5.66, P = 0.06).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Rates per group are not given. The frequency groups are defined among the 792 who had used in the last month (Results, 4th paragraph), so these tests can include at most 792 of the 1285.

key_findings.finding: Of 251 respondents who described their symptoms over time in relation to their ketamine use, 51% (128) reported improvement when they stopped, 43% (108) that symptoms had stayed the same while they continued to use, and 3.8% (8) that symptoms got worse after stopping; none of these outcomes differed significantly between the high-use and low-use groups.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (p. 3, right column); Abstract, Results (p. 1)
key_findings.note: 8 of 251 is 3.2%, and 128 + 108 + 8 = 244, leaving 7 unaccounted for (editors' calculation); how many of the 251 had stopped is not given. The Methods say respondents were asked whether symptoms persisted after stopping (p. 2), but no such figure is reported.

key_findings.finding: Of the 340 respondents with urinary symptoms, 10% (35) had sought help from their general practitioner, 2.9% (10) had been referred to specialist services and 1.8% (6) had attended an accident and emergency department.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Other studies as cited in the Discussion: in a cohort of 90 people who used ketamine, cystitis-like symptoms were reported by 20% of the frequent and 6.7% of the infrequent group, and urinary symptoms by 13.3% of the former group; a survey of UK urologists found that about one-third of cases resolved after stopping, one-third stayed the same and one-third may progress; in one study 12% of people presenting to emergency departments after recent ketamine use had urinary symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (left column, the 4th continuing in the middle column)
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures (references 10, 21 and 22), not read.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a self-nominating, relatively poorly characterized population; self-reported experiences with a substance of uncertain composition; high polydrug use and confounding by other substances; uncertain dose quantification and purity; route unknown for most, which the authors call the most significant of the further limitations they list, so a higher risk with injecting cannot be excluded; symptom misattribution, other substance use, acute polydrug or alcohol use, or pre-existing pathologies cannot be excluded; the dependence figure may be an overestimate because of self-report and a proxy measure.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (middle column)

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: the study clearly highlights that urinary harms are dose related and particularly common among respondents with dependence; symptoms go with more frequent use and larger amounts per session; in most, stopping goes with cessation or improvement of symptoms, which may persist while use continues and in a few progress after stopping; the study shows the link between ketamine and urinary symptoms; people who use ketamine and primary-care providers need education, and a multidisciplinary approach promoting harm reduction, cessation and early referral is needed. The first page labels the study 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)', level of evidence 1b.
key_findings.locator: Study type box and Conclusions (p. 1); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 3, right column, continuing on p. 4) and 8th paragraph (p. 4, right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the survey period as November 2009 to January 2010; the Results say the surveys were completed between 17 November 2010 and 4 January 2010, a start date after the end date.
reporting_issues.consequence: The field period is uncertain; most likely 17 November 2009 to 4 January 2010, but the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: The first page labels the study type 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)' with level of evidence 1b; the Methods describe an online cross-sectional survey, and no respondent was followed up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The natural-history figures were recalled at one survey; claims must not describe them as prospective or cohort findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The 8 respondents whose symptoms worsened after stopping are given as 3.8% of 251 in the abstract and the Results; by the editors' calculation, 8 of 251 is 3.2%, and the three outcome groups (128 + 108 + 8 = 244) leave 7 of the 251 unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the 3.8% is unclear (8 is 3.8% of about 210); cite the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The 340 respondents with at least one symptom are given as 26.6% of 1285; by the editors' calculation, 340 of 1285 is 26.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; perhaps a denominator of about 1278 after missing answers.

reporting_issues.issue: Overall, 44.6% always or 75% of the time drank alcohol with ketamine (31.2% + 13.4%) and 18.6% never did; the sex-specific figures are 44.6% of men against 31.6% of women for always or 75% of the time, and 21.0% of men against 30.8% of women for never. An overall share cannot equal the men's figure when the women's is lower, nor lie below both sexes' figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one set of drinking-with-ketamine figures is wrong; neither the totals nor the sex comparison should be cited without this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: For women, 323 above the AUDIT-C threshold is given as 87.7% and 118 scoring 8 or more as 35.3%; by the editors' calculation, these imply about 368 and about 334 women respectively.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the two figures use different, unstated denominators.

reporting_issues.issue: Among maximum amounts ever used in a session, 674 is given as 54.2%, 307 as 24.6% and 74 as 6.6%; by the editors' calculation, the first two imply a denominator of about 1245 and the third about 1120, and 74 of about 1245 would be 5.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one of the figures is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The association of the dependence proxy with typical amount and with frequency is printed with the percentages missing, as '(%, χ2 = 170.9 ...)' and '(%, χ2 = 122.3 ...)'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the association cannot be read; only the test statistics are available.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name unpaired t-tests and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables; no result of either is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Analyses may have been done and not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says urinary harms are particularly common among respondents with dependence, but the Results give no urinary symptom figures by dependence status.
reporting_issues.consequence: That statement has no data behind it in the paper and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion speaks of over a quarter of people who use ketamine regularly, but the 26.6% is among everyone who used ketamine in the last 12 months, including the 70% of last-month respondents who used on 1–4 days and, by the editors' calculation (1285 minus 792), 493 who had not used it in the last month.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is a past-year figure for any use, not a figure for regular use.
