It enters because it is the authors' own ranking.

design_detail: ELEKT-D: pragmatic, open-label, randomized noninferiority trial at five US sites (a community hospital of the Cleveland Clinic, a VA hospital with Baylor College of Medicine, and Yale, Johns Hopkins and Mount Sinai), March 2017 to September 2022. 403 adults aged 21 to 75 with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant major depression referred to an ECT service were randomized 1:1 (stratified by site) to a 3-week course of intravenous ketamine twice weekly or ECT three times weekly, and were allowed to continue their existing medications. Primary outcome: response on the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 (a fall of at least 50% from the first treatment visit) at the end-of-treatment visit, within 3 days after the last session, in a modified intention-to-treat population; noninferiority margin −10 percentage points. Responders were followed for 6 months while receiving whatever treatment their own clinicians prescribed. Funded by PCORI; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03113968.
can_establish: Whether, in adults referred for ECT with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression (mostly outpatients), a 3-week course of ketamine infusions produced self-rated response at the end of treatment no more than 10 percentage points less often than a course of ECT given as specified here, and how the two courses compared on clinician-rated depression, memory tests and moderate or severe adverse events over those 3 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine works better than no active treatment or placebo (none was included); comparative effects free of expectation and preference (open label, self-rated primary outcome, 31 of 203 assigned to ECT never started it); comparison with ECT given bilaterally from the start or for more sessions; effects in psychotic depression (excluded), in inpatients (11% of the sample) or in older adults (the authors call for studies in older patients); and long-term comparative effectiveness or safety, since follow-up covered responders only, under uncontrolled treatment.

sample.recruitment: Clinic referrals: outpatients or inpatients referred by their own clinicians to the ECT service of one of five sites (an urban community hospital, a VA hospital and three university hospital centres), invited to take part, March 2017 to September 2022 (pp. 2316–2317).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 21 to 75; DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features; unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the lifetime, verified from the referring clinician's information, Antidepressant Treatment History Form guidelines and interview; MADRS above 20; no contraindication to ketamine or ECT. The full criteria are in the protocol (p. 2317), which was not read.
sample.demographics: Mean age 46 (45.6 ketamine, 47.1 ECT); 206 of 403 (51.1%) women; 355 (88.1%) White; 359 (89.1%) outpatients at randomization; median current episode 2.0 years (IQR 0.8 to 6.0); median 5 previous episodes; 157 (39.0%) had attempted suicide; previous ECT 11.5% and 10.3% (the same counts as the inpatient row; see reporting issue 6), previous ketamine 7.0% and 3.9%. Baseline MADRS 32.3 and 32.6, QIDS-SR-16 17.9 and 18.2 (Table 1, p. 2318; Results › Patients, p. 2320). Coexisting diagnoses included generalized anxiety disorder (56.5%, 55.7%), PTSD (19.0%, 24.6%), alcohol use disorder (4.0%, 5.4%) and moderate-to-severe substance use (5.0%, 6.4%).
sample.attrition: 35 did not start the assigned treatment (4 of 200 assigned ketamine, 31 of 203 assigned ECT) and 3 more had no post-treatment QIDS-SR-16 rating (1 and 2), leaving 195 and 170 in the modified intention-to-treat population (p. 2320). The authors attribute the higher withdrawal before ECT to patient preferences and logistic issues (p. 2323) and say the analysed patients were similar to those who dropped out (Table S2, supplement, not read). Of those analysed, 180 of 195 (92.3%) completed all six ketamine sessions and 158 of 170 (92.9%) completed six to nine ECT sessions (p. 2321).
sample.selection_effects: People referred for ECT who accepted randomization between ECT and ketamine; mostly White and outpatients; psychotic depression excluded. Pre-treatment withdrawal was unbalanced (2.0% against 15.3%, editors' calculation), so the analysed ECT group is the subset willing to start ECT.

exposure.measurement: Treatment delivered at the trial sites as assigned; adherence counted as sessions completed (p. 2321). ECT technique changes and ketamine dose changes are summarized in Tables S6 and S7 (supplement, not read).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes (the form, racemic or single enantiomer, is not stated), twice a week for 3 weeks, with dose changes allowed if clinically indicated (kept constant in nearly all patients); ECT three times a week for 3 weeks, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse at six times the seizure threshold set at the first session, with later changes of settings and electrode placement allowed (switched to bilateral in 39%) (pp. 2317, 2321). Treatment could end early by the investigator's judgment or the patient's choice (p. 2317).
exposure.polysubstance: Patients in both groups were allowed to continue previously prescribed psychiatric medications, whose doses and changes were recorded: at enrolment, benzodiazepines 30.0% and 31.0%, anticonvulsants 27.0% and 25.1%, atypical antipsychotics 29.5% and 28.6%, selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors 29.0% and 36.9% (Table 1, pp. 2318–2319). Their influence on either treatment is not analysed in the article. Alcohol use disorder and moderate-to-severe substance use were recorded as coexisting diagnoses (Table 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; ongoing medication allowed.

comparison.controls: Active comparator: ECT as specified (right unilateral ultrabrief pulse first, three sessions a week for 3 weeks). No placebo or sham group.
comparison.matching: Randomization stratified by site; baseline characteristics similar, with small differences (Hispanic 12.0% against 5.4%, OCD 4.5% against 8.9%, PTSD 19.0% against 24.6%, previous ketamine 7.0% against 3.9%) (Table 1, p. 2318).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; treatment preference and expectations, which may differ between a novel infusion and ECT, were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same rules in both groups: existing medications could be continued and were recorded (p. 2317).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: QIDS-SR-16 (16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology, self-report, 0 to 27) response, a fall of at least 50% from the first treatment visit to the end-of-treatment visit. Secondary: MADRS (clinician-rated, 0 to 60) response; remission (QIDS-SR-16 of 5 or lower; MADRS of 10 or lower); Clinical and Patient Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I, PGI-I); changes in QIDS-SR-16 and MADRS; Global Self-Evaluation of Memory (GSE-My, self-rated, 1 to 7) and Squire Memory Complaint Questionnaire (SMCQ, self-rated, −72 to 72) at the end of treatment; change in Hopkins Verbal Learning Test–Revised T-scores (HVLT-R, rater-administered memory test: total, delayed recall, discrimination index); 16-item Quality-of-Life Scale; Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS) on treatment days; adverse events (pp. 2317, 2319). All outcomes were measured after the 3-week course, not during an infusion, except the CADSS, which was rated on treatment days (Fig. S3, supplement, not read). Follow-up of responders at months 1, 3 and 6 (p. 2316).
outcomes.validity_norms: QIDS-SR-16 described as validated and used in large depression trials (p. 2317); HVLT-R scored as T-scores with age-corrected norms (Table 2 footnote, p. 2322).
outcomes.operationalization: Response and remission as above, measured at the end-of-treatment visit within 3 days after the last session. Relapse during follow-up: QIDS-SR-16 above 11 (p. 2323). Memory harm: the end-of-treatment change in HVLT-R T-scores and the self-rated memory scales.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for secondary outcomes: the article states that their confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity and may not be used in place of hypothesis testing (pp. 2319, 2322). 16 counts the primary outcome and the 15 secondary estimates in the text and Table 2; the Supplementary Appendix lists further outcomes and subgroup analyses (Table S3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Patients, attending physicians and research staff knew the assignments (p. 2317); the primary outcome is self-rated, and the MADRS and HVLT-R were rated or administered by staff aware of the assignment.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: QIDS-SR-16 response 108/195 (55.4%) with ketamine against 70/170 (41.2%) with ECT, difference 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2), Farrington–Manning statistic 4.64, P<0.001 for noninferiority; intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation 55.4% against 41.6%, difference 13.8 (3.9 to 23.8) (p. 2320; Table 2, p. 2322). MADRS response 50.8% against 41.4%, 9.3 (−0.9 to 19.4); remission QIDS-SR-16 32.3% against 20.0%, 12.3 (3.4 to 21.2); MADRS 37.9% against 21.8%, 16.2 (7.0 to 25.4). Least-squares mean change QIDS-SR-16 −9.0 against −7.2, difference −1.8 (−2.8 to −0.8); MADRS −15.3 against −13.1, difference −2.2 (−4.1 to −0.3). HVLT-R delayed-recall T-score change −0.9 against −9.7, difference 8.8 (5.7 to 11.9) (pp. 2320, 2322). Editors' calculations: the QIDS-SR-16 change difference is about 0.4 of the baseline SD and the MADRS change difference about 0.4 of its baseline SD; number needed to treat for one additional QIDS-SR-16 response about 7.
analysis.covariates: The mixed model for repeated QIDS-SR-16 scores included treatment, assessment, their interaction and site, with a random intercept per patient (p. 2319). The response analysis is unadjusted apart from site stratification.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03113968 (p. 2315); protocol with the statistical analysis plan published with the article at NEJM.org (p. 2316). Neither the registry record nor the protocol was read for this card, so the match between the registered and reported primary outcome and margin is not verified here; the Methods and the abstract give the same primary outcome and margin.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's statement that ketamine was associated with dissociation rests on a supplementary figure (Fig. S3) with no CADSS values in the article; adverse events in the article are moderate and severe events only (further adverse-event data in Table S8, not read); relapse percentages are given without denominators (Table S9). Subgroup results are in Table S3 only.
analysis.power: Powered for noninferiority: 346 participants for 80% power (one-sided alpha 0.025), margin −10 percentage points, assuming 50% response to ECT and a true difference of 5 percentage points; 400 planned to allow 15% attrition (p. 2319). Observed ECT response (41.2%) was below the assumed 50%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 365 analysed patients referred for ECT, self-rated response at the end of a 3-week course was 55.4% after ketamine and 41.2% after ECT, so the prespecified noninferiority test was met by a wide margin (lower limit 3.9 against a margin of −10); clinician-rated response did not differ significantly (9.3 points, −0.9 to 19.4), while remission rates and change scores favoured ketamine by small to moderate amounts. ECT was followed by a larger fall in verbal memory test scores at the end of treatment; among responders followed up, scores had returned to similar levels by 1 month. More patients assigned to ECT withdrew before starting it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that ketamine was noninferior to ECT for treatment-resistant depression without psychosis, and that ECT was associated with musculoskeletal adverse effects and ketamine with dissociation (p. 2315). This matches the prespecified analysis. Gaps: (1) the abstract says ketamine was administered to 195 and ECT to 170 patients after 38 withdrew before treatment, whereas the Results show 35 never started and 3 started without a post-treatment rating (p. 2320); (2) the abstract states that the trial was open-label and names the self-report primary outcome (QIDS-SR-16), but does not mention that ECT response (41.2%) was lower than the 50% assumed in the power calculation and than other reports, which the Discussion attributes partly to starting with right unilateral placement in mostly outpatients (p. 2324); (3) the dissociation statement has no numbers in the article; (4) the abstract reports the fall in memory recall after ECT 'with gradual recovery during follow-up' without saying that follow-up covered responders only, and the Results say that HVLT-R scores were similar to the ketamine group's by the 1-month visit, while self-rated memory (GSE-My) after ECT stayed lower through the end of follow-up (p. 2323). The Discussion names open-label design, the lack of placebo, flexible treatment and uncontrolled follow-up as limitations (p. 2324) and limits the conclusion to nonpsychotic depression.

timeline.event: Berman et al.: an early placebo-controlled report (by its authors' account the first) of lower depression ratings after one ketamine infusion (7 completers); Amit Anand, first author of this trial, is a co-author.

Murrough et al.: two-site trial of one ketamine infusion against midazolam as an active placebo (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_murrough_2013); James W. Murrough is an author of both trials.

KetECT, a European open-label noninferiority trial of racemic ketamine against ECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022), found remission with ketamine inferior to ECT; this article's Discussion (p. 2323) also credits a meta-analysis (Rhee et al., 2022) with that finding, but Rhee et al. pooled no remission or response result (symptom improvement only; the only remission figures they give are KetECT's counts; sc_rhee_2022).
This trial: noninferiority of ketamine to ECT on self-rated response in 365 analysed patients with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression.

replication.where_it_stands: The two large randomized comparisons of ketamine and ECT point in different directions on remission: the earlier European trial and a meta-analysis (as described here) favoured ECT, this trial favoured or matched ketamine. The authors note that their trial differed from those reports in excluding psychotic depression and in its larger, mostly outpatient sample, without stating that these differences explain the discrepancy (pp. 2323–2324), and they list the ECT protocol that started with right unilateral placement among their limitations (p. 2324). The question of which treatment is better for whom stays open.

funding.funder: Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI), under a contract with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, named as the sponsor (p. 2316); supported by an award (TRD-1511-33648, to Dr. Anand) from PCORI (p. 2324). The article states that the views are the authors' alone and not necessarily PCORI's (p. 2324).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not printed in the article: disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org (p. 2324) and were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Designed and supervised by an executive committee of the first author and the site principal investigators; data coordination and project management by the Cleveland Clinic Center for Clinical Research; statistical analysis by the last author (Cleveland Clinic); first author wrote the manuscript; a data and safety monitoring board and a stakeholder committee oversaw the trial (pp. 2316–2317). No industry funder is named. Several authors are investigators of earlier ketamine trials: Anand is an author of Berman et al. (2000), and Murrough and Mathew of Murrough et al. (2013) (author lists in the reference records). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of ketamine and ECT with a clinician-rated primary outcome scored by raters unaware of the assignment, an ECT protocol at full strength (with a prespecified switch to bilateral placement or more sessions), enrolment of inpatients and older adults, and randomized continuation treatment with relapse over 6 to 12 months as an outcome.

domains.note: Randomization through a secure electronic data-management system, stratified by site (p. 2317), which implies concealed allocation; baseline characteristics similar apart from small differences (Table 1).

Open label for patients, physicians and staff. 31 of 203 assigned to ECT never started it (against 4 of 200 for ketamine), which the authors attribute to preferences and logistics; ECT technique was changed to bilateral in 39% and treatment could stop early; concomitant medications were allowed. The primary analysis excluded those who did not start (modified intention to treat), but an intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation gave the same result.

38 of 403 (9.4%) lack the primary outcome, unevenly (5 of 200 against 33 of 203; editors' calculation); several imputation scenarios supported noninferiority, and the authors report that analysed patients resembled dropouts (Table S2, supplement, not read).

The primary outcome is self-rated by patients who knew which treatment they received, in a comparison where preferences and logistics stopped 15% of those assigned to ECT from starting it; the clinician-rated MADRS and the HVLT-R were scored by staff aware of the assignment. The authors say the open-label design could have influenced response (p. 2324).

Registered, with protocol and analysis plan published alongside; the Methods' primary outcome and margin match the abstract, but neither the registry nor the protocol was read for this card. Secondary estimates are reported without multiplicity adjustment, as stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Allocation was sound and the noninferiority result held in intention-to-treat sensitivity analyses, so random error and attrition are unlikely to explain it. The overall judgment is high because the primary outcome is self-rated in an open-label comparison between treatments that patients view very differently, as the uneven withdrawal before ECT shows; expectation could favour either arm, and its direction cannot be known. The ECT comparator, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse in mostly outpatients, produced a lower response than the authors assumed, which affects how far the result generalizes rather than its internal validity. The source can be cited for noninferiority of a 3-week ketamine course to ECT given this way on self-rated response, for the remission and memory-test differences at the end of treatment, and for moderate and severe adverse event rates; it cannot be cited for comparisons with bilateral or longer ECT, for psychotic or late-life depression, for dissociation magnitudes, or for comparative relapse, which comes from uncontrolled follow-up of responders.

key_findings.finding: Open-label, randomized noninferiority trial at five US sites (one community hospital, one VA hospital, three university centres); patients, attending physicians and research staff knew the assignment; randomization 1:1 through a secure electronic system, stratified by site.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Design and Oversight, 1st paragraph (p. 2316); Methods › Randomization and Treatment, 1st paragraph (p. 2317)

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes, twice a week for 3 weeks (dose modification allowed if clinically indicated), against ECT three times a week for 3 weeks, started as right unilateral ultrabrief pulse at six times the seizure threshold with later changes allowed; patients in both groups were allowed to continue their previously prescribed medications.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Randomization and Treatment, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eligibility: age 21 to 75, DSM-5 major depressive disorder without psychotic features, unsatisfactory response to at least two adequate antidepressant trials, MADRS above 20, referred to an ECT service, March 2017 to September 2022.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Population

key_findings.finding: 403 were randomized (200 ketamine, 203 ECT); 35 did not start treatment (4 ketamine, 31 ECT) and 3 had no post-treatment QIDS-SR-16 rating (1 and 2), leaving 365 in the modified intention-to-treat population (195 and 170).
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sample: mean age 46, 206 (51.1%) women, 355 (88.1%) White, 359 (89.1%) outpatients; median current episode 2.0 years; 157 (39.0%) had attempted suicide; baseline MADRS 32.3 (SD 6.2) and 32.6 (SD 6.0), QIDS-SR-16 17.9 (SD 4.1) and 18.2 (SD 4.2); previous ketamine treatment 14 (7.0%) and 8 (3.9%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2318); Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph (p. 2320)

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: QIDS-SR-16 response at the end-of-treatment visit in 108 of 195 (55.4%) after ketamine and 70 of 170 (41.2%) after ECT, difference 14.2 percentage points (95% CI 3.9 to 24.2; Farrington–Manning statistic 4.64; P<0.001 for noninferiority, margin −10). Intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation: 55.4% against 41.6%, difference 13.8 (3.9 to 23.8).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome (p. 2320); Table 2, primary outcome row (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Clinician-rated MADRS response: 99 of 195 (50.8%) against 70 of 169 (41.4%), difference 9.3 percentage points (95% CI −0.9 to 19.4). Least-squares mean change from baseline: QIDS-SR-16 −9.0 against −7.2 (difference −1.8, 95% CI −2.8 to −0.8); MADRS −15.3 against −13.1 (difference −2.2, 95% CI −4.1 to −0.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Depression, 1st paragraph (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)
key_findings.note: Secondary outcome; the article states that its confidence intervals are not adjusted for multiplicity and may not be used in place of hypothesis testing.

key_findings.finding: Remission: QIDS-SR-16 score of 5 or lower in 63 of 195 (32.3%) against 34 of 170 (20.0%), difference 12.3 (95% CI 3.4 to 21.2); MADRS of 10 or lower in 74 of 195 (37.9%) against 37 of 170 (21.8%), difference 16.2 (7.0 to 25.4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Depression, 2nd paragraph (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Global improvement: CGI-I much improved or better 99/189 (52.4%) against 78/164 (47.6%), 4.8 (−5.6 to 15.3); very much improved 59/189 (31.2%) against 35/164 (21.3%), 9.9 (0.8 to 19.0). PGI-I much improved or better 84/190 (44.2%) against 60/164 (36.6%), 7.6 (−2.6 to 17.8); very much improved 37/190 (19.5%) against 18/164 (11.0%), 8.5 (1.1 to 15.9).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, CGI-I and PGI-I rows
key_findings.note: The footnote's threshold for 'much improved or better' is misprinted; see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: Memory at the end of treatment: change in HVLT-R delayed-recall T-score −0.9 (SE 1.1) after ketamine against −9.7 (SE 1.2) after ECT, difference 8.8 (95% CI 5.7 to 11.9); total 3.2 against −2.1, difference 5.3 (3.1 to 7.4); discrimination index −1.5 against −9.7, difference 8.2 (5.2 to 11.3). Self-rated memory: GSE-My 4.2 against 3.2 (difference 1.1, 0.9 to 1.2); SMCQ 0.2 against −8.8 (difference 9.0, 5.1 to 13.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Cognitive Impairment and Quality of Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2320); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: Among ECT responders, HVLT-R scores that were lower than in the ketamine group at the end of treatment had returned to similar levels by the 1-month visit and stayed stable to 6 months; SMCQ scores recovered gradually, while GSE-My scores remained lower than in the ketamine group through the end of follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Follow-up
key_findings.note: Values are in Table S9 (supplement, not read).

key_findings.finding: Quality of life (16-item scale) rose by 12.3 points after ketamine and 12.9 after ECT, difference −0.6 (95% CI −3.4 to 2.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Cognitive Impairment and Quality of Life, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 2320, the quality-of-life sentences at the top of p. 2321, left column); Table 2 (p. 2322)

key_findings.finding: 180 of 195 (92.3%) completed all six ketamine sessions and 158 of 170 (92.9%) completed six to nine ECT sessions; ECT was changed from right unilateral to bilateral in 39% of patients, and the ketamine dose was kept constant in nearly all.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Sessions

key_findings.finding: Moderate or severe adverse events in the 3-week phase: at least one in 49 of 195 (25.1%) with ketamine against 55 of 170 (32.4%) with ECT; muscle pain or weakness 1/195 (0.5%) against 9/170 (5.3%), P = 0.01; gastrointestinal 6.7% against 5.3%; headache 8.2% against 7.1%; severe or prolonged hypertension 6/195 (3.1%) against 4/170 (2.4%); new suicidal ideation 4/195 (2.1%) against 2/170 (1.2%); no suicide attempts; no deaths during the trial. P>0.05 for all except muscle pain or weakness.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events; Table 3, initial treatment phase
key_findings.note: Table 3 lists moderate and severe events only; the article says adverse events are reported in Table 3 and in Table S8 (supplement, not read).

key_findings.finding: Dissociative symptoms (CADSS) were higher in the ketamine group than in the ECT group on all treatment days; no values are given in the article.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events
key_findings.note: The data are in Fig. S3 of the supplement, not read.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up of responders, treated as their own clinicians prescribed: relapse (QIDS-SR-16 above 11) in 19.0% after ketamine against 35.4% after ECT at month 1, 25.0% against 50.9% at month 3 and 34.5% against 56.3% at month 6. During follow-up, at least one moderate or severe adverse event in 17/108 (15.7%) against 10/70 (14.3%); severe or prolonged hypertension 2/108 (1.9%) against 0/70; suicidal ideation 4/108 (3.7%) against 1/70 (1.4%); one suicide attempt (1/108) in the ketamine group; P>0.05 for each (Table 3 footnote).
key_findings.locator: Results › Follow-up; Table 3, follow-up period and footnote
key_findings.note: Relapse denominators and the treatments received during follow-up are in Tables S9 and S10 (supplement, not read); the comparison is no longer randomized, because it is restricted to responders and follow-up treatment was not controlled.

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations that ECT started with right unilateral placement and might have produced more responses if started bilaterally or given for more sessions, that the open-label design could have influenced response, that maintenance treatment was not studied, and the lack of placebo; they note their ECT response and remission rates were lower than in other reports, resembling community and outpatient settings.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their results differ from those of a recent European trial (KetECT) and a meta-analysis that included it, which showed remission with ketamine inferior to ECT, and that their trial differed from these in including only depression without psychosis, having a larger sample and a mostly outpatient population (89%); they list these as differences without stating that they explain the discrepancy.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 2323, right column, continued on p. 2324)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that after 38 patients withdrew before starting the assigned treatment, ketamine was given to 195 patients and ECT to 170. The Results say 35 did not start (4 and 31) and 3 started but had no post-treatment rating; 195 and 170 are the modified intention-to-treat counts. Editors' arithmetic from p. 2320: 196 started ketamine and 172 started ECT.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but claims should use the Results' flow (35 never started, 31 of them assigned to ECT).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 2 footnotes define a CGI-I or PGI-I rating of 'much improved or better' as a score lower than 2, which on a 1-to-7 scale is a score of 1, the same as 'very much improved'; the table gives different counts for the two (99 against 59 for CGI-I with ketamine).
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold must have been 2 or lower; a typographical error in the footnote, without effect on the numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Table 2 footnote give the range of HVLT-R delayed-recall and discrimination-index T-scores as −300 to 200, which is not the range of a T-score (a metric with mean 50 and SD 10); the footnote adds that age-corrected norms were used.
reporting_issues.consequence: The metric in which the 8.8-point delayed-recall difference is expressed is unclear; claims should give the difference without converting it into standard deviations.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that ketamine was associated with dissociation, but the article gives no CADSS values, only a reference to a supplementary figure; Table 3 lists moderate and severe adverse events only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and duration of dissociation, and the frequency of mild adverse events, cannot be cited from the article itself.

reporting_issues.issue: Relapse percentages during follow-up are printed without denominators, and the follow-up compares responders under treatments chosen by their own clinicians.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower relapse after ketamine (34.5% against 56.3% at month 6) is not a randomized comparison and cannot be cited as one.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the same counts in the row for inpatients at randomization and the row for previous ECT: 23 (11.5%) with ketamine and 21 (10.3%) with ECT in both. The inpatient counts agree with the text (359 of 403, 89.1%, were outpatients, leaving 44 inpatients); the previous-ECT row may repeat the inpatient figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of patients with previous ECT cannot be confirmed from the article; claims should cite it with caution.

design_detail: Brief report of a randomized, double-blind, saline-controlled, two-period crossover trial by a Connecticut (USA) group (Connecticut Mental Health Center, West Haven VA Medical Center, Yale; number of sites not stated). 9 medication-free adults with a DSM-IV major depressive episode were to have two test days at least 1 week apart, in random order: an intravenous infusion over 40 minutes of ketamine hydrochloride (total 0.5 mg/kg) on one day and of saline alone on the other, following the procedure of Krystal et al. (1994). Ratings: 25-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) from baseline to 72 hours, Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) to 72 hours, and a visual analogue scale for feeling 'high' and the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) during the first 2 to 4 hours. Repeated-measures ANOVA (condition × time) on the 7 who completed both days; response (a 50% or greater HDRS fall within 3 days) counted in the 8 who had each condition. Setting (inpatient or outpatient) not stated; no registration or protocol mentioned.
can_establish: Whether, in 7 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode who completed both test days, depression ratings over the 3 days after one 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg differed from those after a saline infusion, and how self-rated 'high' and BPRS positive symptoms changed in the first hours after it.
cannot_establish: Whether the antidepressant effect is specific rather than driven by expectation (saline has none of ketamine's perceptible effects, and the authors say patients readily told the infusions apart); its size free of carryover (washout at least 1 week, while the effect is said to last 1 to 2 weeks) and of a 6-point higher baseline before ketamine; its duration beyond 72 hours (later observations lie outside the rating schedule); effects in treatment-resistant depression as such (treatment history is not reported); any cognitive effect (no cognitive test was given); and any harm rarer than 9 people treated once can show.

sample.recruitment: Not reported. Authors' units: Clinical Neuroscience Research Unit of the Connecticut Mental Health Center (New Haven), Affective Disorders Program of the West Haven VA Medical Center, and the Department of Psychiatry, Yale University; approval by the IRB of the VA Connecticut Healthcare system, West Haven campus (pp. 351–352).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV major depressive episode by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (8 recurrent unipolar major depression, 1 bipolar disorder, depressed); no recent diagnosis of alcohol or substance abuse (2 had a history of alcohol abuse in remission for more than 8 years); no lifetime diagnosis of another Axis I disorder except 1 person with comorbid panic disorder; drug-free, in good health and unmedicated for at least 2 weeks before the first test day, by history, physical examination, routine blood tests, electrocardiogram, urinalysis and urine toxicology (pp. 351–352). No severity threshold, treatment-resistance criterion or exclusion of psychotic features is stated.
sample.demographics: 4 men, 5 women; age 37 (SD 10), range 23–56; 2 Hispanic, 7 Caucasian (p. 351). Baseline 25-item HDRS 33.0 (SD 6.7) before ketamine and 26.9 (SD 5.8) before saline; BDI 29.5 (SD 8.2) and 23.0 (SD 8.2) (pp. 352–353). Illness duration, episode length and prior treatments are not reported.
sample.attrition: 2 of 9 left before their second test day, one after the ketamine day and one after the saline day, to start antidepressant treatment; both were excluded from the ANOVAs (pp. 351–352). The person who had only the ketamine day went from HDRS 33 to 16 (p. 352). The response counts use the 8 people who had each condition (p. 353).
sample.selection_effects: Very small sample of unstated origin; people willing to stay off medication for at least 2 weeks and to accept a challenge described to them at consent as possibly worsening their depression and causing distressing cognitive disturbances (p. 352). Diagnoses are mixed (one bipolar depression, one comorbid panic disorder), treatment history is unknown, and the main analysis keeps completers only.

exposure.measurement: Assigned infusion, ketamine hydrochloride or saline, given under randomized double-blind conditions as described in Krystal et al. (1994); how the solutions were prepared, who gave them and how the blind was kept are not described in this report (p. 352). No blood levels were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: ketamine hydrochloride, total dose 0.5 mg/kg, infused intravenously over 40 minutes, once; saline alone infused the same way on the other test day; the two test days at least 1 week apart (p. 352).
exposure.polysubstance: A recent alcohol or substance abuse diagnosis was an exclusion; 2 participants had alcohol abuse in remission for more than 8 years; urine toxicology at screening (pp. 351–352). Tobacco, caffeine and current alcohol use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Drug-free and unmedicated for at least 2 weeks before the first test day, checked by history and urine toxicology (p. 352). Whether participants stayed off medication between test days is not stated, except that the 2 who left did so to begin antidepressants.

comparison.controls: Each completer's own saline test day: an inert placebo without ketamine's perceptible effects; no active control.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; order randomized, with 4 assigned ketamine first (p. 352). Baseline HDRS was 33.0 before ketamine and 26.9 before saline (paired t test, p = 0.10), and the second test day began lower than the first by 10.3 points (SD 9.0) when ketamine came first and by 3.0 points (SD 7.5) when saline came first (p = .29) (p. 352). Neither difference was adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a between-group comparison; but illness history, previous treatments and participants' expectations were not recorded, and no first-period-only analysis is reported to separate the treatment effect from period and carryover effects.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (same people on both days).

outcomes.instruments: 25-item HDRS (clinician-rated depression severity) at baseline and 80 min, 230 min, 24 h, 48 h and 72 h after the start of infusion; BDI (self-rated depression) at the same times plus 10, 40 and 110 min after infusion; visual analogue scale for feeling 'high' (VAS-high, self-rated intoxication, 0–100 mm) at baseline and 10, 40, 80 and 110 min after infusion; BPRS (clinician-rated psychiatric symptoms, analysed as the positive-symptom score) at baseline and 10, 40, 80, 110 and 230 min after infusion (p. 352). VAS-high and BPRS therefore cover the infusion and the following hours; HDRS and BDI cover the 3 days after it. Whether the times 'after infusion' count from its start or its end is stated only for the HDRS (from the start).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. The BPRS version and the items making up its positive-symptom score are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: Antidepressant effect: the condition × time interaction on HDRS and BDI totals. Response: a 50% or greater HDRS decrease 'during the 3-day follow-up period', without saying whether at 72 h or at any rating (p. 353). Return to baseline: clinical impression and HDRS within 5 points of baseline, observed 1 to 2 weeks after infusion, outside the stated rating schedule (p. 353). Psychotomimetic effects: VAS-high and BPRS positive symptoms. No cognitive test was given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four repeated-measures ANOVAs (HDRS, BDI, VAS-high, BPRS-positive) with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; post hoc contrasts at each time point against baseline and between conditions (Figure 1); a Fisher exact test of response; two correlations; and paired t tests on individual HDRS items (number of items tested not stated), stated to be uncorrected for multiple comparisons (pp. 352–353).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind. Who rated the HDRS and BPRS is not stated and no check of blinding was made; the authors write that patients readily told the active infusion from placebo by its perceptual disturbances and 'high' (p. 353).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. HDRS (7 completers): condition × time F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02; time F = 2.62, p = .09; condition F = 0.157, p = .71 (p. 352). Abstract: HDRS fell by 14 (SD 10) points within 72 hours after ketamine and by 0 (SD 12) after saline (p. 351). BDI: ketamine day 29.5 (SD 8.2) at baseline to 16.8 (SD 10.5); saline day 23.0 (SD 8.2) to 25.2 (SD 6.0); drug × time F = 5.7, df 8,48, p = .0001 (p. 353). Response: 4 of 8 after ketamine against 1 of 8 after saline, Fisher exact p > .05 (p. 353). VAS-high condition × time F = 16.9, df 4,24, p = .0001; BPRS-positive condition × time F = 4.14, df 5,30, p = .068 (p. 353). Editors' calculations: standardized difference in HDRS change about 1.3 (14 against 0 points, pooled SD about 11, treating the two conditions as independent because the SD of within-person differences is not reported); response difference 37.5 percentage points (95% CI about −7 to 68, Newcombe method, conditions treated as independent), two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.28.
analysis.covariates: None. Baseline differences between test days and treatment order were not adjusted for; order effects were examined post hoc only (p > .3) (p. 353).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or named primary outcome is mentioned; the abstract leads with the HDRS change.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the HDRS change but not the non-significant response comparison. The BPRS paragraph opens by calling the BPRS rise significant, while every BPRS-positive test printed is not (p = .06 to .10); BPRS totals are not shown. HDRS item tests are reported only for the items that changed after ketamine. The timing of 'response' and the method of the post hoc between-condition contrasts are not described.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. 7 completers.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 7 completers, HDRS and BDI scores fell over the 3 days after the ketamine infusion and not after saline (condition × time p = .02 and p = .0001). 4 of 8 people reached a 50% HDRS fall after ketamine against 1 of 8 after saline, a difference that was not significant. Self-rated 'high' peaked during or just after the infusion and was gone by 110 minutes; BPRS positive-symptom scores were higher in the first 80 minutes or so and back near baseline by 110 minutes, without a significant condition × time effect. Baseline depression was higher before ketamine than before saline, the second test day started lower than the first in both orders, and the authors state that patients could tell the infusions apart.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the study "the first placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial" of a single NMDA-antagonist dose in depression and reports significant improvement within 72 hours (p. 351). The Discussion speaks of 'robust decreases' in depressive symptoms, reads the item results as a lessening of core symptoms and the timing as showing that the improvement is disconnected from the 'high', and says ketamine induced "profound and transient cognitive deficits" as shown by BPRS increases (p. 353). Gaps: (1) 'double-blinded' stands against the authors' own statement that patients readily recognized the active infusion; (2) 'robust' rests on 7 completers, a non-significant response comparison and a 6-point higher baseline before ketamine; (3) no cognitive test was given and the BPRS-positive effect was not significant; (4) the separation from the 'high' rests on two null correlations in 7 or 8 people; (5) the 1-to-2-week duration comes from observations outside the stated rating schedule. In the authors' favour, the Discussion names the unblinding as a possible confound and the psychotomimetic effects and potential for abuse as limits to clinical use (p. 353), and the conclusion in the abstract is worded as suggesting a potential role.

timeline.event: Krystal et al.: the healthy-volunteer study from the same group whose infusion procedure and rating times this trial follows (p. 352).

Zarate et al.: crossover trial in 18 inpatients with treatment-resistant unipolar depression, the same 0.5 mg/kg infusion against saline, 1 week apart; HDRS lower from 110 minutes to day 7, with carryover into the saline period (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_zarate_2006).

Murrough et al.: two-site parallel trial, 72 analysed, the same dose against midazolam as an active placebo; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours and response 30 of 47 against 7 of 25 (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_murrough_2013). Dennis S. Charney is an author of Berman et al. (2000), Zarate et al. (2006) and Murrough et al. (2013) (reference records).

Short et al.: systematic review of side-effects in 60 depression studies of ketamine, listing this trial first among 20 randomized trials, with short-term BPRS and VAS ratings and 7 patients given ketamine.

Anand et al.: randomized noninferiority trial of six infusions of the same dose (0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, twice weekly for 3 weeks) against ECT in 365 analysed patients; self-rated response 55.4% against 41.2%. Amit Anand is an author of both trials.

replication.where_it_stands: A fall in depression ratings in the first days after one 0.5 mg/kg infusion was found again against saline in a larger crossover trial (Zarate et al., 2006) and against an active placebo in a parallel trial (Murrough et al., 2013); both share investigators with this group. This pilot cannot by itself be cited for the size or the duration of the effect: its estimate rests on 7 completers, an inert placebo with acknowledged unblinding, baseline imbalance and probable carryover.

funding.funder: Supported in part by a Donaghue Foundation (RMB), a Merit Review Grant from the Department of Veterans Affairs (DSC, JHK) and a VA-Yale Alcoholism Research Center; research supported by a VA Merit Award (NNB), an NIMH Program Grant and the State of Connecticut (acknowledgement note, p. 353).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic and VA units in Connecticut; no industry support is declared. The initials NNB in the funding note match none of the seven authors. The infusion procedure is the one this group published in healthy volunteers (Krystal et al., 1994). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A parallel-group trial, or a crossover with a washout longer than the effect, using an active placebo that mimics ketamine's acute perceptible effects; a registered primary outcome at a fixed time; raters kept apart from the infusion sessions; a check of what patients and raters guessed; analysis adjusted for baseline; and ratings on a fixed schedule beyond 72 hours.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two infusions)
domains.note: Order was randomized (4 assigned ketamine first), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described, and first-period baselines by order are not reported. Over both periods, baseline HDRS was 6.1 points higher before ketamine (p = 0.10).

The washout was at least 1 week, while the authors say the improvement lasted 1 to 2 weeks; the second test day began 10.3 points lower than the first when ketamine came first. No first-period analysis or period term is reported, only a post hoc order test in 7 people (p > .3), which has little power to detect carryover.

Saline has none of ketamine's acute effects, and the authors state that patients readily identified the active infusion; how this may have changed behaviour or care is not reported. Whether medication stayed off between test days is not stated.

2 of 9 (22%) missed a test day and were dropped from the ANOVAs; both left to start antidepressants, a reason linked to their depression, and the one with only the ketamine day had improved (HDRS 33 to 16). The response count includes 8 per condition, which partly offsets this.

HDRS (clinician-rated) and BDI (self-rated) are subjective; patients could tell the infusions apart, and raters seeing them during the session probably could too; no blinding check. The consent information warned that the challenge might worsen depression, which runs against a simple expectancy account but does not remove the bias.

No protocol or registered outcome. Many time points and four scales; the response definition does not fix a time; HDRS item tests reported selectively and uncorrected; the abstract omits the non-significant response comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized within-person design and a significant condition × time interaction on two depression scales make a short-term difference between ketamine and saline days likely in these 7 people. The overall judgment is high because the outcomes are subjective ratings under an inert placebo that the authors say patients saw through, because the washout was shorter than the reported duration of benefit and the baselines differed by order and condition, and because the sample is tiny with completers-only analysis. The source can be cited as an early placebo-controlled report (by the authors' account the first) of lower depression ratings within 72 hours after one 0.5 mg/kg infusion, and for the time course of the self-rated 'high' (gone by 110 minutes); the BPRS-positive rise in the first hour was not significant on the interaction test and should be cited only as such; it cannot be cited for the size of the antidepressant effect, its specificity beyond expectation, its duration beyond 72 hours, response rates, or any cognitive effect.

key_findings.finding: 9 adults with a DSM-IV major depressive episode (8 recurrent unipolar, 1 bipolar, depressed) entered; 2 left before their second test day, one after ketamine and one after saline, to start antidepressant treatment, leaving 7 who completed both days for the ANOVAs. The person excluded after the ketamine day only went from HDRS 33 to 16.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 351, right column, continued on p. 352); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 352, left column)

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: two test days at least 1 week apart in randomized, double-blind order; saline alone or ketamine hydrochloride, total dose 0.5 mg/kg, infused intravenously over 40 minutes; 4 participants were randomly assigned ketamine first.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: HDRS (25-item), 7 completers: significant condition × time interaction (F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02), with no significant effect of time (F = 2.62, df 5,30, p = .09) or condition (F = 0.157, p = .71).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The condition df is printed as 1,30; see reporting issue 1.

key_findings.finding: The abstract summarizes the HDRS result as a fall of 14 (SD 10) points within 72 hours after ketamine against 0 (SD 12) after saline.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 352; editors' reading of the plotted means, approximate) shows a mean change of about −8 points at 230 minutes, −11 at 24 hours, −13 at 48 hours and −13 at 72 hours after ketamine, against values between about −2 and +2 after saline; between-condition post hoc contrasts are marked p < .05 at 230 minutes and p ≤ .001 at 24, 48 and 72 hours.

key_findings.finding: Baseline HDRS was 33.0 (SD 6.7) before ketamine and 26.9 (SD 5.8) before saline (paired t test, p = 0.10). The second test day began lower than the first by 10.3 points (SD 9.0) in those given ketamine first and by 3.0 points (SD 7.5) in those given saline first (p = .29).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (right column, below Figure 1)
key_findings.note: A 10-point lower start to the saline day after ketamine is what carryover of the ketamine effect across a washout of at least 1 week would produce; the paper does not discuss it.

key_findings.finding: BDI: ketamine day 29.5 (SD 8.2) at baseline and 16.8 (SD 10.5) at the final rating; saline day 23.0 (SD 8.2) and 25.2 (SD 6.0); drug × time F = 5.7 (df 8,48), p = .0001; drug F = .007, p = .94; time F = 1.63, p = .21. Order effects examined post hoc were not significant for HDRS or BDI (p > .3).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (continued from p. 352), left column

key_findings.finding: Response (a 50% or greater HDRS fall during the 3-day follow-up): 4 of 8 after ketamine (decreases of 7, 30, 45, 47, 52, 52, 63 and 83%) against 1 of 8 after saline (decreases of 3, 6, 7, 8 and 74%; three people 4, 22 and 33% above baseline); Fisher exact p > .05.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.28; difference 37.5 percentage points, 95% CI about −7 to 68 (Newcombe, treating conditions as independent). The counts use 8 people per condition, not the 7 completers of the ANOVAs.

key_findings.finding: Mood improvement after ketamine returned to baseline (clinical impression and HDRS within 5 points of baseline) 1 to 2 weeks after the infusion; one exception, whose HDRS went from 41 at baseline to 7 on day 3, was still at 15 two weeks after the infusion when he started antidepressant medication.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The stated rating schedule ends at 72 hours (p. 352), so these later observations are outside it; how and when they were made is not described.

key_findings.finding: Self-rated 'high' (VAS): condition × time F = 16.9 (df 4,24), p = .0001; scores returned to baseline by 110 minutes after infusion; every patient reached a maximum of at least 50 mm on the ketamine day and none rose at all on the saline day.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 1, middle panel (p. 352; editors' reading, approximate): mean peak about 83 mm at the 10-minute rating, about 44 at 40 minutes and about 13 at 80 minutes.

key_findings.finding: BPRS positive symptoms: the text says ketamine produced significantly greater BPRS scores, especially positive symptoms, but the condition × time (F = 4.14, df 5,30, p = .068), time (p = .06) and condition (p = .10) effects on BPRS-positive scores were not significant; the figure legend gives p = .07 for the interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 353); Figure 1 legend (p. 352)
key_findings.note: Figure 1, bottom panel (editors' reading, approximate): mean score about 4.5 at baseline, about 8.7 at 10 and 40 minutes and back to about 4.5 by 110 minutes after ketamine; about 4 throughout after saline; between-condition contrasts marked p ≤ .01 at 10 and 40 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Changes in BPRS or VAS-high scores did not correlate with the percentage fall in HDRS (R² < .05, p > .65).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Comparing baseline with final scores on individual HDRS items after ketamine: depressed mood (paired t test, p = .0025), suicidality (p = .02), helplessness (p = .008) and worthlessness (p = .015) decreased, uncorrected for multiple comparisons; no HDRS item improved significantly after saline.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that patients readily told the active infusion from placebo by its perceptual disturbances and 'high', and that this limit on the blind may have biased reporting by diminishing placebo effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that clinical use of this strategy may be limited by the psychotomimetic effects and potential for abuse of many NMDA antagonists, and propose testing antagonists without psychotomimetic properties (memantine, eliprodil, 1-aminocyclopropanecarboxylic acid).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The condition main effects are printed with df 1,30 (HDRS), 1,48 (BDI), 1,24 (VAS-high) and 1,30 (BPRS-positive). In a within-person ANOVA of 7 completers the error df for condition is 6, and the printed p values match df 1,6: for example VAS-high F = 26.3 gives p = .002 with df 1,6 against about .00003 with df 1,24, and BPRS F = 3.71 gives p = .10 with df 1,6 against .064 with df 1,30 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The df are misprinted, not the tests; claims should quote F and p, not the printed df.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that ketamine produced significantly greater BPRS scores, especially positive symptoms, while all three BPRS-positive tests in the same paragraph are non-significant (p = .068, .06, .10) and the Figure 1 legend gives p = .07; BPRS total scores are not reported. The Discussion then takes BPRS increases as evidence of 'profound' cognitive deficits, although no cognitive measure was taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims may not describe the BPRS rise in this study as significant or cite it for cognitive effects; the starred contrasts at 10 and 40 minutes follow a non-significant interaction.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall baseline difference (33.0 before ketamine against 26.9 before saline, paired p = 0.10) cannot be reproduced from the order-specific differences in the next sentence (10.3 and 3.0 points), and the paper does not say how many completers had each order or on which sample each baseline mean was computed. Editors' calculation: the overall difference is 6.1 points, while for 7 completers the order-specific values give a mean difference of 4.6 points if 4 had ketamine first, or 2.7 if 3 did.
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline imbalance cannot be quantified exactly; it may come from different samples (8 per condition) than the 7-person ANOVA.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 marks the between-condition HDRS contrasts at 24, 48 and 72 hours as p ≤ .001, and the method of the contrasts is described only as Huynh-Feldt adjusted. Editors' reading and calculation (approximate): at 72 hours the plotted means differ by about 13 points with SEMs of about 4.1 and 4.5; a paired t test with df 6 would need a within-person correlation of about 0.87 between the two days' changes to reach p = .001, and an unpaired comparison gives p of about .05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The starred time-point contrasts probably used a pooled error term and overstate the precision; claims should rest on the interaction (p = .02) and the response counts, not on the stars.

reporting_issues.issue: Response is counted in 8 people per condition (including the 2 who completed only one day), while every other analysis uses the 7 completers; and response is defined only as a 50% fall 'during the 3-day follow-up period', not at a fixed time.
reporting_issues.consequence: Response may have been taken at each person's best rating, which favours the condition with larger fluctuations; the denominators differ between analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 plots the first post-baseline HDRS rating at about 40 minutes on the time axis, level with the 40-minute VAS and BPRS ratings, whereas the Methods schedule the HDRS at 80 minutes after the start of infusion (the BDI, not the HDRS, at 40 minutes). The second HDRS rating is plotted at about 230 minutes, level with the 230-minute BPRS rating, as scheduled from the start of the infusion; so neither the start nor the end of the infusion, taken as time zero, fits both points (editors' measurement at 600 dpi).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the timing of the earliest HDRS rating is uncertain, which does not affect the 24-to-72-hour results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 'seven subjects with major depression', but the sample included one person with bipolar disorder, depressed; whether that person was among the 7 completers is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysed sample's diagnoses are not fully known.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 482 (round-2 check): missed. Minor: Huynh-Feldt epsilons are not reported, so the same F = 3.97 (df 5,30) carries p = .02 for the HDRS interaction (p. 352) and p = .06 for the BPRS time effect (p. 353); the corrected df behind each p cannot be checked.
