design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; no protocol or registration mentioned) of how side-effects of ketamine were assessed and reported in studies of adults with unipolar or bipolar depression who received at least one dose by any route, with a change in depression as the study's primary outcome. MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Database searched from 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, no language limit. 60 studies (20 randomized trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case reports or series, 3 retrospective studies; 899 patients given ketamine) were synthesized qualitatively by counting how many studies assessed and reported each category of side-effect (psychiatric, psychotomimetic or dissociative, cardiovascular, neurological or cognitive, other) over three time frames: acute (within 4 hours of a single dose), cumulative (after repeated doses) and long-term (at least 2 weeks after the last dose). A planned meta-analysis was dropped. The PDF read is the online-first version (Lancet Psychiatry, published online 27 July 2017), paginated 1 to 14.
can_establish: Which side-effects were reported in depression studies of ketamine published up to 2016, in how many studies, over which time frames, and how often harms were actively and systematically assessed rather than recorded only when patients mentioned them.
cannot_establish: How often any side-effect occurs (no incidence figures are extracted or pooled), how much more often it occurs with ketamine than with placebo (no comparative data are given), whether side-effects depend on dose (doses are not tabulated), or what happens with long-term repeated use (rarely assessed in the included studies); the statements about urinary, liver, cognitive and dependence harms in other populations come from literature outside the systematic search.

sample.recruitment: Database search (MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, Cochrane Database), 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, terms combining ketamine with depression, affective, mood or bipolar and with safe, side or adverse; plus 23 records from unspecified other sources; letters reporting a case were eligible (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF). The settings of the included studies are not tabulated; Table 1 gives each study's design, number given ketamine, route and single or multiple dosing, but not setting, diagnosis mix or dose.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with a validated diagnosis of unipolar or bipolar depression given one or more doses of ketamine by any route, frequency and time course, in studies reporting change in depression as a primary outcome. Excluded: animal studies; non-original or mechanistic reports; studies of children or adolescents only; studies whose primary interest was another disorder (pain, fibromyalgia, suicidality, PTSD, recreational drug use) unless a patient with depression was included; studies with ECT as a concomitant intervention; studies of other NMDA-receptor antagonists only (nitrous oxide, MK-0657, AZD6765) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated by study. Routes (Table 2): intravenous 49 articles, about 737 patients (214 given multiple doses); oral 6 articles, 72 patients; intramuscular 3, 7; subcutaneous 4, 25; intranasal 2, 18; sublingual 1, 26; transmucosal 1, 17; total 902, with 3 patients who received more than one route; the authors call these numbers approximate (p. 7 of the online-first PDF).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Withdrawals within studies are summarized by reason (pp. 6–7 of the online-first PDF).
sample.selection_effects: Selection required depression change as a primary outcome, so dedicated safety studies and harms reported only in separate safety papers could be missed. Most included studies were uncontrolled (about three-fifths had no placebo or control, by the editors' reading of the Figure 2 pie chart) and most patients received a single intravenous dose. Table 1 footnotes flag possible sample overlap between several studies from the same groups, so the total of 899 patients may count some people more than once.

exposure.measurement: As given in the primary studies; the review records route and whether dosing was single or multiple, but not the dose (pp. 3–6 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as tabulated: mostly single intravenous doses; multiple doses in about 356 of 899 patients; non-intravenous routes (oral, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intranasal, sublingual, transmucosal) in 17 route entries (Table 2, p. 7 of the online-first PDF). Most studies used racemic ketamine (p. 11 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Concomitant medication was among the data the authors say they collected, but it is not reported in the article (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Whatever the primary studies used: placebo, active control, dose comparison, or none; most studies had no placebo or control group (Figure 2, p. 7 of the online-first PDF).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Health screening before ketamine and pre-existing medical illness were among the data collected, but the authors state it is unclear in many studies whether comprehensive health screening was done (p. 10 of the online-first PDF); no study-level data are shown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: The review's outcome is the reporting of side-effects: for each study and each of four categories, the period assessed (short term within 4 hours, cumulative, long term at least 2 weeks after the last dose), the measures used (for example BPRS, CADSS, YMRS, SAFTEE, PRISE, vital signs, liver function tests) and whether reporting was systematic (presence and absence reported) or ad hoc (only when present), and whether assessment was active or passive (Methods › Analysis; Table 1, pp. 2–6 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.validity_norms: Each article was appraised with a relevant appraisal checklist or tool reported in the appendix (p. 2 of the online-first PDF); the appendix was not read and no appraisal results appear in the article.
outcomes.operationalization: A side-effect counted as having occurred if a study listed it in at least one patient (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). Results are therefore numbers of studies reporting a side-effect, not numbers of patients affected.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; the synthesis consists of counts and proportions of studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Study selection by two authors with consensus and a senior author for discrepancies; data collected by two authors and extracted by four, without a stated duplicate-extraction procedure (pp. 2, 11 of the online-first PDF).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review counts studies: acute side-effects assessed in 55 of 60 (92%), cumulative in 24 (40%), long-term in 12 (20%); acute psychiatric side-effects described in 23 (38%) studies, psychotomimetic or dissociative in 43 (72%), acute cardiovascular changes in 23 (38%), other side-effects in 32 (53%); urinary side-effects assessed in 5 studies, liver function tests in 7 (abnormal in 2), questions about dependence in 2; systematic reporting of psychiatric or psychotomimetic side-effects in 25 (42%), cardiovascular in 19 (32%), neurological or cognitive in 14 (23%) and other in 14 (23%) (pp. 6–8 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. Two study-level comparisons are reported descriptively: intravenous against other routes, and randomized trials against other designs (pp. 7–8 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA reporting is stated. A meta-analysis was planned and then judged inappropriate after data extraction because of clinical diversity, varied routes, doses and comparators, and reporting differences (p. 6 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.selective_reporting: The study-level appraisal is placed in an appendix and never used in the text. Doses are not tabulated, so side-effects cannot be related to dose. The statement that side-effects were reported more often with ketamine than placebo in controlled studies is given without numbers. Figures 2, 4 and 5 present some counts only graphically.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 60 studies of ketamine in depression published from 1999 to 2016, most of them without a control group and most patients given a single intravenous dose, acute side-effects were assessed in almost all, but cumulative effects in 40% and long-term effects in 20%; harms were often recorded passively and reported ad hoc; urinary symptoms were assessed in 5 studies, liver function in 7 and dependence in 2. The most often reported side-effects were headache, dizziness, dissociation, raised blood pressure and blurred vision; psychiatric and psychotomimetic effects and cardiovascular changes were described as short-lived. Withdrawals for side-effects were few and are given as counts of participants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary states that after acute dosing, psychiatric, psychotomimetic, cardiovascular, neurological and other side-effects were reported more frequently after ketamine than after placebo, and that the findings suggest a selective reporting bias (p. 1 of the online-first PDF). The comparison with placebo is asserted in one sentence of the Results without any counts (p. 6). The selective-reporting conclusion is supported by the review's own analysis of how harms were assessed. The Discussion and Conclusion then list urological, hepatic, cognitive and dependence harms reported with high-dose or repeated use in people with chronic pain and in people who use ketamine recreationally (pp. 9–11); these come from a narrative selection outside the systematic search and are cited for the risk of long-term use in depression, which the included studies did not measure. The authors state clearly that only single-dose acute effects could be judged (p. 8).

timeline.event: Berman et al.: the initial pilot placebo-controlled trial, as this review calls it, included here as one of the 20 randomized trials (listed with 7 patients given ketamine and short-term BPRS and VAS ratings).
This review: the authors describe it as the first systematic review of the safety of ketamine in depression after single and repeated doses.
Beck et al.: meta-analysis of BPRS and PANSS ratings after single doses in healthy volunteers (a different population; this round's first-pass card sc_beck_2020).
Dean et al.: Cochrane review of randomized trials of ketamine and other glutamate modulators in unipolar depression (this round's first-pass card sc_dean_2021).

Anand et al.: randomized trial of six ketamine infusions against ECT in 365 analysed patients, reporting moderate and severe adverse events by arm and rating dissociation on every treatment day (CADSS values in its supplement).

replication.where_it_stands: The review documents that the early ketamine-for-depression literature measured harms of repeated or long-term use poorly; it cannot give rates. Later randomized trials and reviews on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023; Anand et al., 2023) report adverse events more systematically, and the authors' group announced a Ketamine Side Effect Tool and a Ketamine Safety Screening Tool (p. 10 of the online-first PDF).

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: C K Loo declares fees for attending a Janssen Advisory Board meeting; all other authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests, p. 11 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the New South Wales Institute of Psychiatry, the School of Psychiatry of the University of New South Wales, the Black Dog Institute, St George and Wesley Hospitals (Sydney) and the University of Otago. Several included studies come from the senior author's group (for example Loo et al., 2016; Galvez et al., 2014; George et al.), and three authors were developing the Ketamine Side Effect Tool that the review recommends (Contributors, p. 11). Janssen was developing esketamine, the S-isomer whose large trials the review notes were under way (p. 11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of repeated ketamine dosing in depression with a structured, pre-specified harms protocol (active questioning at each dose and for months afterwards, including urinary symptoms, liver tests, cognitive testing against a control group and assessment of craving and dependence), reporting numbers of patients affected per arm, and an individual-participant meta-analysis of harms across existing trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, intervention and the harms of interest are described, but no comparator is specified, and the outcome criterion for inclusion is depression change rather than side-effects.
No protocol or registration is mentioned; the planned meta-analysis was abandoned after extraction.
Many types of study design were included because randomized trials are unlikely to detect rare serious or long-term adverse effects (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).

Four databases, the search terms printed, no language restriction, and a search ending about 7 months before online publication; but no trial registries, no stated reference-list or expert searching, and the 23 records from other sources are not described.
Two authors screened and assessed full texts, settling disputes by consensus and discrepancies with a senior author (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
Two authors collected and four extracted data (Contributors), but no duplicate extraction or consensus procedure is described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow diagram gives reasons for the 35 excluded full texts by category only; no list of excluded studies is given or referred to.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, number given ketamine, route, single or multiple dosing and side-effect measures, but not the population (diagnosis, age, setting), the dose or the comparator of each study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article says each study was appraised with a relevant checklist or tool given in the appendix, which was not read; no appraisal results appear in the text. The review separately applied the Cochrane Adverse Effects Methods Group checks (selective outcome reporting, withdrawals, presence of a control group).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
Meta-analysis planned and then judged inappropriate (p. 6 of the online-first PDF).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation rests on the weaknesses of the primary studies' harms assessment (no control group in most, passive monitoring, ad hoc reporting, short follow-up), and the authors limit their conclusions to single-dose acute effects.
Clinical and reporting diversity is described as the reason for not pooling, and route (intravenous against other) and design (randomized against other) are compared descriptively.
No quantitative synthesis; within-study selective reporting of harms is the review's subject.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Conflicts are declared (one author with Janssen advisory-board fees), but the review's funding source is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (no protocol, item 2; no list of excluded studies, item 7), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2 whatever the provisional item 9 turns out to be. For this review the rating says less than usual about usefulness: its question is how harms were measured, and its main finding (harms of repeated and long-term use were rarely assessed in depression studies up to 2016) follows directly from Table 1 and the counts in the Results, which a reader can check. It may be cited for the counts of studies assessing and reporting each category and time frame of side-effect, for the list of most commonly reported side-effects, for the withdrawal counts and for the scarcity of urinary, liver, cognitive and dependence assessment; it may not be cited for incidence of any side-effect, for a ketamine-placebo difference, for dose-dependence, or for the harms in other populations described in its Discussion, which must be cited to their primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Searches of MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Database for articles published 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, without language restriction, with depression change as a required primary outcome; the initial database search was run independently by three authors.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Study flow: 568 records from databases and 23 from other sources, 591 screened; 303 met exclusion criteria and 186 did not meet inclusion criteria; 103 records included; 95 full texts assessed and 35 excluded (26 non-original research, 5 other primary disorders, 1 animal, 1 paediatric, 1 concomitant ECT, 1 other NMDA antagonists); 60 studies included: 20 randomized trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case series or reports, 3 retrospective studies.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The 60 studies included 899 patients who received at least one dose of ketamine; by route, intravenous 49 articles and 737 patients, oral 6 and 72, intramuscular 3 and 7, subcutaneous 4 and 25, intranasal 2 and 18, sublingual 1 and 26, transmucosal 1 and 17 (total 902; the Table 2 footnote says 3 patients received more than one route); about 356 received multiple doses. The 20 randomized trials together included 430 participants given ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 1); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 6); Table 2 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The authors call the per-route numbers approximations, and Table 1 footnotes flag possible sample overlap between several studies, so 899 may count some patients twice.

key_findings.finding: Acute side-effects were assessed in 55 (92%) studies, cumulative side-effects in 24 (40%) and long-term side-effects (at least 2 weeks after the last dose) in 12 (20%); most study reports had no placebo or control group. In studies with a placebo or comparator, side-effects in all categories were said to be reported more commonly with ketamine, without numbers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 (p. 8); Figure 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Acute psychiatric side-effects were described in 23 (38%) studies and psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects in 43 (72%); score changes were generally self-limiting. The most common psychiatric side-effect was anxiety, followed by agitation or irritability, euphoria or mood elevation, delusions or unusual thoughts, panic and apathy; when delayed symptoms (anxiety, worsening depression or suicidality, hypomania) occurred, their link to ketamine was unclear.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Psychiatric reasons for withdrawal across all studies: worsening mood (12 participants), anxiety (6), suicidal ideation (5), panic attack (2), irritability (1); one suicide attempt was reported in one study; dissociation was the only psychotomimetic reason for withdrawal (2 participants); 5 patients were withdrawn for cardiovascular side-effects.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); 4th and 6th paragraphs (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Dissociation was the most commonly reported psychotomimetic side-effect, followed by perceptual disturbance, odd sensations, derealisation, hallucinations, feeling strange or unreal, and depersonalisation; no long-term psychotomimetic effects were reported, but most studies assessed them only within about 4 hours of the dose. Absence of psychosis or mania was reported in 5 (8%) studies and absence of psychotomimetic or dissociative effects in 5 (8%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (end, top of p. 7) and 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies giving ketamine intravenously tended to report more psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects: 72% of intravenous studies against 36% of non-intravenous studies.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The 72% cannot be reconciled with the other counts; see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: Acute cardiovascular changes were reported in 23 (38%) studies, most often raised blood pressure and heart rate, mostly during or immediately after intravenous dosing, generally resolving within 90 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Headache and dizziness were the most common neurological side-effects; cognitive side-effects (poor memory, poor concentration, confusion) were reported over the short term only, and potential cognitive side-effects were not assessed in most studies. Other side-effects were reported in 32 (53%) studies, most often blurred vision and nausea.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th to 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Urinary side-effects were assessed in only 5 studies; liver function tests were reported in 7 studies, 2 of which found abnormalities after dosing; only 2 studies asked about the development of ketamine dependence or abuse; structured scales for other side-effects (such as SAFTEE or PRISE) were used in 15 (25%) studies, and most relied on passive monitoring with little follow-up beyond the acute period.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 7, the 12th continued on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Side-effects were reported systematically (presence and absence) in 25 (42%) studies for psychiatric or psychotomimetic effects, 19 (32%) for cardiovascular, 14 (23%) for neurological or cognitive and 14 (23%) for other side-effects; in randomized trials the common acute side-effects were reported at rates similar to other designs, but long-term risks, cognition, urinary symptoms and dependence were rarely assessed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 13th paragraph; Figure 5 (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Figure 5 (p. 9; editors' reading, approximate): headache was reported in about 21 studies (11 randomized), dizziness about 20 (11), dissociation about 18 (8), raised blood pressure about 17 (9), urinary tract side-effects 5 (2) and dependency risk 2 (none randomized). Figure 5A plots dissociation at 28% of studies, which would be 17 of 60, not 18; see reporting issue 6.

key_findings.finding: The authors summarize ten main findings, including that acute side-effects are common after ketamine, that active assessment and reporting of side-effects in depression trials are inadequate, that most reported side-effects followed intravenous dosing and resolved shortly after the dose, and that conclusions could be drawn only for single-dose acute effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: A meta-analysis was planned but judged inappropriate after data extraction because of clinical diversity, different routes, doses and comparators, differing reporting methods and reporting bias; a qualitative review was done instead.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Analysis, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Conclusion states that acute side-effects of single doses in depression are common but generally transient, that high doses and repeated administration have been associated with urological, hepatic, craving or dependence and cognitive harms in people treated for chronic pain and in people who use ketamine recreationally, that these have not been adequately assessed in depression studies, and that the safety of long-term repeated dosing is uncertain.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: The flow cannot be fully audited, and 288 is used inconsistently: the summary says 288 articles were identified, 60 of which met the inclusion criteria, while the Discussion says 288 published reports were systematically reviewed although 60 studies were included; 288 does not appear in Figure 1 (568 database and 23 other records, 591 screened, 303 and 186 excluded, 103 records included, 95 full texts assessed). Editors' arithmetic: 591 minus 303 and 186 leaves 102, not 103; the step from 103 records to 95 full texts is unexplained; and 288 equals 591 minus 303.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of reports reviewed should be cited as 60 studies, not 288; the flow cannot be fully audited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 72% of intravenous studies against 36% of non-intravenous studies reporting psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects. Editors' calculation: with 49 intravenous and 11 non-intravenous studies (Table 2), 72% is not a whole-number fraction of 49 (35 of 49 is 71%, 36 of 49 is 73%); 36% fits 4 of 11, which would leave 39 of 49 intravenous studies (80%) to make up the 43 studies reporting such effects; 72% equals the overall proportion, 43 of 60. Counting only the 47 studies that used the intravenous route alone (Table 1), 72% fits 34 of 47, but 34 plus 4 of 11, plus at most the 2 mixed-route studies, gives no more than 40, not 43.
reporting_issues.consequence: The route comparison is probably misprinted, and the intravenous figure may be higher than stated; the direction (more reports with intravenous dosing) is unaffected, but the 72% should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary states that side-effects of every category were reported more frequently after ketamine than after placebo, but the only supporting text is one sentence in the Results without counts of studies, patients or comparisons.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for any ketamine-placebo difference in side-effects; primary trials or later meta-analyses must be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the number of patients who received ketamine as 7 for the first randomized trial (Berman et al.). Editors' cross-check against that paper (berman_2000, pp. 352–353): 8 people had the ketamine day, 7 of whom completed both days. Together with the sample overlaps flagged in the Table 1 footnotes, this suggests the per-study numbers are sometimes analysed rather than exposed patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the total of 899 patients is approximate in both directions.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Discussion, urothelial cell apoptosis is cited to reference 93 (Chu et al., 2008, BJU International, a report on lower urinary tract damage) although reference 95 (Baker et al., 2016) is the study of ketamine-induced apoptosis in urothelial cells; the same reference 93 is cited for prevalence figures from both Spain and Hong Kong (46% and 90%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation errors in the narrative part; the urinary-harm figures must be taken from the primary studies, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 5A plots dissociation at 28% of studies, level with raised blood pressure, whereas Figure 5B gives 18 studies for dissociation (30% of 60) and 17 for raised blood pressure (28%). Every other bar in 5A equals its 5B count divided by 60 (editors' measurement at 300 dpi).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the number of studies reporting dissociation is 17 or 18, and dissociation ranks third or ties with raised blood pressure; claims citing 18 should note the discrepancy.

design_detail: Phase 2, double-blind, doubly randomized, delayed-start, placebo-controlled trial (a variant of the sequential parallel comparison design) of intranasal esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine), panel A of a 2-panel study (named SYNAPSE in the registry record read by the first reader; the PDF does not name it), at 14 outpatient sites (13 in the USA, 1 in Belgium), 28 January 2014 to 25 September 2015, sponsored by Janssen Research & Development. 67 adults with DSM-IV-TR major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression (inadequate response to 2 or more antidepressants, at least 1 in the current episode) continued their oral antidepressant unchanged. Period 1 (days 1 to 8): randomized 3:1:1:1 to placebo spray (33) or esketamine 28 mg (11), 56 mg (11) or 84 mg (12) on days 1 and 4. Period 2 (days 8 to 15): the 28 placebo-treated participants with moderate or severe symptoms (QIDS-SR16 of 11 or more) were rerandomized 1:1:1:1 (placebo 6, 28 mg 8, 56 mg 9, 84 mg 5) for days 8 and 11; the others stayed on placebo. Then optional open-label esketamine (days 15 to 74, flexible 28 to 84 mg, twice weekly for 2 weeks, weekly for 3 weeks, then every 2 weeks) and 8 weeks of follow-up without esketamine. Primary end point: MADRS change from each period's baseline to its day 8 (ANCOVA), the two periods combined by a weighted test. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with treatment-resistant depression who continued an oral antidepressant, twice-weekly esketamine nasal spray at 28, 56 or 84 mg for 1 week lowered clinician-rated depression (MADRS) more than a bitter-tasting placebo spray, whether the difference rose with dose, and which adverse effects, blood-pressure rises and dissociative symptoms followed dosing over 2 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether improvement lasts or is maintained by less frequent dosing (the open-label and follow-up phases had no control group and were analysed in those still present, all on their oral antidepressant); the effect without the oral antidepressant or against racemic ketamine; whether blinding held (not assessed); effects in people with psychotic features, PTSD, OCD, a substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year, recent cannabis use or suicidal intent (excluded); or rare and long-term harms (56 people given esketamine double-blind for at most 2 weeks, 57 in the open-label phase).

sample.recruitment: Multiple outpatient referral centres (14 sites); 126 screened and 67 randomized, with 59 screen failures (Figure 1, p. E4: most often MDD judged invalid on the SAFER interview, 13, or withdrawal of consent, 10; a person could have several reasons); financial compensation was provided. How participants were found is not described in the main text (Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Methods › Population, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Medically stable adults aged 20 to 64 with DSM-IV-TR major depressive disorder; treatment-resistant depression defined as inadequate response to 2 or more antidepressants on the Massachusetts General Hospital Antidepressant Treatment Response Questionnaire, at least 1 in the current episode (a failure in a prior episode otherwise acceptable); IDS-C30 of 34 or more at screening and before the day-1 dose. Excluded: recent or current suicidal ideation with intent to act, suicidal behaviour, homicidal ideation or intent, bipolar and related disorders, intellectual disability, psychotic disorder, MDD with psychosis, PTSD, OCD, substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year and recent cannabis use; further criteria only in the eAppendix (not read) (Methods › Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: 38 women of 67; mean age 44.7 (SD 10.0). In the current episode 43 (64%) reported only 1 antidepressant failure (plus 1 in an earlier episode), 15 (22%) 2 and 9 (13%) 3 or more; 26 (39%) had used an atypical antipsychotic as add-on treatment before entry. Other characteristics, by arm, only in eTable 3 (not read); race and ethnicity not given in the main text (Abstract › Results; Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: 63 of 67 (94%) completed period 1 and 60 of 67 (90%) both double-blind periods; 57 entered the open-label phase, 51 (89%) of them the follow-up phase, and 41 (80% of those) completed the week-8 follow-up visit (Results › Participants, p. E3). Figure 1 (p. E4) gives withdrawals by arm: period 1, placebo 1 (other) and 28 mg 3 (1 adverse event, 1 lack of efficacy, 1 withdrawal by participant); period 2, rerandomized 56 mg 1 (adverse event) and continuing 84 mg 2 (1 adverse event, 1 withdrawal by participant); 3 declined the open-label phase, and 16 withdrew during it (1 adverse event, 3 lack of efficacy, 1 lost to follow-up, 5 withdrawal by participant, 6 other). The figure also shows a period-1 withdrawal beside the 84-mg arm and 60 entering follow-up, both in conflict with the text (see reporting issues). Adverse events led to stopping in 3 of 56 esketamine-treated participants in the double-blind phase, none on placebo, and 1 of 57 in the open-label phase (Results › Safety, 1st paragraph, p. E5).
sample.selection_effects: Sponsor-run outpatient sites with paid participation and strict exclusions (suicidal intent, PTSD, OCD, recent substance or cannabis use). The definition of treatment resistance is broad: 64% had failed only one antidepressant in the current episode. The period-2 sample is selected for non-response to placebo. Results apply to esketamine added to an ongoing oral antidepressant.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in disposable nasal spray devices of 200 μL (2 sprays): each 100-μL spray delivered esketamine hydrochloride 16.14 (unit not printed; 14 mg of esketamine base) or placebo (water for injection with the bittering agent denatonium benzoate to mimic the taste). On each double-blind dosing day participants self-administered study drug at 3 time points 5 minutes apart whatever their dose group; in the open-label phase at 1, 2 or 3 time points for 28, 56 or 84 mg (Methods › Study Drug and Administration). No blood levels are reported in this article.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: double-blind esketamine 28, 56 or 84 mg or placebo by nasal spray on days 1 and 4 (period 1) and days 8 and 11 (period 2); open-label 56 mg on day 15, then 28 to 84 mg at the investigator's judgment, twice weekly for 2 weeks, weekly for 3 weeks, then every 2 weeks to day 74 (7 participants enrolled under the original protocol received only 2 weeks of open-label drug). The oral antidepressant taken before entry continued unchanged throughout (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph; Study Drug and Administration; Table 2 footnote a).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance or alcohol use disorder in the past year and recent cannabis use excluded; how this was checked, and tobacco or alcohol use, are not reported in the main text (Methods › Population, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants continued their prescribed oral antidepressant; recent cannabis use was an exclusion.

comparison.controls: Placebo nasal spray (water with a bittering agent) in identical devices on the same schedule, alongside the same continued oral antidepressant. In period 2, placebo-treated participants with moderate or severe symptoms were rerandomized and the others continued placebo, all going through an identical process to keep the blind (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph; Study Drug and Administration, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Two computer-generated randomization schedules (period 1 and period 2), randomly permuted blocks, stratified by centre (Methods › Design, 3rd paragraph); how allocation was concealed is not described. Groups described as similar (eTable 3, not read); period-1 baseline MADRS 35.0 (SD 5.18) placebo, 31.3 (3.80) 28 mg, 33.2 (6.26) 56 mg, 35.0 (4.22) 84 mg (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; all continued their oral antidepressant.

outcomes.instruments: MADRS (clinician-rated depression, 0 to 60, with the SIGMA structured interview guide) on day 1 before and 2 hours after the dose and on days 2, 8 (before the dose), 9 and 15, and in the open-label and follow-up phases; Clinical Global Impression of Severity; GAD-7 (self-rated anxiety; results only in eTables 1 and 2, not read); QIDS-SR16 for rerandomization. Response: a MADRS fall of 50% or more; remission: MADRS of 10 or less. Safety: adverse events throughout; laboratory tests, vital signs and examination at set times; vital signs, the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS, dissociation) and the 4-item BPRS positive symptom subscale (psychotic-type symptoms) before the dose and 40 minutes and 2 hours after it (Methods › Efficacy Assessments; Safety Assessments; Table 2 footnote c). The 2-hour MADRS falls at the end of the acute effects, which the article says resolved by 2 hours; the primary end point (day 8) falls 4 days after the last double-blind dose of the period.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard scales; MADRS with a structured interview guide. Who the raters were, and whether they were kept apart from dosing sessions, is not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit = a larger least-squares mean fall in MADRS from the period baseline to day 8 than on placebo (ANCOVA: period 1 with treatment and country as factors and baseline MADRS as covariate; period 2 adding the QIDS-SR16 stratum), the periods combined by a weighted test; dose-response by the multiple comparison procedure–modelling method (Methods › Efficacy End Points and Analyses).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described for the three dose-against-placebo comparisons at each time point or for the secondary outcomes; the dose-response test used the multiple comparison procedure–modelling method. The sample size assumed an overall one-sided significance level of .05, and every printed P value matches a one-sided test (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, with a bittering agent added to placebo and an identical process before period 2 for everyone, rerandomized or not (Methods › Design and Study Drug and Administration). No check of what participants or raters guessed is reported; the authors list difficulty blinding esketamine despite the bittering agent as a limitation (Discussion › Limitations).

analysis.effect_sizes: Period 1, day 8 (least-squares mean change, SE): placebo −4.9 (1.74); esketamine 28 mg −9.8 (2.72), 56 mg −12.4 (2.66), 84 mg −15.3 (2.56); differences from placebo −5.0 (2.99), P = .05; −7.6 (2.91), P = .006; −10.5 (2.79), P < .001. Period 1 at 24 hours: differences −9.1 (3.08), −10.0 (3.00), −10.7 (2.88). Period 2, day 15: differences −3.1 (2.99), P = .15; −4.4 (3.06), P = .08; −6.9 (3.41), P = .03. Periods combined: −4.2 (2.09), 90% CI −7.67 to −0.79, P = .02; −6.3 (2.07), −9.71 to −2.88, P = .001; −9.0 (2.13), −12.53 to −5.52, P < .001; dose-response P < .001. Editors' calculation: 95% CIs −8.3 to −0.1, −10.4 to −2.2 and −13.2 to −4.8; the printed P values are one-sided, the two-sided equivalents being about .04, .002 and < .001. Period-1 response at day 8: placebo 2 of 33 (6%); 28 mg 1 of 11 (9%), 56 mg 2 of 11 (18%), 84 mg 5 of 12 (42%); remission 1 (3%), 1 (9%), 1 (9%), 3 (25%). No standardized effect sizes are reported.
analysis.covariates: Period 1: country and baseline MADRS; period 2: country, period-2 QIDS-SR16 stratum (moderate or severe) and period-2 baseline MADRS (Methods › Efficacy End Points and Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958 (SYNAPSE), first submitted 25 November 2013 and posted 3 December 2013, before the January 2014 start. Version 1 names as primary outcome the change from baseline to the 1-week end point in MADRS total score, over day 1 to day 8 and day 8 to day 15, which matches the article's primary end point; the headline combined weighted test is described in the article's sample-size section. Version 1 planned about 60 participants with an open-label phase to day 25 and no panels; later versions added panel B (esketamine 14 and 56 mg, with sites in Japan; registry enrolment 108) and extended the open-label phase to day 74. This article reports panel A only. The protocol (Supplement 2) and eAppendix were not read. Read from the registry record and its version 1, not from the article. Not re-checked against the registry in the round-2 PDF check or the card adjudication of 12 November 2026.
analysis.selective_reporting: Panel B of the registered study is not reported in this article. Demographics by arm, double-blind adverse-event counts (eTable 4), CGI-S and GAD-7 results, blood-pressure and CADSS time courses (eFigures 2 to 4) are only in Supplement 1, not read; the statements that dissociation, dizziness and headache were more than twice as frequent on esketamine depend on it. Figures 1 to 3 were read from the PDF for this card: Figure 1's withdrawals by arm are given under attrition, and Figure 3 prints the numbers assessed at each open-label and follow-up visit (key_findings[8] note). The handling of missing day-8 values is not described in the main text.
analysis.power: 60 randomized 3:1:1:1 gave 92.5% power for the combined day-8 and day-15 data, with an overall one-sided significance level of .05, SD 10 and 5% dropout, assuming differences of 9 points in period 1 and 7 or 9 points in period 2 (Methods › Sample Size Determination); 67 were randomized. The combined differences for 28 and 56 mg (−4.2 and −6.3) are smaller than the assumed effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After 1 week of twice-weekly sprays added to an oral antidepressant, MADRS fell more on each esketamine dose than on placebo in period 1 (by 9.8, 12.4 and 15.3 points against 4.9), with larger differences at 2 and 24 hours; in the small rerandomized period-2 groups only 84 mg differed significantly. Combined across periods the differences were 4.2, 6.3 and 9.0 points, with one-sided P values. On day 8 of period 1, 42% met response criteria on 84 mg against 6% on placebo, and fewer on 28 and 56 mg. In the uncontrolled open-label phase 22 of the 34 assessed at day 74 met response criteria, and at week 8 of follow-up 23 of the 41 assessed. Dizziness, headache and dissociation were more than twice as frequent on esketamine; blood pressure rose after dosing (maximum mean rise 19.0/10.3 mm Hg; highest values 199/115 mm Hg).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and abstract say improvement appeared to be sustained with less frequent dosing for up to 9 weeks and that response appeared to persist for more than 2 months (Key Points › Findings, p. E2; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance, p. E1); these rest on open-label and follow-up data without a control group, in those still present, all taking an oral antidepressant, so persistence cannot be attributed to esketamine. The Conclusions cite “evidence of robust and durable efficacy in the double-blind treatment phase” for the 56- and 84-mg doses, a phase that lasted 2 weeks (p. E8). The Discussion compares the 1-week difference with 6- to 8-week differences in antidepressant trials in the FDA database, a cross-trial comparison (1st paragraph, p. E5), and calls the doses apparently safe with no new or unexpected concerns from 56 people treated double-blind for at most 2 weeks (4th paragraph, p. E7). The abstract does not say that its P values are one-sided. The authors acknowledge the small sample, the exclusions and the difficulty of blinding (Discussion › Limitations, p. E8).

timeline.event: Zarate et al.: intravenous racemic ketamine 0.5 mg/kg against saline, crossover, 18 inpatients; Jaskaran B. Singh and Husseini K. Manji, authors here, were among its NIMH authors.
Murrough et al.: intravenous racemic ketamine against midazolam, 72 analysed; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours, no significant difference at day 7.

Singh et al.: double-blind, double-randomization trial of intravenous esketamine in treatment-resistant depression, with authors in common with this trial (Singh, Fedgchin, Daly, per the reference list); cited here for a rapid onset after intravenous esketamine (not read).
This trial, with a linked commentary in the same issue (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.3738, not read).
Popova et al. (TRANSFORM-2): phase 3 trial of flexibly dosed esketamine nasal spray with a newly started oral antidepressant, on the Tier A list; not readable in this round (publisher check page).

replication.where_it_stands: Replication status is not judged on this card. This was the first trial of the nasal spray; its rapid differences are in line with trials of intravenous racemic ketamine read in this round (Zarate et al., 2006; Murrough et al., 2013), but whether the phase 2 differences held in the phase 3 trials could not be checked: Popova et al. (2019) could not be read, and the critiques on the Tier A list (Turner, 2019; Schatzberg, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) were not read.

E8): Drs Daly, Singh, Fedgchin, Cooper, Lim, Van Nueten, Manji and Drevets are employees of Janssen Research & Development, LLC and hold company stock or stock options; Dr Manji holds a patent assigned to Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Yale University and the National Institutes of Health, from which no financial benefit was received; Drs Shelton, Thase and Winokur report no conflicts.

The investigators thanked by name received no financial compensation for the acknowledgment (Article notes › Author Contributions, Additional Contributions).

what_would_settle_it: A large, pre-registered trial run and analysed independently of the manufacturer, with a randomized controlled phase long enough to test whether benefit lasts (including a randomized withdrawal), an active placebo or at least a recorded check of what participants and raters guessed, two-sided analyses, follow-up of every randomized participant, and absolute response and remission rates per arm at fixed times.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedules with randomly permuted blocks stratified by centre, but allocation concealment is not described (protocol not read). Period-1 baseline MADRS ranged from 31.3 to 35.0 across arms, adjusted for in the ANCOVA; other baseline data are only in the supplement.
Double-blind dosing with the oral antidepressant unchanged; analysis sets include everyone dosed with a baseline and at least one later MADRS in each period.

Day-8 data were missing for few people in period 1 (63 of 67 completed), but how missing values entered the ANCOVA is not stated, the groups are small (11 or 12 per dose; 5 to 9 in period 2) so a few missing values matter, and dropouts by arm are only in an image. The open-label and follow-up results describe only those still present.

An inert placebo with a bittering agent cannot mimic esketamine's dose-related dissociation, dizziness and other acute effects; no check of blinding is reported, raters are not described as kept apart from dosing sessions, the outcome is an interview about subjective symptoms, and the authors themselves name the difficulty of blinding as a limitation.

Registered (NCT01998958, p. E1); by the first reader's reading of the registry, prospectively and with a primary end point matching the article (the registry was not re-checked on 12 November 2026). The headline is a combined weighted test of the two periods: the sample-size section shows it was planned (p. E3), but the Methods justify it by the consistency of the two periods' results (p. E3), which reads as a data-dependent choice. Panel B of the study is not reported here (p. E2), and the article does not say that its P values are one-sided.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized period-1 comparison of three doses against placebo, with a dose-ordered result and a primary end point that the first reader found prospectively registered, is reasonable evidence that esketamine nasal spray added to an oral antidepressant lowers MADRS scores over 1 week. The overall judgment is high because an inert placebo could not conceal esketamine's acute effects and blinding was not checked, so expectation may have enlarged the difference on a subjective outcome; the groups are small, the P values one-sided, and the sponsor took part in analysis and writing. The source can be cited for the size of the 1-week MADRS differences by dose, response and remission counts by arm in period 1, and the frequency of blood-pressure rises, dissociation and stopping for adverse events over 2 weeks; it cannot be cited for durable or maintained benefit, which rests on uncontrolled open-label and follow-up data, or for long-term safety.

key_findings.finding: 126 adults screened and 67 randomized in period 1: placebo 33, esketamine 28 mg 11, 56 mg 11, 84 mg 12. Of the 33 on placebo, 28 (85%) had a QIDS-SR16 of 11 or more at the end of period 1 and were rerandomized: placebo 6, 28 mg 8, 56 mg 9, 84 mg 5. 63 of 67 (94%) completed period 1 and 60 of 67 (90%) both double-blind periods; 57 entered the open-label phase, 51 (89%) the follow-up phase, 41 (80%) completed the week-8 follow-up visit.
key_findings.page: p. E1 (Abstract); p. E3 (Results › Participants); p. E6 (Table 1)
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Interventions; Results › Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1, No. rows

key_findings.finding: Sample: 38 women; mean age 44.7 (SD 10.0); 43 (64%) with only 1 antidepressant failure in the current episode (plus 1 earlier), 15 (22%) with 2 and 9 (13%) with 3 or more; 26 (39%) had used an atypical antipsychotic as add-on treatment.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary end point, period 1 (day 1 to day 8; least-squares mean change, SE): placebo −4.9 (1.74), esketamine 28 mg −9.8 (2.72), 56 mg −12.4 (2.66), 84 mg −15.3 (2.56); differences from placebo −5.0 (2.99), P = .05; −7.6 (2.91), P = .006; −10.5 (2.79), P < .001. Baseline MADRS 35.0 (SD 5.18), 31.3 (3.80), 33.2 (6.26) and 35.0 (4.22).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Change at study period end point; Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: P values are one-sided (editors' calculation; see reporting issues): two-sided about .10, .01 and < .001 with a t test on about 57 degrees of freedom (.09, .009 and < .001 with a normal approximation); the printed .006 fits a one-sided t test better than a z test.

key_findings.finding: Period 1, earlier time points: at 2 hours after the first dose, differences from placebo −6.7 (SE 3.03), P = .02 (28 mg); −4.6 (2.96), P = .06 (56 mg); −7.9 (2.84), P = .003 (84 mg); at 24 hours −9.1 (3.08), P = .002; −10.0 (3.00), P < .001; −10.7 (2.88), P < .001. Placebo changes −9.7 (1.76) at 2 hours and −5.7 (1.79) at 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Change at 2 h and Change at 24 h

key_findings.finding: Period 2 (rerandomized placebo non-responders, day 8 to day 15): differences from placebo −3.1 (SE 2.99), P = .15 (28 mg); −4.4 (3.06), P = .08 (56 mg); −6.9 (3.41), P = .03 (84 mg); at 24 hours −4.8 (4.18), −6.1 (4.29) and −7.5 (4.77), P = .13, .09 and .07. Baseline MADRS 29.3, 31.3, 34.9 and 30.4 (placebo, 28, 56, 84 mg); groups of 6, 8, 9 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 2; Table 1 footnote b

key_findings.finding: Periods combined (weighted test): differences from placebo −4.2 (SE 2.09), 90% CI −7.67 to −0.79, P = .02 (28 mg); −6.3 (2.07), −9.71 to −2.88, P = .001 (56 mg); −9.0 (2.13), −12.53 to −5.52, P < .001 (84 mg); ascending dose-response P < .001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Periods 1 and 2 Combined; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 95% CIs −8.3 to −0.1, −10.4 to −2.2 and −13.2 to −4.8; the printed P values match one-sided tests.

key_findings.finding: Response and remission in period 1 (placebo, 28, 56, 84 mg): at 2 hours, responders 6 (18%), 6 (55%), 4 (36%), 7 (58%); at 24 hours 1 (3%), 4 (36%), 3 (27.3%), 5 (42%); at day 8, 2 (6%), 1 (9%), 2 (18%), 5 (42%), with remitters (MADRS of 10 or less) 1 (3%), 1 (9%), 1 (9%), 3 (25%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Period 1, Responders and Remitters rows

key_findings.finding: Completers who had the same treatment in both double-blind periods, day 15: differences from placebo −6.0 (28 mg), −8.3 (56 mg) and −12.5 (84 mg); responders 3 of 8 (38%), 4 of 11 (36%) and 5 of 10 (50%) against 1 of 10 (10%) on placebo; remitters 1 of 8 (13%), 3 of 11 (27%) and 4 of 10 (40%) against 1 of 10 (10%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No SEs or tests are given for these completer comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Open-label phase (no control group): mean MADRS change from open-label baseline to day 74 −7.2 (SE 1.84). Response (50% or more below the period-1 baseline) at day 74 in 22 of the 34 assessed (65%) and at week 8 of follow-up, without esketamine, in 23 of the 41 assessed (56%); remission in 11 of 34 (32%) and 17 of 41 (42%) (by prior treatment sequence, placebo/placebo/open-label 6 of 6 and 5 of 7 responders; placebo/esketamine/open-label 5 of 10 and 3 of 12; esketamine/esketamine/open-label 11 of 18 and 15 of 22).
key_findings.page: p. E5 (text); p. E8 (Table 2); p. E7 (Figure 3)
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and footnote a; Figure 3, numbers of participants
key_findings.note: Denominators are those present at each visit, not the 57 who entered the open-label phase; all continued their oral antidepressant. Figure 3 (p. E7) prints the numbers assessed: 57 at open-label baseline, 34 at day 74, and 49, 46, 44 and 41 at follow-up weeks 1, 2, 4 and 8.

key_findings.finding: Stopping for adverse events: 3 of 56 (5%) esketamine-treated participants in the double-blind phase, none on placebo, and 1 of 57 (2%) in the open-label phase (one event each of syncope, headache, dissociative syndrome and ectopic pregnancy). In the double-blind phase dizziness, headache and dissociative symptoms were the most common treatment-emergent adverse events on esketamine, each more than twice as frequent as on placebo; dizziness and nausea showed a dose-response trend. No deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: Double-blind counts by arm are in eTable 4, which is not in the PDF. Figure 1 (p. E4) places the 3 double-blind withdrawals for adverse events in the 28-mg group (period 1), the rerandomized 56-mg group and the continuing 84-mg group (period 2). The article does not mention serious adverse events at all (neither a count nor a statement that none occurred); it reports only that no death occurred.

key_findings.finding: Open-label phase adverse events in more than 10% of 57: dizziness 22 (39%), dysgeusia 13 (23%), nausea 9 (16%), headache 8 (14%), sedation 6 (11%); 14 of 57 (25%) reported transient dissociative symptoms; most dosing-day events were transient and mild or moderate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure and heart rate on dosing days: most esketamine-treated participants had transient rises, maximum mean change systolic 19.0 mm Hg, diastolic 10.3 mm Hg and heart rate 9.4 beats/min; the highest values (systolic 199, diastolic 115 mm Hg) mostly at 10 or 40 minutes after the dose, usually back to the pre-dose value by 2 hours; no dose effect on heart rate, the largest mean rises in the 84-mg group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dissociative and perceptual symptoms (CADSS) began shortly after dosing, peaked at about 30 to 40 minutes, resolved by 2 hours and became weaker with repeated dosing in all dose groups; no participant had symptoms suggesting psychosis on the BPRS positive subscale. The Discussion adds that these symptoms were dose dependent while the antidepressant effect did not weaken with repeated doses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The time course is in eFigure 4, not read; the Methods list CADSS ratings only before the dose and at 40 minutes and 2 hours (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sample-size plan: 60 randomized (30 placebo, 10 per dose) for 92.5% power on the combined day-8 and day-15 data, with an overall one-sided significance level of .05, SD 10 and 5% dropout, assuming 9-point (period 1) and 7- or 9-point (period 2) differences and 40% moderate and 55% severe QIDS-SR16 scores among placebo-treated participants at the end of period 1.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sample Size Determination, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Registration: NCT01998958 first submitted 25 November 2013, posted 3 December 2013; version 1 primary outcome, change from baseline to the 1-week end point in MADRS total score (day 1 to day 8 and day 8 to day 15), with about 60 participants planned; the current record covers panels A and B (14, 28, 56 and 84 mg; sites in the USA, Belgium and Japan) with 108 enrolled.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958: Study Details (current record) and Record History, version 1 (2013-11-25)
key_findings.note: Read from the registry by the first reader, not from the article; the article prints only the registration number (p. E1) and states that it reports panel A of a 2-panel study (Methods › Design, 1st paragraph, p. E2). Not re-checked in the round-2 PDF check or the card adjudication of 12 November 2026, which did not see the registry record.

reporting_issues.issue: Every P value in Table 1 and the abstract corresponds to a one-sided test: for example the combined 28-mg difference −4.2 (SE 2.09) gives z = −2.01, one-sided P = .022 (printed .02) against two-sided P = .045, and the period-1 day-8 28-mg difference −5.0 (2.99) gives one-sided P = .047 (printed .05) against two-sided .094 with a normal approximation, or .050 against .100 with a t test on about 57 degrees of freedom (editors' calculation). The results never say the tests are one-sided; only the sample-size section mentions an overall one-sided significance level of .05, and the combined estimates carry 90% rather than 95% intervals.
reporting_issues.page: p. E6 (Table 1); p. E1 (Abstract › Results); p. E3 (Methods › Sample Size Determination, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers used to two-sided tests will overrate the evidence; claims should give the differences with the editors' 95% intervals (28 mg −8.3 to −0.1; 56 mg −10.4 to −2.2; 84 mg −13.2 to −4.8) rather than the printed P values.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the combined-period test statistics as −2.02, −3.04 and 4.24; the 84-mg statistic has the wrong sign for a difference of −9.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical sign slip.

reporting_issues.issue: In period 2 at 2 hours, the 56-mg difference from placebo is printed as −4 (SE 3.92), but the group's least-squares mean change (−11.7) minus the placebo change (−6.8) is −4.9, which with that SE matches the printed P = .11 (editors' calculation); every other difference in Table 1 equals its two changes within rounding.
reporting_issues.page: p. E6 (Table 1, Period 2, Change at 2 h)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed −4 is probably −4.9 truncated; use −4.9 with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is titled as response and remission for participants who completed the open-label and follow-up phases, but its group sizes (10, 20, 27; 57) are everyone who entered the open-label phase, while its percentages use those present at each visit (34 at day 74, 41 at week 8), so 6 of 6 is shown as 100% for a group of 10. Two percentages are rounded up: 10 of 22 printed 46% (45.5%) and 17 of 41 printed 42% (41.5%) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The open-label and follow-up rates are observed-case rates among those who stayed, and should not be read as rates among all who started open-label treatment.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods schedule vital signs, CADSS and BPRS ratings only before the dose and at 40 minutes and 2 hours after it, but the Results describe blood-pressure maxima at 10 or 40 minutes and dissociative symptoms that began shortly after dosing and peaked at about 30 to 40 minutes.
reporting_issues.page: p. E3 (Methods › Safety Assessments); p. E5 (Results › Safety, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs)
reporting_issues.consequence: The timing statements rest on measurement times not described in the article (perhaps in the protocol); the peak timing of dissociation and blood pressure should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The strength of the active spray is printed as esketamine hydrochloride 16.14 without a unit (14 mg of esketamine base per 100-μL spray), and the sentence giving 14 of 57 (25%) with transient dissociative symptoms follows the open-label results under the word overall, leaving unclear whether it covers the open-label phase or the whole study.
reporting_issues.page: p. E3 (Methods › Study Drug and Administration, 1st paragraph); p. E5 (Results › Safety, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 25% should be cited as an open-label figure only with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the two higher nasal doses give plasma esketamine levels in the range reached by an intravenous esketamine dose in earlier work, but no pharmacokinetic data are presented in this article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not evidence for blood levels or for any comparison between routes; it must not be used as such.

reporting_issues.issue: According to the registry record as read by the first reader, the registered study (SYNAPSE) had a second panel (esketamine 14 and 56 mg, with sites in Japan; registry enrolment 108 against 67 here) that this article does not report; the article itself states a 2-panel design and reports panel A (p. E2).
reporting_issues.page: registry record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01998958, as read by the first reader; not re-checked on 12 November 2026) and p. E2 (Methods › Design, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The article is not the full record of the registered study; panel B results would have to be sought in the registry.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 (disposition) conflicts with the text twice: it shows a period-1 withdrawal (other) beside the 84-mg arm while all 12 continue into period 2, which with the placebo (1) and 28-mg (3) withdrawals makes 5 period-1 withdrawals, against the text's 63 of 67 completing period 1 and period-2 boxes that sum to 63; and it prints 60 entering follow-up, against the text's 51 of 57 and the 49 assessed at follow-up week 1 (Figure 3).
reporting_issues.page: p. E4 (Figure 1); p. E3 (Results › Participants); p. E7 (Figure 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The text, the period-2 boxes and Figure 3 agree with each other; attrition should be cited from the text (63, 60, 57, 51 and 41), not from these two figure entries.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph cites Figure 1, the disposition chart, for efficacy being better sustained between doses with the 2 higher doses; the MADRS time course is in Figure 2, and no test is reported for this statement.
reporting_issues.page: p. E5 (Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph); p. E7 (Figure 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement rests on visual inspection of Figure 2; cite it only as the authors' description.
