design_detail: Two-site (Baylor College of Medicine, Houston; Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York), parallel-arm, double-blind randomized trial with an active placebo, November 2010 to August 2012. 73 medication-free adults with treatment-resistant major depression (inadequate response to at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials) were randomized 2:1 to one 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg or of midazolam 0.045 mg/kg, a short-acting benzodiazepine anaesthetic chosen to mimic ketamine's nonspecific sedation and disorientation; 72 were analysed (modified intention to treat: 47 ketamine, 25 midazolam). Inpatient on the infusion day with cardiovascular monitoring, discharged at 24 hours, then seen at 48 hours, 72 hours and 7 days; day-7 responders followed biweekly (the article's word; the relapse steps in Figure 3 at about days 3, 7, 10, 14 and 17 suggest twice-weekly visits, editors' inference) until relapse or for 4 more weeks. Primary outcome: MADRS at 24 hours, adjusted for baseline score and site. Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT00768430 (printed in the published article, p. 1141; the registry record was not read).
can_establish: Whether, in medication-free adults with highly treatment-resistant major depression, one 40-minute infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg lowered clinician-rated depression (MADRS) 24 hours later more than an infusion of midazolam chosen to mimic nonspecific anaesthetic effects, and which adverse effects, dissociative symptoms and blood-pressure changes followed the infusion over 7 days.
cannot_establish: Whether the benefit lasts beyond a few days (no significant group difference on MADRS or response at day 7), the effect of repeated infusions or of ketamine added to ongoing antidepressants (all medication was stopped), effects in people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or alcohol or substance abuse in the past 2 years (excluded), whether blinding held (not assessed), or rare and longer-term harms (47 people given one infusion and followed for at most about 5 weeks).

sample.recruitment: Two academic research sites; 116 patients completed informed consent and 73 met all eligibility criteria and were randomized. How patients were recruited (referral, advertisement) is not described in the main text (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 to 80; primary major depressive disorder by SCID-P; inadequate response to at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials on the Antidepressant Treatment History Form, completed by a study psychiatrist from the patient, family or carer, pharmacy and medical records; a previous episode before the current one, or a chronic current episode of at least 2 years, with an IDS-C30 score of 32 or more at screening and within 24 hours of the infusion (the sentence's grouping is ambiguous). Excluded: lifetime psychotic illness or bipolar disorder, alcohol or substance abuse in the previous 2 years, unstable medical illness, serious and imminent suicidal or homicidal risk, MMSE below 27, contraindicated medications. Physical examination, blood tests, urine toxicology and ECG at screening (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Ketamine (47) against midazolam (25): women 26 (55%) and 11 (44%); white 37 (79%) and 23 (92%); Hispanic 7 (15%) and 3 (12%); mean age 46.9 (SD 12.8) and 42.7 (11.6); education 16.5 (2.3) and 16.2 (2.3) years; previous antidepressant failures 5.1 (2.0) and 5.0 (1.8); index episode 146.6 (158.3) and 109.2 (139.0) months, chronic (2 years or more) in 33 (70%) and 16 (64%); prior suicide attempt 14 (30%) and 9 (36%); prior psychiatric hospitalization 23 (49%) and 13 (52%); unemployed 27 (57%) and 15 (60%); body mass index 29.4 (7.5) and 27.0 (6.1); baseline MADRS 32.6 (6.1) and 31.1 (5.6), QIDS-SR16 16.6 (4.1) and 16.3 (4.5), IDS-C30 48 (9) and 48 (10) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: One patient randomized to ketamine received no study medication; the other 72 received it and completed the 24-hour assessment; 67 completed all assessments to day 7. By protocol, non-responders (less than 50% MADRS improvement) were not followed after day 7; day-7 responders who chose to continue (21 ketamine, 4 midazolam) were followed for relapse (Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph; Method › Study Procedures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Durability of drug effect, 4th paragraph). The flow diagram is in the online supplement (Figure SF1, not read).
sample.selection_effects: Highly chronic (mean index episode 9 to 12 years) and resistant (about 5 failed trials) patients at academic research units, mostly white and with about 16 years of education, who could stop all psychotropic medication: 17.2% of screened patients refused or could not tolerate the washout (Discussion, 6th paragraph). People with any psychotic history or alcohol or substance abuse in the past 2 years were excluded. The results describe ketamine given alone, not added to an antidepressant.

exposure.measurement: Assigned infusion prepared from sealed envelopes held by the research pharmacist, given over 40 minutes after an overnight fast through an antecubital catheter, with pulse, blood pressure, pulse oximetry and ECG monitoring in a clinical research unit (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). No blood levels were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one intravenous infusion over 40 minutes of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg or midazolam 0.045 mg/kg; the authors describe the midazolam dose as equipotent to the ketamine dose and chose midazolam for its fast onset and short elimination half-life (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol or substance abuse in the previous 2 years excluded and urine toxicology done at screening; patients were told to abstain from substances and alcohol at home after discharge, without reported verification. Tobacco use not reported (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph; Study Procedures, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Free of antidepressants and other psychotropic medication for at least 1 week before the infusion (at least 4 weeks for fluoxetine) and throughout, except a stable dose of a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic; how this was verified is not stated (Method › Study Procedures, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: An infusion of midazolam as an active placebo: an anaesthetic benzodiazepine intended to mimic the time course of ketamine's nonspecific effects (sedation, disorientation) without specific antidepressant effects, given on the same schedule and with the same monitoring (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 2:1; the research pharmacist prepared sealed envelopes containing the drug identity, and investigators, anaesthesiologists, raters, patients and data analysts were masked. How the sequence was generated is not described (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph). The groups are described as well matched (Table 1), with some differences: women 55% against 44%, index episode 147 against 109 months, atypical features 9% against 24%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population and the same medication-free condition.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: clinician-administered MADRS (0 to 60) 24 hours after the infusion. Secondary: MADRS response (a fall of 50% or more from baseline); QIDS-SR16 (self-rated, 0 to 27); Clinical Global Impression severity and improvement; durability of benefit up to day 7 (MADRS and response at 1, 2, 3 and 7 days); time to relapse in day-7 responders (relapse: MADRS of 20 or more at two consecutive visits and meeting criteria for a major depressive episode for 1 week). Safety: a modified Patient Rated Inventory of Side Effects (general adverse events; sleep and sexual domains excluded) at 40, 120 and 240 minutes and 24 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours and 7 days; Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (dissociation) and BPRS positive symptom subscale (psychotic-type symptoms) at regular intervals; blood pressure at baseline, 40 and 240 minutes (Method › Outcomes; Table 3 footnotes; Table 4; Figure 3 legend). Symptom ratings were made during the infusion and to 240 minutes after its start; the primary outcome at 24 hours was chosen to fall after the acute psychoactive effects (Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Method › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-outcome raters were experienced, trained research staff, with MADRS conventions pilot-tested in earlier ketamine studies; interrater reliability between the two primary raters at each site 0.988 (Method › Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit = lower MADRS at 24 hours after ketamine than after midazolam in a general linear model adjusted for baseline MADRS and site, with Cohen's d; response by exact logistic regression adjusted for site; durability by mixed models of days 1 to 7 with treatment, time and their interaction. Dissociative symptoms are reported as significant in 8 patients without a stated threshold in the main text (Method › Statistical Analysis; Results › Adverse Events, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every test used P ≤ 0.05 (Method › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph). Six efficacy outcomes (MADRS, response, QIDS-SR16, CGI severity, CGI improvement, relapse), several of them at 24 hours, over days 1 to 7 and at day 7.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Investigators, anaesthesiologists, raters, patients and data analysts were masked; primary-outcome raters were not involved in infusion-day procedures and were unaware of infusion-related side effects (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Outcomes, 1st paragraph). No check of what patients or raters guessed is reported; the Discussion notes that dissociative effects right after the infusion were more frequent with ketamine (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: MADRS at 24 hours lower after ketamine by 7.95 points (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) after adjustment for baseline and site, Cohen's d 0.81; means 14.77 (95% CI 11.73 to 17.80) and 22.72 (18.85 to 26.59), t = 3.34, df = 68. Response at 24 hours 30 of 47 (64%) against 7 of 25 (28%), odds ratio 2.18 (1.21 to 4.14), P ≤ 0.006, number needed to treat 2.8. Editors' calculation from these counts: risk difference 35.8 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 54.2, Newcombe method); crude odds ratio 4.54 (1.58 to 13.05). QIDS-SR16 lower by 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01), d 0.63. CGI improvement rated much or very much improved 29 (62%) against 6 (24%), odds ratio 2.31 (1.25 to 4.66); CGI severity minimally or not ill 25 (53%) against 2 (8%), odds ratio 4.08 (1.76 to 13.51). Days 1 to 7: treatment F(1,202) = 5.93, P ≤ 0.02, time F = 7.62, treatment × time F = 0.31 (P ≤ 0.58); mean MADRS across the 4 days 16.93 (14.03 to 19.82) against 23.19 (19.03 to 27.34). Day 7: MADRS, QIDS-SR16, response and CGI improvement not significantly different; CGI severity of 2 or less, odds ratio 2.26 (1.07 to 5.76).
analysis.covariates: Baseline score and site for MADRS, QIDS-SR16 and CGI; site only for response; site in the days 1 to 7 mixed models (Method › Statistical Analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The published article prints ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00768430 (author footnotes, p. 1141); the NIH author manuscript (PMC3992936), from which the card was first written, omits it. The registry record was not read by the first reader, the round-2 checker or the card adjudicator, so the registration date, the registered primary outcome and its time point, and any deviations are not known; that the reported primary outcome (MADRS at 24 hours) was pre-specified cannot be confirmed from the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: The day-7 results (Table ST1), dissociative and psychotic-symptom scores (Table ST2, Figure SF2), serious adverse events (Table ST3) and the flow diagram (Figure SF1) are only in the online data supplement, which is not part of the article PDF and was not read; the day-7 null results and the statement that ketamine did not increase psychotic or manic symptoms depend on it. The durability and relapse results are shown mainly as Figures 1 to 3, with no numbers printed for response after day 1 or for relapse; values read from the plots are given with key_findings[6] and [8]. The midazolam group's rate of dissociative symptoms is not given in the main text. Sensitivity analyses for missing data are mentioned but not reported.
analysis.power: 72 patients (2:1) gave 80% power for a MADRS difference of Cohen's d 0.71 and 96% for response rates of 60% against 15% at 24 hours, two-tailed α 0.05 (Method › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph); 72 were analysed and the observed d was 0.81.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Twenty-four hours after one infusion, MADRS was about 8 points lower after ketamine than after midazolam (7.95, 95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) and 64% against 28% met response criteria (editors' risk difference 36 percentage points, 12 to 54); the self-rated QIDS-SR16 and both CGI measures agreed. Over days 1 to 7 the ketamine group stayed lower on average, but at day 7 the groups no longer differed significantly on MADRS, QIDS-SR16, response or CGI improvement, although Figure 2 shows day-7 response of about 46% against 18%. After ketamine, 17% had dissociative symptoms that resolved within 2 hours, blurred vision, dizziness and nausea were more common than after midazolam, systolic pressure rose from 121.7 to 140.7 mm Hg at 40 minutes, and 2 of 47 infusions were stopped for blood-pressure or heart-rate changes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract (p. 1134) concludes that ketamine showed rapid antidepressant effects in an optimized design and asks for more information on durability and safety, which matches the data; its odds ratio for response (2.18) is smaller than the odds ratio implied by its own percentages (editors' 4.5; see reporting issues). The Discussion goes further: “We consistently demonstrated the magnitude and duration of ketamine’s benefit” across two sites (2nd paragraph, p. 1138), although no group difference remained at day 7, and in the same sentence describes the patients as diverse in ethnicity and race, although 79% of the ketamine group and 92% of the midazolam group were white (Table 1, p. 1136); it suggests that the infusion is safe in the short term for nonpsychotic depressed patients on the basis of 47 people, 2 of whose infusions were stopped (3rd paragraph, pp. 1138-1140); and the conclusion presents the active placebo as showing an effect specific to ketamine apart from its anaesthetic properties (7th paragraph, p. 1140), although blinding was not checked and dissociation was more frequent after ketamine. The authors acknowledge that no control condition is perfect, that only one infusion and a brief follow-up were tested, and that ketamine added to ongoing treatment was not studied (Discussion, 4th and 6th paragraphs, p. 1140). The journal's Clinical Guidance box on the article (p. 1142) is more cautious than the Discussion: it reports that depression scores did not differ between groups 7 days after the infusion, mentions the 17% with dissociative symptoms and the two stopped infusions, and relays the view of an accompanying editorial by Rush (p. 1079, not in the PDF) that ketamine is not ready for clinical use.

timeline.event: Zarate et al.: NIMH crossover trial, 18 inpatients, the same ketamine dose against saline; HDRS lower from 110 minutes to day 7, day-1 response 12 of 17 against 0 of 14. Dennis S. Charney is an author of both trials.
This trial: 72 analysed at two sites against midazolam; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours, response 64% against 28%, no significant difference at day 7.

Daly et al.: esketamine nasal spray added to oral antidepressants, 67 randomized; in period 1, MADRS 9.1 to 10.7 points lower than placebo at 24 hours and 5.0 to 10.5 points lower at day 8 (a different drug form, route and design).

replication.where_it_stands: The 24-hour effect is consistent with the earlier saline-controlled crossover trial (Zarate et al., 2006), which shares one author with this trial, and with the 24-hour results of a later trial of esketamine nasal spray (Daly et al., 2018), which used a different drug form, route and design. The two trials of intravenous ketamine disagree on day 7 (significant against saline, not against midazolam). No later trial of intravenous ketamine against midazolam was read in this round; the systematic reviews on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023) are being read by other readers.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, multi-site trial against an active placebo in which patients and raters record which treatment they think was given, every participant (not only responders) is followed for at least 4 weeks with repeated or single infusions as randomized, ketamine is also tested alongside usual antidepressant treatment, and absolute response and relapse rates are reported per arm at fixed times.

domains.note: Randomized 2:1 with sealed envelopes prepared by the research pharmacist and everyone else masked, but how the sequence was generated is not described. Baseline characteristics are broadly balanced, with modest differences in sex (55% against 44% women), index-episode length and atypical features.

A single masked infusion; one patient randomized to ketamine was not treated and is excluded from the modified intention-to-treat set (1 of 73). Two ketamine infusions stopped early for haemodynamic changes are not described as excluded.

Primary outcome available for 72 of 73 randomized. Later outcomes are less complete (67 at day 7) and relapse was followed in responders only, by design, so relapse data describe only those who responded.

The primary-outcome raters were kept apart from infusion-day procedures and side effects, and midazolam gives some sedation; but patients, whose answers make up the MADRS interview and the QIDS-SR16, could recognise ketamine's dissociative effects (17% had significant dissociative symptoms), and no check of blinding is reported.

The primary outcome and its 24-hour time point are justified in the article, and the analyses are described. The published article prints a registration, NCT00768430 (p. 1141), but the registry record (registration date, registered primary outcome and time point) was not read in this round, so pre-specification cannot be confirmed from the article; the judgment stays at some concerns until it is read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This trial addresses the main weakness of the earlier saline-controlled studies with an active placebo, raters shielded from infusion-day effects, two sites and almost complete 24-hour data. The remaining concerns are that blinding was not checked for a drug whose acute effects patients notice, that the registry record behind the printed registration (NCT00768430) has not been read to confirm the pre-specified outcome, and that sequence generation is not described. The source can be cited for a 24-hour difference of about 8 MADRS points and response in 64% against 28% after one infusion in medication-free adults with highly treatment-resistant depression, and for the transient dissociation, adverse effects and blood-pressure rise that followed; it cannot be cited for benefit lasting a week or more, for ketamine added to other treatment, or for safety beyond the first week.

key_findings.finding: 116 patients consented; 73 were randomized 2:1; one patient randomized to ketamine did not receive study medication; 72 received it and completed the 24-hour assessments (47 ketamine, 25 midazolam); 67 completed all assessments to day 7.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1 column headings

key_findings.finding: Baseline (ketamine against midazolam): women 55% and 44%; mean age 46.9 and 42.7; previous antidepressant failures 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 5.0 (1.8); index episode 146.6 and 109.2 months; prior suicide attempt 30% and 36%; MADRS 32.6 (6.1) and 31.1 (5.6); QIDS-SR16 16.6 (4.1) and 16.3 (4.5).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Study Participants, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: 24 hours after the infusion, MADRS was lower in the ketamine group by 7.95 points (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) after adjustment for baseline score and site, Cohen's d 0.81; mean MADRS 14.77 (95% CI 11.73 to 17.80) against 22.72 (18.85 to 26.59), t = 3.34, df = 68; 24-hour scores did not differ by site (F = 0.63, df = 1, 70, P = 0.43).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome; Table 2, MADRS row and footnote b

key_findings.finding: Response (a MADRS fall of 50% or more) at 24 hours: 30 of 47 (64%) after ketamine against 7 of 25 (28%) after midazolam; odds ratio 2.18 (95% CI 1.21 to 4.14), P ≤ 0.006; number needed to treat 2.8; responder status did not differ by site (exact P = 0.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Table 2, Response row
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: risk difference 35.8 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 54.2, Newcombe method); crude odds ratio 4.54 (1.58 to 13.05). The printed odds ratio is about the square root of the crude one (see reporting issues); cite the counts and percentages.

key_findings.finding: Other 24-hour outcomes: QIDS-SR16 mean 8.38 (95% CI 6.71 to 10.05) against 11.78 (9.63 to 13.92), adjusted difference 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01), P ≤ 0.02, d 0.63; CGI improvement much or very much improved 29 (62%) against 6 (24%), odds ratio 2.31 (1.25 to 4.66); CGI severity minimally or not at all ill 25 (53%) against 2 (8%), odds ratio 4.08 (1.76 to 13.51).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Table 2
key_findings.note: The text calls this CGI category improved or much improved (pp. 1136-1137), while Table 2 defines it as a rating of 2 (much improved) or 1 (very much improved); the finding follows the Table.

key_findings.finding: Days 1, 2, 3 and 7 (mixed model adjusted for site): main effects of time (F = 7.62, df = 1, 202, P ≤ 0.006) and treatment (F = 5.93, df = 1, 202, P ≤ 0.02) but no treatment × time interaction (F = 0.31, P ≤ 0.58); both groups worsened slightly with each day; averaged over the 4 days, MADRS 16.93 (95% CI 14.03 to 19.82) after ketamine against 23.19 (19.03 to 27.34) after midazolam (t = 2.44, df = 202, P ≤ 0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 1st paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Response over days 1 to 7: main effects of time (F = 8.04, P ≤ 0.006) and treatment (F = 6.61, P ≤ 0.02), no treatment × time interaction (F = 0.12, P ≤ 0.73).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 2 (p. 1138; bar heights measured on the rendered page): response about 64%, 61%, 60% and 46% after ketamine and 28%, 23%, 22% and 18% after midazolam on days 1, 2, 3 and 7; only the day-1 rates are printed as numbers (Table 2).

key_findings.finding: Day 7, adjusted for site and baseline: MADRS and QIDS-SR16 no longer differed significantly between groups, nor did the response rate or the proportion much or very much improved on the CGI; CGI severity of 2 or less was more likely after ketamine (odds ratio 2.26, 95% CI 1.07 to 5.76).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The day-7 estimates are in supplement Table ST1, which is not in the PDF; Figure 2 (p. 1138) shows day-7 response of about 46% after ketamine against 18% after midazolam (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: At day 7, 4 patients in the midazolam group and 21 in the ketamine group still met response criteria and chose to continue; their time to relapse over the next 4 weeks is shown only in Figure 3 (relapse: MADRS of 20 or more at two consecutive visits and a major depressive episode for 1 week).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 4th paragraph; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 3 (p. 1138; step heights measured on the rendered page): among the 21 ketamine day-7 responders the proportion without relapse falls to about 0.79 at day 3, 0.74 at day 7, 0.68 at day 10, 0.63 at day 14 and 0.42 at day 17 of the figure's time axis (the 4 weeks after day 7), then stays level to about day 28; among the 4 midazolam responders it falls to 0.5 at day 7 and 0 at day 17. No numbers are printed for this analysis.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events on the infusion day (new or worse, ketamine against midazolam): dizziness 21 (45%) and 5 (20%); blurred vision 20 (43%) and 2 (8%); nausea or vomiting 16 (34%) and 3 (12%); headache 15 (32%) and 5 (20%); dry mouth 12 (26%) and 4 (16%); poor coordination 12 (26%) and 3 (12%); poor concentration 12 (26%) and 2 (8%), rated distressing by 9 (19%) and 0; tremors 6 (13%) and 0; anxiety 7 (15%) and 0; restlessness 10 (21%) and 5 (20%); general malaise 3 (6%) and 7 (28%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Infusion Day columns; Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Modified Patient Rated Inventory of Side Effects at 40, 120 and 240 minutes after the infusion (Table 3 footnotes).

key_findings.finding: Adverse events on days 1 to 7 (new or worse, ketamine against midazolam): restlessness 19 (printed 41%) and 7 (28%); anxiety 14 (30%) and 7 (28%); headache 15 (32%) and 7 (28%); poor concentration 12 (26%) and 3 (12%); dry skin 12 (26%) and 5 (20%); frequent urination 4 (9%) and 0; painful urination 3 (6%) and 0; difficulty urinating 1 (2%) and 0.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Days 1–7 After Infusion columns
key_findings.note: Measured at 24, 48 and 72 hours and 7 days. Editors' calculation: 19 of 47 is 40.4%.

key_findings.finding: Eight of 47 patients given ketamine (17%) had significant dissociative symptoms (feeling outside the body, time passing more slowly or quickly) immediately after the infusion, resolved by 2 hours; no severe psychotic symptoms (paranoia, hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder) occurred in any patient.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The threshold for significant dissociation is not stated in the main text; the CADSS and BPRS data are in supplement Table ST2 and Figure SF2, not read.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure (mean, SD): ketamine systolic 121.7 (13.8) at baseline, 140.7 (17.8) at 40 minutes and 125.4 (17.6) at 240 minutes, diastolic 71.7 (11.3), 80.8 (12.7) and 70.6 (8.9); midazolam systolic 120.8 (17.5), 111.8 (14.8) and 113.9 (13.0), diastolic 72.4 (9.6), 67.9 (9.9) and 71.6 (7.7). Two ketamine infusions were stopped: one after 30 minutes for a rise to 187/91 mm Hg not responding to a beta-blocker (normal within 10 minutes of stopping), and one for transient, pronounced hypotension and bradycardia that resolved, followed by overnight hospital observation.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Adverse Events, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Right after these two events the text refers to supplement Table ST3 (not in the PDF) for a description of the serious adverse events; the article itself does not say how many serious adverse events occurred in each group.

key_findings.finding: Power: 72 patients randomized 2:1 gave 80% power for a MADRS difference of d 0.71 and 96% for response rates of 60% against 15% at 24 hours (two-tailed α 0.05); analysis by modified intention to treat (randomized, baseline and at least one later measurement).
key_findings.locator: Method › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 17.2% of screened patients refused or could not tolerate the psychotropic medication washout before randomization.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The printed odds ratio for response (2.18, 95% CI 1.21 to 4.14; exact logistic regression adjusted for site) does not match the counts: 30 of 47 against 7 of 25 give a crude odds ratio of 4.54 (Woolf 95% CI 1.58 to 13.05), whose square root (2.13, 1.26 to 3.61) is close to the printed value (editors' calculation). Coding treatment as −1 and +1 in a logistic model halves the log odds ratio and would produce this pattern, but the article does not state its coding (editors' inference). The Fisher exact P from the counts (0.006) matches the printed P ≤ 0.006. The CGI odds ratios come from ordinal logistic regression adjusted for baseline and site, so crude 2 × 2 odds ratios are only a rough check there: CGI improvement printed 2.31 against a crude 5.10 (square root 2.26); CGI severity printed 4.08 against a crude 13.07 (square root 3.61).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1136 (Additional 24-hour outcomes; Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs); p. 1137 (Table 2; CGI odds ratios)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed response odds ratio is about half the crude two-group odds ratio on the log scale, whatever the cause, and the CGI odds ratios may share the problem; claims should use the counts, the percentages (64% against 28%) and the risk difference (36 percentage points).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 footnote c gives the QIDS-SR16 test as t = 6.69, df = 68, P ≤ 0.01, while the text gives an adjusted difference of 3.40 (95% CI 0.78 to 6.01), P ≤ 0.02. The interval implies t of about 2.59 and P of about 0.012, and 2.59 squared is 6.7 (editors' calculation), so the printed statistic is probably an F value labelled t. Footnote b gives P ≤ 0.001 for the primary MADRS test (t = 3.34, df = 68), which corresponds to P = 0.0014; the Figure 1 legend gives P ≤ 0.002.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1137 (Table 2 footnotes b and c; Figure 1 legend); p. 1136 (Additional 24-hour outcomes)
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling and rounding errors; the text's P ≤ 0.02 for the QIDS-SR16 and the legend's P ≤ 0.002 for the MADRS are the values consistent with the intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the response rate no longer differed significantly at day 7 (analyses adjusted for site and baseline), yet 21 patients given ketamine and 4 given midazolam still met response criteria at day 7, and Figure 2 shows day-7 response of about 46% after ketamine and 18% after midazolam; the bar heights fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22 (read from the figure; the text gives 67 as completing all assessments through day 7). With those counts Fisher's exact test gives P = 0.03, and with all randomized as denominators (21 of 47 against 4 of 25) P = 0.02 (editors' calculation). The day-7 response figures are only in supplement Table ST1, which is not in the PDF.

design_detail: Single-site, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-period crossover trial at the NIMH Clinical Research Center, Bethesda, November 2004 to September 2005. 18 inpatients with DSM-IV recurrent major depressive disorder without psychotic features and at least 2 failed adequate antidepressant trials were randomized; after a 2-week drug-free period each was to receive one intravenous infusion of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg and one of saline, 1 week apart, in random order (random-numbers chart), each over 40 minutes by an anaesthesiologist from identical 50-mL syringes. Ratings 60 minutes before and at 40, 80, 110 and 230 minutes and 1, 2, 3 and 7 days after each infusion; primary outcome the 21-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) over these 9 time points (linear mixed model, completer, intent-to-treat and first-period-only analyses). Planned for 22, stopped at 18 after an interim analysis. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00088699 (an umbrella NIMH protocol).
can_establish: Whether, in 18 medication-free inpatients with treatment-resistant recurrent unipolar major depression, one 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg lowered clinician-rated (HDRS) and self-rated (BDI) depression compared with a saline infusion from the first hours to 7 days afterwards, and which short-lived psychotic-type, manic-type and perceptual effects were recorded during the first hours after it.
cannot_establish: Whether the effect is specific rather than driven by unblinding and expectation (saline has none of ketamine's perceptual effects and blinding was not checked); its size free of carryover and early stopping; effects beyond 7 days, after repeated infusions, alongside ongoing antidepressants, or in people with bipolar disorder, psychotic features, recent substance use disorder or a shorter illness; blood levels (not measured); and harms rarer than 17 people treated once can show.

sample.recruitment: Referrals from local inpatient psychiatric units, newspaper advertisements in the Washington, DC, area, the Internet, and local and national physician referrals; all studied as inpatients at the NIMH Clinical Research Center. 42 screened; 24 excluded: 11 did not meet the criteria (4 low severity, 2 fewer than 2 failed antidepressant trials, 5 unstable medical illness) and 13 refused (Methods › Patient selection, 1st paragraph, p. 857; Results › Patients, 1st paragraph, and Figure 1, p. 858).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 to 65; inpatients with DSM-IV major depressive disorder, recurrent, without psychotic features (SCID-P); HDRS-21 of 18 or more at screening and at the start of each infusion day; failure of at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials (Antidepressant Treatment History Form). Good physical health on history, examination, blood tests, ECG, chest radiograph, urinalysis and toxicology; no comorbid substance abuse or dependence for at least 3 months and a negative urine toxicology screen; not judged a serious suicide risk; comorbid anxiety disorders allowed if not needing current treatment. Excluded: bipolar disorder or a history of antidepressant- or substance-induced hypomania or mania. Final selection by consensus of the investigator team (Methods › Patient selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: 12 women and 6 men; mean age 46.7 (SD 11.2); length of illness 23.7 (12.5) years; current episode 33.6 (37.4) months; 6.6 (4.7) previous episodes; 5.7 (3.4) lifetime antidepressant trials; 4 had had ECT; 61% a lifetime comorbid anxiety diagnosis, 39% a lifetime diagnosis of any substance abuse or dependence (7 of 18), 28% of alcohol abuse or dependence (5 of 18); all but one had failed an adequate trial in the current episode. Race and ethnicity not reported (Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph; Table, bottom row).
sample.attrition: Of 18 randomized (9 to each order), 17 received ketamine and 14 saline. Saline first: 1 of 9 discontinued on day 2 of the saline phase because of medical illness and never received ketamine; 8 completed both infusions. Ketamine first: 4 of 9 were not crossed over to saline because they maintained a response for 7 days (Results) or because of improved mood (Figure 1), although one of them (Table row 13) had a day-1 HDRS change of −39%, short of the response criterion; 5 completed both. So 13 received both infusions, as Figure 1 gives and the Table's NA cells confirm; the figure's phase-2 box for the ketamine-first arm prints 8 saline infusions, which conflicts with these counts (Results › Patients, 1st paragraph, and Figure 1, p. 858; Table, pp. 859-860).
sample.selection_effects: A small, chronically and severely ill inpatient sample at a national research unit, willing to stop all psychotropic medication for 2 weeks and to be infused, selected by investigator consensus; 13 of 42 screened refused. Two-thirds were women. The authors note that this refractory, late-course group may not respond like people with less severe or shorter illness (Comment, 5th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Assigned infusion: ketamine hydrochloride (Abbott Laboratories) or 0.9% saline, in identical 50-mL syringes, given over 40 minutes by infusion pump by an anaesthesiologist in the perianesthesia care unit (Methods › Study design). No blood levels of ketamine or its metabolites were collected (Comment, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes, once, and saline once, 1 week apart, after a 2-week drug-free period (Methods › Study design). The authors state that the dose was chosen from in vitro NMDA-blockade data, mood effects in healthy volunteers and an earlier pilot study (Comment, 7th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: No comorbid substance abuse or dependence for at least 3 months and a negative urine toxicology screen at entry; 7 of 18 had a lifetime diagnosis of substance abuse or dependence and 5 of alcohol abuse or dependence (Table). Tobacco and current alcohol use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: A 2-week drug-free period before the first infusion, as inpatients; how freedom from psychotropic drugs was verified beyond the screening toxicology is not stated (Abstract › Interventions; Methods › Study design).

comparison.controls: The same participants' saline infusion, an inert placebo with none of ketamine's acute perceptual effects, given 1 week before or after the ketamine infusion.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover; order assigned with a random-numbers chart. Who generated and held the sequence, and how allocation was concealed, is not described (Methods › Study design). Baseline HDRS before the first infusion was similar by order: 24.4 (SD 6.9) for those given saline first and 24.9 (6.9) for those given ketamine first (Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized within-person comparison; but the second-period baseline is not equivalent: in those given ketamine first, HDRS before the saline infusion was 17.2 (SD 6.9) against 24.9 before ketamine (carryover; Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: 21-item HDRS (clinician-rated depression). Secondary: Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, self-rated depression), Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale positive symptoms subscale (BPRS, clinician-rated psychotic-type symptoms), Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS, clinician-rated manic symptoms) and visual analogue scales (self-rated, including depression); single HDRS items as a secondary analysis; adverse effects (how recorded is not described). All rated 60 minutes before and at 40, 80, 110 and 230 minutes and 1, 2, 3 and 7 days after each infusion, so the 40- to 230-minute ratings fall in the hours of acute drug effects and the day 1 to 7 ratings after them (Methods › Outcome measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Raters (research nurses, a physician and a psychologist) trained together; intraclass correlation 0.81 for the HDRS and 0.91 for the YMRS. Response: a decrease of 50% or more in HDRS from baseline; remission: HDRS of 7 or less (Methods › Outcome measures).
outcomes.operationalization: Antidepressant effect = lower HDRS after ketamine than after saline in a linear mixed model of drug and time over the 9 time points, with simple-effects tests at each time point and Cohen's d at chosen points; response and remission compared at each time point by McNemar tests in completers. Psychotic-type and manic-type effects = BPRS positive and YMRS scores; perceptual effects from the HDRS depersonalization/derealization item and the adverse-effect list (Methods › Statistical analyses).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Seven outcome measures (HDRS, BDI, BPRS positive, YMRS, visual analogue scales, response, remission), each at up to 9 time points, plus 20 single HDRS items. Bonferroni correction was applied only to the McNemar tests of responders and remitters across time points; none for the simple-effects tests at each time point or for the item analysis (Methods › Statistical analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind, with identical syringes; how raters were kept unaware is not described, and no check of whether patients or raters guessed the infusion is reported. The authors state that the short-lived perceptual disturbances could have affected the blind and biased patient reporting (Comment, 6th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Completers (13: 8 given saline first and 5 given ketamine first, Figure 1): drug F(1,203) = 58.24, time F(8,203) = 9.48, drug × time F(8,203) = 4.15, all P < .001; ketamine better than saline from 110 minutes through 7 days; Cohen's d 1.46 (95% CI 0.91 to 2.01) at 24 hours and 0.68 (0.13 to 1.23) at 1 week. Intent-to-treat (18): drug F(1,260) = 34.08, time F(8,257) = 8.92, drug × time F(8,257) = 5.29, all P < .001. First period only (between-subjects, 18): drug F(1,16) = 10.44, P = .005; ketamine lower from 80 minutes through day 7. BDI (completers): drug F(1,200) = 50.57, P < .001, drug × time P = .06. Day-1 response 12 of 17 (71%) after ketamine against 0 of 14 after saline; remission 5 of 17 (29%) against 0; 6 of 17 (35%) kept a response for at least a week. Per-patient day-1 HDRS change: mean −56.2% (SD 20.4) after ketamine and −9.8% (20.1) after saline. Editors' calculation from the Table: in the 13 who had both infusions, −53.4% after ketamine and −11.2% after saline.
analysis.covariates: None; within-person comparisons. Carryover was tested on the baseline scores (drug × order interaction), and a first-period-only analysis was added to address it (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00088699 (printed in the abstract), first submitted 30 July 2004, before enrolment began in November 2004. It is an umbrella NIMH protocol (04-M-0222) with several substudies, 67 enrolled up to 2017. The earliest archived version (23 June 2005) lists no primary outcome measure; reduction from baseline of the HDRS between groups was entered on 19 June 2006 (version 2), after the trial had ended and the article had been accepted; the current record names the MADRS at baseline and day 1. The registry's entry criterion is a MADRS of at least 22 at screening and before phase I, against the article's HDRS of 18 or more. Read from the registry record and its history (versions 1 and 2), not from the article. Not re-checked against the registry in the round-2 PDF check or the card adjudication of 12 November 2026.
analysis.selective_reporting: The trial stopped at 18 of a planned 22 after an interim analysis, with no stopping rule or pre-specification described (Methods › Patient selection, 4th paragraph). Adverse effects are listed without counts or denominators. Visual analogue scale results are given for depression only. Response and remission at time points other than days 1 and 7 appear only in Figure 3 (p. 861), read from the bars for this card; the text reports saline-period response for days 1 and 7 only.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation is reported; 22 were planned. With 13 completers the interval for the day-7 effect is wide (d 0.13 to 1.23).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 medication-free inpatients (13 with both infusions), HDRS scores were lower after one ketamine infusion than after saline from 110 minutes to day 7 in the completer analysis, with a standardized difference of 1.46 at 24 hours and 0.68 at day 7; self-rated BDI agreed. On day 1, 12 of 17 met response criteria and 5 of 17 remission criteria after ketamine, against none of 14 after saline; 6 of 17 kept a response for at least a week. Only the day-1 responder difference survived Bonferroni correction, and remission did not differ significantly at any point. Ketamine first lowered the baseline before the saline period (carryover). BPRS positive and YMRS scores rose at 40 minutes only, and depersonalization or derealization was worse from 40 to 110 minutes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract (p. 856) concludes that “robust and rapid antidepressant effects” followed a single dose, with onset within 2 hours and significance for 1 week, without saying that the placebo was saline, that 13 people provided the completer estimates, that remission never differed significantly, or that the trial stopped early. The Comment says no other drug or somatic treatment has been reported to give such a dramatic, rapid and prolonged response, and sets day-1 response here beside week-8 response rates of other antidepressants in other trials (Comment, 1st paragraph, p. 861). The same paragraph calls the self-rated BDI difference statistically significant from 40 minutes through 7 days, where the Results say only that ketamine seemed to improve self-ratings, with a trend-level drug × time interaction (P = .06; p. 860). The Comment also says the improvement is disconnected from euphoria and psychotomimetic symptoms, although a trend linked larger BPRS rises to larger HDRS improvement (r = −0.46, P = .06), and that onset and course were nearly identical for each subject, although the Table shows day-1 changes from −17% to −90% (Comment, 7th paragraph, p. 862; Table, pp. 859-860). The authors do state that limited blinding may have biased patient reporting and that the results may not generalize (Comment, 5th and 6th paragraphs, p. 862).

timeline.event: Berman et al.: placebo-controlled study in 8 people with major depression, as described in this article: a rapid, short-lived effect, with 4 of 8 reaching a 50% or greater HDRS decrease over 3 days of follow-up (not read).
This trial: 18 inpatients, ketamine 0.5 mg/kg against saline, crossover; HDRS lower from 110 minutes to day 7; day-1 response 12 of 17 against 0 of 14.

Murrough et al.: two-site parallel trial, 72 analysed, the same ketamine dose against midazolam as an active placebo; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours, response 64% against 28%, no significant difference on MADRS or response at day 7. Dennis S. Charney is an author of both trials.

Daly et al.: esketamine nasal spray added to oral antidepressants, 67 randomized, Janssen-sponsored; MADRS differences of 4.2 to 9.0 points against placebo after 1 week. Jaskaran B. Singh and Husseini K. Manji, authors of this trial, are among its authors as Janssen employees.

replication.where_it_stands: The effect at 24 hours after a single infusion was found again in a larger two-site trial that used an active placebo (Murrough et al., 2013), with one author in common with this trial; that trial found no significant difference at day 7, so the persistence to 1 week seen here against saline is less secure than the effect at 24 hours. The systematic reviews on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023) are being read by other readers in this round.

funding.funder: Supported by the Intramural Research Program at the National Institute of Mental Health, National Institutes of Health, and Department of Health and Human Services (Article Information › Funding/Support, p. 863). The ketamine used was Abbott Laboratories ketamine hydrochloride (Methods › Study design); no industry funding is reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article information prints correspondence, submission and acceptance dates, author contributions (statistical analysis by Mr Luckenbaugh), funding/support and an acknowledgment of Dennis S. Charney, but no financial disclosure or conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All eight authors (Zarate, Singh, Carlson, Brutsche, Ameli, Luckenbaugh, Charney, Manji) were at the Mood and Anxiety Disorders Program, NIMH; Charney is acknowledged as being at Mount Sinai Medical School at publication and is an author of Murrough et al. (2013). Singh and Manji are authors of the esketamine trial of Daly et al. (2018), in which both are listed as Janssen Research & Development employees holding company stock (that article's disclosures); no such link is stated in this 2006 article.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, multi-site parallel-group trial (no crossover carryover) of one or more infusions against an active placebo that mimics ketamine's acute effects, with a pre-registered primary outcome and time point, raters kept apart from infusion-day events, a formal check of what patients and raters guessed, and follow-up of every participant well beyond 1 week.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two infusions)
domains.note: Order assigned with a random-numbers chart; sequence holding and allocation concealment are not described. First-period baselines were similar by order (HDRS 24.4 and 24.9).

Baseline HDRS before the second infusion fell from 24.9 to 17.2 in those given ketamine first (P = .004; drug × order interaction F(1,16) = 5.05, P = .04), with only 1 week between infusions while 6 of 17 kept a response for at least a week. The first-period-only analysis avoids carryover and gave similar results, but rests on 18 people compared between subjects.

Identical syringes and infusion procedure, but saline lacks ketamine's perceptual effects (depersonalization or derealization worse from 40 to 110 minutes, p. 860), so participants may have been able to tell which infusion they had; the authors say these effects could have affected the blind (p. 862), and no check of guesses is reported. The 4 people given ketamine first who were not crossed over may have been excluded under the protocol itself, which required an HDRS of 18 or more at the start of each infusion (p. 857); either way the missing saline period is outcome-driven, and the intent-to-treat mixed model includes it.

5 of 18 missed one period: 4 because they were still responding after ketamine, 1 for medical reasons after saline. The completer analysis thus drops 4 ketamine responders (which would understate the effect), while the intent-to-treat model assumes data missing at random, which outcome-driven missingness does not satisfy.

Clinician-rated HDRS and self-rated BDI and visual analogue scales with an inert placebo and obvious acute effects; no check of what patients or raters guessed; the authors themselves say limited blinding may have biased patient reporting.

Registered (NCT00088699, p. 856); by the first reader's reading of the registry, before enrolment but with the primary outcome entered only in June 2006, after the trial ended, and a different scale (MADRS) in the current record (the registry was not re-checked on 12 November 2026). The trial stopped at 18 of 22 after an interim analysis with no stated rule (p. 857). The three analysis sets reported all point the same way.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized within-person design and a large, consistent difference in the first 24 hours make a short-term effect likely, and the authors add a first-period analysis to address carryover. The overall judgment is high because the comparison is with saline in a drug whose acute effects are obvious, blinding was not checked, outcomes are subjective, the trial stopped early after an interim look, and ketamine given first carried over into the saline period; together these can inflate the size of the effect and above all its persistence to day 7. The source can be cited for lower HDRS and BDI scores from about 2 hours to 7 days after one 0.5 mg/kg infusion compared with saline in 18 medication-free inpatients with treatment-resistant unipolar depression, for day-1 response in 12 of 17 against 0 of 14, and for BPRS and YMRS rises limited to the first hour; it cannot be cited for an effect specific beyond expectation, for duration beyond a week, for remission, or for safety.

key_findings.finding: 42 people screened, 18 randomized (24 excluded: 11 did not meet criteria, 13 refused); 17 received ketamine and 14 saline; 4 given ketamine first did not receive saline because they kept a response for 7 days, and 1 discontinued for medical reasons after saline. Figure 1: 9 randomized to each order; the 11 not meeting criteria comprised 4 with low severity, 2 with fewer than 2 failed antidepressant trials and 5 with unstable medical illness; the discontinuation was on day 2 of the saline phase in the saline-first arm; completers 8 (saline first) and 5 (ketamine first).
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Figure 1 gives 13 completers (8 + 5), and the Table agrees (rows 1, 3, 9 and 13 have no saline value and row 18 no ketamine value). The figure's phase-2 box for the ketamine-first arm prints 8 saline infusions, which conflicts with these counts (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sample: 12 women and 6 men, mean age 46.7 (SD 11.2); length of illness 23.7 (12.5) years; current episode 33.6 (37.4) months; 6.6 (4.7) episodes; 5.7 (3.4) lifetime antidepressant trials; 4 had had ECT; 61% lifetime anxiety diagnosis, 39% lifetime substance abuse or dependence, 28% lifetime alcohol abuse or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph; Table, bottom row

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, completers: HDRS drug F(1,203) = 58.24, time F(8,203) = 9.48, drug × time F(8,203) = 4.15 (all P < .001); simple effects showed ketamine better than saline from 110 minutes through 7 days; Cohen's d 1.46 (95% CI 0.91 to 2.01) after 24 hours and 0.68 (0.13 to 1.23) after 1 week.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The completer analysis covers the 13 who had both infusions (Figure 1: 8 + 5; the Table agrees); the Figure 2 legend gives n = 18 for it (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Intent-to-treat analysis (all available data): drug F(1,260) = 34.08, time F(8,257) = 8.92, drug × time F(8,257) = 5.29 (all P < .001), described as effects similar to the completer analysis. The next sentence, ketamine better than saline within 2 hours (110 minutes) and through 7 days, cites Figure 2, which shows the completer analysis, so it is not clear that it reports intent-to-treat simple effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 858)

key_findings.finding: Carryover: baseline HDRS before each infusion showed a drug effect, F(1,16) = 6.25, P = .02, and a drug × order interaction, F(1,16) = 5.05, P = .04, without an order effect, F(1,16) = 1.54, P = .23. Saline first: 24.4 (SD 6.9) before the first and 24.9 (6.8) before the second infusion; ketamine first: 24.9 (6.9) and 17.2 (6.9), P = .004.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: First-period data only (between-subjects): drug F(1,16) = 10.44, P = .005; time F(8,126) = 8.25, P < .001; drug × time printed as F(1,126) = 4.66, P < .001; scores lower after ketamine by 80 minutes and through day 7.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The numerator degrees of freedom of the interaction are misprinted (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Self-ratings, completers: BDI drug F(1,200) = 50.57, P < .001, time F(8,200) = 5.82, P < .001, drug × time F(8,200) = 1.90, P = .06 (trend level); the Results say ketamine seemed to improve self-rated depression from 40 minutes through 7 days, with no simple-effects statistics printed, and the Comment calls the BDI difference significant from 40 minutes through 7 days. Visual analogue depression: drug F(1,198) = 59.88, P < .001, time F(8,198) = 4.70, P < .001, drug × time F(8,198) = 1.92, P = .058, with mood described as improved from 40 minutes through 7 days, similar to the BDI.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 4th paragraph; Comment, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Results hedge the self-rated improvement and print no time-point tests for it; the Comment's statement of significance from 40 minutes rests on that hedged result.

key_findings.finding: Single HDRS items: 7 of 20 had significant time × drug interactions; depressed mood, guilt, work and interests and psychic anxiety improved, depressed mood and guilt from 40 minutes; depersonalization or derealization was worse from 40 to 110 minutes; motor retardation and gastrointestinal symptoms were worse at 40 minutes, motor retardation better at day 1. A further 7 items showed only a drug main effect, those named (suicide, insomnia, general somatic, genital symptoms, hypochondriasis) improving after ketamine; no item differed at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The five named symptoms account for the 7 items with only a drug main effect if insomnia covers the three HDRS insomnia items (early, middle and late) (editors' inference); the article does not list the items one by one.

key_findings.finding: Response and remission (intent-to-treat): 1 day after infusion 12 of 17 (71%) met response criteria after ketamine against 0 of 14 after saline; remission 5 of 17 (29%) against 0; 6 (35%) kept a response to ketamine for at least 1 week, 2 of them for at least 2 weeks; no one responded at 1 or 7 days after saline. In completers, McNemar tests showed more responders after ketamine on days 1 and 2, but only day 1 remained significant after Bonferroni correction; remitters did not differ significantly at any time point.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 6th paragraph; Figure 3 and legend
key_findings.note: Figure 3 (p. 861; intent-to-treat, n = 18 in the legend), read from the bars: after saline, about 0.07 met response at 80, 110 and 230 minutes and about 0.14 on day 3 (consistent with 1 and 2 of 14; editors' inference), and about 0.07 met remission on day 3; the text reports saline-period response only for days 1 and 7 (none).

key_findings.finding: Per-patient day-1 HDRS change from baseline: after ketamine mean −56.2% (SD 20.4), ranging from −17% to −90% across the 17; after saline −9.8% (20.1), ranging from −41% to +25% across the 14. Editors' count: 12 of the 17 ketamine values are a fall of 50% or more and none of the saline values; in the 13 who had both infusions the means are −53.4% after ketamine and −11.2% after saline (editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Table, columns % Change in HDRS Score (Day 1), Ketamine and Placebo, and bottom row

key_findings.finding: Psychotic-type and manic-type ratings: BPRS positive scores were higher after ketamine only at 40 minutes (drug F(1,200) = 4.23, P = .04; time F(8,200) = 9.31, P < .001; drug × time F(8,200) = 6.89, P < .001); YMRS scores were higher at 40 minutes only and lower on days 1 to 2 (drug F(1,201) = 3.08, P = .08; time F(8,201) = 3.54; drug × time F(8,201) = 4.68, both P < .001). Peak BPRS positive change during ketamine averaged +3.1 points (SD 3.4), from −2 to +9.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 7th paragraph; Table, column Peak Change in BPRS Positive Symptoms Subscale Score

key_findings.finding: A trend for an inverse relationship between day-1 percentage change in HDRS and the peak change in BPRS positive score (r = −0.46, P = .06): larger psychotic-type rises went with larger improvement; no other characteristic in the Table predicted response.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 8th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the Table's 17 pairs (BPRS change in points): r = −0.43, P = .09; the text calls the predictor a peak percentage change, and the Comment calls it the change to 110 minutes (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects more common after ketamine than saline: perceptual disturbances, confusion, raised blood pressure, euphoria, dizziness and increased libido; more common after saline: gastrointestinal distress, thirst, headache, metallic taste and constipation. Most ceased within 80 minutes; euphoria and derealization or depersonalization never lasted beyond 110 minutes; no serious adverse events. No counts are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse events

key_findings.finding: The study was planned for 22 patients and stopped at 18 because an interim analysis indicated a very large effect even if the remaining data showed no response.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Patient selection, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood levels of ketamine and its metabolites were not collected; the authors say differences in drug metabolism cannot be ruled out as a contributor. They cite half-lives of about 2 hours for ketamine and 5 hours for norketamine from other studies.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Registration: NCT00088699, first submitted 30 July 2004; earliest archived version (23 June 2005) has no primary outcome; HDRS reduction between groups entered as primary outcome on 19 June 2006; current record (umbrella protocol, 67 enrolled, 2004 to 2017) lists the MADRS at baseline and day 1; registry entry criterion MADRS of 22 or more.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00088699: Study Details (current record) and Record History, versions 1 (2005-06-23) and 2 (2006-06-19)
key_findings.note: Read from the registry by the first reader, not from the article; the article prints only the registration number (p. 856). Not re-checked in the round-2 PDF check or the card adjudication of 12 November 2026, which did not see the registry record.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend gives n = 18 for HDRS, BPRS and YMRS values that it says come from the completer analysis, but only 13 people received both infusions: Figure 1 itself gives 8 + 5 completers, and the text and Table give 17 ketamine and 14 saline infusions, with 4 people missing saline and 1 missing ketamine.
reporting_issues.page: p. 861 (Figure 2 legend); p. 858 (Results › Patients, 1st paragraph; Figure 1); pp. 859-860 (Table)
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's sample size is overstated; the completer estimates, including d = 1.46 and 0.68, rest on 13 people.

reporting_issues.issue: In the first-period analysis the drug × time interaction is printed as F(1,126) = 4.66 with P < .001; with 1 and 126 degrees of freedom that F gives P = .03, while with 8 and 126 (as for time) it gives P < .001 (editors' calculation). The carryover test is printed as F15 = 11.80, P = .004, with the degrees of freedom run together (F(1,15) gives P = .004).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the printed P values are consistent with 8 and 126, and with 1 and 15, degrees of freedom.

reporting_issues.issue: The predictor of response is described three ways: the peak percentage change in BPRS positive score (Results), the peak change in points (Table column) and the change from baseline to 110 minutes (Comment, 7th paragraph). From the Table's points the correlation with day-1 HDRS change is r = −0.43 (P = .09), not the printed −0.46 (P = .06) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: p. 861 (Results › Efficacy, 8th paragraph); pp. 859-860 (Table); p. 862 (Comment, 7th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Which BPRS measure was correlated cannot be determined; either way the association is a non-significant trend in 17 people and is not evidence that response is independent of psychotomimetic effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's bottom row gives 6.6 (SD 4.7) previous episodes; the 18 rows give 6.67 (SD 4.58) (editors' calculation), and the text calls the same figure lifetime episodes of depression.
reporting_issues.page: p. 860 (Table, bottom row); p. 858 (Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one table value or the summary row may be misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered eligibility (MADRS of at least 22 at screening and before phase I, with exclusion of anyone whose MADRS fell by more than 25% between the two) differs from the article's (HDRS of 18 or more), and the registered primary outcome was added after the trial ended.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00088699, versions 1 and 2, as read by the first reader; not re-checked on 12 November 2026) and p. 857 (Methods › Patient selection, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary outcome cannot be confirmed as pre-specified; the registry record covers several substudies and does not document this trial's analysis plan.

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse effects are listed by name only, with no counts, denominators or method of collection.
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial cannot be used to estimate how often any adverse effect occurs after this infusion.

reporting_issues.issue: Flow and crossover reporting: Figure 1 prints 8 saline infusions in phase 2 of the ketamine-first arm, although 9 were randomized to that order and 4 were not crossed over, the same figure gives 5 completers for that arm, and the text gives 14 saline infusions in all (9 + 5). The 4 not crossed over are said to have maintained a response for 7 days (Results) or to have had improved mood (Figure 1), but one of them (Table row 13) had a day-1 HDRS change of −39%, short of the 50% response criterion; when or whether that person met response is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: p. 858 (Figure 1; Results › Patients, 1st paragraph); p. 859 (Table, row 13)
reporting_issues.consequence: The phase-2 box conflicts with the text, the Table and the figure's own analysed box, which agree on 5 saline infusions in that arm and 13 completers; the reason for not crossing over is described loosely, which matters because the missing saline periods are outcome-driven.
