design_detail: Retrospective description of deaths in England notified by coroners to the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (NPSAD) at St George's, University of London (J Psychopharmacol 2021;35(11):1324–1348, online 5 June 2021, as recorded from the PubMed Central full text at first reading; checked against the online-first PDF, Journal of Psychopharmacology 1–25, DOI 10.1177/02698811211021588, whose pages the card cites as PDF p. N). Cases were extracted on 31 January 2020 by a text search for 'ketamine' or 'norketamine' in the cause of death, the coroner's verdict and the toxicology results, for deaths from 1 July 1997 to 31 January 2020; deaths in which ketamine had been given for medical reasons, and deaths in which the source of the ketamine could not be determined, were excluded (Methods, 4th paragraph). 283 deaths, none in 1997 or 1998. Descriptive tables: decedents' characteristics beside all NPSAD deaths in England 1999–2019 (33,186; Tables 1 and 3), prescribed medicines (Table 2), underlying cause of death by ICD-10 code (Table 4), the drugs implicated with post-mortem ketamine concentrations (Table 5), substances found at post-mortem by class (Table 6), and the 32 deaths in which ketamine was the only drug implicated (Table 7). The Discussion adds unadjusted Z-tests and t-tests against all NPSAD deaths (Tables 9 and 10), deprivation of area of residence (Figure 3), UK general-register counts (Figure 4) and a crude death rate. The paper opens with a long narrative background ('state-of-the-art' review) on pharmacology, medical uses, UK prevalence, treatment, seizures, prices, purity and effects; its figures are second-hand except for the first author's own analysis of WEDINOS drug-checking results. No denominator of people who use ketamine and no control group.
can_establish: How many deaths with ketamine recorded by a coroner (in the cause of death, the verdict or the toxicology) were notified to NPSAD from England in 1999–2019 and how that annual count changed, as a minimum; who the decedents were (sex, age, employment, living arrangements, drug history) and how they differed descriptively from all NPSAD deaths; which other substances were found; how the deaths were concluded and coded (manner and underlying cause); and the post-mortem ketamine concentrations recorded.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused or contributed to these deaths (the case definition includes deaths in which ketamine was only detected, and other drugs were implicated in most); the risk of death from ketamine use or how that risk changed (no denominator for the NPSAD count; voluntary and changing coroner reporting and toxicology practice; 2019 incomplete); how dangerous ketamine is on its own (only 14 deaths had no other drug found, their causes are not tabulated separately, and concentrations come without specimen or interval); or that the decedents differ from other drug deaths because of ketamine rather than age and other characteristics (all comparisons are unadjusted).

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: deaths notified by coroners to NPSAD on a voluntary basis. At the time, 80.5% of coroners in England reported regularly, data for England are more complete than for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (which are not included), and more than 35,100 deaths had been notified from English jurisdictions since July 1997 (Methods, 1st paragraph). NPSAD records a death if a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, the person had a history of 'dependence or abuse of drugs' (the register's criterion), or a controlled drug was present at post-mortem (Methods, 2nd paragraph). Coroners' files contain witness and family statements, general-practice, ambulance, police, hospital and treatment-service reports, and post-mortem and toxicology reports, varying from case to case (Methods, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: deaths in England from 1 July 1997 to 31 January 2020 in which a text search found 'ketamine' or 'norketamine' in the cause of death, the coroner's verdict or the toxicology results. Excluded: ketamine given for medical reasons (anaesthesia or emergency care) and deaths in which the source of the ketamine could not be determined (Methods, 4th paragraph). The number excluded for either reason is not given. 18 of the deaths were reported earlier by Schifano et al. (2008) (Methods, 5th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Men 238 (84.1%), women 45 (15.9%); mean age 31.2 years (SD 10.0, range 15–67), men 31.1 (SD 9.7), women 32.2 (SD 11.6). Employed 140 (49.5% of all; 56.5% of the 248 with known status), students 28 (9.9%), unemployed 74 (26.1%), not known 35. Living with others 144 (50.9%; 60.3% of the 239 known), alone 87 (30.7%), no fixed abode 5, hostel 3, not known 44. History of drug use 164 (57.9%; 79.6% of the 206 known), of whom 27 (16.5%) had injected; no history 42; not known 77 (Table 1). White 94.4% where ethnicity was known (Results › Socio-demographics; no table or denominator). Prescribed psychoactive medicines: none 118 (41.7%), one or more 81 (editors' sum of Table 2; 28.6% in the text), unknown 84 (29.7%) (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The authors expect more 2019 deaths to be notified (inquests take on average about 7 to 10 months, and about 7 months for these deaths) and show a projected 2019 count in Figures 1 and 2, described only as extrapolated from jurisdiction reporting trends (Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 note; PDF p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Only deaths that went to a coroner who reports to NPSAD (reporting voluntary and varying by area and over time), and whose toxicology included and found ketamine, can appear. Nationally, toxicology was part of 13% of post-mortem examinations in 2011 and 24% in 2019, and ketamine is typically screened for routinely only in some specialised laboratories or on request (Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Deaths in which ketamine was not tested for, or its source was undetermined, are missing, so the count is a minimum and its trend partly reflects testing and reporting. Because any recorded mention qualifies, including toxicology alone, the 283 are deaths with ketamine recorded, not deaths caused by ketamine.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem toxicology, cause-of-death text and coroners' verdicts as recorded in the coroners' information notified to NPSAD, found by a text search for 'ketamine' or 'norketamine' (Methods, 4th paragraph). Laboratory methods, specimens and detection limits are not described. Non-medical ('illicitly sourced') use was inferred from the case records, by excluding deaths after medical administration or with an undetermined source.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no information on amounts, frequency, duration or route of the decedents' ketamine use is reported. Post-mortem ketamine concentrations (mg/L, specimen not stated) are given for 107 to 119 deaths in Table 5 (see key findings); they are measurements after death, not amounts taken. The background section quotes anaesthetic and recreational amounts from secondary sources, including a drug-information website; these are not study data and are not reproduced on this card.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the series. At post-mortem, ketamine was found in 279 (98.6%), alcohol in 117 (41.3%) and cannabis in 51 (18.0%); by class (Table 6, whose counting basis is unclear, see reporting issues), illicit stimulants 251 (88.7%), opioids (prescribed and illicit) 190 (67.1%), anxiolytics and hypnotics 150 (53.0%), antidepressants 56 (19.8%), antipsychotics 24 (8.5%). Mean number of drugs at post-mortem 4.6 (SD 1.30, range 0–13), against 3.3 (SD 2.22) for all NPSAD deaths (Table 3). The Discussion names alcohol 41%, cocaine 41%, heroin or morphine 31%, diazepam 28%, MDMA 20%, cannabis 18% and methadone 10% (Comparison with other studies, 4th paragraph). Ketamine was the only drug implicated in 32 deaths and the only drug found in 14 of them (Table 5). No analysis separates the contribution of each substance.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: No control group of living people. Descriptive comparison with all deaths notified to NPSAD from England in 1999–2019 (33,186), labelled 'other NPSAD deaths' in Tables 9 and 10 although the totals are those of all NPSAD deaths in Table 1, which include the 283 (Tables 1, 3, 9 and 10). Comparisons with published series from New York, San Francisco and Australia (Darke et al., 2021, cited by the paper as 2020) are narrative (Table 8; Discussion › Comparison with other studies).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental and physical health history appears only as prescribed psychoactive medicines (28.6% with one or more, 29.7% unknown). The pattern, amount and duration of ketamine use, tolerance, the setting of use and the timing of each substance are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison deaths are themselves drug-related deaths (mostly involving opioids or stimulants, according to the authors), with a mean of 3.3 drugs at post-mortem.

outcomes.instruments: Manner of death as concluded by the coroner (accidental, suicidal, undetermined, natural, homicidal; Table 3); underlying cause of death in ICD-10 codes (Table 4), with the other cause-of-death fields read for circumstances such as drowning, falls and road traffic collisions; place of death (Table 3); deprivation decile of the area of residence from the English Indices of Deprivation 2019 (Figure 3); post-mortem ketamine concentrations (Table 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: Coroners' conclusions and pathologists' causes of death, recorded without stated criteria for when a drug is 'implicated'; the paper does not say who assigned the ICD-10 underlying cause. Post-mortem concentrations are given without specimen site, interval after death or method, and post-mortem redistribution is not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Ketamine-related death' is any recorded mention of ketamine or norketamine in the cause of death, the verdict or the toxicology. 'Implicated' (Tables 5 and 7) is not defined. 'Ketamine alone' (Table 7) means ketamine was the only drug implicated, not the only drug found.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Nine significance tests: six one-tailed Z-tests of proportions (Table 9) and three unpaired t-tests of age (Table 10), run with online calculators; everything else is descriptive counts.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: coroners and pathologists reached their conclusions with the full case information, and the authors extracted from the records.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages; no confidence intervals except for the age differences. Against all NPSAD deaths (Table 9, one-tailed Z-tests, unadjusted): men 84.1% vs 73.2% (Z 4.1197); employed, of those with known status, 56.5% vs 30.9% (Z 8.6369); living with others 60.3% vs 44.1% (Z 4.997); drug-use history 79.6% vs 69.0% (Z 5.9831); accidental manner 85.5% (242 of 283) vs 77.2% (Z 3.3221), although Table 3 gives 234 (82.7%); dying at home or another private residence 65.6% (179 of 273) vs 69.0% (Z −1.2369, p 0.10749). Age (Table 10, unpaired t-tests): all 31.2 vs 40.2 years, difference −9.000 (95% CI −10.604 to −7.396; t 11.0262, df 33,467); men −7.800 (−9.384 to −6.216); women −12.000 (−16.663 to −7.337). Suicide as the manner of death 5.6% vs 12.5% (Table 3). Crude death rate: 116 deaths with ketamine mentioned registered in England and Wales in 2010–2018 (12.88 a year) over an average Crime Survey estimate of 176,444 people aged 16–59 with last-year use gives 7.3 per 100,000 a year (Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 5th paragraph).
analysis.covariates: None. All comparisons are crude; the 9-year age difference alone could account for much of the difference in employment, living arrangements and manner of death.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; a retrospective extraction from an existing register. Ethical approval was not required for retrospective reviews of death records, the authors state (Methods, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Year-by-year counts appear only in Figure 1 (a bar chart), and the 2019 projection is described only as extrapolated from jurisdiction reporting trends, without further method. Table 5 accounts for 200 of the 283 deaths; the deaths with ketamine detected but not implicated are not described separately. Concentrations are summarized without the specimen. The narrative background is not systematic.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive). Subgroups are small: 32 deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated, 14 with ketamine the only drug found, 16 suicides.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Deaths with ketamine recorded that were notified to NPSAD from England rose from 1 or 2 a year in 1999–2004 to between 13 and 24 a year in 2007–2016 and 31 or 32 a year in 2017–2019 (2019 incomplete; Figure 1, approximate), and their share of all NPSAD notifications rose to about 2%. The decedents were mostly men (84%), mean age 31, nine years younger than other NPSAD decedents. Most had other substances found (mean 4.6 drugs); ketamine was the only drug implicated in 32 and the only drug found in 14. Accidental poisoning was the underlying cause in three quarters, and 16 deaths were suicides. By Table 5, ketamine was implicated in at most 200 of the 283, and it was mentioned in the cause-of-death fields of 119.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that recreational use and related deaths continue to increase and that people who use ketamine need to be more aware of potentially fatal risks; the Conclusions add that “Ketamine on its own can kill” and that the paper should dispel the view that such deaths are rare (Conclusions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Gaps: (1) the Results describe the 283 as deaths in which ketamine was implicated, while the case definition and the Figure 1 legend include deaths in which it was only detected, and Table 5 accounts for 200; (2) the Discussion calls the 32 deaths ones in which ketamine was detected on its own (11.3%) and uses them to question ketamine's safety profile, but Table 5 shows other drugs at post-mortem in 17 of the 32, leaving 14 with ketamine as the only drug found, whose causes of death are not given separately, and the Lethality section gives a third count, 13 deaths with ketamine the sole mention in the cause-of-death fields; (3) the rise in counts may reflect testing and voluntary reporting, which the limitations section describes but the abstract does not mention; (4) differences from other NPSAD deaths are called extremely statistically significant without adjustment for age; (5) the authors' rate of 7.3 deaths per 100,000 people with last-year use combines general-register deaths, which may include deaths after medical use, with a household-survey denominator. Against this, the limitations section is frank about under-ascertainment and calls the numbers a minimum.

timeline.event: Gill and Stajic: 87 deaths with ketamine found in New York City, 1997–1999, of which 12 were non-hospital deaths from acute polydrug intoxication and none from ketamine alone (as summarized in this paper's Discussion, PDF p. 10; its background section describes the same study as reports on 15 deaths, PDF p. 7).
Schifano et al.: 23 UK deaths with ketamine mentioned, 1993–2006, from np-SAD and the general register offices; 18 of those np-SAD cases are among the 283 here.
ACMD review of ketamine, drawing on NPSAD data (key summary results only, according to this paper).
San Nicolas and Lemos: 25 post-mortem cases involving ketamine in San Francisco, 1997–2013 (conference abstract, as summarized in this paper).

Darke et al. (Addiction, online 2020): 68 Australian deaths 2000–2019 in which self-administered ketamine contributed, from the National Coronial Information System; compared narratively in this paper. Not read for this card (publisher full text not accessible in this round).
This paper: 283 deaths with ketamine recorded, England, 1999–2019.

replication.where_it_stands: The largest published series of deaths with ketamine recorded identified by its authors, extending their own earlier counts (Schifano et al., 2008; ACMD, 2013). Other national series use different case definitions (Darke et al. counted deaths to which self-administered ketamine contributed), so counts and proportions cannot be compared directly, as the authors acknowledge for suicide. The paper gives no denominator-based risk beyond its crude rate.

funding.funder: Part-funding of NPSAD for 2004–2019 from the Department of Health, the National Treatment Agency for Substance Misuse (England) and Public Health England (Funding statement; Acknowledgments). Staff of National Records of Scotland, the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency, the Office for National Statistics, the Police Service of Northern Ireland and the Scottish Government's Justice Analytical Services provided unpublished data.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declared: JC, CC, HC and CG are members of the Novel Psychoactive Substances Committee of the UK's Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD); FS was a full ACMD member from 2013 to 2019; JC is also a member of its Technical Committee and was a member of the ACMD ketamine sub-committee in 2003–2004. The authors state the views are their own, not those of their employers or the ACMD.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Hertfordshire (Psychopharmacology, Drug Misuse and Novel Psychoactive Substances Research Unit); King's College London; NPSAD and the Population Health Research Institute, St George's, University of London. The first author co-founded NPSAD in 1997 and a co-author is its current director, so the authors analyse the register they run. The ACMD advises the UK government on drug classification, and the Discussion takes a position on ketamine's classification (no change warranted). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Linked national data that record every death in which ketamine was tested for (with routine screening and a fixed specimen protocol), classify ketamine's role by criteria set in advance and applied without knowledge of the other case features, and relate deaths to a denominator of people using ketamine (a cohort, for example people in treatment, or repeated population surveys), giving age- and sex-specific rates beside those for deaths involving other drugs.

domains.note: Voluntary reporting by coroners (80.5% reporting regularly), toxicology in a minority of post-mortems (13% in 2011, 24% in 2019) and ketamine screened routinely only in some laboratories; England only; late notifications, with 2019 incomplete. The count is a minimum, and its trend depends on testing and reporting.
Any recorded mention of ketamine or norketamine, including toxicology alone; 'implicated' is not defined; the number of deaths excluded for medical use or undetermined source is not given.

Toxicology as recorded in coroners' files, without laboratory methods or specimens; concentrations for 107 to 119 deaths only, without specimen site or interval; the counting basis of Table 6 is unclear.

domains.domain: Attribution of cause and manner of death
domains.note: Coroners' and pathologists' conclusions without stated criteria; who coded the ICD-10 underlying cause is not said; Table 4 accounts for 276 of 283 deaths; the suggestions that ketamine impaired judgement in falls, drownings and collisions, or contributed to suicidal states, are the authors' inferences, not recorded findings.

No denominator for the NPSAD count; the comparison with all NPSAD deaths includes the cases themselves and is unadjusted; the crude rate combines general-register deaths (which may include medical use) with a household-survey denominator.

The 32 deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated are described in the Discussion as ketamine detected on its own and used to question its safety profile; the conclusions that ketamine alone can kill and that the series should dispel a belief that such deaths are rare go beyond counts without a denominator.

Numbers disagree between text and tables in several places: 283 'implicated' against 200 in Table 5 (182 in its total row); accidental manner 234 or 242; death at home 66.8%, 65.6% or 63%; Table 4 sums to 276; four or twelve hangings; Table 7 places sum to 29 (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a description of deaths from a coroners' register (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The paper may be cited for: the number of deaths with ketamine recorded that were notified to NPSAD from England each year, as a minimum; the decedents' characteristics; the other substances found; the manner and underlying cause of death as recorded; and the descriptive differences from all NPSAD deaths (younger, more often men, fewer suicides). It may not be cited for the number of deaths caused by ketamine, for a death rate or trend in risk (the crude rate of 7.3 per 100,000 is the authors' own calculation from mismatched sources), for ketamine being lethal on its own beyond the 14 deaths with no other drug found, for the danger of any particular combination, or for ketamine's role in the suicides and accidents. Its background figures (pharmacology, prevalence, seizures, prices, treatment numbers) are second-hand and should be cited from their sources.

key_findings.finding: Source and case definition: NPSAD receives information on drug-related deaths from coroners on a voluntary basis (80.5% of coroners in England then reporting regularly; more than 35,100 deaths notified from English jurisdictions between July 1997 and 1 February 2020). Ketamine-related deaths were those in which a text search found 'ketamine' or 'norketamine' in the cause of death, the coroner's verdict or the toxicology results, among deaths from 1 July 1997 to 31 January 2020; deaths after medical administration of ketamine, and deaths with an undetermined source of ketamine, were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 283 deaths met the definition, none in 1997 or 1998. Annual counts by year of death (Figure 1): 1999, 2; 2000, 2; 2001, 1; 2002, 2; 2003, 1; 2004, 2; 2005, 5; 2006, 7; 2007, 13; 2008, 21; 2009, 21; 2010, 13; 2011, 21; 2012, 13; 2013, 24; 2014, 14; 2015, 13; 2016, 14; 2017, 32; 2018, 31; 2019, 31, with 2019 projected to about 56. The abstract describes fewer than 5 deaths a year in 1997–2005, a rise to 21 in 2009, a plateau until 2016 and about 30 a year since.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 and its note; Abstract › Findings
key_findings.note: The year-by-year counts are printed nowhere in the text or tables; they were read from the Figure 1 bar chart and are approximate (re-read on the 300 dpi render, PDF p. 8), but the readings sum to 283, the paper's total. The 2019 count is incomplete (inquests take on average 7 to 10 months, Figure 1 note; about 7 months for these deaths, Results, 1st paragraph), and the projection is described only as extrapolated from jurisdiction reporting trends, with no further method given.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine-related deaths also rose as a share of all deaths notified to NPSAD from England, from about 0.1% in 1999–2000 to about 2.2% in 2017 and 2.1% in 2018 (2019: about 1.6% received, projected about 3%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Read from the Figure 2 bar chart (an image); approximate. The share depends on what else coroners notified to NPSAD each year.

key_findings.finding: Decedents (Table 1): men 238 (84.1%) against 73.2% of all NPSAD deaths; mean age 31.2 years (SD 10.0, range 15–67) against 40.2 (SD 13.7); employed 140 (49.5%; 56.5% of those with known status) against 27.9% of all NPSAD deaths; students 28 (9.9%); living with others 144 (50.9%; 60.3% of known); history of drug use 164 (57.9%; 79.6% of known), of whom 27 (16.5%) had injected. White 94.4% where ethnicity was known (text only).
key_findings.locator: Results › Socio-demographics, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The abstract's percentages for employment (56.5%), living with others (60.3%) and drug-use history (79.6%) exclude unknowns (35, 44 and 77 decedents); percentages of all 283 are lower.

key_findings.finding: Prescribed psychoactive medicines (Table 2): none 118 (41.7%), one 52, two 16, three 9, four 2, five 2 (81 with any, editors' sum; 28.6% in the text), unknown 84 (29.7%). Mentions: antidepressants 50 (citalopram 16, sertraline 11, fluoxetine 9, mirtazapine 7), anxiolytics and sedatives 27 (diazepam 16, zopiclone 7), opioids 23 (methadone 10), antipsychotics 14 (olanzapine 5), pregabalin 6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Socio-demographics, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Place and manner of death (Table 3): at home 130 (45.9%), another private residence 49 (17.3%), hospital 45 (15.9%), street or road 13 (4.6%), open space, woodland or campsite 12 (4.2%), river, lake or sea 8 (2.8%), music-festival site 3, hotel 3, pub or club 2, hostel 2, one each in church grounds, public toilets, a derelict property, a bus or railway station, a car park and a motor vehicle, not specified 10 (all 283 accounted for). Manner: accidental 234 (82.7%), suicidal 16 (5.6%), undetermined 31 (11.0%), natural (combined drug-related) 2 (0.7%), homicide 0; for all NPSAD deaths, accidental 77.2%, suicidal 12.5%, undetermined 8.2%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of deaths, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: The text says two-thirds (66.8%) died at home or another residential address; Table 3 gives 179 of 283 (63.3%, editors' arithmetic). See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Underlying cause of death (Table 4, ICD-10): accidental poisoning 211 (74.6%; X42 narcotics and psychodysleptics 143, 50.5%; X44 other unspecified drugs 44, 15.5%; X41 psychotropic and sedative-hypnotic drugs 21, 7.4%; X45 alcohol 3); poisoning of undetermined intent 13 (4.6%); hanging 12 (4.2%: X70 8, Y20 3, W76 1); intentional self-poisoning 6 (X62 5, X64 1); drowning 5; falls 4; road traffic collisions 3; one coded Z90.5, acquired absence of kidney.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of deaths, 3rd paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Group totals are editors' sums of the Table 4 rows; the text's 74.6%, 4.6% and 4.2% match them. Table 4's rows sum to 276, not 283 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Circumstances from the other cause-of-death fields: 16 drownings or immersions in which ketamine intoxication or poisoning was recorded; 15 deaths the authors count as violent (six falls, four hangings, three road traffic collisions, one person hit by a train, one self-harm with a knife); one autoerotic asphyxia. One decedent had a history of bladder problems and one had needed a nephrectomy because of ketamine use. The authors write that intoxication may have impaired judgement in the drownings, adding that this was the case in six falls and three road traffic collisions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of deaths, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Drugs implicated, with post-mortem ketamine concentrations (Table 5; mg/L, specimen not stated): ketamine alone implicated and no drug found at post-mortem, 1 death; ketamine alone implicated and the only drug found, 14 deaths, 10 values, 0.107 to 10.60 (mean 3.59, SD 3.03); ketamine alone implicated with other drugs found, 17 deaths, 12 values, 0.330 to 32.00 (mean 5.73, SD 8.74); ketamine and alcohol implicated and the only substances found, 7 deaths, 3 values, 0.780 to 2.70 (mean 1.54, SD 1.02); ketamine and alcohol implicated with other substances found, 11 deaths, 9 values, 0.150 to 2.30 (mean 0.95, SD 0.77); ketamine and other drugs implicated, no alcohol at post-mortem, 76 deaths, 41 values, 0.011 to 6.90 (mean 1.05, SD 1.68); alcohol at post-mortem, 74 deaths, 44 values, 0.020 to 24.73 (mean 1.89, SD 4.05). The Discussion gives means of 4.757 mg/L (0.107 to 32.000) where ketamine was the only drug implicated and 1.418 (0.011 to 24.730) where it was implicated with other substances.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of deaths, 4th paragraph; Table 5; Discussion › Safety of ketamine, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Concentrations measured after death cannot be translated into amounts taken; ranges overlap widely between groups, the specimen and interval are not given, and post-mortem redistribution is not discussed. The 4.757 mean is reproduced from the two 'ketamine alone' rows (editors' arithmetic); the 1.418 mean and the table's total row are not (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Substances found at post-mortem (Table 6): ketamine 279 (98.6%), alcohol 117 (41.3%), illicit stimulants 251 (88.7%), cannabis 51 (18.0%), hallucinogens 6, synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists 3; opioids (prescribed and illicit) 190 (67.1%), anxiolytics and hypnotics 150 (53.0%), antidepressants 56 (19.8%), antipsychotics 24 (8.5%), gabapentinoids 17 (6.0%), antihistamines 16, anaesthetics and muscle relaxants 16. Mean number of drugs at post-mortem 4.6 (SD 1.30, range 0–13) against 3.3 (SD 2.22, range 0–14) for all NPSAD deaths (Table 3). Named in the Discussion: alcohol 41%, cocaine 41%, heroin or morphine 31%, diazepam 28%, MDMA 20%, cannabis 18%, methadone 10%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of deaths, 4th paragraph; Table 6; Table 3; Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 6 does not say whether it counts decedents or substance mentions within a class; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The 32 deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated (11.3%; Table 7): 29 men; mean age 30.8 years (SD 11.4, range 19–67); White 27 of 29 with known ethnicity (93.1%); employed 21, unemployed 10, student 1; living alone 13, with others 19, not known 1 (the row sums to 33; the text's 61.3% living with others is 19 of 31, editors' arithmetic); history of drug use 15, none 6, not known 11; incident at home 17, other private residence 2; manner accidental 26 (81.3%), suicidal 4, undetermined 1, natural 1. Underlying causes: X44 13, X41 3, X42 1, F19.0 (intoxication, unspecified drugs) 4, F13.0 2, hanging (X70) 4, road traffic collisions 2, fall 1, asphyxia 1, acquired absence of kidney (Z90.5) 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Deaths involving ketamine alone, 1st paragraph; Table 7
key_findings.note: By Table 5, other drugs were found at post-mortem in 17 of these 32 and no drug in 1, so ketamine was the only drug found in 14. Table 7's places sum to 29, and its accidental-poisoning codes to 17 (53.1%), not the 56.3% in the text.

key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison of decedents' characteristics with other NPSAD cases, 2nd paragraph; Tables 9 and 10
key_findings.note: Table 9's accidental numerator (242) disagrees with Table 3 (234); the comparison group is all NPSAD deaths, including the 283.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine-related decedents lived on average in less deprived areas than NPSAD decedents as a whole (English Indices of Deprivation 2019): by decile of residence, about 14% of ketamine-related deaths against about 28% of all NPSAD deaths were in decile 1, with ketamine-related deaths spread more evenly across deciles 1 to 6.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison of decedents' characteristics with other NPSAD cases, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Read from the Figure 3 image; approximate. The legend does not say which end of the scale is most deprived or how many decedents had a known address, and no test is reported.

key_findings.finding: UK general-register deaths with ketamine mentioned in the cause of death (Figure 4; may include deaths after medical use) numbered 0 to 3 a year in 1997–2006, about 7 to 21 a year in 2007–2017 and about 33 in 2018, with ketamine the sole mention in about 2 to 9 a year from 2007. The authors' rate: 116 deaths involving ketamine (of unspecified type of use, as the paper puts it) registered in England and Wales in 2010–2018 (12.88 a year), divided by an average Crime Survey estimate of 176,444 people aged 16–59 with last-year use, gives 7.3 deaths per 100,000 people with last-year use per year.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 2nd and 5th paragraphs; Figure 4
key_findings.note: Figure values read from the image (approximate). The text describes a fourfold rise from 2016 to 2018 in England and Wales; the UK figure shows about 13 in 2016 and 33 in 2018 (about 2.5-fold), and close to fourfold only from 2015 (about 9). The rate's numerator and denominator come from different sources and case definitions (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: Ratio of deaths with ketamine the sole mention to any mention in the cause-of-death fields: 1:9.154 (13 of 119) in this NPSAD series, against 1:2.659 (44 of 117) in Office for National Statistics registrations for England and Wales, 1993–2016 (King and Corkery, 2018); the authors read this as suggesting lower lethality in their sample and as reflecting differences between the registers.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Ketamine was thus mentioned in the cause-of-death fields of 119 of the 283 deaths and was the sole mention in 13, a count the paper does not reconcile with the 32 deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated (Table 7) or the 14 with it the only drug found (Table 5).

key_findings.finding: Compared with the Australian series of Darke et al. (68 deaths, 2000–2019), the English decedents are described as younger (31.2 vs 35.2 years), more often men (84% vs 77%), more often dying of accidental overdose or toxicity (83% vs 59%), less often employed (50% vs 59%), less often with a history of injecting (13% vs 41%) and less often dying in a private residence (63% vs 72%); suicide was the manner of death in fewer than 6% against 32%, with case definitions that are not identical.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Safety of ketamine, 3rd paragraph; Table 8
key_findings.note: Two of these contrasts compare unlike categories (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Completeness: the authors call the counts a minimum, because reporting to NPSAD is voluntary and varies by area and over time, late notifications continue and some inquests had not concluded. Nationally, inquests were held in 61% of deaths reported to coroners in 1995 and 39% in 2019, post-mortems were conducted in 98% and 59% of inquests opened, and toxicology was part of 13% of post-mortem examinations in 2011 and 24% in 2019; the authors put the share of deaths reported to coroners that had toxicology in 2019 at about 9.15%. In a European survey, 94% of forensic laboratories could screen for ketamine routinely and 4% on request, but routine screening is typically done only in specialised laboratories or on request.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The first author's analysis of results posted by the WEDINOS drug-checking service from 15 October 2013 to 31 July 2020 for samples whose purchase intent was ketamine on its own: 321 of 362 (88.7%) contained ketamine, alone in 273; 48 had other components as well (most often cocaine 18, MDMA 16, levamisole 10; 12 had more than one); 32 (8.8%) contained no ketamine (most often cocaine 10, methoxetamine 9, in 2014–2016, and MDMA 4); 9 had no active component or could not be identified.
key_findings.locator: 'State-of-the-art' review › Epidemiology of recreational use › Price, purity and availability, 5th and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Self-selected samples sent in by members of the public; no method beyond the dates is described. Totals check: 321 + 32 + 9 = 362 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: deaths have risen to about 30 a year since 2016, and people who use ketamine need to be more aware of its potentially fatal risks (abstract); polysubstance use, especially with other central nervous system depressants, is called inherently risky, street ketamine is likely to contain undeclared substances, ketamine on its own can kill, and the findings should dispel a belief that such deaths are rare (Conclusions). In the Discussion, the authors judge that the trends do not warrant changing ketamine's status under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, because numbers remain relatively low in the UK compared with other new psychoactive substances.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Findings and Conclusions; Conclusions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Results (1st paragraph) and the Strengths and limitations (1st paragraph) describe the 283 as deaths in which illicit ketamine was implicated in or contributed to death, but the case definition includes a mention in the toxicology results alone (Methods, 4th paragraph) and the Figure 1 legend says ketamine was detected and/or implicated. Table 5's rows account for 200 deaths with ketamine implicated (its own total row gives 182), and ketamine appears in the cause-of-death fields of 119 (Lethality of ketamine, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 7–8 (Methods, 4th paragraph); PDF p. 8 (Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend); PDF p. 12 (Table 5); PDF p. 16 (Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 1st paragraph); PDF p. 18 (Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The 283 must be described as deaths with ketamine recorded, not deaths ketamine caused or contributed to; by the paper's own tables it was implicated in at most 200.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the 32 deaths of Table 7 as cases in which ketamine was detected on its own (11.3% of the total) and uses them to question ketamine's safety profile, while the Results define them as deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated, and Table 5 shows that 17 of the 32 had other drugs at post-mortem and 1 had no drug found. A third count appears in the Lethality section: ketamine was the sole mention in the cause-of-death fields of 13 deaths (of 119 with any mention), and the paper does not reconcile the 13 with the 32 or the 14.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 9 (Results › Deaths involving ketamine alone); PDF p. 12 (Table 5); PDF p. 13 (Table 7; Discussion › Safety of ketamine, 1st paragraph, which continues on PDF p. 16); PDF p. 16 (Discussion › Lethality of ketamine, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about deaths with ketamine alone must say which count they use: 32 with ketamine the only drug implicated, 14 with ketamine the only drug found, or 13 with ketamine the sole mention in the cause-of-death fields; none tells how many of the 14 were poisonings.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5's total row ('K implicated overall': 182 deaths, 107 values, mean 2.17 mg/L) equals the sum of five of its seven rows; with the two ketamine-and-alcohol rows (18 deaths, 12 values) the rows sum to 200 deaths and 119 values. The Discussion's mean of 1.418 mg/L for ketamine implicated with other substances cannot be reproduced from the row means (editors' weighted means: 1.44 with the alcohol rows, 1.49 without), whereas its 4.757 mg/L for ketamine alone is reproduced from the two ketamine-alone rows.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 12 (Table 5); PDF p. 16 (Discussion › Safety of ketamine, 5th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite post-mortem concentrations row by row from Table 5, with the specimen unknown; do not cite the total row or the 1.418 mean as summaries.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4's underlying-cause counts sum to 276, not 283 (editors' sum). It gives F19.0 (intoxication, unspecified drugs) as 1 death, while Table 7 gives 4 for its subset of 32; the text's 'intoxication 1.4%' corresponds to 4 deaths. Even with 4, the table sums to 279.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 9 (Results › Characteristics of deaths, 3rd paragraph); PDF pp. 11–12 (Table 4); PDF p. 13 (Table 7)
reporting_issues.consequence: The underlying causes of 4 to 7 deaths are missing; the group totals for accidental poisoning (211), undetermined poisoning (13) and hanging (12), which match the text, can be cited, but complete distributions cannot.

reporting_issues.issue: Accidental manner of death is 234 (82.7%) in Table 3 and the Results text, 242 (85.5%) in Table 9, where it is the numerator of the Z-test, and 83% in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 8 (Results › Characteristics of deaths, 2nd paragraph); PDF p. 11 (Table 3); PDF p. 16 (Table 9; Discussion › Safety of ketamine, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The Z-test for accidental manner uses a count that disagrees with the table it comes from; cite 234 of 283.

reporting_issues.issue: Death at home or another residential address is given as two-thirds (66.8%) in the Results text, 179 of 273 (65.6%, excluding 10 unspecified) in Table 9, and 63% in the Discussion's comparison with Australia; Table 3 gives 130 + 49 = 179 of 283 (63.3%, editors' arithmetic). Table 9's comparison numerator for all NPSAD deaths (21,836) differs by 2 from Table 3 (18,383 + 3451 = 21,834).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 8 (Results › Characteristics of deaths, 1st paragraph); PDF p. 11 (Table 3); PDF p. 13 (Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 2nd paragraph); PDF p. 16 (Table 9)
reporting_issues.consequence: 66.8% matches no count in the tables; cite 179 of 283 (63%) with the denominator stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The same paragraph gives hanging as the underlying cause in 4.2% of deaths (12 in Table 4: X70 8, Y20 3, W76 1) and then lists four hangings among the 15 deaths it counts as violent.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 9 (Results › Characteristics of deaths, 3rd paragraph); PDF pp. 11–12 (Table 4)
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of violent deaths (15) is unreliable as printed; cite hangings from Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 7 (32 deaths with ketamine the only drug implicated) lists places of incident for 29, and its accidental-poisoning codes (X41 3, X42 1, X44 13) sum to 17 (53.1%), while the text gives accidental poisoning as the main underlying cause in 56.3% (18 deaths). Its living-arrangements row (alone 13, with others 19, not known 1) sums to 33; the text's 61.3% living with others matches 19 of 31 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 9 (Results › Deaths involving ketamine alone, 1st paragraph); PDF p. 13 (Table 7)
reporting_issues.consequence: Small discrepancies within the subgroup that the authors use to argue ketamine's lethality on its own.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 6 gives illicit stimulants in 251 deaths (88.7%), opioids in 190 (67.1%) and anxiolytics and hypnotics in 150 (53.0%) without naming the substances in each class, and does not say whether it counts decedents or mentions; the Discussion names cocaine (41%) and MDMA (20%) as the main stimulants, and at least 22 decedents had no stimulant by Table 5 (ketamine, or ketamine and alcohol, the only substances found).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 12 (Tables 5 and 6); PDF p. 13 (Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 4th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The class percentages in Table 6 should not be cited as proportions of decedents with that class present until the counting basis is known.

reporting_issues.issue: In the comparison with Darke et al., 'less likely to be employed (50% vs. 59%)' sets NPSAD's employed excluding students (140 of 283) against the Australian 'employed/student' count (40 of 68, as this paper's Table 8 gives it); with students included the English figure is 168 of 283, 59.4% (editors' arithmetic). 'Accidental overdose/toxicity (83% vs. 59%)' sets NPSAD's accidental manner of death, which includes falls and drownings (234 of 283), against Australian accidental drug toxicity (40 of 68); NPSAD's accidental poisoning as underlying cause is 74.6%. The toxicology profile in the same paragraph (opioids 59%, hypnotics or sedatives 58%, psychostimulants 50%) is the Australian series', whose counts Table 8 gives in its Darke et al. row (opioids 39, hypnosedatives 38, psychostimulants 33, alcohol 18, among 68 deaths), and which the first reader also found in Darke et al.'s abstract on the publisher page; it is not NPSAD's (alcohol 41%, Table 6).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 13 (Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 2nd paragraph); PDF p. 9 (Table 1); PDF pp. 11–12 (Tables 3 and 4); PDF p. 15 (Table 8, Darke et al. row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The English–Australian differences in employment and accidental toxicity are overstated by mismatched categories and should not be cited as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Periods and trend wording vary: the title says 1997–2019, the Methods give deaths from 1 July 1997 to 31 January 2020, Tables 1, 9 and 10 say 1999–2019, and Figure 1 shows no deaths before 1999. The abstract and Discussion say fewer than 5 deaths a year until 2005, while Figure 1 appears to show 5 in 2005; the Discussion's summary that there have been about 30 deaths a year since the end of the 2000s conflicts with Figure 1 (13 to 24 a year in 2007–2016).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 1 (title; Abstract › Findings); PDF pp. 7–8 (Methods, 4th paragraph); PDF p. 8 (Figure 1); PDF p. 9 (Table 1; Discussion, 2nd paragraph); PDF pp. 16–17 (Tables 9 and 10)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the series as deaths occurring in 1999–2019 (2019 incomplete) and the annual counts from Figure 1 as approximate; the plateau was at 13 to 24 deaths a year before the rise to about 30 in 2017–2019.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say 83 of these deaths (including the 18 of Schifano et al.) were reported by the ACMD in its earlier assessment of 2004 as well as in its 2013 review, but by Figure 1 only about 10 of the 283 deaths occurred before 2005.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overlap with earlier publications is misdescribed for the 2004 report; overlap with Schifano et al. (2008) and the ACMD (2013) stands.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller points: the 94.4% White (Socio-demographics) appears in no table and has no denominator; Tables 9 and 10 call the comparison 'other NPSAD deaths' but use the totals of all NPSAD deaths in Table 1 (33,186), which include the 283; the estimate that about 9.15% of deaths reported to coroners in 2019 had toxicology cannot be reproduced from the three national rates quoted beside it (0.39 × 0.59 × 0.24 gives about 5.5%, 0.39 × 0.24 about 9.4%; editors' arithmetic); the background dates ketamine's reclassification to Class B both to 10 June 2014 (Legal status) and to 2013 (Confiscations/seizures, 3rd paragraph); the Results text says the prescribed psychoactive medicines were mostly benzodiazepines, hypnotics or sedatives, opioids and antipsychotics, but the largest class in Table 2 is antidepressants (50 of 129 mentions, against anxiolytics and sedatives 27, opioids 23 and antipsychotics 14; editors' sum); and the background counts 15 deaths in the New York series of Gill and Stajic (2000), which the Discussion describes as 87 ketamine-positive deaths, 12 of them non-hospital polydrug deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 4 ('State-of-the-art' review › Legal status; Confiscations/seizures, 3rd paragraph); PDF p. 7 (Rationale for studying deaths, 3rd paragraph); PDF p. 8 (Results › Socio-demographics); PDF p. 9 (Table 1); PDF p. 10 (Table 2; Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 1st paragraph); PDF pp. 16–17 (Tables 9 and 10); PDF p. 18 (Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; none changes the main counts, but the ethnicity figure and the 9.15% should not be cited from this paper, prescribed medicines should be cited from Table 2, and the Gill and Stajic series from its own report.

design_detail: Systematic review with multivariable mixed-effects (multilevel) meta-regression of randomized controlled trials of racemic ketamine or esketamine against a control condition for depression (eClinicalMedicine 2023;62:102127, published online 3 August 2023; pp. 1–15). PROSPERO CRD42021221157. Four databases (Embase, Medline/PubMed, PsycINFO and CENTRAL; the Summary lists Medline and PubMed separately, and Fig. 1 gives counts for four) searched to 13 April 2023 in any language, plus reference lists, trial registries and communication with authors. 49 trials (45 published, 3 known only from registry results, and the authors' own KADS trial, then under review), 3299 participants, 72 ketamine arms and 52 control arms. Model: R metafor, restricted maximum likelihood, study as random effect, linear and quadratic time, formulation (racemic or esketamine), a two-level dose category and their interaction as fixed effects; every reported time point within a window entered the model. Outcomes: standardised mean difference (SMD) in depression severity and odds ratios (OR) for response, remission and all-cause dropout, in three windows: acute (4 hours to 3 days after the first dose), during repeated dosing (day 4 to the last dose) and after the last dose of a course (up to 28 days). The dose category is the review's classification of trial conditions: 'High' for an intravenous racemic-equivalent dose of 0.5 mg/kg or more (or titration up to it) or intranasal dosing predominantly at 84 mg or more, 'Low' otherwise. For crossover trials, data from before the crossover were prioritised; by the Table 1 footnotes, four trials designed with repeated doses contributed first-dose data only. No funding.
can_establish: The average difference between ketamine (racemic or esketamine, as given in randomized trials up to April 2023) and control conditions in depression scores, response, remission and all-cause dropout, by time window after the first dose, during repeated dosing and up to four weeks after the last dose, and how those averages differ across the review's formulation and dose categories within one model.
cannot_establish: Whether racemic ketamine is more effective than esketamine, or a 'High' dose more effective than a 'Low' one, because no included head-to-head comparison exists beyond one small pilot trial, formulation is confounded with route, as the authors state, and also travels with trial size, sponsor and add-on design (see selection effects), and the article reports no statistic for either difference (the Discussion says only that a statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate high-dose racemic ketamine from esketamine); whether any effect lasts beyond four weeks after the last dose (only seven studies contributed after the last dose and none later); adverse effects other than all-cause dropout (not analysed); and the size of the effect free of unblinding and small-study bias, which the authors' own funnel-plot analysis suggests inflates the acute estimates.

sample.recruitment: Database search by two authors of Embase, Medline/PubMed, PsycINFO and CENTRAL from inception to 13 April 2023 in any language, with strategies peer-reviewed by a librarian against the PRESS checklist (full strategies in Appendix pp 5-7, not read), plus reference lists of included studies and trial registries; Fig. 1 shows 1041 database records and 4 from communication with authors or reference lists, 683 after de-duplication (the text's 687 identified articles are these 683 plus the 4), 144 full texts and 49 RCTs included (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1, p. 4). Esketamine trial data were also obtained from the Yale University Open Data Access (YODA) Project, which has an agreement with Janssen Research & Development (Acknowledgements). Two-thirds of the trials (33 of 49) recruited treatment-resistant samples (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As stated: randomized controlled trials of ketamine used primarily as a treatment for participants with a clinical diagnosis of major depressive disorder, any language, no start date (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria). The included set is wider than the criterion: Table 1 lists two trials whose entry criteria required failure of a mood stabiliser (Diazgranados 2010; Zarate 2012) and a third whose reference title names bipolar depression (Grunebaum 2017, ref 38), an adolescent trial using the Children's Depression Rating Scale (Dwyer 2021), and trials selected for suicidal ideation (Sinyor 2018; Domany 2020). By the first reader's reading of the PROSPERO record on 27 October 2026 (not in the PDF; not re-checked in this round), the registered protocol specified unipolar or bipolar depression at any age, while its condition field says adults.
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article: Table 1 gives design, diagnostic entry criteria, arm sizes, route, formulation, doses and control for each trial, but no age, sex, setting or country, although age, sex and treatment resistance were extracted (Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. For the after-last-dose window the authors report dropouts of 0.0% to 35.5% in the contributing studies and note that this could bias the estimate in either direction (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: The ten esketamine trials include most of the large industry-run trials (seven with 72 to 233 participants in their esketamine arm or arms, Table 1), several of them adding intranasal esketamine or placebo spray to an oral antidepressant (titles of refs 16, 17, 45, 50 and 62), whereas the racemic trials are mostly small single-site intravenous trials, two of them with more than 72 participants in the ketamine arm or arms (Fava 2018; KADS). Three trials enter only through registry results and one through the authors' own then-unpublished trial; data on Janssen trials came partly through YODA. These differences travel with the formulation contrast the review emphasises.

exposure.measurement: Ketamine as given in each trial, classified by the review by formulation, route, number of treatments and dose; doses were converted to an intravenous racemic equivalent using a published review of formulation and route (ref 23) to place each arm in the 'High' or 'Low' category (Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph; Appendix pp 7-8, not read). The authors note that this classification rests on estimates of the parent drug's bioavailability (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as listed in Table 1: single doses or courses of 2 to 9 treatments (one oral trial listed with 84 treatments; see reporting issues); intravenous racemic ketamine from 0.1 to 1.0 mg/kg, intravenous esketamine 0.2 and 0.4 mg/kg, intranasal racemic ketamine 50 or 100 mg, intranasal esketamine 28 to 84 mg, subcutaneous racemic ketamine 0.1 to 0.9 mg/kg, intramuscular racemic ketamine, and oral racemic ketamine 50 mg/day or 1.0 mg/kg. The 'High'/'Low' boundary (0.5 mg/kg intravenous racemic equivalent; 84 mg intranasal) is the review's classification of these trial conditions, reported here only as such.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Concomitant medication is not tabulated. Several of the large esketamine trials were add-on designs in which both arms took an oral antidepressant, newly started in two of them (titles of refs 16, 17, 45, 50 and 62; Dean et al., 2021, describe the same design for these trials), which Table 1 does not show; the control in those trials is placebo spray plus an antidepressant, not placebo alone.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The trials' control arms: saline placebo (27 trials), saline placebo with a bittering agent (5 intranasal esketamine trials), midazolam (14 trials), remifentanil (1), diphenhydramine (1) and an unspecified intranasal spray (1) (Table 1; editors' count). Control type (active or saline) was examined as an effect modifier only in the appendix (pp 49-58, not read).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Depression severity on standardised clinician-rated scales (the review names the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), pooled as SMD of ketamine relative to control (negative favours ketamine); response, defined as a reduction of 50% or more in depressive symptoms; remission, whose definition is not given in the article; acceptability as all-cause dropout at each trial's primary endpoint, only for trials with repeated dosing (Methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard depression scales. The article gives no definition of remission (text searched). By the first reader's reading of the PROSPERO record on 27 October 2026 (not in the PDF; not re-checked in this round), the registered protocol defined remission as a HAM-D-17 score of 7 or 8 or less or a MADRS score of 10 or 11 or less; the article does not say which definition was applied.
outcomes.operationalization: Three windows (Methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph): acute, from 4 hours after the first dose to 3 days or the second treatment, whichever came first; repeated dosing, from day 4 to the last treatment (trials with 2 or more sessions); after the last treatment of a course, up to 28 days. Every reported time point inside a window entered the model, with time as linear and quadratic terms, so each window's estimate is an average over time points rather than a value on a fixed day. All effects are measured after dosing, in patients with depression; the review contains no healthy-volunteer data.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p < 0.05 for each estimate. The 10 counts outcome-by-window models (severity, response and remission in three windows, and dropout); together they report about 35 formulation-by-dose estimates plus the time terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening, risk-of-bias assessment and extraction were done by two authors (SN, AS) with consensus; the Summary says they worked independently, the Methods says they screened 'successively' (Summary › Methods; Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria; Contributors).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed-effects meta-regression estimates with 95% CIs and I-squared; no tau-squared or prediction intervals; no absolute rates. Depression severity (SMD): acute: Rac-High -0.73 (-0.91 to -0.56), Esket-Low -0.55 (-0.87 to -0.24), Esket-High -0.48 (-0.75 to -0.20), Rac-Low -0.33 (-0.54 to -0.12), k = 43, I2 = 60.5%, significant quadratic time term (peak about one day after the dose, then return towards baseline); repeated dosing: Rac-High -0.61 (-1.02 to -0.20), Rac-Low -0.55 (-1.09 to -0.00), Esket-Low -0.15 (-0.49 to 0.19), Esket-High -0.22 (-0.54 to 0.10), k = 16, I2 = 84.2%; after the last dose: racemic -0.65 (-1.23 to -0.07), esketamine -0.33 (-0.96 to 0.31), k = 7, I2 = 87.6%; without the single low-dose arm, racemic -0.87 (-1.43 to -0.31), esketamine -0.32 (-0.81 to 0.16). Response (OR): acute Rac-High 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), Esket-Low 3.48 (1.66 to 7.27), Rac-Low 2.69 (1.56 to 4.64), Esket-High 2.27 (1.24 to 4.14), k = 37, I2 = 44.0%; repeated Rac-High 2.83 (1.68 to 4.76), Esket-High 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90), Rac-Low 1.56 (0.57 to 4.26), Esket-Low 1.37 (0.91 to 2.05), k = 16, I2 = 37.8%; after the last dose racemic 2.53 (1.00 to 6.37), esketamine 1.76 (0.89 to 3.49), k = 7, I2 = 61.6%. Remission (OR): acute Esket-Low 5.05 (2.41 to 10.54), Rac-Low 3.31 (1.57 to 7.01), Rac-High 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), Esket-High 2.17 (1.43 to 3.29), k = 25, I2 = 9.9%; repeated Rac-High 2.44 (1.49 to 3.99), Esket-High 1.52 (1.27 to 1.82), Rac-Low 1.05 (0.35 to 3.12), Esket-Low 1.30 (0.91 to 1.85), k = 16, I2 = 5.7%; after the last dose esketamine 1.80 (1.14 to 2.82), racemic 1.31 (0.52 to 3.28), k = 7, I2 = 37.7%. All-cause dropout (repeated-dose trials): OR 1.18 (0.85 to 1.64), k = 20, I2 = 17.3%; Rac-Low 0.94 (0.06 to 15.83), Rac-High 1.23 (0.47 to 3.22), Esket-Low 1.06 (0.48 to 2.34), Esket-High 1.20 (0.83 to 1.74).
analysis.covariates: Formulation, dose category and their interaction, with linear and quadratic time, in one model per outcome and window; dose was dropped from the after-last-dose models because only one arm there was low-dose. Other modifiers (control type, treatment resistance, route) were added one at a time to a base model with time only, and their results are only in the appendix (pp 49-58, not read). The authors state that formulation was often confounded with route and that this limits the ability to quantify each modifier within a single comprehensive multivariable model (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 12).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021221157 (Summary and Methods, pp. 1 and 3); the data sharing statement says the review protocol is available (p. 13), and the article mentions no deviation from it. The rest of this field is the first reader's reading of the registry record on 27 October 2026; the record is not in the PDF and was not re-read in this round. As the first reader recorded it: first submitted 16 November 2020, version 1.0 published 14 January 2021, still shown as planned or ongoing. Differences between the record and the article, none of them mentioned in the article: planned search of MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO in English only, done as four databases (five as the Summary lists them) in any language; planned risk-of-bias tool RoB 2, used the 2011 Cochrane tool; planned outcomes of suicidality and adverse events (VAS-high, BPRS, CADSS, YMRS, serious adverse events) not reported; planned time points (2-4 hours, 24 hours, day 3-4 and 1 week after a single dose; up to 4 weeks after the first of repeated doses) replaced by three windows including one after the last dose; planned random-effects models and subgroups (titration, route, enantiomer, control type, treatment resistance) replaced by a multivariable meta-regression on a high/low dose category that the record does not mention; planned sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk-of-bias studies not reported; funding given in the record as NHMRC APP1105089 but as none in the article; review team in the record Nikolin and Schwaab with collaborators Loo, Rodgers and Alonzo, while the article adds Bahji, Zarate and Vazquez.
analysis.selective_reporting: The article reports only the formulation-by-dose model; the effect-modifier analyses, per-study risk-of-bias judgments, funnel plots and trim-and-fill estimates are only in the appendix. GRADE is named as the method for rating the body of evidence (Methods › Data analysis, 6th paragraph) but no certainty rating appears anywhere in the article. Suicidality and adverse-event outcomes, which the first reader found planned in the PROSPERO record (not re-checked here), are absent without comment. None of the key findings on this card depends on the appendix, except that the risk-of-bias summary and the trim-and-fill result are reported in the article only in outline, with their details in the appendix.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The after-last-dose window rests on seven studies (four racemic, three esketamine, Discussion 4th paragraph) with one low-dose arm, so dose could not be modelled there. The authors say the acute Esket-Low point estimates are exaggerated by small, underpowered trials (Results › initial effects).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In randomized trials of people with depression, mostly treatment-resistant, ketamine was associated with lower depression scores and higher response and remission than control conditions in the first three days after a first dose for every formulation and dose category (SMD -0.33 to -0.73), with a peak about a day after dosing and a return towards baseline. During repeated dosing, differences in depression scores were significant for racemic ketamine (-0.61 and -0.55) but not for esketamine (-0.15 and -0.22), while response and remission were significant for both 'High' categories and neither 'Low' one. After the last dose (seven studies, up to four weeks) racemic ketamine kept a significant difference in scores and response, esketamine only in remission. All-cause dropout did not differ (OR 1.18). Differences between formulations and doses are comparisons of separate cell estimates from mostly different trials; the article reports no statistic for either difference, and the Discussion says only that a statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate high-dose racemic ketamine from esketamine; heterogeneity was high in the severity models (I2 60.5% to 87.6%); and the funnel-plot analysis suggested missing null results in the acute window.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that higher doses were more effective than low doses and that differences were evident in initial, ongoing and lasting effects after the final dose, and the 'Research in context' panel says higher doses improved outcomes at all stages, including lasting effects. The results give no support to this for the after-last-dose window, where dose was not modelled (the closing Discussion paragraph itself says little benefit of dose or formulation was detected there), and the point estimates do not bear it out for esketamine in the acute window, where the low-dose estimates exceeded the high-dose ones in all three outcomes, with overlapping intervals; no test of the dose term is reported in the article. The Discussion opens by calling racemic ketamine superior to esketamine in onset and ongoing treatment, but its next paragraph says the statistical comparison did not differentiate them, and the comparison is confounded with route, trial size, sponsor and add-on design (the authors list several of these confounders as limitations). The abstract calls all acute effects moderate-high, including an SMD of -0.33 that the Results call modest. The conclusion that all doses and formulations were acceptable rests on all-cause dropout alone, which the authors themselves call a coarse measure of safety, and an interval as wide as 0.06 to 15.83 for one cell. The implication for practice, that clinics should adopt protocols ensuring adequate dosing, is drawn from these indirect and confounded comparisons. The Discussion's paragraph on lasting effects misstates which formulation kept a significant effect on depression scores and calls the effects small.

timeline.event: Xu et al., meta-analysis of low-dose and very-low-dose ketamine (9 RCTs, 201 participants, as described in this review's introduction; ref 1); the article calls itself an updated review (Research in context; Introduction, p. 2), and the first reader recorded that the PROSPERO record calls it an update of Xu et al. by the same group (not re-checked).
Correia-Melo et al., pilot non-inferiority RCT of esketamine against racemic ketamine (ref 66), the only head-to-head trial the authors cite.
Bahji, Vazquez and Zarate, meta-analysis comparing racemic ketamine and esketamine (ref 3; three of its authors are authors of this review).

Dean et al., Cochrane review of ketamine and other glutamate receptor modulators in unipolar depression (searched to July 2020), read in this batch as sc_dean_2021; it overlaps heavily with this review's trials.
Loo et al., KADS trial of repeated subcutaneous racemic ketamine (ref 9), the authors' own trial and the only low-dose arm in the after-last-dose window.
This review (published 3 August 2023).

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent pooled analysis in this batch and the only one that models time windows and a dose category together. Its pooled acute effects agree in direction with the Cochrane review of Dean et al. (2021), which shares most of its trials, so the two are not independent confirmations. Its formulation and dose conclusions rest on indirect comparisons of different trials and have not been tested in an adequately sized head-to-head randomized trial.

funding.funder: Summary: Funding: None. Acknowledgements: carried out under YODA Project #2021-4658, using data from the Yale University Open Data Access Project, which has an agreement with Janssen Research & Development, L.L.C.; interpretation and reporting are the authors' responsibility. The first reader recorded that the PROSPERO record gives the funding source as the National Health and Medical Research Council, Australia, APP1105089 (2015); this is not in the PDF and was not re-checked in this round.
funding.declared_conflicts: AB: doctoral research funding from a Canadian Institutes of Health Research Fellowship and research funding through the Calgary Health Trust; a small honorarium for teaching medical trainees at the Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary; unpaid member of the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments editorial committee, the International Society of Addiction Journal Editors, the Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine policy committee and the Addiction Psychiatry section of the Canadian Psychiatric Association; unpaid associate editor of the Canadian Journal of Addiction; mental health educator for TED-Ed (small honorarium).
