funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of New South Wales and Black Dog Institute, The George Institute for Global Health, Maastricht University, the University of Calgary and the intramural programme of the US National Institute of Mental Health. Review authors are authors of included trials: the KADS trial, called 'our recent phase 3 RCT' (Research in context), and Loo 2016 (Loo first author); Zarate is first author of two included trials (Zarate 2006 and Zarate 2012, refs 13 and 28); Bahji, Vazquez and Zarate wrote the earlier racemic-versus-esketamine meta-analysis (ref 3). No procedure for appraising their own trials is described. CL advises Janssen, the esketamine manufacturer, and CZ holds ketamine-use patents. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An adequately powered randomized head-to-head trial of racemic ketamine against esketamine, each at two doses, on the same route and schedule, with an active control, measured blinding and expectancy, several weeks of repeated dosing and at least three months of follow-up after the last dose, with adverse events (dissociation, blood pressure, bladder, cognition) recorded systematically; and, for the existing trials, an individual-participant meta-analysis that separates formulation from route, trial design, sponsor and population.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (major depressive disorder), intervention (racemic ketamine or esketamine), control conditions and outcomes (severity, response, remission, dropout) are stated; the included set is wider than the stated population (bipolar, adolescent and suicidal-ideation trials), which is recorded as a reporting issue rather than here.

The article states registration with PROSPERO (CRD42021221157; pp. 1 and 3) and that the review protocol is available (Data sharing statement, p. 13), and mentions no deviation from it. The first reader read the record on 27 October 2026 (not in the PDF; not re-checked in this round) and found it submitted before the review began, with the question, search, eligibility, risk-of-bias tool and a synthesis plan, and found substantial deviations that the article neither mentions nor justifies (risk-of-bias tool, search languages, dropped suicidality and adverse-event outcomes, new time windows, a dose classification and meta-regression not in the record, missing risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis, funding). The judgment rests on that reading.
Randomized trials only, without a stated reason; the choice is conventional for an efficacy question but is not explained.

Four databases (Embase, Medline/PubMed, PsycINFO and CENTRAL; the Summary lists five, counting Medline and PubMed separately), no language or date limit, peer-reviewed strategies (appendix), reference lists and trial registries searched, registry-only results and an unpublished trial included, and 4 records identified through communication with authors or reference lists (Fig. 1, p. 4), taken here as consulting content experts; search less than four months before online publication (13 April to 3 August 2023). Raised from partial-yes in the adjudication of 12 November 2026, because Fig. 1 shows the contact with authors that the first reading, without the figure, found missing.
Two authors with disagreements resolved by consensus; the Summary says independently, the Methods says successively.
Two authors extracted (SN, AS) and three verified (SN, AS, CL) (Summary; Contributors).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article gives no list of excluded full-text studies: Fig. 1 (p. 4) gives the 95 full-text exclusions by reason with counts only (7 non-randomised; 72 re-analyses of published data; 10 cohorts without clinical depression; 4 ketamine combined with another compound; 1 anaesthetic use; 1 lanicemine in place of ketamine). The appendix, which may hold a list, is not part of the PDF and was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each trial's design, diagnostic entry criteria, arm sizes, formulation, route, doses, number of treatments and control; it gives no age, sex, setting, country, background medication or follow-up times, and not the outcome scale used for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The 2011 Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting), assessed by two authors; per-study judgments are only in the appendix, which was not read, and the article summarises them in one sentence (most studies low or unclear risk).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the article; whether the appendix reports them could not be checked.

A multilevel model with study as random effect and restricted maximum likelihood handles several time points per study; data from before the crossover were prioritised for crossover trials. Weaknesses not scored by this item: cell estimates are compared without a reported test of the difference, the I-squared of a multilevel model is not explained, and no prediction intervals are given.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias is reported; the sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies that the first reader found in the PROSPERO record (not re-checked) does not appear, and the control-type moderator (relevant to blinding) is only in the appendix.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Met narrowly: the limitations discuss compromised blinding in crossover trials and suggest that better-blinded controls in larger trials may explain smaller effects (Discussion, 6th paragraph), but the conclusions on formulation and dose do not carry this through.
I-squared reported for every model (5.7% to 87.6%); effect modifiers examined (results in the appendix) and the confounded parameter space of the trials discussed.

Egger test, contour-enhanced funnel plots and trim-and-fill; the authors report likely missing null results in the acute window and discuss the likely direction (inflated acute effects) and an alternative explanation.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (none) and each author's interests are declared; the authors' own included trials are not mentioned, nor is the NHMRC funding that the first reader recorded from the PROSPERO record (not re-checked).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 (a critical item) can be judged only from the appendix, which was not read; if it lacks a list of excluded studies with reasons, confidence falls to low. On the items that could be judged, no critical item fails outright (item 2 is met in part, items 4, 9, 11, 13 and 15 are met), and there are several non-critical weaknesses (items 3 and 12 not met, item 8 met in part, item 10 unknown), which under AMSTAR 2 gives moderate confidence. The rating concerns the pooling, not the conclusions: the review is registered, searched widely, worked in duplicate and examined publication bias, but, by the first reader's reading of the registry record (not re-checked here), it departed from its protocol without saying so, and its headline conclusions on formulation and dose go beyond its own estimates. Cite it for the pooled differences by time window and for the scarcity of data after the last dose; do not cite it for racemic ketamine being more effective than esketamine, for a dose-response relationship, or for safety.

key_findings.finding: Study selection (Fig. 1): 1041 records from four databases (EMBASE 145, Medline 291, PsycINFO 270, CENTRAL 335) and 4 from communication with authors or reference lists; 683 after removal of duplicates (the text's 687 identified articles are these 683 plus the 4); 184 excluded by article type and 359 on title and abstract; 144 full texts assessed and 95 excluded with reasons (7 non-randomised; 72 re-analyses of published data; 10 cohorts not diagnosed with clinical depression; 4 ketamine combined with another compound; 1 anaesthetic use; 1 lanicemine in place of ketamine). 49 RCTs with 3299 participants were included (52 control arms, called placebo arms in the text, and 72 ketamine arms): 45 peer-reviewed trials, 3 trials known from registry results (NCT02106325, NCT03434041, NCT03539887) and one recently completed trial (the authors' KADS trial). 13 trials (27%) were crossovers, for which data from before the crossover were prioritised; 27 (55%) gave a single dose and 22 (45%) repeated doses; 39 (80%) used racemic ketamine and 10 (20%) esketamine; 33 (67%) recruited treatment-resistant samples; ketamine arms were intravenous in 48, intranasal in 17, subcutaneous in 4, oral in 2 and intramuscular in 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (pp. 3–4); Fig. 1 (p. 4); Table 1 and its footnotes (pp. 5–7)
key_findings.note: Table 1 footnotes (p. 7): only first-dose data were analysed for three crossover trials of up to 5 treatments (Lai 2014, Loo 2016, George 2017) and data before the second dose for Singh 2016a, so 4 of the 22 trials counted as repeated-dose contributed first-dose data only; Shiroma 2020 contributed its first five of six treatments, Cao 2018 its two dose arms (0.2 and 0.5 mg/kg) combined into one weighted average, and the 20 lanicemine participants of Downey 2016 were not analysed. The Summary lists Medline and PubMed as separate databases (five), the Methods name Medline Pubmed among four, and Fig. 1 gives counts for four.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (2011 Cochrane tool) was low or unclear for most studies (details in Appendix pp 27-28, not read). Contour-enhanced funnel plots showed possible publication bias, and trim-and-fill suggested missing null findings at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, that is, possible bias towards larger acute effects favouring ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Acute window (4 hours to 3 days after the first or single dose), depression severity: SMD Rac-High -0.73 (95% CI -0.91 to -0.56; p < 0.0001), Esket-Low -0.55 (-0.87 to -0.24; p = 0.0006), Esket-High -0.48 (-0.75 to -0.20; p = 0.0007), Rac-Low -0.33 (-0.54 to -0.12; p = 0.0019); k = 43, I2 = 60.5%. The quadratic time term was significant (0.81, 0.10 to 1.52; p = 0.025), which the authors read as a rapid fall in depression scores peaking about one day after treatment and then returning towards baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome—change in depression severity: initial effects after a single/first dose; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The authors add that the Esket-Low point estimates from simple meta-analyses at each time point are exaggerated by small, underpowered trials and exceed the model's confidence limits at 4 hours; the model borrows strength from trials that tested both esketamine dose levels.

key_findings.finding: Repeated-dosing window (day 4 to the last treatment), depression severity: racemic ketamine differed from control (Rac-High SMD -0.61, -1.02 to -0.20, p = 0.0038; Rac-Low -0.55, -1.09 to -0.00, p = 0.049); esketamine did not (Esket-Low -0.15, -0.49 to 0.19, p = 0.40; Esket-High -0.22, -0.54 to 0.10, p = 0.18); k = 16, I2 = 84.2%; no significant linear or quadratic time trend.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in depression severity: effects of repeated doses

key_findings.finding: After the last dose of a course (up to 4 weeks): data from 7 studies and 8 ketamine arms, only one of them low-dose (fixed-dose subcutaneous racemic ketamine, the KADS trial), so dose was not modelled. Racemic SMD -0.65 (-1.23 to -0.07; p = 0.029); esketamine -0.33 (-0.96 to 0.31; p = 0.31); k = 7, I2 = 87.6%; trend-level decline over time (p = 0.051). Excluding the low-dose arm: racemic -0.87 (-1.43 to -0.31; p = 0.0023), esketamine -0.32 (-0.81 to 0.16; p = 0.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in depression severity: effects following the final dose of a course of treatments

key_findings.finding: Response (50% or greater reduction in symptoms), acute window: OR Rac-High 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), Esket-Low 3.48 (1.66 to 7.27), Rac-Low 2.69 (1.56 to 4.64), Esket-High 2.27 (1.24 to 4.14); k = 37, I2 = 44.0%; no significant time terms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Response rates, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Response during repeated dosing: Rac-High OR 2.83 (1.68 to 4.76) and Esket-High 1.42 (1.07 to 1.90) differed from control; Rac-Low 1.56 (0.57 to 4.26) and Esket-Low 1.37 (0.91 to 2.05) did not; k = 16, I2 = 37.8%. After the last dose: racemic 2.53 (1.00 to 6.37; p = 0.049), esketamine 1.76 (0.89 to 3.49; p = 0.10); k = 7, I2 = 61.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Response rates, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Remission (definition not stated in the article): acute window OR Esket-Low 5.05 (2.41 to 10.54), Rac-Low 3.31 (1.57 to 7.01), Rac-High 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), Esket-High 2.17 (1.43 to 3.29), k = 25, I2 = 9.9%; repeated dosing Rac-High 2.44 (1.49 to 3.99) and Esket-High 1.52 (1.27 to 1.82) significant, Rac-Low 1.05 (0.35 to 3.12) and Esket-Low 1.30 (0.91 to 1.85) not, k = 16, I2 = 5.7%; after the last dose esketamine 1.80 (1.14 to 2.82; p = 0.011), racemic 1.31 (0.52 to 3.28; p = 0.56), k = 7, I2 = 37.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Remission rates, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Acceptability, measured only as all-cause dropout at the primary endpoint of trials with repeated dosing, did not differ between ketamine and control: OR 1.18 (0.85 to 1.64; p = 0.31), k = 20, I2 = 17.3%; Rac-Low 0.94 (0.06 to 15.83), Rac-High 1.23 (0.47 to 3.22), Esket-Low 1.06 (0.48 to 2.34), Esket-High 1.20 (0.83 to 1.74). Adverse events were not meta-analysed; the authors call dropout a coarse measure of safety and note that adverse events are dose-dependent in the literature they reviewed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acceptability; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Definitions used throughout: primary outcome the change in depression severity relative to control on a standardised scale (SMD); response a reduction of at least 50%; three windows (acute from 4 hours after the first dose to day 3 or the second treatment; repeated from day 4 to the last treatment; after the last treatment up to 28 days); acceptability as all-cause dropout in repeated-dose trials. Dose was converted to an intravenous racemic equivalent and classed as 'High' at 0.5 mg/kg or more (or titration up to it), intranasal arms as 'High' when dosing was predominantly at 84 mg or more; this is the review's classification of trial conditions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Only one small pilot RCT had compared esketamine directly with racemic ketamine (non-inferiority after a single session, ref 66). The authors write that the active-control differences were larger for high-dose racemic ketamine than for esketamine but that the statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate them, and call for large head-to-head RCTs.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; reference 66

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: possible publication or small-study bias (which they suggest may instead reflect a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to large trials with better-blinded controls in treatment-resistant samples); dose categories based on estimated bioavailability of the parent drug; compromised blinding and carry-over in crossover trials (handled by prioritising data from before the crossover); many trial features confounded with one another, for example formulation with route, which limits the ability to quantify each modifier within a single comprehensive multivariable model.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Registration as reported in the article: the Summary and the Methods state that the review is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42021221157), and the data sharing statement says the review protocol is available as supplementary material or from the corresponding author. The article mentions no deviation from the protocol (text searched).
key_findings.locator: Summary › Methods; Methods › Data analysis, last paragraph; Data sharing statement
key_findings.note: The registry record itself is not in the PDF and was not re-read in this round. What the first reader recorded from it on 27 October 2026 (planned searches, population, outcomes, risk-of-bias tool, synthesis plan and funding) is kept, marked as the first reader's reading, in analysis.preregistration_detail; it is not a finding of this PDF.

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests as printed: no funding source; data from the Yale University Open Data Access Project under an agreement with Janssen Research & Development (YODA Project #2021-4658); one author (CZ) is co-inventor on patents for ketamine and its metabolites in depression, with rights assigned to the US government and a share of royalties; another (CL) has served on an advisory board for Janssen Cilag; a third (GV) has been a speaker or advisory-board member for companies including Janssen.
key_findings.locator: Role of the funding source; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgements

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Research in context' panel says higher doses improved outcomes at all stages of a treatment course, including lasting effects, and the abstract says dose differences were evident in lasting effects after the final dose; the Results say dose could not be included in the after-last-dose models because only one arm was low-dose, and the Discussion says data were insufficient to explore dose effects in that period. The closing Discussion paragraph itself says that little benefit of dose or formulation was detected for the durability of effects after the final dose.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1 (Summary › Interpretation); p. 2 (Research in context › Added value of this study); p. 8 (Results › effects following the final dose); p. 11 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); p. 12 (Discussion, closing paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim may say this review found a dose effect on lasting benefit.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose conclusion (higher doses more effective) is not borne out by the point estimates for esketamine in the acute window, where the low-dose estimates exceed the high-dose ones for all three outcomes (SMD -0.55 against -0.48; response OR 3.48 against 2.27; remission 5.05 against 2.17), or for acute racemic remission (Low 3.31 against High 2.97); the intervals overlap throughout. The article reports no test of the dose term; the effect-modifier analyses are in the appendix.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1 (Summary › Interpretation); p. 7 (Results › initial effects); pp. 8–9 (Response rates, 1st paragraph); p. 10 (Remission rates, 1st paragraph); p. 11 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose finding is at most a pattern in some cells during repeated dosing (response and remission significant for 'High', not 'Low'), not a demonstrated dose-response relationship.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion paragraph on lasting effects says the follow-up data showed a significant benefit of esketamine and a similar benefit of racemic ketamine once the low-dose arm was excluded, and calls both effects small; in the Results, for depression severity after the last dose racemic ketamine was significant with or without the low-dose arm (SMD -0.65 and -0.87) and esketamine was not (-0.33, p = 0.31; -0.32, p = 0.19); only remission favoured esketamine (OR 1.80) and not racemic ketamine (1.31).
reporting_issues.page: p. 8 (Results › effects following the final dose); p. 10 (Remission rates, 3rd paragraph); pp. 11–12 (Discussion, 4th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The text and the estimates disagree on which formulation kept an effect after the last dose; claims must use the numbers from the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the acute standardised mean differences moderate-high for all conditions, but one of them is -0.33 (Rac-Low), which the Results call modest; the abstract's interpretation says response and remission were numerically greater for racemic ketamine than esketamine, whereas the largest acute remission estimate is Esket-Low (OR 5.05) and after the last dose only esketamine reached significance for remission.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1 (Summary › Findings; Summary › Interpretation); p. 7 (Results › initial effects); p. 10 (Remission rates)
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's summary of formulation differences holds for depression scores, not for remission.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's first paragraph says racemic ketamine is superior to esketamine in acute onset and ongoing benefit; its second paragraph says the statistical comparison did not significantly differentiate high-dose racemic ketamine from esketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Superiority is not shown by the review's own analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated inclusion criterion is a clinical diagnosis of major depressive disorder, but Table 1 includes trials requiring failure of a mood stabiliser (Diazgranados 2010; Zarate 2012), a trial whose title names bipolar depression (Grunebaum 2017, ref 38; refs 14 and 28 also name bipolar depression), an adolescent trial (Dwyer 2021) and trials defined by suicidal ideation (Sinyor 2018; Domany 2020); by the first reader's reading of the PROSPERO record on 27 October 2026 (not in the PDF; not re-checked in this round), the registered protocol allowed bipolar depression of any age.
reporting_issues.page: p. 2 (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria); pp. 5–6 (Table 1); pp. 13–14 (references 14, 28 and 38); PROSPERO record, Population (first reader's reading, 27 October 2026; not re-checked)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimates describe a mixed population (unipolar and bipolar depression, adults and adolescents), not major depressive disorder alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample sizes in Table 1 sum to 3279 when crossover participants are counted once and the 20 lanicemine participants of Downey 2016 (not analysed, footnote b) are left out; the reported total of 3299 equals the sum only if those 20 are included (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: p. 3 (Results, 1st paragraph); pp. 5–7 (Table 1 and footnote b)
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant total probably includes 20 people who received a different drug; the analysable total is about 3279.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists the authors' KADS trial as 'Loo et al. (under review)', while reference 9 cites it as published in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 2023.
reporting_issues.page: p. 6 (Table 1, last row of that page, Loo et al. (under review)); p. 7 (Table 1 continued: the three registry-only trials, two of them racemic); p. 13 (reference 9)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the trial is the published KADS study.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives Arabzadeh 2018 as 84 treatments twice weekly with oral racemic ketamine 50 mg/day and a saline placebo; Dean et al. (2021) describe the same trial as 25 mg twice daily for 6 weeks alongside sertraline, and 84 doses equal 6 weeks of twice-daily dosing (editors' arithmetic), so 'weekly' appears to be an error for 'daily' and the oral comparator cannot have been a saline infusion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled estimates; the row should not be cited for the trial's schedule.

reporting_issues.issue: GRADE is named as the method for rating the quality of the body of evidence, but no GRADE certainty rating is reported anywhere in the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claim writers must rate certainty themselves; the review offers none.

reporting_issues.issue: The article states that there was no funding source; the first reader recorded that the PROSPERO record gives the National Health and Medical Research Council, Australia (APP1105089), as the funding source (not in the PDF; not re-checked in this round). The article mentions no deviation from the registered protocol (text searched); the deviations listed in the preregistration detail rest on the first reader's reading of the record.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 1, 3 (Summary › Funding; Role of the funding source); PROSPERO record, Funding source (first reader's reading, 27 October 2026; not re-checked)
reporting_issues.consequence: A transparency flag; it does not change the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Research in context' panel says earlier meta-analyses did not examine single versus repeated dosing or route of administration, while the Introduction credits earlier meta-analyses with information on sustained benefit after repeated sessions (ref 2) and on routes of administration (ref 8).
reporting_issues.page: p. 2 (Research in context › Evidence before this study; Introduction, 1st paragraph, which begins on p. 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the novelty claim is overstated.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 describes the comparators of the intranasal esketamine trials only as saline placebo (with a bittering agent in five of the nine) or an intranasal spray (NCT03434041); the titles of refs 17 and 50 (and Dean et al., 2021, for the same trials) show that these were add-on trials in which both arms started a new oral antidepressant, and the titles of refs 16, 45 and 62 also describe esketamine added to an oral antidepressant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The esketamine-control differences in these five trials are differences on top of an oral antidepressant (newly started in both arms in two of them), which is one reason why they are not comparable with the racemic-control differences; by their titles, most racemic trials did not start a new antidepressant in both arms (an exception is Hu 2016, ref 34, ketamine added to newly initiated escitalopram).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the intravenous esketamine trial of 0.2 and 0.4 mg/kg 'Singh et al. (2016a)' and the twice- or thrice-weekly intravenous racemic ketamine trial 'Singh et al. (2016b)'; Dean et al. (2021) use the opposite labels for the same two trials (Singh 2016 a racemic, Singh 2016 b esketamine). The two reviews also describe the racemic trial's regimen differently: 4 twice-weekly or 6 thrice-weekly treatments here, infusions on days 1 to 25 or 26 (8 or 12 infusions) in Dean et al.
reporting_issues.page: p. 5 (Table 1, Singh et al. rows); p. 14 (references 36 and 37)
reporting_issues.consequence: Risk of mis-citation when the two reviews are compared; identify these trials by journal (Am J Psychiatry 2016 for racemic ketamine, Biol Psychiatry 2016 for esketamine), not by letter.

No correction or erratum was linked from the PMC page.

design_detail: Secondary quantitative text analysis of two existing collections of retrospective written reports; nobody was studied directly. (1) 625 near-death-experience (NDE) narratives (623,926 words) collected by anonymous voluntary questionnaire through the Division of Perceptual Studies, University of Virginia, and the Coma Science Group, Liège. (2) About 15,000 drug-experience reports for 165 substances (each with more than 10 reports; reports of combinations excluded) from the Erowid Experience Vaults. Substance names, slang and route words were deleted from both. All reports for one substance were merged into one document, and all NDE narratives into one; after tf-idf weighting, latent semantic analysis (singular value decomposition keeping 20 singular values) gave a correlation of word use between the NDE document and each substance document, which was used to rank the substances. Robustness checks: 5 to 145 singular values, NDE subsets by cause, closeness to death and emotional tone, and removal of the 500 most relevant terms of each of two context topics. Appraised with ROBINS-E as the closest instrument, because the paper compares substances (the exposure) on how closely their reports resemble NDE narratives (the outcome) in observational data and estimates no prevalence.
can_establish: Which substances' Erowid reports, pooled by substance, use words in patterns most like the pooled NDE narratives in these two collections, and how stable that ranking is to the analysis settings the authors varied.
cannot_establish: That any drug produces an experience like a near-death experience, or that NDEs are caused by an endogenous ketamine-like or DMT-like substance (the authors say the analysis neither validates nor refutes such models, p. 65); how individual experiences compare (reports were merged by substance, so there is no person-level comparison and no measure of uncertainty); whether differences reflect the drugs themselves, doses, settings, expectations, the writers or the conventions of drug-report writing; or whether ketamine is safe as an experimental model (not studied).

sample.recruitment: NDE narratives: people who reported an NDE and volunteered to complete an anonymous questionnaire through the University of Virginia Division of Perceptual Studies or the Liège Coma Science Group; how they were reached is not described (p. 54). Drug reports: downloaded from the Erowid Experience Vaults, a curated public website holding more than 20,000 reports written by people who chose to submit them (p. 54). The number of drug reports analysed is given as about 15,000 in the abstract (p. 52) and as more than 15,000 in the introduction (p. 54); per-substance counts are in supplementary tables that were not read (n_total is therefore left empty).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: NDE narratives: a score of 7 or more on the NDE Scale (mean 15.2, SD 7), except 182 accounts collected before the scale existed, which the authors judged detailed enough to have qualified (p. 54). Erowid reports: single-substance reports only, duplicates removed, substances with more than 10 reports; 165 substances classified by mechanism and subjective effects as serotonergic psychedelics, dissociatives, entactogens, deliriants, depressants or sedatives, stimulants, antipsychotics or antidepressants, oneirogens and others (MAOIs appear as a further class in the figures) (pp. 54-55).
sample.demographics: NDE experiencers: 68% women; mean age at the NDE 31 (SD 15; 7 missing) and when the account was collected 52 (SD 13; 2 missing). Cause to which loss of consciousness was attributed: head injury 13%, anaesthesia or drug use 30%, cardiac arrest 10% (228 missing; the base is not stated, and Fig. 1, p. 55, shows the rest as other or unknown). Self-rated closeness to death: not serious 27%, serious 37%, loss of vital signs 35% (209 missing). Emotional tone: pleasant 82%, neutral 8%, unpleasant 9% (279 missing) (p. 54). Demographic information is not commonly available for the writers of Erowid reports (p. 65).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. NDE background information was missing for 209 to 279 of the 625 narratives, which limits the subgroup analyses (p. 54).
sample.selection_effects: Both collections are self-selected written accounts: people who volunteered NDE accounts to research groups that study NDEs (one author, Greyson, is at the University of Virginia Health System, where part of the collection was gathered), and people who chose to write drug reports for Erowid, which curates them (two authors, Fire Erowid and Earth Erowid, are from the Erowid Center). NDE accounts were written on average about two decades after the event (p. 65). Neither collection represents people who have had such experiences in general, and the authors note the relative cultural homogeneity of the writers (p. 65).

exposure.measurement: The substance named by the writer of each Erowid report; identity and dose were not verified in a laboratory and may have been unknown to the writer (p. 65). For NDEs, the circumstances were self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Unknown for every report; words naming routes were deleted from the texts (p. 55).
exposure.polysubstance: Reports describing combinations were excluded (p. 54); the writers' other drug use is unknown. In 30% of NDEs (base not stated) loss of consciousness was attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (p. 54), so part of the NDE collection may itself describe drug-related states; these narratives stay in the main analysis and the anaesthetics or drugs are not named, but Fig. 8A (p. 62) analyses them as a separate subset, with results like those of the other subsets (p. 60).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: No control group. Each substance's merged reports are compared with the merged NDE narratives and the substances are ranked against each other; cocaine and heroin serve as contrasts in the radar plots (Fig. 6C, p. 60).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: For the Erowid writers: age, sex, culture, beliefs, expectations, knowledge of the NDE literature and writing habits are unknown; dose and setting are unknown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Latent semantic analysis: a term-document matrix of lemmatized words of three or more letters (substance names, slang and route words removed), tf-idf weighting keeping terms found in more than 5% and less than 95% of documents, singular value decomposition keeping 20 singular values; similarity is the correlation between the reduced columns for the NDE document and each substance document (pp. 55-56). Principal component analysis of the same matrix gave five topics, named automatically with a word2vec-based engine (Datamuse) and shown as word clouds and radar plots (p. 56).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite earlier work using this method to classify drug reports and to compare drug states with dreams, and state that it has not been established that ratings drawn from free narratives are equivalent to those from psychometric scales (p. 63). No validation of the similarity index against standardized NDE or altered-state questionnaires is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Phenomenological similarity is operationalized as correlated word use between merged documents. The authors note that the method measures word co-occurrence rather than meaning: a word such as fear could appear in reports of fear and of its absence (footnote 2, p. 56).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported for the pairwise comparisons between the seven drug categories (21 pairs, editors' count) (each at p<0.05, Fig. 4B, p. 58) or for the one-way ANOVAs on NDE background variables (number not stated, p. 61). The ranking of substances itself carries no statistical test or uncertainty estimate.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (automated analysis). Preprocessing choices, such as the word lists to delete and the drug categories, were made by hand by the authors (p. 55).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or intervals are reported. With 20 singular values (Fig. 3, p. 57), ketamine reports had the highest similarity to the NDE narratives (about 0.9, read from the figure), followed, in the figure's zoomed panel of top-ranked substances (which shows 21), by Salvia divinorum, L. williamsii (peyote), LSD, 5-MeO-DMT, psilocybin mushrooms, DMT, iboga, ibogaine, nitrous oxide, cannabis, ayahuasca, MDMA, DXM, mescaline, PCP, methoxetamine, E. peruviana, 5-AcO-DMT, DPT and Datura species (about 0.72); the lowest was betel nut (about 0.08). By category (Fig. 4A, p. 58), dissociatives ranked best, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics; dissociatives differed from every category except deliriants. Averaged over 5 to 145 singular values (Fig. 7C, p. 61), ketamine had a mean similarity of about 0.64, LSD about 0.62, psilocybin mushrooms about 0.61, Salvia divinorum and cannabis about 0.59 to 0.60, followed by 5-MeO-DMT, DMT, ayahuasca and MDMA (values read from the figure, approximate). Ketamine ranked first for most choices of the number of singular values, followed by LSD, ibogaine, L. williamsii and PCP (p. 59; Fig. 7D, shares not printed; editors' measurement of the slices: about 79%, 13%, 6%, 1% and under 1%). In Fig. 7C L. williamsii is 18th and methamphetamine 17th (editors' reading). After deleting the 500 most relevant terms of each of two context topics the top ten were ketamine, ayahuasca, Salvia divinorum, L. williamsii, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, cannabis, psilocybin mushrooms, iboga and nitrous oxide (p. 61).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The choice of 20 singular values is justified by the number of drug categories and by earlier work with the same data (p. 56), although there are nine or ten categories; rankings computed with very different numbers of singular values (for example 20 vs 100) compared poorly (p. 59). The full ranking, the number of reports per substance and the curation details are in supplementary material that was not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the ranking involves no sampling-based inference.

interpretation_gap.results_show: When all Erowid reports for each substance were merged into one document and compared with all 625 NDE narratives merged into one, ketamine reports had the most similar pattern of word use, with LSD, psilocybin mushrooms, Salvia divinorum and, on the average across settings, cannabis close behind; dissociatives ranked best as a class and sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics worst. Below the top ranks the ordering changed with the number of singular values. The NDE narratives also loaded heavily on a topic made of words about preparing materials (the make/stuff component).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says ketamine consistently produced the reports most similar to NDEs, that the analysis suggests ketamine could be used as a safe and reversible experimental model of NDE phenomenology, and that it supports the speculation that endogenous neuroprotective NMDA antagonists are released near death (p. 52); the discussion repeats that such drugs could be tools for the safe and temporary induction of NDE-like states (p. 65), the introduction calls these substances very safe under most circumstances, citing other studies (p. 53), and the conclusion says ketamine can produce an altered state resembling near-death (p. 66). But the discussion itself states that the analyses neither validate nor refute neurochemical models of NDEs (p. 65); safety was not studied; ketamine's lead over LSD was small, and LSD ranked comparably for NDEs after cardiac arrest (p. 61); and similarity of word use in merged, unverified, retrospective reports has not been shown to measure similarity of experience: the authors treat it as a proxy resting on a stated assumption (p. 55) and note only that ratings drawn from free narratives have not been shown equivalent to psychometric-scale ratings (p. 63). In 30% of NDEs (base not stated) loss of consciousness was attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (p. 54), a possible source of shared vocabulary; the paper analyses these narratives as a separate subset, with a class ranking like the others' and ketamine most often first (Fig. 8A, p. 62; text p. 60), but keeps them in the main analysis and does not name the anaesthetics or drugs. A headline that ketamine simulates dying, or that near-death experiences come from a ketamine-like brain chemical, goes well beyond these data: what was measured is how similar the words are in two collections of written reports.

timeline.event: Corazza and Schifano retrospectively compared reports of 36 people with cardiac-arrest NDEs with 36 people's ketamine experiences and concluded that ketamine can reproduce some aspects of NDEs (as summarized in this paper, pp. 53-54; not appraised)

Timmermann and colleagues gave DMT to 13 volunteers in a placebo-controlled within-person study and found NDE Scale differences from placebo and overlap with a matched group of NDE experiencers (as summarized in this paper, p. 54; not appraised)
Sanz and colleagues applied the same Erowid collection and text-similarity method to compare drug reports with dream reports (the method source for this paper; not appraised)
This paper: ketamine reports most similar to NDE narratives in word use among 165 substances

replication.where_it_stands: A single exploratory text-mining study. The prior evidence the authors cite is one retrospective comparison of reports (Corazza & Schifano, 2010) and one small laboratory study with DMT (Timmermann et al., 2018). No replication with other collections of reports, person-level comparisons or validated questionnaires is reported in this paper.

funding.funder: University and University Hospital of Liège; Belgian National Funds for Scientific Research (FRS-FNRS); European Union Horizon 2020 (Human Brain Project SGA2, grant agreement 785907); the Luminous project (EU-H2020-fetopenga686764); the European Space Agency; Fonds Léon Frédéricq; the Bial Foundation; the Mind Science Foundation; the European Commission; and CONICET, Argentina (p. 66).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors (Fire Erowid and Earth Erowid) are from the Erowid Center, which curates the drug-report collection used. Bruce Greyson is at the University of Virginia Health System (Department of Psychiatry and Neurobehavioral Sciences), whose Division of Perceptual Studies supplied part of the NDE narratives, and the NDE Scale used for inclusion is his (Greyson, 1983, in the reference list). No ethics approval statement for the NDE questionnaire is reported. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective comparison of individual NDE accounts, collected soon after the event, with accounts from people given ketamine, DMT, psilocybin or an active placebo at known doses in a laboratory, all rated blind on validated NDE and altered-state questionnaires as well as by text analysis, with person-level estimates of uncertainty.

domains.note: Writers, doses, settings and expectations differ between substances and none were measured or adjusted for. The paper itself describes a long cultural tradition comparing ketamine experiences with dying (p. 53), which could shape how such reports are written. The number of reports merged per substance also differs (more than 10 each; counts only in the unread supplement), and whether document size affects the similarity is not examined (editors' observation).
The substance is as named by the writer, without laboratory verification; dose and route are unknown (p. 65).
Self-selected volunteers and Erowid contributors, with curation by Erowid; NDE accounts from centres that study NDEs, 182 of them included without the NDE Scale.
Not applicable to this design: nothing was done to the writers after the exposure.
NDE background information missing for 209 to 279 of 625 narratives in the subgroup analyses; substances with 10 or fewer reports were dropped.

Similarity of word use between merged documents is an unvalidated proxy for similarity of experience; one number per substance, with no uncertainty estimate; results depend on hand-made preprocessing choices.

No protocol; the number of singular values was chosen with a stated rationale and then varied, but rankings at very different settings compared poorly; 21 category comparisons with no correction for multiple comparisons reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison rests on unverified, self-selected, retrospective reports merged by substance, with no adjustment for who wrote them, at what dose or in what setting, and with an outcome (correlated word use) that has not been validated as a measure of experience; the analysis yields a ranking without any estimate of uncertainty. The paper may be cited for what this word-use comparison found in these two collections (ketamine reports closest to the NDE narratives, with LSD, psilocybin mushrooms and others close behind) and as a hypothesis-generating study; not as evidence that any drug reproduces near-death experiences, that NDEs have a neurochemical cause, or that ketamine is a safe experimental model.

key_findings.finding: What was compared: 625 written accounts of near-death experiences (623,926 words) and about 15,000 drug-experience reports covering 165 substances from an online collection (the Erowid Experience Vaults); nobody was given a drug or interviewed for this study.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 52); 1. Introduction, 6th paragraph, and 2.1 NDE corpus (p. 54)

key_findings.finding: Who wrote the NDE accounts: volunteers (68% women) who had had the experience at a mean age of 31 and wrote about it at a mean age of 52. Loss of consciousness was attributed to head injury in 13%, anaesthesia or drug use in 30% and cardiac arrest in 10% of cases (228 missing; the base of these percentages is not stated, and Fig. 1 shows the remaining share, about half, as other or unknown); 35% rated their closeness to death as involving loss of vital signs; 82% of rated experiences were pleasant and 9% unpleasant. Background details were missing for 209 to 279 of the 625.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 NDE corpus (p. 54); Fig. 1 (p. 55)

key_findings.finding: How similarity was measured: all reports for each substance were merged into one document and all NDE narratives into another, drug names, slang and route words were deleted, and a text-mining method (latent semantic analysis with 20 dimensions) scored how strongly the patterns of word use correlated.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Corpora preprocessing (p. 55); 2.4 Latent semantic analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, and 3.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 56)

key_findings.finding: Main ranking: ketamine reports were the most similar to the NDE narratives, followed by Salvia divinorum and a series of serotonergic psychedelics (peyote, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, psilocybin mushrooms, DMT, iboga, ibogaine, ayahuasca, mescaline and others). The text names nitrous oxide, PCP, methoxetamine and Datura species as also in the top 20, but the zoomed 'top 20' panel of Fig. 3 shows 21 substances, with Datura species 21st, and also includes DXM (14th, coloured as a dissociative with a deliriant secondary category), MDMA and cannabis, which the text does not name. The 20 least similar substances were mostly sedatives and stimulants.
key_findings.locator: 3.1, 3rd paragraph (p. 56, continuing on p. 57); Fig. 3 (p. 57)
key_findings.note: Approximate similarity values read from Fig. 3: ketamine about 0.9, Datura species (21st in the zoomed panel) about 0.72, betel nut (lowest) about 0.08. See reporting issue 7.

key_findings.finding: By class, dissociatives ranked best, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics; in pairwise tests dissociatives differed from all classes except deliriants, and all three hallucinogen classes ranked better than sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics or antidepressants.
key_findings.locator: 3.1, 4th paragraph (p. 57, continuing on p. 58); Fig. 4 (p. 58)

key_findings.finding: The twist in the robustness checks: rankings computed with very different settings (for example 20 vs 100 dimensions) compared poorly, although the top of the list was fairly stable. Averaged over all settings, ketamine came first only narrowly, ahead of LSD and psilocybin mushrooms, with Salvia divinorum and cannabis next; ketamine ranked first in most settings, LSD in most of the rest.
key_findings.note: Approximate mean similarity read from Fig. 7C: ketamine about 0.64, LSD about 0.62, psilocybin mushrooms about 0.61, Salvia divinorum and cannabis about 0.59 to 0.60. Fig. 7D prints no shares; editors' measurement of its slices: ketamine first in about 79% of settings, LSD about 13%, ibogaine about 6%, L. williamsii about 1%, PCP under 1%. Below the top few, the averaged order departs from Fig. 3, which the text calls similar (p. 59): in Fig. 7C L. williamsii, 3rd at 20 singular values, is 18th, and methamphetamine, a stimulant, is 17th (editors' reading).

key_findings.finding: Splitting the NDE accounts by cause (head injury, anaesthesia or drug use, cardiac arrest), closeness to death or emotional tone, ketamine stayed first in almost all subsets; for NDEs after cardiac arrest, LSD ranked comparably to ketamine. One-way ANOVA found no significant effect of these background variables on the drug ranking.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 (p. 60, continuing on p. 61); Fig. 8 (p. 62)
key_findings.note: In the cardiac-arrest pie of Fig. 8A, LSD's slice (about 48%) is slightly larger than ketamine's (about 46%) (editors' measurement, approximate). No test statistics are printed for the ANOVA; see reporting issue 8.

key_findings.finding: After deleting the 500 most relevant words of each of two context topics (preparation of materials, and dependence), the ten most similar substances were ketamine, ayahuasca, Salvia divinorum, peyote, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, cannabis, psilocybin mushrooms, iboga and nitrous oxide; the ten least similar included betel nut, atomoxetine, triazolam, yohimbe, passion flower, etizolam and olanzapine.

Words frequent in both the NDE and ketamine reports concerned perception (face, vision, saw), emotion (fear), reality and consciousness (reality, universe, memory), self and others, and surroundings (door, floor, inside, outside).
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 58); Fig. 5 (p. 59)

key_findings.finding: Five topics explained more than 60% of the variation in word use; the NDE narratives loaded on three of them, one about perception and self, one about disease and religion, and one made of words about preparing materials (the make/stuff topic).
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 58); Fig. 6 (p. 60)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that it has not been established that ratings drawn from free narratives are equivalent to those from psychometric scales.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their analyses neither validate nor refute neurochemical models of NDEs, because they rest on retrospective reports with no examination of anyone at the time of the NDE.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 12th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: NDE accounts were given on average about two decades after the event; demographic information is not commonly available for the writers of Erowid reports, and the reports may reflect expectations and mostly lack laboratory verification of the substance and dose, which the writer may not have known; dose differences between substances could bias the results; the population was relatively homogeneous culturally.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 14th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The number of drug reports is given as about 15,000 in the abstract and as more than 15,000 in the introduction, and the exact number analysed is not given in the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the drug-report collection cannot be checked from the paper itself.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction speaks of ten pharmacological classes, the methods list nine, and the figures add MAOIs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the category comparisons should be read from the figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The choice of 20 singular values is said to be based on the number of drug categories, which is nine or ten, and on earlier work with the same data (Sanz et al., 2018).
reporting_issues.consequence: The main ranking rests on a setting whose category-based rationale does not fit; rankings at very different settings compared poorly (p. 59).

reporting_issues.issue: Categories containing different substances were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, which are designed for paired data; all pairs of the seven categories in Fig. 4B (21 pairs, editors' count) were tested at p<0.05 (12 marked significant, editors' count), and no correction for multiple comparisons is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The category significance pattern in Fig. 4B may not be valid as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentages for the cause of the NDE (13%, 30%, 10%) are given with 228 missing values but without a stated denominator; they add to 53% (editors' sum), the rest presumably being other or unknown causes (Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of NDEs that followed anaesthesia or drug use cannot be stated precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence describing how each drug category projects onto the five topics is garbled in the printed text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The projections have to be read from the radar plots in Fig. 6.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the other dissociatives in the top 20 were nitrous oxide, PCP and methoxetamine and that the only deliriants were Datura species, but the zoomed 'top 20' panel of Fig. 3 shows 21 substances: Datura species are 21st, and DXM (14th, coloured as a dissociative with a deliriant secondary category), MDMA and cannabis appear without being named in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Membership of the top 20 should be read from Fig. 3, not the text: by the figure, Datura species are just outside the top 20 and DXM is a further dissociative near the top.

reporting_issues.issue: No test statistics or exact p values are printed for the pairwise Wilcoxon tests (Fig. 4B marks only p<0.05) or for the one-way ANOVAs on the NDE background variables, whose number is not stated; the error bars in the Fig. 8 sub-panels are not defined.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statistical statements about drug classes and NDE subsets cannot be checked from the paper.
