design_detail: KetECT: randomized, parallel-group, open-label, multicentre non-inferiority trial at six Swedish clinics (Lund, Malmö, Örebro, Helsingborg, Linköping and one patient in Halmstad). 199 hospitalized adults aged 18 to 85 with DSM-IV unipolar depression (MADRS 20 or more) who were already scheduled for ECT were randomized 1:1 to racemic ketamine infusions or ECT, each three times a week for up to 12 sessions, until remission or maximal effect as judged by the treating psychiatrist, with a stop after 6 sessions for less than 25% MADRS reduction; 186 who received at least one session were analysed (95 ketamine, 91 ECT). Primary outcome: remission (MADRS 10 or lower, sustained over at least 2 sessions or 5 days) after the completed series, rated by unblinded treating staff; the non-inferiority margin was stated as a ketamine remission rate of 40% against an assumed 60% with ECT. Remitters were followed for 12 months for relapse. Psychotic depression was included. Registered in EudraCT (2011-001520-37) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02659085); funded by the Swedish Research Council and Swedish foundations.
can_establish: Whether, in inpatients with unipolar depression (psychotic depression included) already scheduled for ECT at Swedish university clinics, a flexible course of up to 12 ketamine infusions led to clinician-rated remission as often as a course of ECT given in the same setting, and how the two courses compared on symptom change, early discontinuation and adverse events judged treatment-related.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine works better than placebo (no placebo arm); comparative effects free of rater and patient expectations (open label, depression rated by the treating staff); effects in outpatients or in people with bipolar disorder, primary psychosis or substance use disorder (not recruited or excluded); whether ECT's advantage is really confined to patients over 50 and absent in younger or present in psychotic depression (post hoc subgroups of 14 to 59 patients); comparative relapse or long-term outcome (only remitters were followed, under continuation treatment the article does not describe); or rare harms.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: hospitalized patients scheduled for ECT at the participating university hospitals were screened and told of a study comparing ECT with a new experimental treatment; none were recruited through referrals or advertisements (p. 340; p. 347). Of 622 screened, 283 did not meet the criteria (67 bipolar disorder, 63 coercive care, 30 primary psychosis, 25 substance use disorder, 17 severe personality disorder, 17 severe somatic illness, 16 DSM criteria not fulfilled, 48 other reasons) and 140 of the 339 eligible declined (Figure 1, p. 342). Most analysed patients were treated in Lund (58 ECT, 56 ketamine; Table 1, p. 343). The article gives no recruitment period.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Hospitalized patients aged 18 to 85 with DSM-IV unipolar depression and MADRS 20 or more, scheduled for ECT (p. 340). The full criteria are in supplementary Table 1, not read. Suicidal patients and patients with comorbid psychiatric conditions were not excluded, and there was no medication washout (p. 347). Psychotic depression was included. Earlier treatment failure is not named as a criterion in the main text.
sample.demographics: ECT 91 and ketamine 95: mean age 50 (SD 18, range 20 to 85) and 55 (SD 18, range 18 to 84); women 58/91 (64%) and 61/95 (64%); body mass index 27.6 and 25.5; psychotic symptoms 14/91 (15%) and 18/95 (19%); previous ECT 34/91 (37%) and 40/95 (42%); previous suicide attempt 46/90 (51%) and 38/95 (40%); self-harm 21/89 (24%) and 12/92 (13%); median current episode 14 weeks in both; antidepressants at inclusion 77 (85%) and 75 (79%) (Table 1, p. 343). Patients older than 50: 39 of 91 and 59 of 95 (Table 2, p. 344).
sample.attrition: 13 of 199 randomized were excluded from the main analysis (8 erroneous inclusions, 5 who regretted participation and received no treatment); the arms of the 8 are not reported. Before the 2-week (6-session) evaluation, 21 of 95 stopped ketamine (2 serious adverse events, 10 adverse events, 8 dropped out, 1 non-compliant) and 4 of 91 stopped ECT (2 serious adverse events, 1 adverse event, 1 non-compliant); they remain in the analysed totals, since Figure 1 classifies all 95 and 91 as remitters, responders or non-responders (p. 342). In follow-up, time to relapse or continued remission was obtained for all but 1 remitter, and 27 patients missed at least one visit (p. 341).
sample.selection_effects: Inpatients already scheduled for ECT who accepted randomization to a new treatment; 140 of 339 eligible declined, some because of good earlier experience of ECT, which the authors say may have favoured ketamine (p. 347). Bipolar disorder, coercive care, primary psychosis and substance use disorder were common reasons for ineligibility. All sites had long experience of ECT and none of ketamine (p. 347). Randomization left the ketamine group older (more than half over 50: 59 of 95 against 39 of 91), which matters because age interacted with treatment in a post hoc analysis; standardized to the combined age distribution, remission is 65.5% after ECT and 48.6% after ketamine (editors' calculation from Table 2), so the age imbalance does not explain the overall difference.

exposure.measurement: Treatments were given in hospital by the trial sites; the number of sessions was recorded (Table 2, p. 344). Concomitant medications were unrestricted and changes were recorded from 4 weeks before to 2 weeks after inclusion (p. 341; p. 342).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: racemic ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes; ECT under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants and oxygenation, stimulus set by age and sex (electrode placement and other parameters are in supplementary Table 2, not read; Rhee et al., 2022, Table 1, describe it as right unilateral). Both three times a week in the morning, up to 12 sessions over about 4 weeks, until remission or maximal effect as judged by the treating psychiatrist; less than 25% MADRS reduction after 6 sessions ended study treatment (p. 341). Sessions given: ECT mean 7.8 (SD 2.4), median 8 (IQR 6 to 10); ketamine mean 6.8 (SD 3.3), median 6 (IQR 5 to 9) (Table 2, p. 344).
exposure.polysubstance: Concomitant psychiatric medications were allowed without restriction: at inclusion, ECT and ketamine groups took antidepressants 85% and 79%, anxiolytics 69% and 61%, hypnotics 75% and 64%, antipsychotics 20 patients (printed 24%) and 18 (19%), mood stabilizers 16% and 9% (Table 1, p. 343). Changes in medication around inclusion did not differ between groups (P = .91) (p. 342). Substance use disorder was a reason for ineligibility (Figure 1, p. 342); participants' alcohol and other drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; ongoing medication allowed and no washout (p. 347).

comparison.controls: Active comparator: ECT as given at the sites; no placebo or sham arm. The authors justify the absence of placebo by earlier placebo-controlled ketamine trials and by the ethics of withholding active treatment from inpatients (p. 347).
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1 in blocks of 6 per site, by sequentially numbered sealed envelopes opened after consent, from a scheme made by a statistician not otherwise involved (pp. 340–341). Baseline differences: age (mean 55 against 50), previous suicide attempt (40% against 51%), self-harm (13% against 24%), previous psychotherapy (55% against 69%), body mass index (Table 1, p. 343). The primary comparison is unadjusted.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison. Expectations were measured after randomization: hope of improvement 6.3 with ECT and 5.8 with ketamine (P = .32), fear of negative outcomes 4.2 and 4.6 (P = .37) (Table 2, p. 344).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same rules in both arms: concomitant medications unrestricted, with drug adjustments following the same procedures (p. 341).

outcomes.instruments: MADRS, clinician-rated, at baseline, 4 to 5 hours after the first session, the day after each later session and at follow-up; remission: MADRS 10 or lower persisting over at least 2 sessions or 5 days (temporary scores of 10 or lower followed by higher ones did not count); response: at least 50% fall after a complete series of 1 to 12 sessions; relapse: the clinical judgment that a patient again met criteria for depression, from patient information at follow-ups at 1 week and 3, 6 and 12 months, confirmed from medical records if needed; modified Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (items 7 to 11, 14, 15, 20 and 22 to 24) and CADSS at baseline, 1 hour, 4 to 5 hours, the next day and after 6 sessions; adverse events listed by patients at each MADRS rating, with causality classified by the investigator and only events judged very likely or probably related analysed; visual analogue scales of expectations and fears after randomization (p. 341).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments (MADRS, BPRS, CADSS) cited; raters trained with video material and discussion; no inter-rater reliability reported (p. 341).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit as remission and MADRS change after the completed series; harm as investigator-attributed adverse events, their duration and serious adverse events. Memory was not tested: amnesia appears only as a reported adverse event.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: all P values are uncorrected (Table 2 footnote, p. 344). 64 counts the between-group P values in Table 2 (27, of which 4 are baseline comparisons) and Table 3 (33 adverse-event types and 4 summary rows); the text adds more (long-lasting events by type, CADSS and BPRS at several times, sessions in non-responders). The age, sex and site interactions and the psychotic-depression subgroup were not prespecified in the protocol (p. 341; Table 2 footnote a).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: neither raters nor patients were blinded (p. 341). MADRS ratings were made by the treating staff as part of the clinical interaction, together with adverse-event recording, and the authors rejected independent raters (p. 347). The treating psychiatrist also judged when maximal effect was reached.

analysis.effect_sizes: Remission 57/91 (63%) after ECT against 44/95 (46%) after ketamine: chi-square 5.0, P = .026, odds ratio 0.51 (0.29 to 0.92), 95% CI of the difference 2.0% to 30% (Newcombe) (p. 341). Editors' calculations: difference 16.3 percentage points; about 6 patients treated with ECT rather than ketamine for one more remission; the upper limit of 30 points exceeds the margin of about 20 points implied by the design. With the 5 who regretted participation: 57/94 (61%) against 44/97 (45%), P = .034, CI 1.1% to 29%. Final MADRS 12.2 (SD 11.1) against 16.9 (SD 13.1), P = .009, difference CI 1.2 to 8.2, Cohen d 0.40; MADRS fall 22.4 (SD 11.4) against 16.1 (SD 12.0), P < .001, CI 2.9 to 9.7, d 0.53 (p. 342; Table 2, p. 344). Post hoc: aged 18 to 50, remission 26/52 (50%) against 22/36 (61%), P = .39; aged 51 to 85, 31/39 (printed 77%) against 22/59 (37%), P < .001; treatment by age-group interaction Wald chi-square 12.6, P < .001 (Table 2 gives ExpB 12.6, 95% CI 3.1 to 51.2); psychotic depression 11/14 (79%) against 9/18 (50%), P = .15. Editors' Newcombe intervals for ECT minus ketamine: aged 18 to 50, −11.1 points (−30.4 to 9.8); aged 51 to 85, 42.2 (22.5 to 57.0); psychotic depression 28.6 (−5.0 to 53.7). Relapse among remitters 36/56 (64%) against 31/44 (70%), hazard ratio 0.83 (0.51 to 1.34), direction of the ratio not stated (p. 345).
analysis.covariates: Primary comparison unadjusted (chi-square). Post hoc binary logistic regression with treatment, age group (18 to 50, 51 to 85), sex and site, and the interaction of each with treatment (p. 341).
analysis.preregistration_detail: EudraCT 2011-001520-37 and ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02659085 (p. 340); ethics approval Lund 2011/796. Neither registry record nor the protocol was read, and the article gives no recruitment period, so whether registration preceded enrolment and whether the registered outcome and margin match cannot be checked here. Analyses not specified in the protocol are named as post hoc (p. 341).
analysis.selective_reporting: No test against the non-inferiority margin is reported: the Results give a chi-square test of difference and the interval of the difference, and the statement that non-inferiority was not demonstrated appears only in the Conclusion (p. 348). CADSS and BPRS values are not given, only P = .01 at 1 hour (p. 345). Blood pressure is not reported and Table 3 has no row for raised blood pressure, although the introduction lists hypertension among common acute effects of ketamine (p. 340). The abstract's median days in remission (57 and 61) appear nowhere else. Additional outcomes and outcome by site are in supplementary Tables 3 and 4 (not read).
analysis.power: Planned 97 per group (5% significance, 80% power), assuming 60% remission with ECT and a 40% limit for ketamine; the authors state that ketamine would have needed about 54% remission to show non-inferiority (p. 340). Analysed 91 and 95. ECT remission (63%) was close to the assumption; ketamine remission (46%) was below 54%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 186 inpatients scheduled for ECT, remission after a flexible course of up to 12 sessions was 63% with ECT and 46% with ketamine infusions (difference 16 points, 95% CI 2 to 30), so ECT did better and the trial's non-inferiority margin could not be met. Depression scores fell more with ECT (d 0.53). Remission came no faster with ketamine: cumulative remission was 11% and 10% after 3 sessions and 39% and 25% after 6 (Figure 3B). Ketamine was stopped early far more often (21 of 95 against 4 of 91 before 2 weeks, mostly for adverse events), while more ECT patients reported long-lasting adverse events (49 against 21 patients), more headache, muscle pain and amnesia, with amnesia unresolved at 12 months in 3 patients; serious adverse events were 23 against 14 patients (P = .09). In post hoc subgroups the difference was concentrated in patients over 50. About two-thirds of remitters in each group relapsed within 12 months.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract calls ketamine a safe and valuable tool (p. 339) and the Significance Statement says racemic ketamine is safe and effective, including in psychotic depression (p. 340): effectiveness cannot be shown without a placebo arm, the psychotic-depression evidence is 18 patients given ketamine in a post hoc subgroup with 50% remission, and 95 patients cannot establish safety beyond common events. The abstract also says serious adverse events were more common with ECT, a difference that was not statistically significant (23/90 against 14/91, P = .09; p. 345). (2) The Significance Statement says younger patients seem to respond as well to ketamine as to ECT (p. 340), from a post hoc subgroup whose difference the editors estimate at −11 points (−30 to 10); the Conclusion says ECT's high remission in older and psychotic patients was "confirmed in this study" (p. 348), though both analyses were post hoc and the psychotic comparison was not significant. (3) The abstract says no head-to-head trial had been performed (p. 339) and the Introduction calls this the first trial with an active control (p. 340), qualified elsewhere as the first with an adequate sample size (pp. 340, 345); its own reference list includes an earlier small comparison of repeated ketamine with ECT in hospitalized patients (Ghasemi et al., 2014). (4) The abstract gives relapse of 70% with ketamine and 63% with ECT, P = .52, and median days in remission of 57 and 61 (p. 339); the Results give 36/56 (64%) for ECT, a log-rank P of .44 and a time-to-relapse P of .30, and no median days (p. 345). (5) The Conclusion's statement that ketamine's effect was "not necessarily transient" (p. 348) rests on 13 of 44 ketamine remitters relapse-free at 12 months under unreported continuation treatment. Against this, the abstract and Conclusion state plainly that ketamine was inferior and that non-inferiority was not demonstrated.

timeline.event: Berman et al.: cited by KetECT among trials showing ketamine's superiority over placebo infusions and among studies reporting 30% to 50% remission after one infusion (pp. 346–347).
Zarate et al.: randomized trial in treatment-resistant depression, cited by KetECT for the same two points (pp. 346–347).
Ghasemi et al.: small randomized comparison of repeated ketamine with ECT in hospitalized patients (18 patients, per Rhee et al., 2022, Table 1), in KetECT's reference list.
This trial: remission 63% after ECT against 46% after ketamine in 186 inpatients; non-inferiority of ketamine not shown.

Rhee et al.: meta-analysis of six ketamine–ECT trials in which KetECT supplies 186 of 340 patients and about half the weight of the pooled symptom-severity estimate favouring ECT (SMD −0.69); remission was not pooled.

Anand et al. (ELEKT-D): 403 mostly outpatients with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression, ketamine twice weekly for 3 weeks against ECT; self-rated response noninferior (55.4% against 41.2%) and remission higher with ketamine (a secondary outcome whose intervals, by the table footnote, are not adjusted for multiple comparisons; Anand et al., 2023, Table 2, p. 2322), as recorded on the card sc_anand_2023.

replication.where_it_stands: The two large randomized comparisons disagree. KetECT (inpatients, psychotic depression included, older on average, ketamine three times a week for up to 12 sessions, clinician-rated remission) favoured ECT; ELEKT-D (mostly outpatients without psychosis, ketamine twice a week for 3 weeks, self-rated response) found ketamine noninferior and remission higher with ketamine, a secondary outcome not adjusted for multiple comparisons (per sc_anand_2023). Both were open label with unblinded ratings, and they differ in population, schedule, ECT technique and outcome, so neither design can show why. The meta-analysis by Rhee et al. (2022) predates ELEKT-D and is half KetECT, so it is not independent support for KetECT. KetECT's age interaction is post hoc and untested elsewhere in the sources read here.

funding.funder: Swedish Research Council (grant 2015-00799), the Crafoord Foundation, Skåne Regional Council, the Königska Foundation, Lions forsknings foundation Skåne and the OM Perssons donation foundation (p. 348); the funding sources had no role in any aspect of the study (p. 341). The paper was edited by a commercial editing service (p. 348).
funding.declared_conflicts: Three authors (A.N., J.E. and P.M.R.) have received lecture honoraria from Lundbeck (p. 348).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Lund, Linköping and Örebro universities and the participating psychiatric clinics; the sites had long experience of ECT and none of ketamine (p. 347). No industry funding of the trial. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of ketamine and ECT with depression rated by assessors unaware of the assignment, a prespecified narrow non-inferiority margin, both inpatients and outpatients with randomization stratified by age and psychotic features so that the age interaction is tested as a primary hypothesis, the same session frequency in both arms, and randomized continuation treatment with relapse followed over 12 months in all patients.

domains.note: Sequentially numbered sealed envelopes opened after consent, blocks of 6 per site, scheme from an independent statistician (pp. 340–341); opacity of the envelopes is not stated. Eight patients were excluded after randomization as erroneously included, arm not reported. The ketamine group was older (59 of 95 against 39 of 91 over 50), a prognostic imbalance given the age interaction, though age standardization does not remove the difference (editors' calculation).

Open label for patients and staff; the number of sessions was left to the treating psychiatrist, who knew the assignment; 21 of 95 stopped ketamine before 2 weeks, which the authors partly attribute to staff and patients being unprepared for ketamine's effects and to knowing ECT was available afterwards (p. 347). Patients who stopped were kept in the analysis as not remitted; medication changes did not differ (P = .91).

Remission was available for all 186 treated; the 5 who regretted participation were added in a sensitivity analysis with the same result; the 8 erroneous inclusions (4% of 199) are unlikely to change it. How final MADRS was obtained for patients who stopped early is not stated.

Remission is a clinician rating made by the treating staff, who knew the assignment, also recorded adverse events and decided how many sessions to give, at sites with long experience of ECT and none of ketamine; the authors rejected independent raters (p. 347). The direction of any bias cannot be known.
Registered, with post hoc analyses labelled, but the registry records and protocol were not read, the recruitment period is not given, and no test against the stated margin is reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Allocation was concealed in sealed envelopes and the primary outcome was available for nearly all randomized patients, with early stoppers counted as not remitted, so attrition is unlikely to explain the result. The overall judgment is high because remission was rated by unblinded treating staff who also controlled how much treatment each patient received; expectation could have favoured either arm. The source can be cited for the remission and MADRS differences between these two courses in inpatients scheduled for ECT, for early discontinuation, and for adverse events judged treatment-related; it cannot be cited for ketamine's efficacy against placebo, for age or psychotic-depression effects as established findings (post hoc, small), for comparative relapse (remitters only, continuation treatment unreported), or for rare harms.

key_findings.finding: Randomized, parallel, open-label, multicentre non-inferiority trial at six Swedish clinics; allocation 1:1 by sequentially numbered sealed envelopes opened after consent, in blocks of 6 per site, from a scheme made by a statistician not otherwise involved; neither patients nor raters were blinded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design (p. 340); Methods › Patients and Randomization, 2nd paragraph (pp. 340–341); Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 341)

key_findings.finding: Non-inferiority margin: assuming 60% remission with ECT, the margin for ketamine was set at a remission rate of 40%; 97 patients per group were planned (5% significance, 80% power), and the authors state that about 54% remission with ketamine would have been needed to show with 95% confidence that it was not below 40%.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with 97 per group, 60% against 54% gives an upper 95% limit for the difference of 19.9 percentage points, so the margin works as a difference of about 20 points; the article does not state it as a difference.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 622 inpatients scheduled for ECT screened; 283 did not meet criteria (67 bipolar disorder, 63 coercive care, 30 primary psychosis, 25 substance use disorder, 17 severe personality disorder, 17 severe somatic illness, 16 DSM criteria not fulfilled, 48 other); 140 of 339 eligible declined; 199 randomized; 13 excluded after randomization (8 erroneous inclusion, 5 regretted participation); 95 received ketamine and 91 ECT and form the main analysis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 341); Figure 1 (p. 342)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image without a text layer; its numbers were read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: racemic ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously over 40 minutes, or ECT under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants, stimulus set by age and sex; both three times a week, up to 12 sessions, until remission or maximal effect as judged by the treating psychiatrist; less than 25% MADRS reduction after 6 sessions ended study treatment; concomitant medications unrestricted.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Treatments

key_findings.finding: Baseline (ECT 91, ketamine 95): mean age 50 (SD 18; range 20–85) and 55 (SD 18; range 18–84); women 64% in both; psychotic symptoms 14/91 (15%) and 18/95 (19%); previous ECT 34/91 (37%) and 40/95 (42%); previous suicide attempt 46/90 (51%) and 38/95 (40%); self-harm 21/89 (24%) and 12/92 (13%); MADRS 34.5 (SD 5.7) and 33.1 (SD 6.3), P = .11.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 343); Results › Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 342)

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: remission in 57 of 91 (63%) after ECT and 44 of 95 (46%) after ketamine (chi-square 5.0, P = .026; odds ratio 0.51, 0.29 to 0.92); 95% CI of the difference 2.0% to 30% (Newcombe). Including the 5 randomized patients who regretted participation: 57/94 (61%) against 44/97 (45%), P = .034, CI 1.1% to 29%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome: Remission Rates (p. 341); Table 2, remission rows (p. 344)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: difference 16.3 percentage points; about 6 patients treated with ECT rather than ketamine for one more remission. The authors conclude that non-inferiority of ketamine was not demonstrated (Conclusion, p. 348).

key_findings.finding: Depression scores: final MADRS 12.2 (SD 11.1) after ECT against 16.9 (SD 13.1) after ketamine (P = .009; difference CI 1.2 to 8.2; Cohen d 0.40); fall from baseline 22.4 (SD 11.4) against 16.1 (SD 12.0) (P < .001; CI 2.9 to 9.7; d 0.53).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 342); Table 2, MADRS rows (p. 344)

key_findings.finding: Cumulative remission by session, ECT against ketamine: 0% and 0% 4 to 5 hours after the first session; 0% and 3% after session 1; 11% and 10% after session 3; 39% and 25% after session 6; 57% and 41% after session 9; 63% and 46% after session 12. Remitters needed a mean of 6.0 (SD 2.3) ECT and 6.0 (SD 2.7) ketamine sessions (median 6 in both; P = .84).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3B (p. 345); Table 2, number of treatments (p. 344); Results › Secondary Outcomes, 4th paragraph (p. 345)

key_findings.finding: Sessions given: ECT mean 7.8 (SD 2.4), median 8 (IQR 6–10); ketamine mean 6.8 (SD 3.3), median 6 (IQR 5–9) (P = .02); the difference was confined to non-responders (7.2 against 5.2, P = .002).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 344); Results › Secondary Outcomes, 4th paragraph (p. 345)

key_findings.finding: Discontinuation before the 2-week (6-session) evaluation: 21 of 95 with ketamine (2 serious adverse events, 10 adverse events, 8 dropped out, 1 non-compliant) against 4 of 91 with ECT (2 serious adverse events, 1 adverse event, 1 non-compliant); at the evaluation 15 and 10 more were stopped for less than 25% MADRS reduction. Final classification: ketamine 44 remitters, 10 responders, 41 non-responders; ECT 57, 8 and 26.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 and Results › Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 342); Results › Adverse Events (p. 345)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: early discontinuation 22% against 4%. Eight ketamine discontinuations are attributed to a combination of lack of improvement and discomfort from the infusions (p. 345). The breakdowns and final classification come from Figure 1, an image read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Post hoc age subgroups: aged 18–50, remission 26/52 (50%) after ECT and 22/36 (61%) after ketamine (P = .39; final MADRS 14.8 against 12.9, P = .41); aged 51–85, 31/39 (printed 77%) against 22/59 (37%) (chi-square 16.8, P < .001; odds ratio 0.15; final MADRS 8.7 against 19.4, P < .001). Treatment by age-group interaction: Wald chi-square 12.6, P < .001; no interaction with sex (P = .19) or with site.
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 342, 344); Table 2 (p. 344)
key_findings.note: Not prespecified in the protocol (p. 341; Table 2 footnote a). 31/39 is 79.5% (editors' arithmetic). Editors' Newcombe intervals for ECT minus ketamine: aged 18–50, −11.1 points (−30.4 to 9.8); aged 51–85, 42.2 points (22.5 to 57.0).

key_findings.finding: Post hoc psychotic depression subgroup: remission 11/14 (79%) after ECT against 9/18 (50%) after ketamine (P = .15; odds ratio 0.27, 0.056 to 1.3); final MADRS 10.1 against 19.4 (P = .069; d 0.68); no interaction between treatment and psychotic symptoms (P = .41). The authors report no indications of adverse reactions particular to these patients.
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 342, 344–345); Table 2 (p. 344); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 347)
key_findings.note: Editors' Newcombe interval for ECT minus ketamine: 28.6 points (−5.0 to 53.7).

key_findings.finding: Expectations, rated after randomization and before treatment on a visual analogue scale: hope of improvement 6.3 (SD 2.7) with ECT and 5.8 (SD 3.1) with ketamine (P = .32); fear of negative outcomes 4.2 (SD 3.0) and 4.6 (SD 2.9) (P = .37).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 4th paragraph (p. 341); Table 2 (p. 344)
key_findings.note: The text on p. 345 gives 5.3 for ketamine; only Table 2's 5.8 fits the printed P and interval (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Adverse events judged very likely or probably treatment-related, counted as patients reporting them (ECT n = 90, ketamine n = 91): any, 85 and 85 patients; events per participant 7.8 (SD 5.4) and 12.0 (SD 10.9) (P < .001); lasting more than 24 hours, 49 and 21 patients (P < .001). More frequent with ECT: headache 72 against 20, muscle pain 48 against 13, amnesia 26 against 8, desaturation 12 against 4, tachycardia or bradycardia 6 against 0. More frequent with ketamine: vertigo 63 against 22, dissociative symptoms 55 against 14, anxiety 41 against 16, diplopia 28 against 2, salivation or dry mouth 22 against 1, euphoria 19 against 0, blurred vision 18 against 0, affect lability 11 against 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events (p. 345); Table 3 (p. 346)

key_findings.finding: 19 ECT patients and no ketamine patient reported amnesia lasting more than 24 hours (median duration 28 days, range 1 to 365, where 365 means unresolved at 12 months); the text says 21 ECT recipients reported prolonged amnesia, which resolved only after 3 to 6 months in 3 and persisted through the 12-month follow-up in 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events (p. 345); Table 3 and footnote a (p. 346)

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events: at least one in 23 of 90 ECT patients and 14 of 91 ketamine patients (chi-square 2.6, P = .09); 11 and 2 were judged very likely or probably treatment-caused. With ECT: hypertonia, amnesia (4), deep-vein thrombosis, hypoxia, post-treatment catatonia and seizures (the last two in one patient); with ketamine: two panic attacks during the first infusion, after which both patients declined further infusions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events (p. 345); Table 3 (p. 346)

key_findings.finding: Aggregated CADSS and BPRS scores were higher with ketamine 1 hour after the first session (P = .01) but not at other time points; no values are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events

key_findings.finding: Suicide: one ECT patient died by suicide 3 months after remitting following 12 sessions; 9 other patients attempted suicide during follow-up (5 ECT, 4 ketamine). Table 3 lists 6 and 4 patients attempting suicide and 1 and 0 suicides.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events (p. 345); Table 3 (p. 346)
key_findings.note: Denominators for the follow-up period are not stated; only remitters were followed.

key_findings.finding: Relapse within 12 months among remitters: 36 of 56 (64%) after ECT against 31 of 44 (70%) after ketamine (log-rank P = .44; hazard ratio 0.83, 0.51 to 1.34); time to relapse did not differ (chi-square 0.061, P = .30). Relapse was the clinical judgment that a patient again met criteria for depression; continuation treatment is not described.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 341); Table 2, relapse rows (p. 344); Results › Relapse (p. 345); Figure 4 (p. 347)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: in remission without relapse at 12 months, 20 of 91 treated with ECT (22%) and 13 of 95 treated with ketamine (14%), the one ECT remitter without follow-up not counted as relapse-free; difference 8.3 points (−2.8 to 19.3). The relapse comparison itself is among remitters only and is not randomized.

key_findings.finding: Medication changes (dose changes, switches or added antidepressants from 4 weeks before to 2 weeks after inclusion) did not differ between groups (P = .91) or between remitters, responders and non-responders (P = .62).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: no placebo group; open label, with MADRS rated together with adverse-event recording as part of the physician–patient interaction and independent raters rejected; some potential participants declined because of good earlier experience of ECT, which the authors say might have introduced a small potential bias in favour of ketamine; the sites had long experience of ECT and none of ketamine, and staff, and some patients, were less prepared for ketamine's psychological adverse effects, which, with knowing ECT was available after the study, probably contributed to the higher dropout with ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe an intention-to-treat analysis of all randomized patients, but it includes 94 ECT and 97 ketamine patients, short of the 199 randomized: the 8 erroneously included patients are left out and their arms are not reported (editors' arithmetic: 191 of 199 analysed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The intention-to-treat result is a modified analysis, and the number randomized to each arm is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The non-inferiority margin is stated as a ketamine remission rate (40%) against an assumed ECT rate (60%), and no test against the margin is reported: the Results give a chi-square test of difference and the interval of the difference, and the statement that non-inferiority was not shown appears only in the Conclusion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers must infer that the upper 95% limit of the difference (30 points) exceeds an implied margin of about 20 points (editors' calculation). Claims should say that ECT did better and non-inferiority was not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: Relapse is reported three ways: the abstract gives 70% (ketamine) and 63% (ECT) with P = .52 and median days in remission of 57 and 61; the Results give 31/44 (70%) and 36/56 (64%), log-rank P = .44 and, for time to relapse, chi-square 0.061 with P = .30; Figure 4's legend gives 57 ECT remitters.
reporting_issues.consequence: A chi-square of 0.061 corresponds to P of about .80 (editors' calculation). The median days appear nowhere else, and Figure 4's curves fall to 50% only at about 100 days with ketamine and about 180 days with ECT (read from the figure, approximate), so they cannot be the median time to relapse of all remitters. Cite the counts in the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse-event counts differ between the text and Table 3: patients with long-lasting adverse events 48/90 and 20/91 in the text against 49 and 21 in the table; long-lasting muscle pain 28/90 in the text against 26; prolonged amnesia in 21 ECT recipients in the text against 19 with long-lasting amnesia in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the table values and note the discrepancy; no conclusion changes.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's denominators (90 ECT, 91 ketamine) differ from the treated groups (91 and 95) without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Adverse-event data are missing for 1 ECT and 4 ketamine patients (editors' arithmetic); rates should use 90 and 91.

reporting_issues.issue: Values that do not match each other: ketamine hope of improvement is 5.3 in the text and 5.8 in Table 2; the ECT MADRS fall in psychotic depression is 27.8 in the text and 27.0 in Table 2 (baseline 37.1 minus final 10.1 gives 27.0); the upper limit of the baseline MADRS interval is 3.4 in the text and 3.2 in Table 2; Table 2 prints the final-MADRS interval for psychotic depression with the opposite sign to the other rows; Table 1 prints 6/95 as 9% and 20/91 as 24%; and 31/39 is printed as 77% in the text and Table 2 (editors' arithmetic: 79.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors without effect on the conclusions; cite table values and recompute percentages from counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Several P values do not match the chi-square statistics printed beside them: aged 18–50 (chi-square 1.1, P = .39), psychotic depression (2.7, P = .15) and the ketamine age contrast (5.1, P = .034). The printed P values agree with Fisher's exact test, while the chi-square values correspond to P of about .30, .10 and .024 (editors' calculation); the Methods name only chi-square tests.
reporting_issues.consequence: No conclusion changes, but the tests used are not fully described.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals printed with Cohen's d for final MADRS in the age subgroups (0.18 [0.036, 0.40] for ages 18–50; 0.91 [0.68, 1.13] for ages 51–85) match d plus or minus one standard error rather than 95% intervals (editors' calculation: about −0.25 to 0.60 and 0.45 to 1.30); the first appears to have lost a minus sign and excludes zero although P = .41.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the subgroup effect sizes is overstated in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The article gives no recruitment period, and the registration dates are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether registration preceded enrolment cannot be checked from the article (the registry records were not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote of Table 3 says only adverse events judged very likely or probably treatment-related are included, yet its serious-adverse-event row (23 and 14 patients) exceeds the 11 and 2 serious adverse events the text says were so judged; the printed chi-square of 2.6 corresponds to a P of about .11, not the printed .09 (editors' calculation from the counts: chi-square 2.9, P = .09).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which serious adverse events the table counts is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results report a treatment by psychotic-symptoms interaction (P = .41, p. 342), but psychotic symptoms are not among the regression terms the Methods name (treatment, age group, sex, site and their interactions with treatment, p. 341).
reporting_issues.consequence: How that interaction was tested is not described.

design_detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022338045) of clinical trials comparing ketamine with ECT in people with a major depressive episode. PubMed, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library and Embase were searched from inception to 19 April 2022 without language limits, with US and EU trial registries, Google Scholar and reference lists searched by hand. Six trials with 340 patients (162 ECT, 178 ketamine; five randomized, one non-randomized open-label) were included, KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022) supplying 186 of them. Primary outcome: improvement in depressive symptoms as Hedges g, pooled in two stages (several measures combined within a trial by a 3-level model, then one effect per trial), with a fixed-effect model when I² was below 50% and a random-effects model above 50%; adverse events as Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios; meta-regression and subgroup moderator analyses; RoB 2; Egger and Begg-Mazumdar tests. Remission and response were not pooled.
can_establish: The average standardized difference in end-of-course improvement in depressive symptoms between ECT and ketamine across six trials in inpatient ECT candidates published up to April 2022, and the relative risks of common acute adverse events reported in three of those trials.
cannot_establish: Whether ketamine brings remission or response less often than ECT (neither was pooled); anything independent of KetECT, which supplies 186 of 340 patients and about half the weight of the main estimate (editors' calculation); what the later ELEKT-D trial adds (not yet published, described as ongoing); effects in outpatients, or patient-level effects of age or psychotic features (moderators are study-level, with six trials); relapse, long-term outcome or cognition (one or two trials each, not pooled); or freedom from small-study bias (six trials, small trials showing the largest effects: the smallest trial (18 patients) shows the smallest effect and the two largest effects come from the 22- and 25-patient trials).

sample.recruitment: Database search (PubMed, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Embase) from inception to 19 April 2022 with MeSH terms and keywords and no language limits; US and EU trial registries and Google Scholar searched by hand by two authors; reference lists. 1248 records, 60 eligible after screening, 56 excluded at full text, 2 added by hand search (pp. 1162–1164).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human clinical trials of patients with depression diagnosed by standardized criteria (DSM or ICD-10), with ECT and ketamine as intervention and comparator, and depressive symptom severity on a standardized measure (for example MADRS, HDRS); suicidal ideation, cognition or memory, and adverse events as further outcomes. Excluded: non-human studies and studies without standardized depression measures (p. 1163).
sample.demographics: Trials from Germany (Basso et al., 2020: 50 patients, non-randomized open-label), Sweden (KetECT: 186, open-label randomized), Iran (Ghasemi et al., 2014: 18, blind randomized; Kheirabadi et al., 2019: 22, blind randomized; Kheirabadi et al., 2020: 39, open-label randomized, intramuscular and oral ketamine) and India (Sharma et al., 2020: 25, blind randomized, bipolar or unipolar depression). All inpatients and ECT candidates; mean ages 37.6 to 52.5; men 33% to 59%. Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously in five trials and 0.5 mg/kg intramuscularly or 1.0 mg/kg orally in one; ECT right unilateral in two trials, bilateral in three, bifrontal or right unilateral in one; courses of 1 to 4 weeks (Table 1, p. 1165).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within trials is not tabulated (KetECT's higher dropout with ketamine is mentioned under risk of bias, p. 1168).
sample.selection_effects: Six trials, four from Iran or India with 18 to 39 patients; two of the six were found only by hand search, not by the database search (p. 1164). KetECT carries 49% of the fixed-effect weight (editors' calculation from Figure 1B). Inpatient ECT candidates only. ELEKT-D, a planned 400-patient trial in unipolar treatment-resistant depression, was ongoing and is described but not included (p. 1169).

exposure.measurement: As delivered in each trial; numbers of infusions or sessions are given in Table 1 where the trials reported them (p. 1165).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, from Table 1 (p. 1165): ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously (five trials) or 0.5 mg/kg intramuscularly or 1.0 mg/kg orally (one trial), two or three times a week; ECT three times a week in most trials; courses of 1 to 4 weeks. Table 1's KetECT row gives ketamine three times a week for 2 weeks with a range of 5 to 9 infusions; the KetECT article gave both treatments three times a week for up to 12 sessions and reports 5 to 9 as an interquartile range (see reporting issues).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: concomitant medications in the trials are not extracted.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: ECT in each trial (right unilateral, bilateral, or bifrontal or right unilateral); no placebo.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; one included trial (Basso et al., 2020) was not randomized.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; patient-level predictors were not extracted, and moderators were study-level (sample size, mean age, % men, region, randomization, ECT type, inclusion of psychotic features).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Depression: MADRS (2 trials), HDRS (4 trials) and BDI (2 trials), combined as Hedges g of improvement; suicidal ideation: Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation (1 trial); cognition (1 trial) and memory (Wechsler Memory Scale, 1 trial), described, not pooled; adverse events as risk ratios (headache, muscle pain, blurred vision, diplopia or nystagmus, vertigo, dissociative or depersonalization symptoms, nausea); serious adverse events from KetECT only (pp. 1164–1167).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard depression rating scales; trials appraised with RoB 2.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy is the end-of-course difference in symptom improvement as a standardized mean difference (negative values favour ECT). Remission and response are not analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two-sided P < .05, p. 1164). 18 counts the pooled depression estimates (3 by measure and 1 overall), 7 adverse-event risk ratios and 7 moderator tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Titles, abstracts and full texts were screened and data extracted independently by two reviewers (pp. 1163–1164).

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall pooled SMD, ECT against ketamine, −0.69 (95% CI −0.89 to −0.48), 6 trials, fixed effect, Cochran Q P = .15, I² 39%, τ² 0.0368. By measure: MADRS −0.59 (−0.85 to −0.33), 2 trials, I² 0%; HDRS −0.83 (−1.22 to −0.44), 4 trials with 5 comparisons, I² 22%; BDI −0.86 (−1.50 to −0.22), 2 trials, I² 60% (pp. 1164, 1166). Editors' calculations from Figure 1B: KetECT carries 49% of the fixed-effect weight; a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model gives −0.73 (−1.02 to −0.44) with an approximate 95% prediction interval of −1.47 to 0.01; without KetECT the fixed-effect estimate is −0.79 (−1.08 to −0.50). Risk ratios, ketamine against ECT: headache 0.37 (0.18 to 0.76), muscle pain 0.23 (0.13 to 0.38), blurred vision 26.47 (3.62 to 193.67), diplopia or nystagmus 10.88 (3.52 to 33.63), vertigo 2.99 (2.03 to 4.40), dissociative or depersonalization symptoms 5.04 (3.03 to 8.36), nausea 0.64 (0.25 to 1.62) (Figure 2, p. 1167). No moderator was significant (Table 2, p. 1168).
analysis.covariates: None; meta-regression (restricted maximum likelihood) on study-level sample size, mean age and % men, and subgroup comparisons by region, randomization, ECT type and inclusion of psychotic features (pp. 1164, 1168).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022338045 (p. 1163); PRISMA checklist in eTable 2 (not read). The registration date and the registered analysis plan are not given in the article, and the record was not read, so deviations (for example, the absence of a remission analysis) cannot be checked.
analysis.selective_reporting: Remission and response were not analysed (remission was KetECT's primary outcome), and the article does not say why. The abstract says no significant differences were observed for cognition or memory, while the Results report a significant advantage for ketamine in the one trial that measured neurocognition. Only 4 of 6 trials reported adverse events and only KetECT reported serious adverse events.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally; the authors call the included trials small and possibly underpowered (p. 1169). With six trials, the meta-regressions and funnel-plot tests have little power (editors' note).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across six trials with 340 inpatient ECT candidates, depressive symptoms improved more by the end of a course of ECT than of ketamine, by about 0.7 standard deviations (fixed effect; about 0.73 with random effects, editors' calculation). KetECT carries half the weight; four small trials from Iran and India (18 to 39 patients) give the most variable effects; the two largest effects come from the 22- and 25-patient trials, and the smallest trial (18 patients) gives the smallest (Figure 1B, p. 1166). Headache and muscle pain were less frequent with ketamine, blurred vision, diplopia, vertigo and dissociative symptoms more frequent, with these pooled risks resting mostly on KetECT. No remission, response, relapse or cognitive comparison was pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract's conclusion that ECT may be superior for depression severity in the acute phase (p. 1162) matches the analysis and is hedged. (2) The abstract says no significant differences were observed for cognition or memory (p. 1162), but the Results report that Basso et al. found better neurocognitive performance after ketamine (Cohen d 0.40, P = .04), with no difference only in the other trial (p. 1166). (3) The Discussion says KetECT found no difference in remission rates by the 12-month follow-up (pp. 1168–1169); KetECT compared relapse among remitters (64% against 70%), not remission. (4) The review calls the trials' quality low to moderate but rated measurement of the outcome at low risk in every trial, including open-label trials whose depression ratings were made by unblinded staff, and its Limitations section does not discuss risk of bias (pp. 1168–1169). (5) The finding of no moderating effects (age, psychotic features, ECT type; p. 1168) is reported without saying that six trials give these tests little power, or that study-level mean age cannot show the patient-level age interaction reported within KetECT. The Discussion also gives ketamine's faster antidepressant effect as a reason to individualize treatment (p. 1168), citing qualitative reports from three trials against one that found faster recovery with ECT; speed of response was not analysed, and the largest trial, KetECT, found no faster remission with ketamine (11% and 10% after 3 sessions; Ekstrand et al., 2022, Figure 3B, p. 345). The review reports no pooled remission or response result: its only remission figures are KetECT's counts in Table 1 (p. 1165).

timeline.event: Ghasemi et al. (Iran): blind randomized trial, 18 patients; included.
Kheirabadi et al. (Iran): blind randomized trial, 22 patients; included.

Basso et al. (Germany): non-randomized open-label trial, 50 patients; Kheirabadi et al. (Iran): open-label randomized trial of intramuscular and oral ketamine, 39 patients; Sharma et al. (India): blind randomized trial, 25 patients; all included.
Ekstrand et al. (KetECT, Sweden): open-label randomized non-inferiority trial, 186 inpatients; remission 63% after ECT against 46% after ketamine; included, with about half the weight here.
This review: pooled symptom-severity SMD −0.69 favouring ECT; remission not pooled.

Anand et al. (ELEKT-D), described in this review as ongoing: 403 mostly outpatients with nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression; self-rated response with ketamine noninferior to ECT and remission higher with ketamine (a secondary outcome whose intervals, by the table footnote, are not adjusted for multiple comparisons; Anand et al., 2023, Table 2, p. 2322), as recorded on the card sc_anand_2023.

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the first meta-analysis of ketamine against ECT. It predates ELEKT-D, the largest randomized comparison, which found ketamine noninferior on self-rated response in mostly outpatients without psychosis (per sc_anand_2023); an update adding ELEKT-D would be dominated by two large open-label trials pointing in different directions. KetECT and this review are largely the same evidence and must not be counted as two confirmations. The card sc_anand_2023 records Anand et al.'s Discussion as saying that KetECT and a meta-analysis found remission with ketamine inferior to ECT, and names this review: if this review is the one meant, it pooled symptom severity, not remission, and its only remission figures are KetECT's own (Anand et al.'s reference list was not read here).

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the randomized ketamine–ECT trials, including KetECT and ELEKT-D, analysing remission and response with common definitions, testing age, psychotic features, inpatient status and ECT technique at the patient level, and comparing blinded with unblinded ratings; ideally alongside a new trial with blinded raters.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (depression diagnosed by standardized criteria), intervention and comparator (ketamine and ECT) and outcomes (symptom severity on standardized measures; suicidal ideation, cognition, adverse events) are stated (p. 1163).

Registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022338045), with inclusion criteria set before article review (p. 1163); the registration date, the registered analysis plan and any deviations (for example, why remission and response were not analysed) are not reported, and the record was not read.
Clinical trials of any design were eligible, and one non-randomized open-label trial was pooled with five randomized trials, without a stated reason for including non-randomized designs (p. 1163).

Four databases without language limits, trial registries, Google Scholar and reference lists, with the search less than 24 months before publication; strategies in eTable 1 (not read). Consultation with content experts is not reported, and two of the six trials were found only by hand search, which suggests the database strategy missed eligible trials (p. 1164).
Titles, abstracts and full texts screened independently by two reviewers, discrepancies resolved by discussion (p. 1163).
Independent extraction by two reviewers on a pilot-tested form, then corroborated (pp. 1163–1164). The KetECT values used differ from those printed in KetECT's Table 2 (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 56 full-text exclusions are only counted; the supplementary items named in the article (search strategies, PRISMA checklist, study-selection details in eFigure 1, risk-of-bias reasons, funnel plot) do not include a list of excluded studies with reasons, and the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, size, sex, age, condition, both interventions, course duration, setting and country, and the outcome measures appear in Figure 1; the timing of outcome assessment is not given per trial, and the KetECT row misstates the ketamine schedule and prints interquartile ranges as ranges.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 applied by domain, covering allocation and blinding, with reasons in eTable 3 (not read); but measurement of the outcome was rated low in every trial, including open-label trials whose depression ratings were made by staff aware of the assignment, with a justification that concerns selective reporting, and the non-randomized trial was assessed with RoB 2 rather than a tool that addresses confounding (p. 1168).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Inverse-variance pooling of Hedges g, a random-effects model planned for I² above 50%, heterogeneity investigated by meta-regression and subgroups, and a separate estimate for the five randomized trials (−0.692, Table 2). Judged met on balance, a close call: the main estimate used a fixed-effect model chosen by an I² cut-off for clinically diverse trials (intravenous, intramuscular and oral ketamine; blind and open designs) with no other justification; the rule was not followed for the BDI subgroup; and combining correlated measures within trials narrowed their intervals. A random-effects model gives a similar estimate (editors' calculation: −0.73, −1.02 to −0.44).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis excluding trials at high risk; the randomization moderator compares one non-randomized trial with five randomized ones and does not test the effect of the rated risk of bias (p. 1168).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Two of six trials, including KetECT with about half the weight, were at high overall risk by the review's own rating, but the Discussion's limitations name sample size, differing criteria and differing protocols, not risk of bias, and its likely effect on the pooled result is not discussed; the abstract mentions only low to moderate methodological quality (pp. 1162, 1169).
I² and Q reported for every pool; moderator analyses run (none significant); differing criteria and protocols discussed as limitations (pp. 1166, 1168–1169).

Funnel plot (eFigure 2, not read), Egger P = .32 and Begg-Mazumdar P = .57, with the conclusion that no publication bias was found (p. 1168). With six trials these tests have little power, the 22- and 25-patient trials give the two largest effects (the smallest trial, 18 patients, the smallest) (−1.415 and −1.297) against −0.577 for the largest, and the likely impact is discussed in one sentence.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Authors' disclosures are extensive, but the review's own funding is not stated and no management of conflicts is described (pp. 1169–1171).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (no list of excluded studies; risk of bias not taken into account when interpreting the results) and three more (protocol, search, risk-of-bias assessment) are only partly met, which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2's rule. In practice, the pooled advantage of ECT in symptom improvement can be reproduced from the forest plot and survives a random-effects model, but it is half KetECT's own result, otherwise rests on small trials whose effects vary widely (the largest from trials of 22 and 25 patients), and was appraised without considering unblinded outcome ratings. The source can be cited for a pooled difference in end-of-course symptom improvement favouring ECT among inpatient ECT candidates in trials published up to April 2022, and for acute adverse-event profiles that come mostly from KetECT; it cannot be cited for remission or response, for cognition or relapse, for patient-level moderators, or as evidence independent of KetECT.

key_findings.finding: Search: PubMed, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library and Embase from inception to 19 April 2022 with MeSH terms and keywords, no language limits; US and EU trial registries and Google Scholar searched by hand by two authors; protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022338045); PRISMA followed; search strategies in eTable 1 (supplement, not read).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Data Sources (p. 1162); Methods › Search Strategy and Reporting Criteria, 1st paragraph (p. 1163)

key_findings.finding: Titles, abstracts and full texts screened independently by two reviewers; data extracted independently by two reviewers on a pilot-tested form and corroborated; risk of bias assessed with RoB 2 (5 domains); publication bias by funnel plot, Egger test and Begg-Mazumdar test.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Extraction (pp. 1163–1164); Methods › Assessment of Bias and Methodological Quality (p. 1164)

key_findings.finding: Models: Hedges g for improvement in depressive symptoms with inverse-variance weights; random effects when I² was above 50% and fixed effects when below 50%; trials with several depression measures combined first by a 3-level model, then one effect per trial pooled; Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios for adverse events; meta-regression with restricted maximum likelihood for moderators.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 1248 records; 60 eligible after screening; 56 excluded at full text; 2 more found by hand search of trial databases and reference lists. Six trials with 340 patients (162 ECT, 178 ketamine): five randomized and one naturalistic open-label trial (Basso et al., 2020, Germany); two European and four from Asia or the Middle East; five single-site; sizes 18 to 186; all inpatient ECT candidates; one trial (Sharma et al., 2020) included bipolar depression.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the Studies Included, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1164); Table 1 (p. 1165)

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists KetECT (Ekstrand et al., 2022) as 186 patients (36% men), mean age 52.5, ketamine 0.5 mg/kg intravenously 3 times a week for 2 weeks (infusions mean 6.8, SD 3.3, range given as 5–9) against right unilateral ECT 3 times a week for 4 weeks (mean 7.8, SD 2.4, range given as 6–10), with remission 57/91 (62.6%) against 44/95 (46.3%), P = .03. These are the only remission figures in the review.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Ekstrand et al. row
key_findings.note: The KetECT article gave both treatments three times a week for up to 12 sessions and reports 5–9 and 6–10 as interquartile ranges (Ekstrand et al., 2022, pp. 341, 344); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Overall pooled SMD for depressive symptoms, ECT against ketamine: −0.69 (95% CI −0.89 to −0.48), 6 trials, fixed effect, Cochran Q P = .15, I² 39% (τ² 0.0368). By measure: MADRS −0.59 (−0.85 to −0.33; 2 trials, I² 0%); HDRS −0.83 (−1.22 to −0.44; 4 trials, 5 comparisons, I² 22%); BDI −0.86 (−1.50 to −0.22; 2 trials, I² 60%). Negative values favour ECT.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 1162); Results › Efficacy Outcome: Depressive Symptoms (p. 1164); Figure 1A and 1B (p. 1166)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations from Figure 1B: KetECT carries 49% of the fixed-effect weight; a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model gives −0.73 (−1.02 to −0.44) with an approximate 95% prediction interval of −1.47 to 0.01; leaving out KetECT gives −0.79 (−1.08 to −0.50).

key_findings.finding: Trial-level SMDs (Figure 1B): Basso et al. −0.636 (n = 50); KetECT −0.577 (n = 186); Ghasemi et al. −0.259 (n = 18); Kheirabadi et al. 2019 −1.415 (n = 22); Sharma et al. −1.297 (n = 25); Kheirabadi et al. 2020 −0.684 (n = 39).
key_findings.locator: Figure 1B

key_findings.finding: KetECT's inputs in Figure 1A: MADRS change −22.300 (SD 9.6100) with ECT (n = 91) and −16.200 (SD 11.3500) with ketamine (n = 95), SMD −0.577 (−0.870 to −0.283).
key_findings.locator: Figure 1A, MADRS rows
key_findings.note: KetECT's own Table 2 gives 22.4 (SD 11.4) and 16.1 (SD 12.0) (Ekstrand et al., 2022, p. 344), which give a Hedges g of about 0.54 (editors' calculation); the review does not say where its values came from.

key_findings.finding: Suicidal ideation: one trial (ref. 40, Kheirabadi et al.) measured it with the Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation; all three groups improved, with no group differences at 1 week and 1 month (P = .99 and P = .69).
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Outcome: Suicidal Ideation

key_findings.finding: Cognition and memory, not pooled: Basso et al. found better neurocognitive performance after ketamine than after ECT (Cohen d 0.40; P = .04), with better attention, verbal memory and executive functions and no difference in immediate or visual memory; Kheirabadi et al. (2019) found no difference on the Wechsler Memory Scale.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognition and Memory

key_findings.finding: Safety: 4 of 6 trials reported adverse events and only KetECT reported serious adverse events (23 of 90 with ECT against 14 of 91 with ketamine, P = .09; suicide attempts 6 of 90 against 4 of 91; suicide deaths 1 of 90 against 0 of 91).
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pooled risk ratios, ketamine against ECT (3 trials unless stated): headache 0.37 (0.18 to 0.76; random effects, I² 73%); muscle pain 0.23 (0.13 to 0.38); blurred vision 26.47 (3.62 to 193.67; 2 trials); diplopia or nystagmus 10.88 (3.52 to 33.63); vertigo 2.99 (2.03 to 4.40; 2 trials); dissociative or depersonalization symptoms 5.04 (3.03 to 8.36); nausea 0.64 (0.25 to 1.62; random effects, I² 53%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (pp. 1166, 1168); Figure 2 (p. 1167)
key_findings.note: KetECT carries 46.7% to 98.0% of the weight in these pools (vertigo 98.0%, dissociative symptoms 92.5%; Figure 2).

key_findings.finding: Moderators (k = number of effect sizes), none significant: sample size P = .51; mean age P = .47; % men P = .36; region, Asia or Middle East −0.839 against Europe −0.589 (P = .25); randomization, yes −0.692 against no −0.636 (P = .86); ECT type, right unilateral −0.589, bilateral −0.655, mixed −1.297 (P = .12); psychotic features, yes −0.709 against no −0.649 (P = .78).
key_findings.locator: Results › Moderator Analysis; Table 2
key_findings.note: All moderators are study-level with six trials; for psychotic features, the yes category means trials that included patients with psychotic features, not those patients' own results.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2): overall high for Basso et al. (non-randomized) and KetECT, some concerns for Ghasemi et al. and both Kheirabadi trials, low for Sharma et al.; measurement of the outcome and selection of the reported result rated low in all six trials; four trials had some concerns for deviations from intended interventions, attributed partly to difficulty blinding; KetECT flagged for missing outcome data because of higher dropout with ketamine. Publication bias: Egger P = .32, Begg-Mazumdar P = .57.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3; Results › Quality Assessment and Risk of Bias

key_findings.finding: The Discussion says KetECT found remission rates not different between groups by the 12-month follow-up, and suggests treatment effects may wane similarly in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: KetECT compared relapse among remitters (64% against 70%), not remission rates at 12 months (Ekstrand et al., 2022, p. 345); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: most trials had small samples and lacked long-term follow-up, so the designs may be underpowered; differing inclusion criteria (bipolar depression, psychotic features); differing ketamine and ECT protocols (frequency, route, pulse width, anaesthetic medications). Two ongoing randomized trials are described: CAN-BIND (planning to recruit 240 patients with unipolar or bipolar depression, single-blinded crossover, ketamine or ECT thrice weekly for 3 to 4 weeks) and ELEKT-D (aiming to recruit 400 patients with unipolar treatment-resistant depression, open label, ketamine twice a week up to 6 sessions against ECT three times a week up to 9 sessions, over 3 to 5 weeks), expected to finish by March 2023 and December 2022.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Remission and response were not pooled: the efficacy outcome is the standardized difference in symptom improvement, and the only remission figures in the article are KetECT's, quoted in Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Outcome: Depressive Symptoms (p. 1164); Table 1 (p. 1165); Figure 1 (p. 1166)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says no significant differences were observed for cognition or memory, but the Results report that Basso et al. found better neurocognitive performance after ketamine (Cohen d 0.40; P = .04), with no difference only in Kheirabadi et al. (2019).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract contradicts the Results on the only significant cognitive finding, which favoured ketamine; cite the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says KetECT found remission rates not different by the 12-month follow-up; KetECT reported relapse among remitters (36/56 after ECT against 31/44 after ketamine), not remission at 12 months (Ekstrand et al., 2022, p. 345).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement should not be cited; KetECT's follow-up compared relapse in remitters, a non-randomized subgroup.

reporting_issues.issue: KetECT's inputs in Figure 1A (MADRS change 22.300, SD 9.6100, against 16.200, SD 11.3500) differ from KetECT's Table 2 (22.4, SD 11.4, against 16.1, SD 12.0; Ekstrand et al., 2022, p. 344), and the source of the review's values is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small effect on the pooled result (editors' calculation: KetECT's Hedges g about 0.54 from its printed values, against 0.577 used here).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's KetECT row gives ketamine three times a week for 2 weeks and ECT three times a week for 4 weeks, with ranges of 5–9 and 6–10 sessions; KetECT gave both treatments three times a week for up to 12 sessions, and 5–9 and 6–10 are its interquartile ranges (Ekstrand et al., 2022, pp. 341, 344).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table understates the ketamine course KetECT allowed; compare schedules from the KetECT article.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated rule (random effects when I² is above 50%) was not applied to the BDI subgroup, pooled with fixed effects at I² 60%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Applying the rule gives −0.84 (−1.86 to 0.17), an interval that includes zero (editors' calculation); the BDI result is less certain than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The first-stage combination of two ratings of the same patients gives intervals narrower than either rating alone: Ghasemi et al., HDRS −1.131 to 0.723 and BDI −1.245 to 0.618, combined −0.916 to 0.398; Sharma et al., HDRS −2.115 to −0.376 and BDI −2.233 to −0.466, combined −1.916 to −0.677. Kheirabadi et al. (2020) combine two ketamine arms against one shared ECT group of 12.
reporting_issues.consequence: Correlated ratings are treated as if they added information, overstating these trials' precision; their weight in the pooled result is modest (editors' calculation: 9.8%, 11.0% and 12.9%).

reporting_issues.issue: The number of depression effect sizes is given as 6 in the Results and 11 in the Discussion, while Figure 1A shows 9 comparisons.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the number of comparisons entering each stage is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the coefficient for % men as −4.490 with a 95% CI of −4.687 to 1.708, so the estimate is not at the centre of its interval; the mixed ECT category has k = 2 but its estimate (−1.297, −1.916 to −0.677) is Sharma et al.'s single-trial result, and k sums to 7 across ECT types for six trials.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors (editors' calculation: an estimate of −1.49 at the interval's centre gives P = .36, as printed); the mixed category rests on one trial.

reporting_issues.issue: Risk-of-bias reporting is internally inconsistent: the text justifies low risk for measurement of the outcome by the absence of selective reporting, which is a different domain; Figure 3 shows green circles with a some-concerns symbol for missing data in Ghasemi et al. and Kheirabadi et al. (2019); the text says 4 of the 5 randomized trials had robust allocation concealment while Figure 3 rates randomization low in all 5; the Methods name high, low or unclear judgments while Figure 3 uses some concerns.
reporting_issues.consequence: The domain judgments cannot be taken at face value; in particular, outcome measurement was not appraised for unblinded ratings (the reasons in eTable 3 were not read).

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: the Discussion gives Kheirabadi et al. (2019) a total sample of 32, while Table 1 and Figure 1 give 22; Basso et al. have 24 ECT patients in Figure 1A and 25 in Table 1; Figure 1B dates Kheirabadi et al. (ref. 40) to 2022, elsewhere 2020.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the pooled estimates.

(3) The Discussion says KetECT found no difference in remission rates by the 12-month follow-up (pp. 1168–1169); KetECT compared relapse among remitters (64% against 70%), not remission. (4) The review calls the trials' quality low to moderate but rated measurement of the outcome at low risk in every trial, including open-label trials whose depression ratings were made by unblinded staff, and its Limitations section does not discuss risk of bias (pp. 1168–1169). (5) The finding of no moderating effects (age, psychotic features, ECT type; p. 1168) is reported without saying that six trials give these tests little power, or that study-level mean age cannot show the patient-level age interaction reported within KetECT.
