design_detail: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, randomized withdrawal trial (SUSTAIN-1; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02493868), sponsored by Janssen, October 2015 to February 2018; 99 sites randomized patients (outpatient clinics in the United States, Canada and Europe, with Brazil and Mexico in Table 1). Adults with prospectively confirmed treatment-resistant depression received esketamine nasal spray (flexible, 56 or 84 mg) plus a new oral antidepressant: direct-entry patients in a 4-week open-label induction phase, and transfer-entry patients who had responded to esketamine in one of two short-term trials, which this paper calls TRD3001 (fixed dose; cited as a conference abstract by Fedgchin et al., whose full report is titled TRANSFORM-1) and TRD3002 (flexible dose; cited as a conference presentation by Popova et al.); the names TRANSFORM-1 and TRANSFORM-2 are not printed in this paper. Responders had 12 weeks of optimization (dosing weekly, then weekly or every 2 weeks). After 16 weeks, patients in stable remission (primary analysis set) and patients with stable response without remission (secondary set) were randomized separately, 1:1, to continue esketamine or switch to a placebo spray, both keeping their oral antidepressant. The maintenance phase was event-driven with a two-stage group-sequential design; primary outcome: time to relapse in stable remitters.
can_establish: Whether, among adults with treatment-resistant depression who had remitted or responded after 16 weeks of esketamine nasal spray plus an oral antidepressant, continuing esketamine delayed relapse compared with stopping it (switching to a placebo spray) while the oral antidepressant continued.
cannot_establish: Whether esketamine prevents relapse in people not selected for having responded to it (only 297 of 705 enrolled were randomized); whether relapse after the switch reflects the return of depression or an effect of stopping the drug (the design cannot separate them, and the authors argue against withdrawal without trial data, PDF pp. 8-9); how much participants' recognition of the switch contributed (blinding was not assessed); effects beyond the median 17.7 to 19.4 weeks of maintenance treatment; or how esketamine compares with other maintenance strategies.

sample.recruitment: Outpatients in treatment or referred, at academic and non-academic clinics in the United States, Canada and Europe; they were approached by their treating physician or answered ethics-approved recruitment materials, and a web-based prescreening tool helped sites (PDF p. 2). Direct-entry patients came through a 4-week prospective screening phase; transfer-entry patients came from the fixed-dose and flexible-dose short-term trials (TRD3001 and TRD3002, Table 1 footnotes e and f) after responding (at least a 50% MADRS reduction) (PDF pp. 2-3, 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 to 64; DSM-5 recurrent or single-episode (at least 2 years) major depression; IDS-C 34 or more and MADRS 28 or more; non-response to at least 1 and no more than 5 antidepressants in the current episode, plus non-response to a different antidepressant confirmed by at least 4 weeks of observed treatment. Excluded: history of psychotic disorder or depression with psychotic features, suicidal behaviour in the prior year, current or recent homicidal or suicidal ideation or intent, moderate or severe substance or alcohol use disorder within 6 months, and lifetime ketamine use disorder; urine drug screening was done intermittently before dosing (PDF p. 2). Randomization required stable remission (MADRS 12 or less in at least 3 of the last 4 weeks of optimization, with one excursion or one missed rating allowed at week 13 or 14) or stable response (MADRS reduction of at least 50% in the last 2 weeks without remission) (PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: Randomized: mean age 46.3 (SD 11.13); 197 (66.3%) women (PDF p. 1). By group (Table 1, PDF p. 5): White 88.9% / 88.4% (remitters, esketamine / placebo spray) and 91.9% / 93.2% (responders); Europe 54.8% to 59.3%; mean baseline MADRS 37.4 / 37.6 and 40.1 / 38.9; more than two previous antidepressants 21.1% / 26.2% and 33.9% / 42.4%; suicidal ideation in the previous 6 months 20.0% / 16.3% and 32.3% / 23.7%.
sample.attrition: Before randomization (Figure 1, PDF p. 4): of 1097 assessed, 800 were excluded: 378 screen failures, 86 transfer-entry patients from placebo arms of the short-term trials, 14 for Good Clinical Practice issues, and 322 withdrawn during induction or optimization (221 did not meet criteria to continue, 27 adverse events, 23 withdrew, 14 MADRS of 22 or more at 2 visits, 10 lack of efficacy, 6 protocol violations, 3 lost to follow-up, 18 other). After randomization: stable remitters 8 vs 9 discontinued, none lost; stable responders 4 (1 lost to follow-up) vs 3; all randomized patients analysed. 13 vs 12 were censored because they left before relapsing; most other censoring was administrative, when the study stopped at its target number of relapses (Table 2 note, PDF p. 6).
sample.selection_effects: Strong enrichment: only people who responded to and tolerated 16 weeks of esketamine were randomized (297 of 705 enrolled, 42%; editors' calculation), and, by the footnotes of Table 1, 115 of the 297 had already responded to esketamine in TRD3001 or TRD3002 (the table's dose sub-rows give a different split; see reporting issues). The result applies to people who have already benefited from esketamine. Median 2 randomized patients per site (range 1-25) across 99 sites (PDF p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, self-administered at the clinic; maintenance dosing frequency (weekly or every 2 weeks) was set by a MADRS-based algorithm reviewed every 4 weeks (PDF p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: induction twice weekly at 56 or 84 mg (flexible) for 4 weeks; optimization at the dose reached in induction, weekly for 4 weeks and then weekly or every 2 weeks; maintenance weekly or every 2 weeks; each device 200 microlitres, two sprays, 28 mg esketamine base; placebo with denatonium benzoate as a bittering agent (PDF p. 3). Stable remitters who continued esketamine: 40 (44.4%) on 56 mg and 50 (55.6%) on 84 mg, 62 (68.9%) dosed every 2 weeks most of the time; stable responders: 20 (32.3%) and 42 (67.7%), 34 (54.8%) weekly most of the time. Median maintenance exposure to esketamine 17.7 weeks (remitters) and 19.4 weeks (responders); to placebo 10.2 and 10.1 weeks (PDF pp. 4-6).
exposure.polysubstance: Recent moderate or severe substance or alcohol use disorder and lifetime ketamine use disorder excluded; urine drug screens before dosing (PDF p. 2). One participant received one intravenous dose of ketamine (10 mg) for nephrolithiasis during the study (PDF p. 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (treatment trial).

comparison.controls: Patients randomized to stop esketamine and switch to a placebo nasal spray (bittering agent), continuing the same oral antidepressant at an unchanged dose (PDF p. 3).
comparison.matching: Separate 1:1 randomization for stable remitters and stable responders by computer-generated schedule in randomly permuted blocks, stratified by country (PDF p. 3). One patient with stable response was randomized in the remission set, and one who met neither definition in the response set (Figure 1 notes, PDF p. 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusions and urine screening as the esketamine arms.

outcomes.instruments: Relapse: a MADRS of 22 or more on 2 consecutive assessments 5 to 15 days apart, or hospitalization for worsening depression, a suicide attempt, suicide prevention or completed suicide, or another clinically relevant event judged by a relapse adjudication committee (PDF p. 4). MADRS was rated weekly by independent, blinded, remote raters (PDF p. 3). Safety: adverse events, laboratory tests, physical examination, ECG, C-SSRS, vital signs, CADSS and the BPRS positive-symptom subscale at every dosing visit, and the 20-item Physician Withdrawal Checklist after stopping; cognitive results to be reported separately (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard rating scales; the relapse definition is the trial's own.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: time to relapse in stable remitters (Kaplan-Meier; weighted combination log-rank test across the interim and final analyses; weighted hazard ratio). Secondary: time to relapse in stable responders (log-rank test; Cox model with treatment as factor) (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Group-sequential plan for the primary set: interim analysis after 31 relapses at two-sided 0.0097 (superiority not shown), then final analysis at an adjusted two-sided 0.046 (Wang-Tsiatis alpha-spending) after the target was re-estimated to 59 relapses (PDF p. 3). No multiplicity procedure is stated for the secondary (stable responder) comparison; post hoc analyses are labelled as such.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Independent, blinded, remote MADRS raters; double-blind maintenance phase, with a bittering agent (denatonium benzoate) in the placebo solution to simulate the taste of esketamine; the paper does not say the devices were identical (PDF p. 3). Whether participants or staff could tell who had been switched was not assessed; the authors note that the dissociative and sedative effects are difficult to blind and could have biased the staff who observed dosing (PDF p. 9).

analysis.effect_sizes: Stable remitters: relapse in 24 of 90 (26.7%) who continued esketamine vs 39 of 86 (45.3%) switched to placebo spray; hazard ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.84; weighted estimate), two-sided P=.003; NNT 6. Time to relapse, 25th percentile 153.0 (95% CI 105.0 to 225.0) vs 33.3 (22.0 to 48.0); median not estimable vs 273.0 (97.0 to not estimable). Stable responders: 16 of 62 (25.8%) vs 34 of 59 (57.6%); hazard ratio 0.30 (0.16 to 0.55), P<.001; NNT 4; median 635.0 (264.0 to 635.0) vs 88.0 (46.0 to 196.0) (Table 2, PDF p. 6). Post hoc: both sets combined, hazard ratio 0.38 (0.26 to 0.57); remission cut-off of MADRS 10, P=.005; leaving out one site at a time, 0.42 to 0.57 against an unweighted overall 0.47, no intervals or P values printed (PDF p. 6); censoring the 3 relapsing patients with a clear change in CADSS score around randomization, 0.50 (0.30 to 0.84), P=.008, unweighted Cox model (PDF p. 9). By study entry (not labelled post hoc): direct-entry 0.49 (0.27 to 0.90) and transfer-entry 0.45 (0.17 to 1.18) (PDF p. 6). Editors' calculation: differences in the proportion relapsing of 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 4.7 to 32.6) in remitters and 31.8 points (15.2 to 48.5) in responders, over variable, event-driven follow-up without a fixed time horizon. The time units in Table 2 are not printed; they are consistent with days given the weekly axis of Figure 2 (273 days is 39 weeks).
analysis.covariates: None for the primary weighted log-rank analysis; Cox model with treatment as the only factor for the secondary analysis (PDF p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02493868 (PDF p. 1); the trial protocol is in Supplement 1, which was not read. Planned: 211 stable remitters to yield 84 relapses, 90% power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.49 at two-sided 0.05; after the interim analysis the target was re-estimated to 59 relapses (PDF p. 3). Observed: 176 remitters randomized and 63 relapses (Table 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Primary and secondary results reported as planned, with several post hoc sensitivity analyses. Supplementary eTables and eFigures (MADRS over time, early relapses by dosing frequency, blood pressure, CADSS) were not read. Cognitive results deferred to another paper.
analysis.power: The trial stopped at its re-estimated number of relapses (59 planned; 63 observed in remitters), fewer than the 84 originally planned.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people who had remitted after 16 weeks on esketamine plus an oral antidepressant, those switched to a placebo spray relapsed more often (39 of 86, 45.3%, vs 24 of 90, 26.7%) and sooner (hazard ratio 0.49); among stable responders, 57.6% vs 25.8% relapsed (hazard ratio 0.30). About half of the relapses among remitters switched to placebo (19 of 39) came within 4 weeks of the switch, 6 of them by week 2. Only 42% of the people enrolled reached randomization.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say that continuing esketamine gave clinically meaningful superiority in delaying relapse and that it decreased the risk of relapse by 51% and 70% (PDF pp. 1, 6, 9); these percentages are 1 minus the hazard ratios, not reductions in absolute risk, which were 18.7 and 31.8 percentage points (editors' calculation). The abstract does not say that the randomized population was selected for response to esketamine, that the comparison is continuing versus stopping a drug with noticeable acute effects whose disappearance participants could detect (during maintenance, dissociation 23.0% vs 0 and dysgeusia 27.0% vs 6.9%), or that blinding was not assessed. The discussion argues that early relapses after the switch are unlikely to be withdrawal or rebound, citing esketamine's half-life, intermittent dosing and an analogy with stopping ECT (PDF pp. 8-9); this is reasoning, not data from the trial. The conclusion that the trial supports a positive benefit-risk ratio of long-term treatment rests on a median maintenance exposure of under 20 weeks. A headline that esketamine prevents relapse in treatment-resistant depression overstates it: the trial shows that, in people who had done well on esketamine, stopping it was followed by more and earlier relapse.

timeline.event: Flexible-dose short-term trial, called TRD3002 in this paper (TRANSFORM-2 on the other cards, a name not printed here); a source of transfer-entry patients for this trial
Fixed-dose short-term trial, called TRD3001 in this paper (titled TRANSFORM-1 in its own report; primary endpoint not met); 150 of its responders entered this trial (Fedgchin et al., Figure 1)
This trial (SUSTAIN-1): continuing esketamine vs switching to placebo spray after 16 weeks; hazard ratio for relapse 0.49 in stable remitters and 0.30 in stable responders
Long-term open-label safety study (SUSTAIN-3, NCT02782104), which patients who relapsed in this trial could enter (cited by this paper; no results reported here)
Turner, critique of the efficacy evidence and of the FDA approval of esketamine (to be appraised from the full text)
Horowitz and Moncrieff, critical review of the evidence for esketamine, with a published corrigendum (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first controlled maintenance study of esketamine (PDF p. 2). It is not independent of the short-term trials: by the footnotes of Table 1, 115 of its 297 randomized patients came from TRD3001 and TRD3002, the fixed-dose and flexible-dose trials (Fedgchin et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2019); the table's dose sub-rows conflict with this count (see reporting issues). No replication with an active placebo, a taper arm or an unselected population is reported in this paper. The paper does not mention regulatory approval. Published critiques (Turner, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) are listed for appraisal and not summarized here.

funding.funder: Funded by Janssen Research & Development LLC. Sponsor employees were involved in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis and interpretation of the data; preparation, review or approval of the manuscript; and the decision to submit it (PDF p. 10). Medical writing by Sandra Norris (Norris Communications Group LLC, supported by Janssen and compensated) and editorial support by Ellen Baum (a Janssen employee) are acknowledged.
funding.declared_conflicts: Twelve of the 23 authors (Daly, Janik, H. Li, Zhang, X. Li, Lim, Hough, Manji, Drevets, Singh, Lane, Duca) are employees of Janssen Research & Development LLC and hold company equity; Manji holds a patent assigned to the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Yale University and the National Institutes of Health, from which no financial benefit was received. Trivedi, Thase, Zajecka, Divacka, Fagiolini, Cubała, Bitter, Blier, Shelton, Molero and Winokur report consulting, advisory, speaker, grant or royalty relationships with pharmaceutical companies, in each case including Janssen or Johnson & Johnson (PDF pp. 9-10).
funding.affiliations_note: Sponsor statisticians (Zhang, X. Li, Lane, Lim) did the statistical analysis (PDF p. 9). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized discontinuation trial with an active placebo that reproduces esketamine's acute sensations, a blinding check, a gradual-taper arm to separate withdrawal effects from relapse, and at least a year of follow-up; or a trial that randomizes unselected patients from the start to long-term esketamine or another maintenance strategy.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedule in permuted blocks, stratified by country, separately for remitters and responders (PDF p. 3); how the allocation was concealed is not described, and the paper does not say the devices were identical (the placebo contained a bittering agent); groups comparable at baseline (Table 1). Two patients were randomized into the wrong set and analysed as randomized.

Participants switched to placebo stopped experiencing effects they had felt for 16 weeks, and the authors note that staff observing dosing could have been biased (PDF p. 9). No deviations arising from the trial context are reported; all randomized patients were analysed in their groups.
One patient lost to follow-up; 13 vs 12 censored after leaving before relapse; other censoring administrative at the study's end (Figure 1; Table 2 note).

Relapse was defined mainly by telephone MADRS ratings that rest on participants' reports. After 16 weeks of esketamine, participants switched to placebo were likely to notice the loss of familiar acute effects (during maintenance, dissociation 23.0% vs 0, dysgeusia 27.0% vs 6.9%, vertigo 25.0% vs 5.5%), and their awareness was not assessed; the only analysis addressing this censored 3 relapsing patients with a clear change in CADSS score (PDF p. 9).
Registered, with a prespecified primary analysis and group-sequential plan reported as planned; the protocol in Supplement 1 and the registry record were not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization (although its concealment is not described), retention and analysis are sound. But in a withdrawal design comparing continued esketamine with a switch to placebo, people who had taken the drug for 16 weeks could plausibly tell they had been switched, and the outcome depends on what they reported; this was not measured. Relapses clustered in the first month after the switch, which fits either a return of depression in vulnerable patients or an effect of stopping the drug, and the trial cannot tell them apart. The card may be cited for the observed relapse rates and hazard ratios in people who had already responded to esketamine, and for maintenance-phase adverse events; not as evidence that esketamine prevents relapse in treatment-resistant depression generally.

key_findings.finding: Of 1097 people assessed, 705 were enrolled, 455 entered the 12-week optimization phase and 297 were randomized after 16 weeks of esketamine: 176 in stable remission (90 continued esketamine, 86 switched to placebo spray) and 121 with stable response (62 vs 59). By the footnotes of Table 1, 54, 56, 31 and 41 patients in the four groups had entered directly and 36, 30, 31 and 18 had transferred from the fixed-dose (TRD3001) or flexible-dose (TRD3002) short-term trials; the table's dose sub-rows, as labelled, give other counts (69 direct-entry and 228 transfer-entry patients), and the paper does not say which is right (reporting issue 0).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Figure 1 (p. 4); Table 1, footnotes b, c, e and f and dose sub-rows (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' sums of the footnote counts: 182 direct-entry and 115 transfer-entry patients among the 297 randomized. The paper calls the source trials TRD3001 (ref. 15, Fedgchin et al., cited as a 2018 conference abstract; that trial's full report is titled TRANSFORM-1) and TRD3002 (ref. 12, Popova et al., cited as a 2018 conference presentation); it does not print the names TRANSFORM-1 or TRANSFORM-2.

key_findings.finding: Main result in people in stable remission: 24 of 90 (26.7%) who continued esketamine relapsed vs 39 of 86 (45.3%) switched to placebo spray; hazard ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.84), P=.003; NNT 6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: absolute difference 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 4.7 to 32.6), over variable, event-driven follow-up.

key_findings.finding: In people with stable response but not remission: 16 of 62 (25.8%) vs 34 of 59 (57.6%) relapsed; hazard ratio 0.30 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.55), P<.001; NNT 4.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: absolute difference 31.8 percentage points (95% CI 15.2 to 48.5).

key_findings.finding: How fast relapse came: among remitters, a quarter of those switched to placebo spray had relapsed by 33.3 vs 153.0 among those continuing esketamine; median time to relapse 273.0 after the switch, not reached with esketamine. Among responders, the median was 88.0 vs 635.0.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 6); Figure 2 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: Table 2 does not print the unit; the values fit days, given the weekly axis of Figure 2 (273 days is 39 weeks).

key_findings.finding: Half of the relapses after switching came early: 19 of the 39 relapses among remitters switched to placebo spray occurred in the first month after stopping esketamine (6 by week 2), and 11 of those 19 had needed weekly dosing in the last 4 weeks before randomization.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Further analyses gave hazard ratios in the same direction: post hoc, both sets combined 0.38 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.57), 0.42 to 0.57 when each site was left out in turn (unweighted overall 0.47; no intervals printed), and 0.50 (0.30 to 0.84; unweighted Cox model) after censoring the 3 relapsing patients whose dissociation scores clearly changed around randomization; by study entry (not labelled post hoc), direct-entry 0.49 (0.27 to 0.90) and transfer-entry 0.45 (0.17 to 1.18).
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Limitations (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The interim analysis after 31 relapses did not show superiority at two-sided 0.0097; the study continued with the relapse target re-estimated to 59 (originally 84 relapses among 211 remitters) and a final significance level of 0.046.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis › Sample Size Determination, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Treatment during maintenance (study conditions): among remitters who continued esketamine, 44.4% were on 56 mg and 55.6% on 84 mg, and 68.9% were dosed every 2 weeks most of the time; median exposure was 17.7 weeks to esketamine and 10.2 weeks to placebo spray. Among responders, 67.7% were on 84 mg and 54.8% were dosed weekly; median exposure 19.4 and 10.1 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continuing on p. 6) and 2nd paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events in the maintenance phase, esketamine (n=152) vs placebo spray (n=145): dysgeusia 41 (27.0%) vs 10 (6.9%), vertigo 38 (25.0%) vs 8 (5.5%), dissociation 35 (23.0%) vs 0, somnolence 32 (21.1%) vs 3 (2.1%), dizziness 31 (20.4%) vs 7 (4.8%), nausea 25 (16.4%) vs 1 (0.7%), blurred vision 24 (15.8%) vs 1 (0.7%). Most were mild or moderate and resolved the same day; no respiratory depression or interstitial cystitis was observed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Results, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Table 3 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: No deaths. Serious adverse events judged related to the study drug occurred in 6 patients, all during open-label induction: autonomic imbalance, disorientation, hypothermia, a lacunar stroke (day 1, 6 hours after dosing), sedation, simple partial seizures (day 5, 45 minutes after dosing, no previous seizures) and suicidal ideation; none was reported during optimization or maintenance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: During maintenance, adverse events led 4 of 152 (2.6%) on esketamine and 3 of 145 (2.1%) on placebo spray to stop the spray (mostly worsening depression). Blood pressure of 180 mmHg systolic or more occurred in 1 (0.7%) and 110 mmHg diastolic or more in 2 (1.3%) esketamine-treated patients, none on placebo spray.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Suicidality (C-SSRS, on which 1 to 5 denote suicidal ideation and 6 to 10 suicidal behaviour): during maintenance a higher score than at baseline was recorded in 3 (2.4%) on esketamine (maximum 4) vs 6 (4.5%) on placebo spray (maximum 1); during open-label induction, 42 (11.6%) of the direct-entry patients without suicidal ideation or behaviour at baseline had a higher score at some point, one of them reaching 8; during optimization, 22 (5.7%) direct- and transfer-entry patients did (maximum 3). No suicidal behaviour was reported in optimization or maintenance, and among patients who relapsed the highest score was 2 with esketamine and 3 with placebo spray.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Safety Assessments (p. 3, scale ranges); Results › Safety Results, 5th paragraph (p. 8, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: The score of 8 during induction lies in the paper's own suicidal-behaviour range (6 to 10); the text's statement that no suicidal behaviour was reported covers only optimization and maintenance, and the event is not described further.

key_findings.finding: Dissociation scores peaked 40 minutes after dosing, resolved by about 1.5 hours and became smaller with repeated sessions; no psychotic symptoms. No distinct withdrawal syndrome was seen in the 2 weeks after esketamine was stopped (20-item Physician Withdrawal Checklist), and no adverse events related to misuse of ketamine were reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Results, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Blinding relied on a placebo solution containing a bittering agent (denatonium benzoate) to simulate the taste of esketamine; the paper does not say whether the devices were identical in appearance; the authors acknowledge that the dissociative and sedative effects are difficult to blind and could have biased the staff who observed dosing. No check of whether participants could tell their allocation is reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Intranasal Study Drug and Administration (p. 3); Limitations (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the early relapses after switching are unlikely to be a withdrawal or rebound effect, because esketamine levels fall quickly (mean terminal half-life 7 to 12 hours) and never reach steady state with intermittent dosing, and because early relapse after stopping ECT is similar; this is their reasoning, not a trial measurement.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 contradicts itself on how many randomized patients entered directly and how many transferred from the short-term trials. Its footnotes b and c give, for the four groups (stable remission: esketamine, placebo spray; stable response: esketamine, placebo spray), direct-entry 54, 56, 31 and 41 (182 in all) and transfer-entry 36, 30, 31 and 18 (115 in all). Its dose sub-rows, as labelled, give direct-entry 26, 20, 15 and 8 (69 in all; 14 + 12, 9 + 11, 7 + 8, 6 + 2), transfer-entry 3001 10, 10, 16 and 10 (46) and transfer-entry 3002 54, 56, 31 and 41 (182), that is 228 transfer-entry patients. The rows labelled 3002 equal the footnote direct-entry counts in every column, and the other two sub-rows sum to the footnote transfer-entry counts (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not say which set is correct. As labelled, the sub-rows would place 182 randomized patients from TRD3002, more than the 115 who received esketamine in that trial (Popova et al., 2019, PDF p. 7), so they cannot be right as labelled; how the transfer-entry patients split between TRD3001 and TRD3002, and the dose distribution by entry route, cannot be recovered. Entry-route counts elsewhere on this card are the footnote counts and are attributed to the footnotes. Results by analysis set are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The NNTs (6 and 4) correspond to the crude proportions relapsing over variable, event-driven follow-up and are given without a time horizon.
reporting_issues.consequence: They cannot be read as the number treated for a stated period to prevent one relapse.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results say that esketamine decreased the risk of relapse by 51% and 70%; these figures are 1 minus the hazard ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: They are relative reductions in the hazard, not in the absolute risk; the absolute differences were 18.7 and 31.8 percentage points (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints times to relapse (for example 273.0 and 635.0) without a unit.
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit has to be inferred (days, from Figure 2's week axis).

reporting_issues.issue: Two randomization errors are reported only in the notes to Figure 1: one patient with stable response was randomized in the stable-remission set, and one who met neither definition in the stable-response set.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both were analysed as randomized, slightly diluting the definitions of the two analysis sets.

reporting_issues.issue: The leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis (99 sites, median 2 randomized patients per site, range 1 to 25) is reported only as a range of hazard ratios, 0.42 to 0.57, against an unweighted overall 0.47, with no confidence intervals or P values.
reporting_issues.consequence: It shows that the point estimate changes little when any one site is dropped, but not whether the result stays statistically significant, which cannot be checked from the paper.

verification.source_read: Online-first PDF (JAMA Psychiatry, published online June 5, 2019), 11 pages printed E1-E11, cited as PDF p. design_detail: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multicentre trial (TRANSFORM-1; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02417064), sponsored by Janssen, at outpatient centres in Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Estonia, France, Hungary, Mexico, Slovakia and the United States (countries from Table 1), September 2015 to February 2018. Adults aged 18 to 64 with non-psychotic major depression and prospectively confirmed non-response stopped their antidepressants and were randomized 1:1:1 to a nasal spray twice weekly for 4 weeks: esketamine fixed at 56 mg, esketamine 84 mg (56 mg on day 1, then 84 mg), or a placebo spray; every arm also started a new open-label oral antidepressant. Adaptive two-stage design: a prespecified interim analysis after 121 patients re-estimated the sample size, and the primary analysis used a weighted combination test that gives the two stages equal weight. Fixed-sequence testing: 84 mg was tested first, and 56 mg could be formally tested only if 84 mg was significant. The PDF read is the accepted manuscript.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with treatment-resistant depression, esketamine at a fixed 56 or 84 mg plus a newly started oral antidepressant lowered MADRS scores after 4 weeks more than a newly started antidepressant plus a placebo spray, under a prespecified testing order, and the short-term adverse-effect profile of each dose.
cannot_establish: Efficacy of 56 mg in a formal test (testing stopped when 84 mg failed, so its p-value is nominal); durability beyond 4 weeks; whether the weaker 84 mg result reflects the dose, that arm's higher early withdrawal, its larger share of people with three or more earlier failed antidepressants, changes in trial conduct between stages, or chance; how much participants' recognition of the drug's acute effects contributed (blinding was not assessed); or effects in the excluded groups.

sample.recruitment: Outpatient centres; how patients were found is not described. Entry required moderate to severe depression (a total score of 34 or more on the Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology, the version not named, and MADRS 28 or more) and, besides at least one antidepressant that had failed (no more than 25% improvement) in the current episode by history (MGH-ATRQ, from patient report and medical or pharmacy records), a prospectively observed failure of a different antidepressant over at least 6 weeks; those with no more than 25% MADRS improvement from week 1 to week 4 and a MADRS of 28 or more at weeks 2 and 4 stopped all antidepressants and were randomized (PDF pp. 7-8).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 to 64; DSM-5 recurrent or single-episode (at least 2 years) major depression without psychotic features (MINI); treatment-resistant depression defined as non-response to adequate trials of at least two antidepressants in the current episode. Key exclusions: suicidal ideation with intent to act in the prior 6 months or suicidal behaviour in the prior year; psychotic disorder, bipolar or related disorders; moderate or severe substance use disorder in the prior 6 months; positive tests for specified drugs. The full list is in supplementary material that was not read (PDF p. 8).
sample.demographics: Efficacy set, 56 mg / 84 mg / placebo spray (Table 1, PDF pp. 40-41): mean age 46.4 / 45.7 / 46.8; women 70.4% / 69.3% / 71.7%; White 79.1% / 74.6% / 76.1%; United States 39.1% / 39.5% / 39.8%; mean duration of the current episode 202.8 / 212.7 / 193.1 weeks; three or more earlier failed antidepressants 30.1% / 48.2% / 40.7% (one or two: 69.9% / 51.8% / 59.3%); mean baseline MADRS 37.4 / 37.8 / 37.5 (Table 2, PDF p. 42).
sample.attrition: 315 of 346 (91.0%) completed the double-blind phase; withdrawals 6 of 117 (5.1%), 19 of 116 (16.4%) and 6 of 113 (5.3%), and 11 of the 19 in the 84 mg arm withdrew after only the first dose, which was 56 mg (PDF p. 15). Reasons (Figure 1, PDF p. 46): 56 mg arm, adverse event 1, lack of efficacy 1, protocol violation 2, withdrawal by patient 1, other 1; 84 mg arm, adverse event 7, lack of efficacy 1, lost to follow-up 1, protocol violation 1, withdrawal by patient 5, other 4; placebo arm, adverse event 2, protocol violation 1, withdrawal by patient 1, other 2. A day-28 MADRS was available for 111 of 115, 98 of 114 and 108 of 113 (Table 2, PDF p. 42).
sample.selection_effects: Trial population selected for prospectively confirmed non-response, excluding psychotic and bipolar disorders, recent moderate or severe substance use disorder and suicidal intent; about 70% women and three-quarters White, which the authors list among the limits on generalizability with the exclusion of people with significant comorbidity or imminent suicide risk (PDF p. 23). 150 patients who responded went on to the SUSTAIN-1 relapse-prevention trial (Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, self-administered at the study site under the supervision of a staff member (PDF p. 9). Adherence to the open-label oral antidepressant is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: three nasal spray devices per session in all arms (an active device gives two sprays and 28 mg esketamine base; the placebo solution contained a bittering agent); 56 mg arm fixed at 56 mg; 84 mg arm 56 mg on day 1, then 84 mg from day 4 in a blinded manner; twice weekly for 4 weeks. The open-label oral antidepressant (duloxetine, escitalopram, sertraline or extended-release venlafaxine) was chosen by the investigator, could not be one the patient had failed in the current episode or not tolerated, and followed a mandatory titration schedule (PDF pp. 8-9).
exposure.polysubstance: Positive tests for specified drugs and recent moderate or severe substance use disorder excluded people at entry; concomitant medications and alcohol or other drug use during the trial are not reported in the paper.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (treatment trial). MADRS ratings were done within 2 days before a dosing visit (PDF p. 10).

comparison.controls: A newly started open-label oral antidepressant plus a placebo nasal spray (bittering agent; three devices per session) on the same twice-weekly schedule. Both arms switched to a new antidepressant, so the comparison isolates the spray.
comparison.matching: 1:1:1 randomization by computer-generated schedule in randomly permuted blocks, stratified by country and oral antidepressant class (SNRI or SSRI); identical devices and packaging (PDF p. 8).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison. A chance imbalance in earlier treatment failures (three or more failed antidepressants in 30.1% / 48.2% / 40.7%) was not adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusions as the esketamine arms.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: MADRS change from baseline (day 1) to day 28, by independent telephone raters blind to protocol details, study visit, clinical status and side effects. Key secondary endpoints in a fixed order: onset of clinical response by day 2 maintained to day 28, Sheehan Disability Scale, PHQ-9. Other: response, remission, CGI-S, GAD-7, EQ-5D-5L. Safety: adverse events, laboratory tests, ECG, vital signs, C-SSRS, CADSS, BPRS positive-symptom subscale, MOAA/S, a discharge-readiness scale, nasal examination and symptom questionnaire, and the Physician Withdrawal Checklist (PWC-20); cognitive results to be reported separately (PDF pp. 9-11).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated rating scales.
outcomes.operationalization: Response: MADRS reduction of at least 50%. Remission: MADRS of 12 or less. Onset of clinical response: a reduction of at least 50% by day 2 kept to day 28, with one excursion allowed if the reduction stayed at least 25%; patients with missed assessments or early discontinuation counted as not having onset. Moderate or greater sedation: MOAA/S of 3 or less, with a score of 4 called mild (PDF pp. 14, 19, 43).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Truncated fixed-sequence procedure across the primary and three key secondary endpoints and the two doses: 84 mg first at two-sided 0.05; 56 mg at 0.0425 only if 84 mg was significant; if only 84 mg was significant, further endpoints were tested for that dose at 0.0075 (PDF pp. 12-13). Because 84 mg failed the primary test (p=0.088), no other dose or endpoint was formally tested; every other p-value is nominal.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Remote telephone MADRS raters blind to protocol details, visit, clinical status and side effects; spray assignment double-blind with identical devices and a bittering agent in the placebo (PDF pp. 8-10). Whether participants or staff could tell the allocation was not assessed; the authors say the adverse-event profile may have affected the blind for patients (PDF p. 23).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (weighted combination; median unbiased estimate; two-sided flexible 95% CI): 84 mg vs placebo spray −3.2 (−6.88 to 0.45), p=0.088; 56 mg vs placebo spray −4.1 (−7.67 to −0.49), nominal p=0.027 (Table 2, PDF p. 42). Raw mean change at day 28: −19.0 (SD 13.86, n=111), −18.8 (SD 14.12, n=98), −14.8 (SD 15.07, n=108). Unweighted MMRM differences at days 2, 8, 15, 22 and 28 (Figure 2, PDF p. 47): 84 mg −2.2, −2.7, −3.6, −3.7, −3.6; 56 mg −3.0, −3.0, −3.8, −5.0, −4.0. By stage at day 28 (Figure 3, PDF p. 48): stage 1 (n=121) 84 mg 0.0 (SE 3.08), 56 mg −3.6 (SE 3.13); stage 2 (n=221) 84 mg −5.6 (SE 2.31), 56 mg −4.5 (SE 2.21). Post hoc, both doses combined (unweighted): −3.8 (SE 1.58; 95% CI −6.92 to −0.70) (Table 4, PDF p. 44). Onset of response by day 2 maintained to day 28: 12 of 115 (10.4%), 10 of 114 (8.8%), 2 of 113 (1.8%); odds ratios 6.47 (1.38 to 60.45) and 5.34 (1.09 to 50.91). Sheehan Disability Scale −2.5 (−5.25 to 0.20) and −2.2 (−4.91 to 0.53); PHQ-9 −2.3 (−4.34 to −0.31) and −2.2 (−4.26 to −0.20) (Table 3, PDF p. 43). Response at day 28 54.1%, 53.1% and 38.9% (NNT 7 and 7); remission 36.0%, 38.8% and 30.6% (NNT 18 and 12) (PDF p. 16). GAD-7 differences −1.5 (−2.84 to −0.20) and −1.4 (−2.77 to −0.12) (PDF p. 17). Editors' calculation: standardized differences about 0.28 (56 mg) and 0.22 (84 mg), dividing the weighted differences by the pooled SD of day-28 change (14.5 and 14.6); the response and remission percentages match 60/111, 52/98 and 42/108, and 40/111, 38/98 and 33/108, that is, patients with a day-28 rating; counting those without one as not responding gives response 52.2%, 45.6% and 37.2% (84 mg vs placebo spray 8.4 points, 95% CI −4.3 to 21.2) and remission 34.8%, 33.3% and 29.2%.
analysis.covariates: MMRM with baseline MADRS as covariate; treatment, region, oral antidepressant class, day and day-by-treatment as fixed effects; a random patient effect; changes at days 2, 8, 15, 22 and 28 as repeated measures; treatment comparisons by a weighted combination test giving the pre- and post-interim test statistics equal weight (Cui et al., 1999; Lehmacher & Wassmer, 1999) (PDF p. 13). GAD-7 by ANCOVA.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02417064 (PDF pp. 4, 6). The paper does not compare registered with reported outcomes; the registry record was not read. Planned maximum sample 348 (about 116 per arm for 90% power, assuming a 6.5-point difference, SD 12, two-sided 0.025 and 25% dropout). After the interim analysis of 121 patients, the independent data monitoring committee recommended a final sample of 234; once 234 had been randomized, the sponsor let patients already in screening continue, so 346 were randomized (PDF pp. 11-12).
analysis.selective_reporting: The failed primary result is stated plainly in the abstract and text. The 56 mg result is reported with a nominal p-value as informative for practitioners. The stage-by-stage split is shown. The subgroup forest plot (Figure 4) gives no numerical estimates. Response and remission denominators are not printed. Supplementary material and cognitive results not available here.
analysis.power: Planned for 90% power to detect 6.5 points with either dose; the weighted differences were 3.2 and 4.1 points. The final sample (346) exceeded the re-estimated 234.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 4 weeks, 84 mg esketamine plus a new antidepressant did not significantly beat a new antidepressant plus placebo spray (MADRS difference −3.2, 95% CI −6.88 to 0.45; p=0.088); 56 mg gave −4.1 (−7.67 to −0.49) but could not be formally tested. In the first 121 patients the 84 mg difference was 0.0; in the 221 enrolled after the interim analysis it was −5.6. The 84 mg arm lost 16.4% of its patients (11 after the first dose) and had more people with three or more earlier failed antidepressants (48.2% vs 30.1% and 40.7%). Remission at day 28 was 36.0% and 38.8% vs 30.6% (NNT 18 and 12). The rapid-onset endpoint favoured esketamine numerically (10.4% and 8.8% vs 1.8%) but was not testable. Dissociation was reported by 26.1% and 27.6% vs 3.5%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states the primary result accurately but concludes that the study provides supportive evidence for esketamine as a new, rapid-acting antidepressant and that both doses exceeded what is considered clinically meaningful for approved antidepressants against placebo (PDF pp. 3-4); the summary repeats both points (PDF pp. 23-24). The clinical-meaning claim sets point estimates, one of whose intervals includes no effect, against a 2-point threshold taken from other trials (PDF p. 21), and rapid action rests on an endpoint that was never formally tested. The discussion explains the null 84 mg result by withdrawals, a large comparator response, a difference between stages that coincided with mid-trial changes (audio-recording of MADRS interviews, new experienced sites, extra training, and the availability of an open-label long-term esketamine study) and the one-in-three placebo allocation (PDF pp. 21-23); these explanations are offered without supporting analyses, and the stage-1 null is not mentioned in the abstract. The text calls the groups similar at baseline (PDF p. 15) although Table 1 shows the imbalance in earlier treatment failures. A headline that this trial confirmed esketamine overstates it: it is negative on its primary endpoint, and its supportive numbers are exploratory.

timeline.event: Phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine against placebo spray, added to existing antidepressants, on which this trial's sample size and dose-testing order were based (to be appraised from its own card)
TRANSFORM-2, the flexible-dose sister trial with the same design: MADRS difference −4.0 at day 28 (p=0.020), primary endpoint met
This trial (TRANSFORM-1): 84 mg −3.2 (p=0.088), primary endpoint not met; 56 mg −4.1 nominal
SUSTAIN-1 relapse-prevention trial; 150 responders from this trial entered it (Figure 1)
Turner, critique of the efficacy evidence and of the FDA approval of esketamine (to be appraised from the full text)
Horowitz and Moncrieff, critical review of the evidence for esketamine, with a published corrigendum (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: This trial and TRANSFORM-2 differed mainly in fixed versus flexible dosing; TRANSFORM-2 reached significance (−4.0) and this one did not (−3.2 for 84 mg), with point estimates of similar size. The paper notes the US approval of esketamine nasal spray for treatment-resistant depression (PDF p. 5) and cites a 2019 NEJM article (Kim et al.) on the first FDA-approved antidepressant in a new class for the statement that the phase 3 studies, including this one, provided evidence of clinically meaningful efficacy with a newly started antidepressant (PDF p. 21); it does not detail what the approval rested on. Published critiques (Turner, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) are listed for appraisal and not summarized here.

funding.funder: Supported by Janssen Research and Development, LLC, Titusville, NJ (PDF p. 25). Medical writing assistance by Sandra Norris (Norris Communications Group LLC, supported by Janssen) and editorial support by Ellen Baum (Janssen Global Services) are acknowledged.
funding.declared_conflicts: Ten of the 18 authors (Fedgchin, Daly, Melkote, Lane, Lim, Vitagliano, Manji, Hough, Drevets, Singh) are employees of Janssen Research & Development and hold company equity. Trivedi reports consulting or advisory roles for many companies including Johnson & Johnson Pharmaceutical Research & Development, royalties from Janssen Research and Development, and grants including from Johnson & Johnson. Blier, Liebowitz, Ravindran, Gaillard, van den Ameele and Preskorn report consulting, advisory, trial-contract or grant relationships with companies including Janssen; Fava's disclosures are given only as a web link. Sponsor employees were involved in trial design, patient recruitment, data collection, analysis and interpretation (PDF pp. 26-28).
funding.affiliations_note: Sponsor statisticians (Melkote, Lane, Lim) ran the analyses (PDF p. 26). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An independent trial with fixed doses and enough power to compare them, an active placebo that mimics esketamine's acute sensations, blinding checked by asking participants, raters and staff to guess allocation, stable trial procedures throughout, intention-to-treat response and remission, and follow-up of 6 to 12 months.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedule in permuted blocks, stratified by country and antidepressant class; identical devices and packaging. The imbalance in three or more earlier failed antidepressants (30.1% / 48.2% / 40.7%; editors' chi-square p of about 0.02) is one variable among many and is compatible with chance, but it could have disadvantaged the 84 mg arm.

Dissociation (26.1% and 27.6% vs 3.5%), sedation and blood-pressure rises could have shown participants and staff the allocation (PDF p. 23). No deviations arising from the trial context are reported. The efficacy analysis excluded 4 randomized patients who received no esketamine or no oral antidepressant (Table 2 note).

Day-28 MADRS missing for 16 of 114 in the 84 mg arm (14%) vs 4 and 5 in the other arms; 11 of 19 withdrawals in that arm came after the first dose; the MMRM assumes data missing at random, and no missing-data sensitivity analysis is reported.
Raters were remote and blind to visit, clinical status and side effects, but a telephone MADRS rests on participants' own reports, and their awareness of allocation was not assessed.
The primary analysis, testing order and adaptive weighting were prespecified, and the failed primary result is reported as such; the registry record was not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design and prespecified analysis are sound and the negative primary result is reported transparently. Possible functional unblinding and unequal missing data in the 84 mg arm leave some concerns, although unblinding would tend to favour esketamine and so does not explain the null primary result. Under the trial's own rules, the 56 mg estimate and every secondary result are exploratory. The card may be cited for the failed primary comparison, the nominal 56 mg result as exploratory, the stage-by-stage split, response and remission with their denominators, and the short-term adverse-effect profile; not as confirmation of efficacy for either dose.

key_findings.finding: Of 710 people screened, 346 were randomized: 117 to esketamine 56 mg, 116 to esketamine 84 mg and 113 to placebo spray, each with a new oral antidepressant; 115, 114 and 113 entered the efficacy analysis.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 1st paragraph (p. 14); Table 1 (p. 40); Figure 1 (p. 46)

key_findings.finding: Who took part: adults aged 18 to 64 (mean 46, about 70% women) with moderate to severe non-psychotic depression and an average current episode of about 4 years (202.8 / 212.7 / 193.1 weeks), whose depression had not responded to an antidepressant by history plus a different one watched prospectively for at least 6 weeks (no more than 25% MADRS improvement). Three or more earlier failed antidepressants: 30.1% (56 mg), 48.2% (84 mg), 40.7% (placebo spray), although the text calls the groups similar.
key_findings.locator: Study Population, 2nd paragraph (pp. 7-8); Study Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 15); Table 1 (pp. 40-41)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation for the three-way imbalance: chi-square 7.9 on 2 degrees of freedom, p about 0.02.

key_findings.finding: What each arm got (study conditions): a supervised self-administered nasal spray on days 1, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22 and 28 according to the text (twice weekly for 4 weeks), three devices per session: esketamine 56 mg, esketamine 84 mg after 56 mg on day 1, or a placebo spray with a bitter taste added; every arm started a new oral antidepressant on day 1.
key_findings.locator: Randomization and Blinding; Intranasal Study Drug and Administration, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Newly-Initiated Oral Antidepressant
key_findings.note: Figures 5 and 6 (PDF pp. 50-51) show dosing sessions on days 1 to 25, not day 28.

key_findings.finding: Primary result: the 84 mg dose did not significantly beat the comparator at day 28 (MADRS difference −3.2, 95% CI −6.88 to 0.45; p=0.088). Under the prespecified testing order, the 56 mg dose (−4.1, 95% CI −7.67 to −0.49; nominal p=0.027) and all key secondary endpoints could therefore not be formally tested.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 4th paragraph (p. 15, continuing on p. 16); Table 2 (p. 42)

key_findings.finding: Mean MADRS scores fell from 37.4, 37.8 and 37.5 by 19.0 points (SD 13.86, n=111) with 56 mg, 18.8 points (SD 14.12, n=98) with 84 mg and 14.8 points (SD 15.07, n=108) with placebo spray.
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: The result depended on when people joined. In the 121 patients enrolled before the interim analysis, the day-28 difference was 0.0 for 84 mg (SE 3.08) and −3.6 for 56 mg (SE 3.13); in the 221 enrolled afterwards it was −5.6 (SE 2.31) and −4.5 (SE 2.21), mainly because the placebo-spray arm improved less in the second stage.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 5th paragraph (p. 16); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 22); Figure 3 (p. 48)

key_findings.finding: During the trial, before and independently of the interim analysis, several initiatives were introduced to improve the quality of study conduct (the paper does not say by whom): audio-recording of the independent MADRS interviews, new experienced sites, enhanced site education and training, and the availability of an open-label long-term esketamine safety extension study; all were considered to have had an impact on the patients enrolled in stage 2.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 22, continuing on p. 23)

key_findings.finding: Sample size: the interim analysis after 121 patients led the independent data monitoring committee to set a final sample of 234; when 234 had been randomized the sponsor let patients already in screening continue, so 346 were randomized, close to the planned maximum of 348.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Methods › Sample Size Determination; Interim Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Dropouts: 6 (5.1%), 19 (16.4%) and 6 (5.3%) withdrew before the end of the 4 weeks; 11 of the 19 in the 84 mg arm left after only the first dose, which was 56 mg, and 7 of the 19 left because of adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 15); Figure 1 (p. 46)

key_findings.finding: Unweighted differences by visit (not adjusted for multiplicity or sample-size re-estimation): 84 mg −2.2, −2.7, −3.6, −3.7 and −3.6, and 56 mg −3.0, −3.0, −3.8, −5.0 and −4.0, at days 2, 8, 15, 22 and 28. Post hoc, both doses pooled: −3.8 (SE 1.58; 95% CI −6.92 to −0.70).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 legend, note (p. 38); Table 4 (p. 44); Figure 2, table beneath the graph (p. 47)
key_findings.note: The unweighted day-28 values (−3.6 and −4.0) differ from the weighted primary estimates in Table 2 (−3.2 and −4.1); the weighted estimates are the prespecified primary result.

key_findings.finding: Key secondary endpoints, none formally testable: a MADRS reduction of at least 50% by day 2 kept to day 28 in 12 of 115 (10.4%), 10 of 114 (8.8%) and 2 of 113 (1.8%); disability (Sheehan) differences −2.5 (95% CI −5.25 to 0.20) and −2.2 (−4.91 to 0.53); self-rated depression (PHQ-9) −2.3 (−4.34 to −0.31) and −2.2 (−4.26 to −0.20).
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Response at day 28 (MADRS down at least 50%): 54.1% (56 mg), 53.1% (84 mg), 38.9% (placebo spray), NNT 7 and 7. Remission (MADRS 12 or less): 36.0%, 38.8% and 30.6%, NNT 18 and 12.
key_findings.locator: Secondary Efficacy Endpoints and Analyses, 3rd paragraph (definitions, p. 14); Study Results, 7th paragraph (p. 16)
key_findings.note: Denominators are not printed; the percentages match patients with a day-28 rating (60/111, 52/98, 42/108; 40/111, 38/98, 33/108; editors' calculation). Counting those without a rating as not responding: response 52.2%, 45.6%, 37.2%; remission 34.8%, 33.3%, 29.2%.

key_findings.finding: Anxiety (GAD-7) differences −1.5 (95% CI −2.84 to −0.20) and −1.4 (−2.77 to −0.12); the odds of a less severe CGI-S at day 28 were 3.2 (56 mg) and 2.5 (84 mg) times those with placebo spray, with no intervals printed.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 8th paragraph (p. 16, continuing on p. 17) and 9th paragraph (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events, 56 mg / 84 mg / placebo spray (N=115/116/113): nausea 27.0% / 31.9% / 10.6%, dissociation 26.1% / 27.6% / 3.5%, dizziness 27.8% / 22.4% / 8.8%, vertigo 20.9% / 20.7% / 1.8%, somnolence 20.9% / 18.1% / 11.5%, headache 20.0% / 20.7% / 16.8%. Most occurred on dosing days, were mild or moderate and resolved the same day; dissociation scores peaked at 40 minutes and resolved by 1.5 hours; no psychotic symptoms were reported.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 11th and 12th paragraphs (pp. 17-18); Table 5 (p. 45)

key_findings.finding: The spray was stopped for adverse events by 1 (0.9%), 7 (6.0%) and 2 (1.8%); 5 of the 7 in the 84 mg arm stopped after only the 56 mg dose of day 1. There were no deaths; two serious adverse events, both in the 56 mg arm, were judged possibly (worsening depression on day 15) or probably (headache on day 12) related to the spray.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 13th and 14th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Largest mean maximum blood-pressure rise across dosing days: systolic +14.3 and +15.0 mmHg vs +7.2 mmHg, diastolic +8.9 and +9.4 vs +5.3 mmHg; no respiratory depression. Moderate or greater sedation (MOAA/S 3 or less) in 11 of 115 (9.6%) and 14 of 116 (12.1%) vs 1 of 113 (0.9%); sedation was mostly mild (score 4) and resolved by 1 to 1.5 hours.
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Treatment-emergent suicidal ideation (C-SSRS): 12 (10.4%), 8 (7.1%) and 13 (11.5%); one participant on 56 mg reported preparatory behaviour (keeping sleeping tablets under the pillow), recorded as an adverse event that resolved the same day. By 1 hour after dosing at least 56% (56 mg), at least 44% (84 mg) and at least 88% (placebo spray) were judged ready to go home. The authors report no evidence of withdrawal symptoms in the 2 weeks after stopping (PWC-20).
key_findings.locator: Study Results, 17th paragraph (p. 19, continuing on p. 20), 19th and 20th paragraphs (p. 20)

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that the comparator's higher response and remission may reflect participants' high expectation of receiving a novel drug and frequent, lengthy clinic visits (in some cases up to 4 hours twice weekly); they report that dissociation scores (CADSS) rose from baseline in 28.3% of the placebo-spray arm, which they take to show a nocebo effect, and say these factors may have contributed to a smaller effect than in the phase 2 trial on which the sample size was based.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 21, continuing on p. 22)

key_findings.finding: On the regulator, the paper notes that esketamine nasal spray has been approved in the United States for treatment-resistant depression and cites a 2019 NEJM article (Kim et al.) on the first FDA-approved antidepressant in a new class for the statement that the phase 3 studies, including this one, provided evidence of clinically meaningful efficacy with a newly started antidepressant; it gives no further detail of what the approval rested on.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 20, continuing on p. 21)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 gives 30 (13.3%) for hypoesthesia in the total esketamine group; 30/231 is 13.0%, as printed for paresthesia (30, 13.0%) in the next row (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic slip; the arm-level figures (14/115 and 16/116) are consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the treatment groups were similar in baseline characteristics, but Table 1 shows three or more earlier failed antidepressants in 30.1% (56 mg), 48.2% (84 mg) and 40.7% (placebo spray).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 84 mg arm was more treatment-resistant at baseline, a possible contributor to its weaker result that the discussion does not mention.

reporting_issues.issue: The text lists dosing on days 1, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22 and 28, but Figures 5 and 6 show dosing sessions on days 1, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22 and 25.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typographical error for day 25; the day-28 MADRS was the primary endpoint and would follow the last dose.

reporting_issues.issue: Two day-28 estimates are printed for each dose: the weighted median unbiased estimates of Table 2 (−3.2, −4.1) and the unweighted MMRM estimates under Figure 2 (−3.6, −4.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers should cite Table 2 for the prespecified primary result; the equal weighting gives the 121 stage-1 patients as much weight as the 221 stage-2 patients, which lowers the 84 mg estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The response and remission percentages are printed without denominators, and the NNTs are computed from them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages match completers with a day-28 rating; on all analysed patients, the 84 mg response difference falls from 14.2 to 8.4 points (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The CGI-S odds ratios (3.2 and 2.5) are printed without confidence intervals or a described model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Their precision cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: This paper counts MOAA/S 3 or less as moderate or greater sedation and calls 4 mild, whereas the TRANSFORM-2 paper counts 4 or less as moderate or greater.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sedation rates (9.6% and 12.1% here vs 57.4% in TRANSFORM-2) are not comparable as printed.
