design_detail: Four-page 'Analysis' article (critical narrative review) in The British Journal of Psychiatry, published online in 2020 (received 11 November 2019, accepted 23 April 2020), arguing that the licensing evidence for intranasal esketamine in 'treatment-resistant depression' did not establish efficacy and that safety signals were played down. Sources: the FDA review documents and Janssen's advisory-committee briefing document, published trial reports, commentaries (including Turner, 2019), news items, a Public Health England report and NICE draft guidance; three tables of deaths and adverse events taken from the FDA and Janssen documents. Background sections on ketamine's anaesthetic use, recreational use and harms cite one review (Morgan and Curran, 2012) for most of their statements. No search strategy. A corrigendum (Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618, online 2 July 2021; read as PDF) qualifies Table 1, adds long-term and post-marketing data on suicidality and qualifies the statement on anaesthetic use. The PDF read is the online-first version, 'Page 1 of 4' to 'Page 4 of 4'.
can_establish: What the FDA and Janssen documents, as reproduced by the authors, show about deaths, worsening of depression and suicidality, common adverse events and bladder symptoms in the esketamine licensing programme, and the authors' arguments that the short-term trials were weak and the discontinuation trial confounded by withdrawal.
cannot_establish: That esketamine caused the deaths or suicides (the corrigendum states that Table 1 is not a randomized comparison and that exposure was larger and longer with esketamine); that relapse in the discontinuation trial was withdrawal (an untested hypothesis); or anything about ketamine's recreational harms beyond the secondary sources it cites.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The licensing programme as described: three 4-week efficacy trials, one discontinuation trial and one 60-week safety trial submitted by Janssen to the FDA (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF); 1861 participants exposed to esketamine and 486 to placebo in stage 2 and 3 trials up to 4 September 2018 (Table 1, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the authors chose the evidence.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen to support the critique. The regulatory documents are a defined source, but the background on recreational harms and several key arguments rest on secondary sources (one review, commentaries, a news item), and the case for efficacy made by the sponsor and the FDA is reported only where the authors rebut it.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited trials: intranasal esketamine against placebo (a nasal spray with an embittering agent) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as described by the authors: in the 4-week and discontinuation trials, esketamine 56 to 84 mg twice a week intranasally; in the 60-week safety study, weekly or fortnightly; the discontinuation trial enrolled people in stable remission after 16 weeks of esketamine (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF). The authors call the trial doses in line with recreational doses of ketamine and state that esketamine is twice as potent as ketamine, citing secondary sources (pp. 1–2).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed (the trials added esketamine to oral antidepressants, as the titles of the cited trial reports show).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Placebo nasal spray in the trials; for deaths (Table 1), all placebo-exposed against all esketamine-exposed participants across stage 2 and 3 trials, including open-label periods, as the corrigendum states.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: MADRS change and relapse in the trials; Clinical Global Impression thresholds linked to MADRS change (from a separate equipercentile-linking study); Physician Withdrawal Checklist; adverse events, deaths, worsening of depression and suicidal ideas, blood pressure, bladder symptoms and cognitive impairment from the FDA and Janssen documents (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note the FDA's statement that adverse events were misclassified, under-reported and misrepresented, so Table 2 likely underestimates their incidence (Table 2 footnote, p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy judged by statistical significance across trials and by comparing the 4-point MADRS difference with change thresholds for individual patients; harm judged by counts of events in esketamine-exposed and placebo-exposed participants across different trial sets.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As reproduced from the FDA and Janssen documents (pp. 2–3 of the online-first PDF): in the only positive 4-week trial, MADRS fell by 19.8 points with esketamine and 15.8 with placebo (baseline mean 37); deaths 6 of 1861 esketamine-exposed (0.3%; 3 suicides) against 0 of 486 placebo-exposed; worsening of suicidal ideas 5/570 (0.9%) against 2/432 (0.5%); worsening of depression 8/570 (1.4%) against 1/432 (0.2%); increased blood pressure 368/3646 (printed 10.0%; 10.1% by editors' calculation) against 15/432 (3.5%); in trials 3001 and 3002, dissociation 48.3% against 18.9%, dizziness 29.5% against 8.1%, nausea 28.9% against 8.6%, vertigo 22.5% against 2.7%, cystitis-suggestive events 10.7% against 2.7%. No confidence intervals or tests. Corrigendum (PDF, p. 618): in the long-term safety study, whose population was selected for lack of active suicidality, 114 of 784 (14.5%) reported treatment-emergent suicidal ideation; for post-marketing reports to the FDA in the first 12 months, a cited analysis found a 24-fold increased risk of report for suicidal ideation and a 6-fold increased risk for completed suicide compared with other drugs (the statistic is not named).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Arguments are one-sided by design. Table 1 compared deaths across unequal, partly open-label exposure without saying so until the corrigendum. Table 2 uses different denominators for different rows (570 against 3646 esketamine-exposed). Several statements are attributed to secondary sources that do not contain them (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The figures reproduced from the regulatory documents show one significant 4-week trial out of three with a 4-point MADRS difference, a discontinuation trial in an enriched group whose significance depended on one site, six deaths (three suicides) among esketamine-exposed participants and none among the fewer placebo-exposed participants, small excesses of worsening depression and suicidal ideas, and common acute adverse effects (dissociation in about half in two 4-week trials, against about a fifth with placebo), with bladder symptoms in about a fifth in the 60-week open-label study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary states that the licensing trials "did not establish efficacy" and that safety signals, including deaths, suicides and bladder damage, were "minimised" (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the conclusion speaks of patients as unwitting guinea pigs in an unregulated experiment (p. 3). Gaps: (1) the deaths are presented as occurring only in those assigned to esketamine, without saying that Table 1 pools open-label and placebo-controlled periods with much larger and longer esketamine exposure; the authors' own corrigendum (2021) concedes that no definitive causal inference can be drawn from it; (2) withdrawal as the explanation for relapse after stopping esketamine is the authors' argument, and withdrawal as the explanation for the suicides comes from a commentary; neither was tested; (3) the 4-point between-group difference is compared with change thresholds for individual patients, which are not the same quantity; (4) several statements are attributed to Turner (2019), whose Comment does not make them. The criticisms of the trial evidence that come from the FDA's own documents (one positive short-term trial, enrichment, the outlier site, unblinding) are documented.

timeline.event: Daly et al.: phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine (this round's first-pass card sc_daly_2018).
Turner: Comment with seven concerns about the efficacy evidence and the FDA approval, including the outlier-site re-analysis that this article cites.
Schatzberg: commentary cited here for the timing of the three suicides and the possibility of a withdrawal reaction (not read).
NICE draft guidance (January) recommending against esketamine for treatment-resistant depression, as described here; this article published online.

Corrigendum (Br J Psychiatry 219(5), p. 618, online 2 July 2021): Table 1 pools phase 2 and phase 3 data including open-label periods, is not a randomized comparison and allows no definitive causal inference; adds long-term safety-study and post-marketing data on suicidality; qualifies the statement on anaesthetic use.
Dean et al.: Cochrane review of randomized trials of ketamine, esketamine and other glutamate modulators in unipolar depression (this round's first-pass card sc_dean_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The efficacy criticisms overlap with Turner (2019) and rest on the same FDA documents; the safety criticisms rely on non-randomized counts, which the authors' corrigendum acknowledges. Randomized long-term safety data remain the gap both articles identify.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: J.M. (Joanna Moncrieff) is co-chairperson of the Critical Psychiatry Network; ICMJE disclosure forms are in the online supplementary material (Declaration of interest, p. 4 of the online-first PDF), which was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Division of Psychiatry, University College London, and North East London Foundation Trust. M.A.H. wrote the article; J.M. edited it and supervised (Author contributions, p. 4). The Critical Psychiatry Network position is relevant to a critique of a new psychiatric drug. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the article.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of esketamine lasting a year or more, with placebo or active comparator arms of equal exposure, pre-specified collection of deaths, suicidal ideation and behaviour, urinary and cognitive outcomes, and a discontinuation design that tapers treatment and measures withdrawal symptoms separately from relapse.

domains.note: No search or criteria; regulatory documents mixed with commentaries, news items and one review chosen by the authors.

The trials are appraised critically (unblinding, enrichment, outlier site, possible withdrawal confounding), but the sources for the harm claims are not, and non-randomized death counts were presented as a comparison until the corrigendum.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No studies by the authors are cited.

The withdrawal explanations for relapse and for the suicides are presented beside the data without being marked as untested; the Summary's wording goes beyond what the tables show; several statements are attributed to a source that does not contain them.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against esketamine's efficacy and safety (the sponsor's and the FDA's case is under-represented)
domains.note: The FDA's reasons for approval and its assessment of the deaths are reported only to be rebutted; positive data (the significant trial, the overall relapse result) are mentioned only with their weaknesses.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative critique (METHODS §5.3). The article usefully brings together regulatory data that are hard to find (deaths, worsening of depression and suicidality, common adverse events, bladder symptoms) and states the main weaknesses of the efficacy evidence; but its selection is unsystematic and one-sided, its central safety table needed a corrigendum to say it allows no definitive causal inference, and several attributions to secondary sources do not check out. It may be cited for the counts it reproduces from the FDA and Janssen documents (with their denominators and the corrigendum's caveat) and as a published critique; it may not be cited for esketamine causing deaths or suicides, for withdrawal as the cause of relapse, or for ketamine's recreational harms, which must be cited to primary studies.

key_findings.finding: The authors' Summary: licensing trials did not establish efficacy (two negative trials, one statistically significant but clinically uncertain, and a flawed discontinuation trial accepted against FDA precedent), and safety signals including deaths, suicides and bladder damage were minimised.
key_findings.locator: Summary

key_findings.finding: Janssen submitted five studies to the FDA: three 4-week efficacy trials, one discontinuation trial and one 60-week safety trial. The authors state that in the 4-week and discontinuation trials doses of 56 to 84 mg were given intranasally twice a week. Only one of the three short-term trials showed a statistically significant difference from placebo.
key_findings.locator: Evidence submitted to the FDA, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' statement. The discontinuation trial's report (Daly et al., 2019, SUSTAIN-1, which the article cites as reference 24 for this trial) describes twice-weekly dosing only in its 4-week induction phase, then weekly and later weekly or every 2 weeks, so dosing in that trial should be cited to the trial report, not to this article.

key_findings.finding: In the only positive 4-week trial, the MADRS (0 to 60, baseline mean 37) fell by 19.8 points with esketamine and 15.8 with placebo, a 4-point difference; the authors compare this with a 7 to 9 point change corresponding to 'minimally improved' and 16 to 17 points to 'much improved' on the Clinical Global Impression scale, and note that dissociation would have unmasked participants.
key_findings.locator: The single positive efficacy trial
key_findings.note: Turner (2019, p. 1 of its online-first PDF), citing FDA slide 24, gives 20.8 and 16.8 for the same trial; both give a 4-point difference. The CGI thresholds describe change in individual patients, not differences between group means.

key_findings.finding: Discontinuation trial: people in stable remission after 16 weeks of esketamine were randomized to continue or stop. The authors argue that withdrawal effects could be mistaken for relapse, noting that Physician Withdrawal Checklist scores are not reported, that 48.7% of relapses occurred in the first 4 weeks after stopping, and that the FDA observed the placebo relapse rate moving closer to esketamine week by week. Separately, the FDA highlighted unblinding (participants switched to placebo noticing the absence of psychoactive effects), and the authors cite the correlation of higher dissociation scores on treatment with shorter time to relapse as consistent with that unblinding hypothesis.
key_findings.locator: The discontinuation trial, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The FDA raised the concern that the discontinuation trial's result was driven by one site in Poland, where all 16 placebo participants relapsed, against 33% in the placebo arm elsewhere (printed as n = 81); without that site the P value changes from 0.012 to 0.48 (citing Turner's Comment, reference 18).
key_findings.locator: The discontinuation trial, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The n = 81 for the placebo arm elsewhere does not fit; see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: Six deaths occurred in the licensing trials, all among participants assigned to esketamine: 3 suicides, 1 fatal motor vehicle accident (a motorcycle accident 26 hours after a dose), 1 myocardial infarction (6 days after a dose) and 1 death from acute respiratory and cardiac failure (5 days after a dose, in a person with risk factors); Table 1 gives 6/1861 (0.3%) esketamine-exposed against 0/486 placebo-exposed participants in stage 2 and 3 trials up to 4 September 2018. For the two cardiovascular deaths, the FDA argued that one participant's cardiovascular parameters had been normal before and after the last dose and that esketamine raises blood pressure only briefly, and judged these deaths difficult to consider drug-related.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The authors' corrigendum (2021, p. 618) states that Table 1 pools phase 2 and phase 3 data including open-label periods, is not a randomized comparison, and that more and longer esketamine exposure may be one reason for the higher number of suicides in the esketamine group.

key_findings.finding: The three suicides occurred 4, 12 and 20 days after the last dose; two of the three had shown no suicidal ideas at study entry or at the last visit (no data for the third); the FDA attributed the deaths to the severity of the underlying illness and accepted Janssen's view that they were not drug-related; a cited commentary argued they might fit a severe withdrawal reaction.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: One esketamine participant had a non-fatal cerebral haemorrhage and five more in the esketamine arms had non-fatal motor vehicle accidents.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, continued on p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Selected adverse events (Table 2; 4-week trials 3001, 3002, 3005 and discontinuation trial 3003 unless stated): worsening of suicidal ideas 2/432 (0.5%) with placebo against 5/570 (0.9%) with esketamine; worsening of depression 1/432 (0.2%) against 8/570 (1.4%); non-fatal motor vehicle accidents 0 against 5 (denominators not reported); increased blood pressure 15/432 (3.5%) against 368/3646 (printed 10.0%; 10.1% by editors' calculation), both denominators in this row being participants in completed stage 3 studies (footnote d), whereas 432 in the other rows counts the 4-week and discontinuation trials (footnote b). The FDA noted misclassification, under-reporting and misrepresentation of adverse events, so these figures likely underestimate incidence.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnotes
key_findings.note: The text gives six, not eight, participants with worsening depression and calls these short-term-trial figures, although footnote b includes trial 3003; see reporting issues 1 and 2.

key_findings.finding: Most common adverse events in the 4-week trials 3001 and 3002 (placebo against esketamine, % of exposed): dissociation 18.9 against 48.3; dizziness 8.1 against 29.5; nausea 8.6 against 28.9; headache 18.0 against 19.7; sedation 9.9 against 23.1; anxiety 7.7 against 13.3; vertigo 2.7 against 22.5; hypoaesthesia 1.8 against 12.7; blood pressure increase 1.4 against 10.7; vomiting 1.4 against 11.3; cystitis-suggestive adverse events 2.7 against 10.7.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Signs of bladder irritation (urinary tract infections, pain, discomfort, cystitis, nocturia) occurred in esketamine participants; in the 60-week study with weekly or fortnightly dosing, a fifth reported bladder effects, and some cognitive impairment was detected among older participants; the FDA argued that the lack of a comparison arm and individual variability made it difficult to conclude that these effects were attributable to esketamine.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: When licensing esketamine, the FDA recommended a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy because of concerns about sedation, dissociation and diversion; the strategy requires administration in a healthcare setting with monitoring for at least 2 hours.
key_findings.locator: The safety of esketamine in trials submitted to the FDA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The MHRA licensed esketamine; NICE's draft guidance of January 2020 recommended against its use for treatment-resistant depression, citing a lack of evidence that it was more effective than existing treatments including psychological treatment, a lack of long-term evidence and unlikely cost-effectiveness.
key_findings.locator: MHRA and NICE reviews of esketamine, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Corrigendum (2021): Table 1 combines phase 2 data (open-label and placebo-controlled periods) with phase 3 data (placebo-controlled efficacy studies, a maintenance-of-effect study and a long-term open-label safety study), so it is not a randomized comparison and definitive causal inferences cannot be drawn; more patients were exposed to esketamine, and for longer, which may be one reason for the higher number of suicides in that group. The corrigendum adds that in the long-term safety study, whose population was selected for lack of active suicidality, 114 of 784 (14.5%) esketamine patients reported treatment-emergent suicidal ideation and 6 attempted suicide besides the one completed suicide; and that an analysis of post-marketing reports to the FDA in the 12 months after US licensing found 64 reports of suicidal ideation, 11 completed suicides and 6 attempts attributed to esketamine, described as a 24-fold increased risk of report for suicidal ideation and a 6-fold increased risk for completed suicide compared with other drugs, and whose authors concluded that esketamine's safety needed urgent clarification. It also states that ketamine is not used routinely as an anaesthetic in high-income countries such as the UK, because of its unfavourable balance of risks and harms, but is used more often in low-income countries.
key_findings.locator: Corrigendum, The British Journal of Psychiatry (2021) 219, 618, doi 10.1192/bjp.2021.40: 1st paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column) and 2nd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Read from the corrigendum PDF (PDFs/Ketamine/Horowitz_2021_Corrigendum.pdf). The statistic behind the 24-fold and 6-fold figures is not named. The post-marketing figures are spontaneous reports, which cannot give incidence; the corrigendum cites Wajs et al. (2020) and Gastaldon et al. (2020, by its title a disproportionality analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System reports), not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says six participants (1.4%) in the esketamine group of the short-term trials became more depressed, against one on placebo (0.2%), while Table 2 gives 8/570 (1.4%) for worsening of depression. Editors' calculation: 6 of 570 is 1.1%, so the text's count and percentage disagree, and the percentage matches Table 2's eight. The text also calls these short-term-trial figures, although Table 2's denominators (footnote b) include discontinuation trial 3003.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of esketamine participants with worsening depression is 8 (Table 2) or 6 (text); claims should use the table and say the text differs. The corrigendum does not address it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives increased blood pressure as 368/3646 with esketamine, footnoted as participants in completed stage 3 studies, while Table 1 gives 1861 participants exposed to esketamine in all stage 2 and stage 3 trials up to September 2018, and the other rows of Table 2 use 570. Editors' calculation: 368 of 3646 is 10.1%, printed as 10.0; and the placebo denominator 432 is defined by footnote b (4-week and discontinuation trials) in two rows and by footnote d (completed stage 3 studies) in this one.
reporting_issues.consequence: 3646 cannot be a count of esketamine-exposed participants on the article's own figures; the 10.0% rate and its comparison with 3.5% on placebo (432) should not be cited from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The placebo arm at the sites other than the outlier site is given as n = 81. Editors' cross-check with Turner (2019), whose figure the cited P values come from: 86 placebo participants overall and 16 at the outlier site leave 70; Turner's P values are reproduced with 23 of 70 placebo relapses (33%) and 22 of 81 esketamine relapses, so 81 is the esketamine arm at those sites, a label swapped in Turner's figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 33% relapse rate in the placebo arm elsewhere is right, but its denominator is 70, not 81.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements are cited to reference 18 (Turner, 2019) that its Comment does not contain: the phrase that the FDA requires two positive trials each convincing on its own, the statement that the FDA loosened its rules to accept a discontinuation trial (and the Summary's 'against FDA precedent'), and the conclusion that a 4-point difference has doubtful clinical relevance. Editors' check against turner_2019, read in full: none of these appears; Turner refers to the FDA requirement for substantial evidence of effectiveness and only wonders whether the drug's novel mechanism encouraged leniency regarding the concerns he lists (Turner, p. 2 of its online-first PDF), which is close to, but not, a statement that the FDA loosened its rules.
reporting_issues.consequence: These points must be cited to the FDA documents or other sources, not to Turner (2019) through this article.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that dissociation was reported by the majority of participants, in the section on the single positive trial (3002), and later that half of participants experienced it, while Table 3 gives 48.3% with esketamine for trials 3001 and 3002 pooled and no figure for trial 3002 alone, so the statement about a majority cannot be checked from the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; claims should give 48.3% (against 18.9% with placebo), for the two trials pooled.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 6, the source given for the figure that 3.1% of 16- to 24-year-olds in England and Wales used ketamine in 2017–2018, names the Office for National Statistics and its Crime Survey for England and Wales but gives as its location Computer Fraud and Security 2018(11): 4, a journal item rather than the survey publication; and the trial showing rapid-onset antidepressant effects within 2 hours is cited to a pharmacology review (reference 13), not to a trial.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prevalence figure must be taken from the Crime Survey for England and Wales directly; the background section cannot be used to trace primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 and the text present the six deaths as occurring only among participants assigned to esketamine, without saying that the data pool open-label and placebo-controlled periods with unequal exposure; the authors' corrigendum supplies this and states that definitive causal inferences cannot be drawn.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about deaths in esketamine trials must carry the corrigendum's caveat and cannot present 6/1861 against 0/486 as a randomized comparison.

design_detail: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multicentre trial (called TRANSFORM-2 on this card, a name this paper does not print; it gives only ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02418585, PDF p. 10), sponsored by Janssen, at 39 outpatient referral centres in the Czech Republic (6), Germany (9), Poland (7), Spain (7) and the United States (10), August 2015 to November 2017. Adults aged 18 to 64 with non-psychotic major depression whose current antidepressant had failed in a 4-week prospective phase stopped all antidepressants and were randomized 1:1 to a self-administered nasal spray twice weekly for 4 weeks, either esketamine (flexible, 56 or 84 mg) or a placebo spray with a bittering agent, each together with a newly started open-label oral antidepressant chosen by the investigator (duloxetine, escitalopram, sertraline or extended-release venlafaxine). Primary outcome: change in MADRS from baseline to day 28, rated by blinded remote telephone raters. A post-treatment follow-up of up to 24 weeks is mentioned; only withdrawal-symptom and misuse observations from it are reported here.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate to severe depression that had not responded to at least two antidepressants in the current episode (one of them observed prospectively), switching to esketamine nasal spray plus a newly started oral antidepressant lowered clinician-rated depressive symptoms after 4 weeks more than switching to a newly started oral antidepressant plus a placebo spray, and how often short-term adverse effects occurred in each arm.
cannot_establish: Whether any benefit lasts beyond 4 weeks or what the longer-term harms are (not studied here); the effect of esketamine alone or added to an ongoing antidepressant; the effect of 56 versus 84 mg (doses were flexible, so dose-response was not evaluated, PDF p. 9); how much of the 4-point difference reflects participants recognising their allocation from the drug's acute effects (blinding was not assessed); or effects in people with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, recent moderate or severe substance use disorder, prior non-response to ketamine or esketamine, or imminent suicide risk (all excluded).

sample.recruitment: Outpatients at 39 referral centres (clinic); how patients were found (referral, advertising) is not described. Entry required documented non-response (no more than 25% improvement) to one to five antidepressants in the current episode on the MGH Antidepressant Treatment Response Questionnaire, and current treatment with a different antidepressant taken adequately (fewer than 4 missed days) for at least 2 weeks. That antidepressant was continued for 4 more weeks (at least 6 weeks in all), and people with no more than 25% MADRS improvement from week 1 to week 4 and a MADRS score of 28 or more at weeks 2 and 4 were randomized; an independent psychiatrist or psychologist confirmed the adequacy of the prospective treatment and the ratings (PDF p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 to 64; DSM-5 single-episode (at least 2 years) or recurrent major depression without psychotic features (MINI); IDS-C score of 34 or more; non-response to adequate trials of at least two antidepressants in the current episode, one prospective; medically stable; able to self-administer the spray. Excluded: homicidal ideation, or suicidal ideation with intent to act, in the past 6 months, or suicidal behaviour in the past year; psychotic disorder, bipolar or related disorders, borderline, antisocial, histrionic or narcissistic personality disorder, current obsessive-compulsive disorder, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder; uncontrolled hypertension; seizures; moderate or severe substance use disorder in the past 6 months, or lifetime ketamine use disorder; a positive urine test for specified drugs (cannabinoids, barbiturates, methadone, opioids, cocaine, phencyclidine, amphetamine or methamphetamine), with no urine test for ketamine available; prior non-response to esketamine or ketamine, to the study's oral antidepressant options, or to ECT. The full list is in an online supplement that was not read (PDF pp. 2-3).
sample.demographics: Efficacy set, esketamine vs comparator (Table 1, PDF p. 5): mean age 44.9 (SD 12.58) vs 46.4 (SD 11.14); women 65.8% vs 57.8%; White 93.0% vs 93.6%; United States 39.5% vs 40.4%; mean duration of the current episode 111.4 vs 118.0 weeks; mean baseline MADRS 37.0 (SD 5.69) vs 37.3 (SD 5.66); one or two failed antidepressants besides the prospective one 68.4% vs 66.1%, three or more 31.6% vs 33.9% (as corrected by the journal, Am J Psychiatry 176(8):669; the PDF read prints 39.9%, see reporting issues); an SNRI as the new antidepressant 67.5% vs 68.8% (duloxetine 52.6% vs 56.0%).
sample.attrition: 197 of 227 randomized (86.8%) completed the 4-week phase; by-arm disposition is in a supplementary figure that was not read. A day-28 MADRS was available for 101 of 114 in the esketamine arm and 100 of 109 in the comparator arm (Figure 1, Table 2, PDF p. 6), so 13 and 9 lacked one. The nasal spray was stopped for adverse events by 8 of 115 (7.0%) vs 1 of 109 (0.9%). In addition, 9 patients randomized at one Polish site were excluded from all analyses for Good Clinical Practice violations, and of the 227, 3 received no study drug and 1 no oral antidepressant (PDF p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: A trial population selected for prospectively confirmed non-response that excluded people with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, recent moderate or severe substance use disorder, significant comorbidity or imminent suicide risk; 93% White and mostly from European sites. The authors suggest that media coverage of ketamine as a new treatment may have raised patients' expectations of benefit (PDF p. 9).

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, self-administered at the clinic under the investigator's direct supervision (PDF p. 3). Adherence to the open-label oral antidepressant is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: three nasal spray devices at every session in both arms (each device gives two sprays; an active device holds 28 mg esketamine; placebo devices contain a bittering agent), twice weekly for 4 weeks. Esketamine started at 56 mg on day 1 and could be raised to 84 mg on day 4, 8, 11 or 15 at the investigator's judgement, then stayed fixed; on day 4, 58 of 107 (54.2%) stayed at 56 mg and 49 of 107 (45.8%) moved to 84 mg, and 66.7% were on 84 mg at the end. The new oral antidepressant followed a fixed titration schedule from day 1 (PDF pp. 3-4).
exposure.polysubstance: Positive urine tests for specified drugs excluded people at entry (no ketamine test was available) and recent moderate or severe substance use disorder was excluded. Concomitant benzodiazepine use occurred; response did not differ notably by benzodiazepine use (PDF p. 6). Alcohol and other drug use during the trial are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (treatment trial). The timing of MADRS ratings relative to the last spray is not stated in this paper.

comparison.controls: Active comparator: a newly started open-label oral antidepressant (the same four options and titration) plus a placebo nasal spray with a bittering agent, three devices per session twice weekly on the same schedule (PDF p. 3). Both arms switched to a new antidepressant, so the comparison isolates the spray, not esketamine against no treatment.
comparison.matching: 1:1 randomization by computer-generated schedule in randomly permuted blocks, stratified by country and by class of oral antidepressant (SNRI or SSRI); identical devices and packaging (PDF p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison. Prior experience with ketamine or esketamine is not described beyond the exclusion of prior non-response and of ketamine use disorder.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusions as the esketamine arm.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: MADRS (0-60) change from baseline to day 28, by independent remote telephone raters blind to protocol details, study visit, clinical status and side effects. Key secondary endpoints in a fixed order: onset of clinical response by day 2 maintained to day 28 (a reduction of at least 50% by day 2, one excursion to a reduction of at least 25% allowed on day 8, 15 or 22); Sheehan Disability Scale; PHQ-9. Other: response (MADRS reduction of at least 50%) and remission (MADRS 12 or less) at day 28; CGI-S; GAD-7; EQ-5D-5L (supplement). Safety: adverse events, laboratory tests, ECG, vital signs, C-SSRS, CADSS, BPRS positive-symptom subscale, the Modified Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation (MOAA/S, 0-5), a discharge-readiness scale developed for the programme, nasal examination and symptoms, and the Physician Withdrawal Checklist; cognitive results are left to separate publications (PDF pp. 3-4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated rating scales, except the discharge-readiness scale, which was developed for the esketamine programme.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: difference in least-squares mean MADRS change at day 28 (MMRM). Response: MADRS reduction of at least 50%. Remission: MADRS of 12 or less. In this paper a MOAA/S score of 4 or less after dosing is called moderate or greater sedation (PDF p. 7), which counts any drop from fully alert (5); the companion fixed-dose trial counted only scores of 3 or less as moderate or greater and called 4 mild (Fedgchin et al., 2019).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Serial gatekeeping (fixed sequence) across the primary and the three key secondary endpoints, each at two-sided 0.05 only if all earlier ones were significant (PDF p. 4). The first key secondary endpoint failed (p=0.321), so the Sheehan Disability Scale and PHQ-9 results are numerical only. Response, remission, CGI-S, GAD-7 and EQ-5D-5L were outside the hierarchy; the response and remission NNTs are post hoc.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: MADRS raters were remote, by telephone, and blind to protocol details, visit, clinical status and side effects; patients, investigators, site personnel, outcome assessors and data analysts are described as blind to assignment (PDF p. 3). Participants were not asked which treatment they thought they had received (PDF p. 10).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: least-squares mean difference in MADRS change at day 28 −4.0 (SE 1.69; 95% CI −7.31 to −0.64; p=0.020); raw mean change −21.4 (SD 12.32, n=101) vs −17.0 (SD 13.88, n=100) (Table 2, PDF p. 6); effect size 0.30 as printed (PDF p. 5). Differences by visit: day 2 −3.3 (−5.75 to −0.85), day 8 −2.9 (−5.17 to −0.59), day 15 −2.0 (−4.78 to 0.82), day 22 −3.8 (−6.87 to −0.65) (PDF p. 5). First key secondary: onset of response by day 2 sustained to day 28 in 9 of 114 (7.9%) vs 5 of 109 (4.6%), p=0.321; Sheehan Disability Scale −4.0 (−6.28 to −1.64) and PHQ-9 −2.4 (−4.18 to −0.69), not formally testable (PDF pp. 5-6). Post hoc at day 28: response 70 of 101 (69.3%) vs 52 of 100 (52.0%), odds ratio 2.4 (95% credible interval 1.30 to 4.54), NNT 6; remission 53 of 101 (52.5%) vs 31 of 100 (31.0%), NNT 5. GAD-7 difference −1.0 (−2.35 to 0.28); CGI-S odds ratio 2.8 (95% credible interval 1.14 to 7.68) (PDF p. 6). Editors' calculation: 4.0 divided by the pooled SD of day-28 change (13.1) gives 0.30, matching the printed effect size; Wald 95% CIs for the post hoc risk differences are 17.3 points (4.0 to 30.6) for response and 21.5 points (8.2 to 34.8) for remission; counting the 13 and 9 patients without a day-28 rating as not responding gives response 61.4% vs 47.7% (13.7 points, 0.7 to 26.7; NNT about 7) and remission 46.5% vs 28.4% (18.1 points, 5.6 to 30.5; NNT about 6).
analysis.covariates: MMRM with baseline MADRS as covariate; treatment, country, oral antidepressant class, day and day-by-treatment as fixed effects; a random patient effect. A delta-adjustment tipping-point analysis of the missing-at-random assumption is reported only in the supplement (not read). GAD-7 by ANCOVA on last observation carried forward (PDF p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02418585 (PDF p. 10). The paper does not give the registration date or compare registered with reported outcomes, and the registry record was not read. The sample size assumed a 6.5-point difference with SD 12, two-sided 0.05 and 25% dropout: 98 per group for 90% power (PDF p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The primary and key secondary results are reported as prespecified, including the failed first key secondary endpoint. Response and remission NNTs and odds ratios are post hoc and use only patients with a day-28 rating; the odds ratios carry credible intervals from a model the methods do not describe. EQ-5D-5L, nasal tolerability, the tipping-point analysis, the individual-patient scatterplot, by-arm disposition and the blood-pressure guidance are only in the supplement (not read); cognitive results are deferred to other papers.
analysis.power: Planned for 90% power to detect 6.5 points; the observed difference (4.0) was smaller than planned (PDF p. 8). No power calculation for the key secondary endpoints.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 223 analysed adults with prospectively confirmed treatment-resistant depression, switching to esketamine spray plus a new oral antidepressant lowered MADRS scores by 4.0 points more than switching to a new oral antidepressant plus a placebo spray at day 28 (95% CI 0.64 to 7.31 points; standardized 0.30), less than the 6.5 points the trial was designed to detect. The day-15 difference was 2.0 points with an interval including zero. The prespecified test of rapid onset (response by day 2 sustained to day 28) failed: 7.9% vs 4.6%. Post hoc, among patients rated at day 28, 69.3% vs 52.0% responded and 52.5% vs 31.0% remitted. Dissociation (26.1% vs 3.7%), nausea, vertigo, dizziness and sedation were far more common with esketamine; 7.0% vs 0.9% stopped the spray for adverse events; one participant was injured in a motorbike accident on day 16 and died on day 55.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports clinically meaningful improvement at earlier time points and concludes that the study supports esketamine as a rapidly acting antidepressant (PDF p. 1), without saying that the prespecified rapid-onset endpoint was not significant (p=0.321) and that the other key secondary endpoints therefore could not be formally tested (PDF pp. 5-6). The discussion does report the failure, attributing it to the endpoint's strict definition and to the remote raters, who did not know the patients and could assess only reported symptoms, and reads the 3.3-point day-2 difference as clinically meaningful and suggestive of rapid onset (PDF p. 9). The results text says response increased over time with repeated dosing (PDF p. 5), although the between-arm difference was smallest at day 15, with an interval including zero. The discussion takes the rise in dissociation ratings in the placebo arm as evidence of adequate blinding (PDF p. 10) while stating that participants were never asked which treatment they thought they had; with dissociation reported by 26.1% vs 3.7% and any MOAA/S drop in 57.4% vs 10.1%, participants' awareness of allocation is unknown, not shown to be low. The discussion also compares the response odds ratio and NNTs with other drugs and trials (PDF p. 9): cross-trial comparisons with different comparators, and NNTs computed on completers only. Against this, the paper states the shortfall against the planned difference, the active comparator, the 4-week duration, the flexible dosing that rules out dose-response conclusions, and the exclusions that limit generalizability. A headline that esketamine relieves treatment-resistant depression within a day overstates this trial: the day-2 difference was 3.3 points and the prespecified rapid-onset test failed.

timeline.event: Phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine added to an existing oral antidepressant in treatment-resistant depression; with clinical judgement, the basis of this trial's 6.5-point assumption (PDF p. 4; the discussion also cites an intravenous esketamine study, PDF p. 8) (to be appraised from its own card)

TRANSFORM-3 (a name not printed in this paper) in patients aged 65 or older (Ochs-Ross et al., conference abstract cited by this paper): MADRS difference −3.6, not statistically significant, as reported in this paper's discussion (PDF pp. 8-9)

This trial (TRANSFORM-2, a name not printed in this paper; NCT02418585): flexible-dose esketamine plus a new oral antidepressant vs a new antidepressant plus placebo spray; MADRS difference −4.0 at day 28 (p=0.020); rapid-onset endpoint not met
TRANSFORM-1, the fixed-dose sister trial run in parallel: 84 mg vs comparator −3.2 (95% CI −6.88 to 0.45; p=0.088), primary endpoint not met; 56 mg −4.1 with a nominal p-value only

SUSTAIN-1 randomized withdrawal trial: continuing esketamine after 16 weeks delayed relapse compared with switching to placebo spray (HR 0.49 in stable remitters); part of its randomized sample transferred from this trial and from TRANSFORM-1
Commentary by Schatzberg in the same issue of the American Journal of Psychiatry (p. 422, signalled on PDF p. 1 of this paper); not among the files read (to be appraised from the full text)
Turner, critique of the efficacy evidence and of the FDA approval of esketamine (to be appraised from the full text)
Horowitz and Moncrieff, critical review of the evidence for esketamine, with a published corrigendum (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: Of the three phase 3 short-term trials of esketamine plus a new antidepressant against a new antidepressant plus placebo spray, this is the only one whose primary endpoint was statistically significant (this paper, PDF pp. 8-9; Fedgchin et al., 2019); the MADRS differences were similar in size across the three (−3.2 to −4.1). The paper says the US Food and Drug Administration recently approved esketamine for treatment-resistant depression in adults (PDF p. 2) but does not say what the approval rested on. Published critiques (Schatzberg, 2019; Turner, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) are listed for appraisal and not summarized here.

funding.funder: Supported by Janssen Research and Development, Titusville, N.J. (PDF p. 10). Medical writing assistance by Sandra Norris (Norris Communications Group) and editorial support by Ellen Baum (Janssen Global Services) are acknowledged.
funding.declared_conflicts: Ten of the 16 authors (Popova, Daly, Cooper, Lane, Lim, Mazzucco, Hough, Manji, Drevets, Singh) are employees of Janssen Research and Development and hold company equity. Trivedi reports consulting or advisory roles for many companies including Janssen Pharmaceutical and Johnson & Johnson, royalties from Janssen Research and Development, and research support including from Janssen and Johnson & Johnson. Thase reports consulting for many companies and grant or research support including from Janssen Pharmaceuticals and Johnson & Johnson (including for the present study); his spouse is employed by a company that does business with pharmaceutical companies. Shelton, Molero, Vieta and Bajbouj report consulting, advisory, lecture or grant relationships with several companies including Janssen. Manji is named on a patent assigned to the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Yale University and NIH, from which no financial benefit was received (PDF p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: A sponsor-run trial with ten sponsor employees among the authors; study data are available on request through the YODA Project (PDF p. 10). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An independent, adequately powered trial of esketamine against an active comparator that mimics its acute effects (an active placebo producing dissociation or sedation), with blinding checked by asking participants, raters and staff to guess allocation, and with remission, function and harms followed for 6 to 12 months; or an individual-participant meta-analysis of all esketamine trials using intention-to-treat denominators.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedule in permuted blocks, stratified by country and antidepressant class; concealment through identical devices and packaging (no central allocation system is described); baseline characteristics balanced (Table 1, PDF p. 5).

Dissociation, sedation and blood-pressure rises could have shown participants and the staff supervising dosing which spray was given (the authors call the dissociative effects difficult to blind, PDF pp. 3, 10). No deviations arising from the trial context are reported. The efficacy analysis left out 4 randomized patients who received no study drug or no oral antidepressant, and 9 patients randomized at one Polish site were excluded from all analyses for GCP violations; a sensitivity analysis including that site is reported only in the supplement (PDF p. 4).

Day-28 MADRS missing for 13 of 114 vs 9 of 109; adverse-event discontinuations were more frequent with esketamine (8 vs 1); MMRM assumes data missing at random, and the tipping-point sensitivity analysis is only in the supplement (not read).

Raters were remote and blind to visit, clinical status and side effects, but a telephone MADRS rests entirely on what participants report, and participants' awareness of their allocation was not assessed (PDF p. 10).
Registered trial with a prespecified primary endpoint, analysis and testing hierarchy, reported as planned, including the failed first key secondary endpoint. The registry record was not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization, concealment by identical devices and the prespecified analysis are sound, and remote blinded raters reduce assessor bias. The main unresolved threat is that esketamine's acute effects (dissociation 26.1% vs 3.7%; any MOAA/S drop 57.4% vs 10.1%) may have told participants and staff which spray they received while the outcome rests on participants' own reports; the trial did not measure this. With a 4.0-point difference whose interval reaches −0.64, a modest bias of this kind could account for much of the effect. The card may be cited for the 4-week MADRS difference against an active comparator, the response and remission figures with their denominators, the failed rapid-onset endpoint and the short-term adverse-effect profile; not for durability, dose-response, efficacy outside the trial's exclusions, or rapid onset.

key_findings.finding: Of 435 people screened, 227 were randomized and counted (9 more, randomized at one Polish site, were excluded from all analyses for Good Clinical Practice violations). The efficacy analysis had 114 people on esketamine spray plus a new antidepressant and 109 on a new antidepressant plus placebo spray; 197 of 227 (86.8%) completed the 4 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Who took part: adults aged 18 to 64 with moderate to severe non-psychotic depression whose current episode had not responded to at least two antidepressants, one of them watched prospectively for 4 more weeks (no more than 25% MADRS improvement and a MADRS of at least 28). One or two earlier failed antidepressants (besides the prospective one) in 78 of 114 (68.4%) vs 72 of 109 (66.1%), three or more in 36 of 114 (31.6%) vs 37 of 109 (33.9%, as corrected by the journal; the PDF read prints 39.9%, see note); mean baseline MADRS 37.0 vs 37.3; current episode lasting on average more than 2 years (111.4 vs 118.0 weeks).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design, 2nd and 4th paragraphs, and Study Population, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1 (p. 5); Correction to Popova et al., Am J Psychiatry 176(8), p. 669
key_findings.note: Table 1 of the PDF read prints 39.9% for 37 of 109 in the comparator arm; the journal's correction (Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(8):669) gives 33.9%, which matches 37/109.

key_findings.finding: What each arm got (study conditions): a supervised self-administered nasal spray twice weekly for 4 weeks, three devices per session, either esketamine starting at 56 mg with the option of 84 mg from day 4 to day 15 at the investigator's judgement, or a placebo spray with a bitter taste added; both arms started a new oral antidepressant (duloxetine in 52.6% vs 56.0%). By the end, 66.7% of the esketamine arm were on 84 mg.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Randomization and Blinding; Intranasal Study Drug and Administration, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 3); Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 4); Table 1 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Primary result: at day 28 the MADRS (0-60) had fallen 4.0 points more with esketamine than with the comparator (least-squares mean difference −4.0, SE 1.69; 95% CI −7.31 to −0.64; p=0.020). Raw mean falls were 21.4 points (SD 12.32, n=101) vs 17.0 points (SD 13.88, n=100) from baselines of 37.0 and 37.3; the printed effect size is 0.30.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 5); Table 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: The trial had been sized to detect a 6.5-point difference (SD 12; 98 per arm for 90% power); the observed 4.0 fell short. The authors note that the 6.5-point assumption came from phase 2 studies, not from a threshold of clinical meaningfulness, state that 4.0 exceeded minimum clinically important differences reported in the literature, and list factors that may have contributed to the smaller difference and to the comparator arm's higher than expected response and remission: a newly started antidepressant rather than a true placebo, frequent clinic visits, a novel nasal spray, expectations raised by media coverage of ketamine, and a nocebo response.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis › Sample size determination (p. 4); Discussion, 2nd and 7th paragraphs (pp. 8-9)

key_findings.finding: Differences by visit were −3.3 at day 2 (95% CI −5.75 to −0.85), −2.9 at day 8 (−5.17 to −0.59), −2.0 at day 15 (−4.78 to 0.82, interval including zero), −3.8 at day 22 (−6.87 to −0.65) and −4.0 at day 28 (−7.31 to −0.64).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 5); Figure 1 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: The prespecified test of rapid onset failed: a MADRS reduction of at least 50% by day 2 that was kept to day 28 occurred in 9 of 114 (7.9%) vs 5 of 109 (4.6%), p=0.321. Under the fixed testing order, the disability (Sheehan, −4.0, 95% CI −6.28 to −1.64) and self-rated depression (PHQ-9, −2.4, −4.18 to −0.69) results could not be formally tested. A 50% reduction at day 2 alone was seen in 18 of 109 (16.5%) vs 11 of 102 (10.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Post hoc response and remission at day 28, among patients rated that day: response (MADRS down at least 50%) 70 of 101 (69.3%) vs 52 of 100 (52.0%), odds ratio 2.4 (95% credible interval 1.30 to 4.54), NNT 6; remission (MADRS 12 or less) 53 of 101 (52.5%) vs 31 of 100 (31.0%), NNT 5.
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation counting the 13 and 9 patients without a day-28 rating as not responding: response 61.4% vs 47.7% (difference 13.7 points, 95% CI 0.7 to 26.7; NNT about 7) and remission 46.5% vs 28.4% (18.1 points, 5.6 to 30.5; NNT about 6).

key_findings.finding: Anxiety (GAD-7) fell 7.9 vs 6.8 points from 13.2 and 13.1 (difference −1.0, 95% CI −2.35 to 0.28); the median CGI-S change was −2.0 in both arms (odds ratio for a better CGI-S 2.8, 95% credible interval 1.14 to 7.68).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th and 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Adverse events with esketamine vs comparator: dissociation 30 (26.1%) vs 4 (3.7%), nausea 30 (26.1%) vs 7 (6.4%), vertigo 30 (26.1%) vs 3 (2.8%), dysgeusia 28 (24.3%) vs 13 (11.9%), dizziness 24 (20.9%) vs 5 (4.6%), increased blood pressure 11 (9.6%) vs 0, feeling drunk 9 (7.8%) vs 1 (0.9%). Most were mild or moderate, began soon after dosing and resolved by 1.5 hours; the number needed to harm for dissociation was 5.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (p. 7); Table 3 and Results, 17th paragraph (p. 8)
key_findings.note: The header of Table 3 gives N=114 for the esketamine arm, but its percentages correspond to 115, the safety set (for example 30/115 = 26.1%; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Sedation: a MOAA/S score of 4 or less after dosing (called moderate or greater sedation in this paper) occurred at some point in 66 of 115 (57.4%) vs 11 of 109 (10.1%); it peaked 30 to 45 minutes after dosing, resolved by 1 to 1.5 hours and was not accompanied by low oxygen. By 1 hour after dosing at least 44.3% vs at least 92.0% were judged ready to go home; by 1.5 hours 93.2% vs 98.9%; all by 3 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (p. 7); Results, 18th paragraph (p. 8)
key_findings.note: The companion fixed-dose trial counted only scores of 3 or less as moderate or greater sedation (Fedgchin et al., 2019, PDF p. 19), so the two papers' sedation rates are not comparable.

key_findings.finding: The spray was stopped because of adverse events by 8 of 115 (7.0%) on esketamine vs 1 of 109 (0.9%) on the comparator. One participant on esketamine was injured in a motorbike accident on day 16, about 28 hours after a dose, and died on day 55, 40 days after the last dose; the investigator judged the events doubtfully related to treatment. No other deaths or treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 12th and 13th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure rose after each esketamine dose, peaking at about 40 minutes and returning to or near pre-dose levels by 1.5 to 2 hours; the largest mean maximum rise across dosing days was +11.6 vs +5.0 mmHg systolic and +8.1 vs +4.5 mmHg diastolic.
key_findings.locator: Results, 14th paragraph (p. 7, continuing on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Dissociation scores (CADSS, change from before dosing to 40 minutes) fell with repeated dosing, from 7.8 (SE 0.84) on day 1 to 3.5 (SE 0.55) on day 25; no psychotic symptoms were reported. Response at day 28 was similar in patients with dissociation on day 1 (maximum CADSS score above 4) and without it (4 or less): 68.5% vs 70.2%. Treatment-emergent suicidal ideation: 6 of 112 (5.4%) vs 7 of 109 (6.4%); no suicidal behaviour.
key_findings.locator: Results, 16th and 17th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: On the Physician Withdrawal Checklist after esketamine was stopped, the most frequently reported (25% or more) new or worsened symptoms in the esketamine arm were fatigue, lethargy or lack of energy, weakness, dysphoric mood, loss of appetite and restlessness or agitation (comparator arm: insomnia, irritability and dysphoric mood); the authors judge these changes consistent with changes in depression and anxiety and report no clear evidence of withdrawal 1 or 2 weeks after stopping. No misuse of the drug or craving was reported during follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results, 19th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding was not checked: participants were not asked which spray they believed they had received. The authors instead cite the rise in dissociation ratings after the placebo spray (which contained a bittering agent) as evidence that blinding was adequate, while noting that esketamine's side effects may have affected the blind.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 12th paragraph (p. 9, continuing on p. 10)

key_findings.finding: The authors report that the two other short-term phase 3 trials run at the same time found similar MADRS differences, −4.1 (56 mg) and −3.2 (84 mg) in the fixed-dose trial and −3.6 in patients aged 65 or older, neither statistically significant.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9)

key_findings.finding: On the regulator, the paper says only that esketamine was recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for treatment-resistant depression in adults; it does not describe the evidence the approval rested on.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 of the PDF read (the AJP in Advance version) prints 39.9% for the 37 of 109 comparator patients with three or more previous failed antidepressants. The journal's published correction (Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(8):669) states that this percentage should have been 33.9%, which matches 37/109 (72 + 37 = 109), and that the article was corrected and reposted on July 11, 2019.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 5; correction, Am J Psychiatry 176(8), p. 669
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical, corrected by the journal; the arms were balanced on this variable (31.6% vs 33.9%), and the card uses 33.9%.

reporting_issues.issue: The header of Table 3 gives N=114 for the esketamine arm, but its percentages are computed on 115 (the safety set), as in the text (66/115, 8 of 115).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; adverse-event percentages should be read against 115.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says response increased over time with repeated dosing, but the between-arm difference was smaller at day 15 (−2.0, 95% CI −4.78 to 0.82) than at days 2, 8, 22 and 28.
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-arm effect did not grow steadily; the statement describes within-arm improvement, not the drug effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The response and CGI-S odds ratios are given with 95% credible intervals, and the CGI-S figure comes from an ANCOVA on ranks; neither a Bayesian model nor how an odds ratio was derived from a rank ANCOVA is described in the methods, which call these endpoints descriptive.
reporting_issues.consequence: These two odds ratios cannot be reproduced or appraised from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Nine patients randomized at one Polish site were excluded from all analyses for Good Clinical Practice violations, and the abstract's 227 randomized excludes them; the sensitivity analysis including the site is only in the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: A post-randomization exclusion of about 4% of randomized patients; the paper states it did not change the conclusions, which could not be checked here.

reporting_issues.issue: This paper counts a MOAA/S score of 4 or less as moderate or greater sedation (57.4% vs 10.1%), whereas the companion TRANSFORM-1 paper calls 4 mild and counts 3 or less (9.6% and 12.1% vs 0.9%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sedation rates from the two trials cannot be compared or pooled as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The response and remission NNTs (6 and 5) are computed only on patients with a day-28 rating (101 and 100), and the discussion compares them with NNTs of other treatments from other trials.
reporting_issues.consequence: With all analysed patients as denominators the NNTs are about 7 and 6 (editors' calculation); cross-trial NNT comparisons are not like for like.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF read is the AJP in Advance version, which carries the uncorrected Table 1. The journal's one-page correction (Correction to Popova et al., Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(8):669) states that one percentage in Table 1 was misreported: the share of the antidepressant plus placebo group treated with three or more antidepressants should have been 33.9% (the PDF read prints 39.9%; see reporting issue 0); the article was corrected and reposted on July 11, 2019.
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 1; correction, Am J Psychiatry 176(8), p. 669
reporting_issues.consequence: The notice describes no other change, so no other number on this card is affected as far as the notice states. The correction page prints no DOI of its own; the erratum DOI in the reference record comes from PubMed.

verification.source_read: Online-first PDF (AJP in Advance, doi 10.1176/appi.ajp.2019.19020172), 11 pages, cited as PDF p. N (the printed AJP in Advance page numbers 1-11 equal the PDF pages); pages differ from the version of record (Am J Psychiatry 176(6):428-438). All pages read; tables, Figures 1-2 and every sign and inequality checked on rendered pages, because the text layer prints minus signs as the digit 2 and the less-or-equal and greater-or-equal signs as # and $ (so a mechanical search will not find negative values on these pages). Online supplement and the erratum (doi 10.1176/appi.ajp.2019.1768correction1) not among the files and not read. At card adjudication (2026-11-12) the journal's correction (Correction to Popova et al., Am J Psychiatry 2019;176(8):669, one page, on file as PDFs/Ketamine/Popova_2019_Correction.pdf) was read with the paper.
