design_detail: Commentary (3 pages, single author, 10 references) in the American Journal of Psychiatry on the intranasal esketamine development programme, written to accompany the phase 3 trial report by Popova et al. in the same issue; read in the journal's online-first ('ajp in Advance') version, pages 1–3. No search or appraisal method. The author draws on the trial report (Popova et al., 2019), the FDA briefing document for the joint meeting of the Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee and the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee of 12 February 2019 (cited once with a page, p. 42), the package insert (not in the reference list), his own group's naltrexone study of ketamine (Williams et al., 2018), his own 2014 commentary on ketamine, two rodent studies (Moda-Sava et al., 2019; Pacheco et al., 2014), a study whose title names the NMDA antagonist MK-801 and morphine tolerance (Trujillo & Akil, 1991), a review of ketamine for pain (Jonkman et al., 2017), a biosensor study of where opioid drugs act (Stoeber et al., 2018) and a 1993 paper on protracted withdrawal (Satel et al.) (References, PDF pp. 2–3).
can_establish: What one academic psychopharmacologist argued in 2019 (accepted 24 April 2019), alongside a pivotal esketamine trial, about the strength of the efficacy evidence presented for approval, the use of a relapse-prevention (discontinuation) study as the second positive trial, the suicides reported after the last esketamine dose and esketamine's possible opioid-related risks; and which sources (the trial report and the FDA briefing document of 12 February 2019) hold the figures he cites.
cannot_establish: How well esketamine works (it gives one trial's effect size without a metric or interval and no figures for the two other pivotal trials), whether stopping esketamine caused the three suicides (no numbers exposed, follow-up or comparison with expected rates are given), or whether esketamine's antidepressant effect depends on opioid receptors (one blockade study of ketamine by the author's own group, summarized without its size or design).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The figures discussed come from Popova et al. (2019), described as a pivotal phase 3 trial of esketamine plus a newly started oral antidepressant against placebo plus antidepressant in refractory depression, and from the FDA briefing document of 12 February 2019, which reported the manufacturer's relapse-prevention (discontinuation) study (PDF pp. 1–2). No sample size is given for any study.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the author chose the sources (10 references; PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen by the author for a critical reading. The two other pivotal trials are mentioned without names, numbers or citations (PDF p. 1). Two of the ten references are the author's own (his group's naltrexone study, Williams et al., 2018, and his 2014 commentary), and the opioid-mechanism argument rests mainly on the first of them and on rodent studies (PDF pp. 1–2).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. As described: intranasal esketamine with an oral antidepressant started at the same time, against placebo with the antidepressant (Popova et al.; PDF p. 1); in the relapse-prevention study, 16 weeks of esketamine with an antidepressant, then less frequent administration, then randomization to continue esketamine or to switch to placebo while the antidepressant continued (FDA briefing document as described; PDF p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as described: in Popova et al., intranasal esketamine twice weekly for 4 weeks (PDF p. 1); in the relapse-prevention study, 16 weeks of treatment before less frequent administration (once weekly to once every 2 weeks) and randomization (PDF p. 2). No amounts are given. The commentary also notes that the label sets a schedule of progressively less frequent administration without settling how long treatment should last (PDF p. 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: In the trials described: placebo (a saline nasal spray, per the commentary) plus a newly started antidepressant (Popova et al.); in the relapse-prevention study, placebo plus the continued antidepressant after 16 weeks of esketamine (PDF pp. 1–2).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized trials, as described).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Not named. The commentary refers to each trial's primary endpoint and change scores (rating instrument not named), relapse, suicides after the last dose, and side effects such as dissociation (PDF pp. 1–2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy as statistically significant separation from placebo on each trial's primary endpoint and as an effect size (metric not named); harm as relapse after stopping, suicide after the last dose, and the potential for non-medical use and dependence, argued from pharmacology.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed as such. The commentary notes that the saline control produced few side effects resembling esketamine's, although some people given placebo seemed to experience dissociation (PDF p. 1), which bears on whether participants could tell their allocation (editors' reading).

analysis.effect_sizes: Numbers given, with the source the commentary names (none are its own data): (1) separation from placebo by 24–48 hours, maintained with repeated administration up to 28 days, with no further gain after the initial separation (Popova et al., including its Figure 1; PDF p. 1); (2) of three pivotal phase 3 trials only Popova et al. separated significantly from placebo on the primary endpoint, the other two showing similar mean differences in change scores (no names, numbers or source; PDF p. 1); (3) an effect size of 0.30 in Popova et al., called mild (metric, interval and page not given; PDF p. 1); (4) in the relapse-prevention study (FDA briefing document): significantly more relapse after switching to placebo by 2 weeks, against 1 month or more in discontinuation studies of established antidepressants (the latter from the author's 2014 commentary), and relapse reaching 40% by 3–4 months after stopping esketamine (no denominators, no rate in the group that continued, no hazard ratio; PDF p. 2); (5) three suicides 4–20 days after the last esketamine dose and none in the placebo group, two of the three people having shown no signs of suicidality at baseline or at the last visit (no study, denominators or follow-up given; PDF p. 2); (6) the FDA's request that the company track patients for 3 years and the 2-hour observation for side effects under restricted distribution (no source; PDF p. 2).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: The efficacy figures of the two non-significant pivotal trials and the denominators behind the relapse and suicide figures are not given; the FDA's reasons for not attributing the suicides to the drug are quoted and rejected without the data they rest on (PDF p. 2).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As cited: one of three pivotal short-term trials showed a statistically significant difference from placebo on its primary endpoint, with an effect size of 0.30 (metric and interval not given); in the relapse-prevention study, relapse was more frequent after switching to placebo within 2 weeks and reached 40% by 3–4 months; three suicides occurred 4–20 days after the last esketamine dose and none in the placebo group, without denominators; in the author's group's study, naltrexone pretreatment blocked ketamine's acute antidepressant effect (design and size not given).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The closing verdict is hedged and largely in proportion to the figures cited: evidence of efficacy 'Maybe?', its strength 'Apparently mild', how long and how often to prescribe unclear, stopping possibly problematic, care advised, and possible benefit for many patients with refractory depression acknowledged (PDF p. 2). Two interpretations go further than the evidence the commentary gives. The naltrexone result is said to be "indicating that ketamine's antidepressant effects are mediated by mu opioid agonism" (PDF p. 1), although the same paragraph says the study could not tell release of endogenous opioids from receptor binding and did not rule out a role for NMDA antagonism, the cited paper's own title speaks of attenuation rather than blocking (reference 3, PDF p. 2), and the study concerned ketamine, not esketamine. The three suicides, two without earlier signs of suicidality, are read as suggesting a protracted withdrawal reaction like that described with opioids, and the FDA's contrary assessment is said to appear misguided (PDF p. 2), without the numbers of people exposed and followed in each group, any report of withdrawal symptoms, or a comparison with the expected rate of suicide in refractory depression. The comparison with four decades of supposedly safer new opioids (PDF p. 2) is an analogy, not evidence about esketamine.

timeline.event: The author's earlier commentary in the same journal, 'A word to the wise about ketamine' (Am J Psychiatry 171:262–264), cited for ketamine's potential for non-medical use and for the timing of relapse in discontinuation studies of established antidepressants (reference 8; not read)

Williams et al. (Am J Psychiatry 175:1205–1215), the author's group, titled as showing attenuation of ketamine's antidepressant effects by opioid receptor antagonism; this commentary describes the effect as blocked by naltrexone pretreatment (reference 3; not read)
Popova et al., the phase 3 trial this commentary accompanies (reference 1)
FDA briefing document for the joint PDAC and DSaRM advisory committee meeting of 12 February 2019, the source of the relapse and suicide figures (reference 9; not among the files)

Fedgchin et al., by its title a fixed-dose esketamine trial with a newly started oral antidepressant (TRANSFORM-1); the commentary does not name the two pivotal trials that missed significance, so whether this is one of them is to be checked from that trial's own report

Daly et al., by its title a randomized relapse-prevention trial of esketamine nasal spray plus an oral antidepressant; apparently the published report of the discontinuation study that the commentary describes from the FDA briefing document, which it cites instead
Reply by Drevets et al. in the same journal, a comment on this commentary (DOI 10.1176/appi.ajp.2019.19070688); not among the files, not read
Turner, a separate critique of the efficacy evidence for esketamine and of its FDA approval (seven concerns, per its title); not read for this card
Horowitz & Moncrieff, a review of the evidence for esketamine asking whether past mistakes are being repeated (per its title); not read for this card

replication.where_it_stands: A single-author commentary written shortly after the FDA approved esketamine for refractory depression (PDF p. 1). Its figures come from Popova et al. (2019) and the FDA briefing document of 12 February 2019, which are the sources to cite for them; its opioid-mechanism argument rests on one study by the author's group (Williams et al., 2018). A reply by Drevets et al. (2019) was published in the same journal (not read). Later critiques of the esketamine evidence (Turner, 2019; Horowitz & Moncrieff, 2021) are on the library's list.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the commentary).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Author and article information, PDF p. 2): Dr. Schatzberg has received grant support from Janssen; he has served as a consultant for Alkermes, Avanir, Brain Resource, Bracket, Compass, Delpor, Epiodyne, GLG, Jazz, Janssen Pharmaceuticals, Lundbeck/Takeda, McKinsey and Company, Merck, Myriad Genetics, Neuronetics, Owl Analytics, Pfizer, Sage, Sunovion and Xhale; he holds equity in Corcept (co-founder), Delpor, Dermira, Epiodyne, Gilead, Incyte Genetics, Intersect ENT, Madrigal, Merck, Owl Analytics, Seattle Genetics, Titan and Xhale; and he is listed as an inventor on patents for pharmacogenetics and antiglucocorticoid use in the prediction of antidepressant response.
funding.affiliations_note: Stanford University School of Medicine (PDF p. 2). The commentary calls the drug's maker only 'the manufacturer' and 'the company'; the author declares grant support from Janssen and consultancy for Janssen Pharmaceuticals, and the library's card for an earlier randomized trial of intranasal esketamine (sc_daly_2018) records Janssen Research & Development as that trial's funder and esketamine nasal spray as the sponsor's product. He also declares equity and patents in other antidepressant-related ventures (Corcept co-founder; patents on antiglucocorticoid use in predicting antidepressant response). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: For efficacy: replicated, adequately powered trials of esketamine against an active control that mimics its dissociative effects, with blinding assessed. For the discontinuation question: a randomized discontinuation trial with prespecified, systematic monitoring of suicidal ideation and behaviour and of withdrawal symptoms for several months after stopping, reporting events with denominators and person-time in each arm. For the mechanism: a larger, blinded opioid-antagonist study with esketamine itself.

domains.note: No search or criteria; ten references chosen by the author.

The efficacy evidence is appraised (one of three pivotal trials significant, a small effect, a saline control, no gain after the first separation; the discontinuation design questioned), but the evidence for the author's own hypotheses is not: the naltrexone study, the rodent studies and the three suicides are taken at face value, without sizes, designs or denominators.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The opioid-mechanism argument rests on the author's group's study (Williams et al., 2018), and the concern about non-medical use and the argument about the timing of relapse in discontinuation studies rest on his own 2014 commentary (2 of 10 references).

Most conclusions are framed as questions or hedged, but opioid mediation of the antidepressant effect is stated as indicated by one blockade study, and the protracted-withdrawal reading of the suicides is offered from three cases.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on esketamine's benefit and harm
domains.note: A critique: the benefit side is represented by one effect size; the other trials' results, the relapse figures in the group that continued esketamine and the base rate of suicide in refractory depression are absent, and the FDA's reasons are quoted only to be rejected. Under-represented: evidence and context bearing on benefit and on the suicide comparison. The commentary does acknowledge possible benefit for many patients and cites evidence that ketamine may reduce opioid tolerance, against its own concern.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3). The piece is a hedged critical opinion by an experienced psychopharmacologist who declares ties to the manufacturer and to many other companies; its selection of evidence is unsystematic and its figures are second-hand. It may be cited for the concerns it raised in 2019 (only one of three pivotal short-term trials significant; a small effect against a saline control; a discontinuation study used as the second positive trial; suicides after the last dose; a possible opioid component), as an informed critic's view, and as a pointer to Popova et al. (2019) and the FDA briefing document of 12 February 2019. It should not be cited as the source of those figures (cite the trial reports or the FDA document), nor for the claims that esketamine's antidepressant effect is opioid-mediated or that stopping esketamine caused the suicides.

key_findings.finding: A single-author commentary by Alan F. Schatzberg, M.D. (Stanford University School of Medicine), accompanying the report of the phase 3 esketamine trial by Popova et al. in the same issue; 10 references; accepted 24 April 2019.
key_findings.locator: Title block and text, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 1); Author and article information (PDF p. 2); References (PDF pp. 2–3)

key_findings.finding: As described, the pivotal phase 3 trial of Popova et al. gave intranasal esketamine twice weekly for 4 weeks with a newly started oral antidepressant, against placebo plus antidepressant; esketamine separated from placebo by 24–48 hours and stayed separated with repeated administration up to 28 days, but, according to the author's reading of the trial's Figure 1, the advantage did not grow after the initial separation.
key_findings.locator: Text, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Figures from Popova et al. (reference 1); not checked against the trial report for this card.

key_findings.finding: Of three pivotal phase 3 trials, only Popova et al. separated significantly from placebo on the primary endpoint; in the other two, mean differences in change scores were similar but not statistically significant. The commentary names neither trial and gives no numbers or source for them.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: The effect size in Popova et al. is given as 0.30, which the author calls mild (and, in the same paragraph, small); with saline as the control and so small an effect, he questions whether efficacy has been truly demonstrated.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The metric, interval and source page of 0.30 are not given.

key_findings.finding: The saline control produced few side effects resembling esketamine's, although some people given placebo seemed to experience dissociation; no numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Because every participant also started an antidepressant, the author questions whether the trial design shows that esketamine needs to be continued beyond the first administrations, and he notes that the label, as he describes it, sets no end point, only progressively less frequent administration aimed at keeping the response.
key_findings.locator: Text, 4th paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: Opioid mechanism: the author's group (Williams et al., 2018) reported that pretreatment with oral naltrexone blocked ketamine's acute antidepressant effect, which he takes to indicate mediation by mu-opioid agonism; the same paragraph says the study could not distinguish release of endogenous opioids from binding to the mu receptor and did not rule out that NMDA antagonism is needed to maintain the response. He suggests that the opioid properties may explain the drug's potential for non-medical use and raise concern about longer-term use.
key_findings.locator: Text, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 1, right column); reference 3 (PDF p. 2)
key_findings.note: The study's design, size and route of administration are not given in the commentary; it concerned ketamine, not esketamine. The cited paper's title speaks of attenuation by opioid receptor antagonism, the commentary of blocking (reference 3, PDF p. 2).

key_findings.finding: Evidence weighed on both sides of the opioid question: a rodent pain study in which naloxone blocked ketamine's antinociception (Pacheco et al., 2014) would suggest risks of tachyphylaxis and withdrawal; against that, ketamine is said to reduce opioid tolerance and, at anaesthetic doses, opioid use after surgery, and endogenous and synthetic opioids are said to act differently at Golgi membranes (Stoeber et al., 2018). The author concludes that this pharmacology may not be a problem with intermittent use and that animal and human studies are needed.
key_findings.locator: Text, 6th paragraph (PDF p. 1, right column, continuing at the top of PDF p. 2)
key_findings.note: The reference given for reduced opioid tolerance (Trujillo & Akil, 1991) is, by its title, a study of the NMDA antagonist MK-801 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Relapse-prevention study, as reported by the manufacturer in the FDA briefing document: patients treated for 16 weeks with esketamine (called ketamine in two places) plus an antidepressant, then given it once weekly to once every 2 weeks, were randomized to continue esketamine or switch to placebo while the antidepressant continued; the study served as the second positive trial supporting proof of efficacy, which the author calls a somewhat unusual application. Relapse was significantly more frequent with placebo by 2 weeks, a much shorter time frame, he writes, than in discontinuation studies of established antidepressants in which patients are taken off all drugs and differences appear by 1 month or more (citing his 2014 commentary), and relapse after stopping esketamine reached 40% by 3–4 months even though patients were receiving antidepressants.
key_findings.locator: Text, 7th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: No numbers randomized, no relapse rate in the group that continued esketamine and no hazard ratio are given; the briefing document is cited without a page for these figures.

key_findings.finding: Three suicides occurred 4–20 days after the last dose of esketamine, and none in the placebo group; two of the three people had shown no signs of suicidality during the study, at baseline or at the last visit. The author takes this to suggest a protracted withdrawal reaction, as described with opioids (Satel et al., 1993), distinct from acute physical withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Text, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 2, left column); reference 10 (PDF p. 3)
key_findings.note: The commentary does not say in which study or studies the deaths occurred, how many people were exposed to esketamine or to placebo, or how long each group was followed.

key_findings.finding: The FDA briefing document (p. 42), as quoted, judged it difficult to consider the suicides drug-related, given the small number of cases, the severity of the patients' illness and the lack of a consistent pattern; the author says this appears misguided, holding that discontinuation reactions can be caused by a drug that is no longer being taken, and argues that a long-term discontinuation design may not suit a drug with potential for non-medical use, where stopping may be more informative than taking it.
key_findings.locator: Text, 8th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: As reported, with no source cited: the FDA asked the company to track patients for 3 years, and restricted distribution limits the drug to approved medical settings, with patients observed for side effects for 2 hours.
key_findings.locator: Text, 8th paragraph (end, right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: intranasal esketamine is easier to give than intravenous ketamine; clear evidence of efficacy, 'Maybe?'; its strength, apparently mild; how long and how often to prescribe it, not entirely clear; raising the frequency after loss of response could be problematic, and data suggest that stopping could be an issue; there are more questions than answers and care is advised in clinical practice; still, it could help many patients with refractory depression, and efforts to develop rapidly acting agents are applauded.
key_findings.locator: Text, 9th paragraph (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: Numbers are given without their sources or details: the effect size of 0.30 without metric, interval or page; the two non-significant pivotal trials without names, numbers or citation; the relapse figures (2 weeks; 40% by 3–4 months) without denominators or page; the 3-year tracking and the 2-hour observation without any source.
reporting_issues.consequence: The commentary is a secondary source for every figure in it; claims must take the figures from Popova et al. (2019), the other trial reports or the FDA briefing document.

reporting_issues.issue: The three suicides are reported without the study or studies in which they occurred, the numbers exposed to esketamine and to placebo, or the follow-up of each group; the text places them directly after the discontinuation study and ties them to stopping esketamine, but does not say that they occurred in that study.
reporting_issues.consequence: 'None in the placebo group' cannot be read as a comparison of rates; a claim must not place the suicides in the discontinuation study, or compare the arms, on the strength of this commentary.

reporting_issues.issue: In describing the relapse-prevention study, the commentary twice calls the study drug ketamine (treatment with ketamine plus antidepressant; continuing with antidepressant plus ketamine) and in the following sentences esketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording slip; the paragraph's later sentences show that the drug was esketamine, but a quotation of the first sentences would attribute the findings to racemic ketamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 5 (Trujillo & Akil, 1991) is cited for ketamine reducing the risk of tolerance with opioids, but its title names a different NMDA antagonist, MK-801.

design_detail: Two-page Comment (The Lancet Psychiatry, published online 31 October 2019) by a former FDA medical officer, setting out seven concerns about the efficacy evidence behind the US approval of intranasal esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine) for treatment-resistant depression on 5 March 2019. The evidence is the public record of the 12 February 2019 FDA advisory committee meeting (FDA briefing document, Janssen briefing document, slides and transcript), cited by page, plus the published trial reports and one meta-analysis of other drugs. The author adds his own re-analyses: a Fisher's exact test of relapse proportions with and without one outlier site in the relapse-prevention trial (study 3003), named but with no counts printed; a pooled standardized mean difference for the three short-term phase 3 trials, without stated methods; and a placebo-to-drug ratio of mean MADRS change. No search strategy. The PDF read is the online-first version, paginated 1 to 2.
can_establish: What the public FDA advisory-committee documents show on the points the author selected: how treatment resistance was defined and distributed in the esketamine phase 3 trials, which trials were positive, how the relapse-prevention trial was enriched and how far its result depended on one site, and how small the reported rapid-response rates were.
cannot_establish: Whether esketamine works less well than other treatments (the comparison with other drugs is across different trials and populations), how the author's pooled effect size and sensitivity analysis were computed (no methods are given), or the evidence for esketamine's efficacy in full, since the Comment presents concerns only.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The cited trials: three short-term phase 3 trials (3001, 3002 and 3005, the last in people aged 65 or older) that together entered 702 patients, and the randomized withdrawal trial 3003 (p. 1 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the author chose the points.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The source documents are a defined and complete public record of the phase 3 programme, which limits selection of trials; the selection of points within them is the author's and is limited to concerns.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited trials: intranasal esketamine (fixed doses of 56 mg and 84 mg are named in a quoted FDA sentence on trial 3001), combined with a newly started oral antidepressant in trials 3001 and 3002 according to the titles of their cited reports (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the cited trials; for the author's comparison of effect sizes, published standardized mean differences for olanzapine-fluoxetine, aripiprazole and quetiapine from a separate meta-analysis (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) change in the short-term trials; relapse in the withdrawal trial; rapid clinical response (definition not given in the Comment) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy is judged from the drug-placebo difference in mean MADRS change, the share of the drug group's change also seen with placebo, a pooled standardized mean difference, relapse proportions and rapid-response proportions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. The author reports his own Fisher's exact tests (three in the figure) without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited from the FDA documents (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF): in trial 3002, mean MADRS decrease 20.8 with esketamine against 16.8 with placebo; trial 3005 (65 or older) p = 0.06; in 3003, relapse 22% printed for esketamine (n = 90) against 45% for placebo (n = 86), Fisher's exact p = 0.012; at the outlier site, 22% (n = 9) against 100% (n = 16), p = 0.0001; excluding that site, 27% against 33%, p = 0.48; rapid response in about 10% of patients given esketamine overall, and in 3002 8% against 5% with placebo (Fisher's exact p = 0.32). Author's own pooling of the three short-term trials: standardized mean difference 0.28 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.44), compared with olanzapine-fluoxetine 0.26 (0.04 to 0.45), aripiprazole 0.35 (0.23 to 0.48) and quetiapine 0.40 (0.26 to 0.53) from a published meta-analysis. Editors' calculation: 16.8 divided by 20.8 is 0.81, the basis of the author's 81%; the printed p values are reproduced exactly by relapse in 24 of 90 (27%) against 39 of 86 overall, 2 of 9 against 16 of 16 at the outlier site, and 22 of 81 against 23 of 70 elsewhere; the overall counts are those of the trial report (Daly et al., 2019, p. E1).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: By design the Comment reports concerns only; the sponsor's case is mentioned in one clause (the sponsor argues the 3002 difference is clinically meaningful) and the FDA's site inspection in another. Methods for the pooled effect size (which arms, which model, which SDs) are not given; the sensitivity analysis names its test and data source but prints no counts.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: From the FDA's own documents: two of the three short-term phase 3 trials were not statistically significant (one, in older adults, p = 0.06); in the positive trial the MADRS change with placebo was about four-fifths of that with esketamine; the relapse-prevention trial enrolled only people who had remitted on esketamine and its significance depended on one site where every placebo patient relapsed; most participants had failed antidepressants from one or two classes only; and rapid response was uncommon and did not differ significantly from placebo in trial 3002.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The author concludes that esketamine's novel mechanism does not appear to confer efficacy beyond that of cheaper alternatives, wonders whether the novelty encouraged regulatory leniency, and suggests clinicians and patients temper their expectations (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). The first conclusion rests on comparing a pooled effect size, computed by methods not shown, with effect sizes of other drugs from different trials in different populations (adjunctive treatment of depression), which cannot show that esketamine is no better than those drugs. The point about leniency is framed as a question. The opening paragraph announces concerns about the safety of esketamine, while all seven concerns, and the title, are about efficacy and approval. His sensitivity analysis drops, after the fact, the one site most favourable to esketamine and compares relapse proportions, because time to relapse and the hazard ratio could not be recalculated without patient-level data (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the concern about that site comes from the FDA briefing document, which he quotes.

timeline.event: Daly et al.: phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine with continued oral antidepressants, sponsored by Janssen (this round's first-pass card sc_daly_2018).

FDA advisory committee meeting (12 February) and approval of intranasal esketamine for treatment-resistant depression (5 March), as described in this Comment; the phase 3 reports cited are Popova et al. (2019, trial 3002) and Fedgchin et al. (2019, trial 3001).
This Comment: seven concerns about the efficacy evidence and the approval.
Horowitz and Moncrieff: a critical review of the same phase 3 evidence (online first 2020), with a published corrigendum.

replication.where_it_stands: The Comment's factual points are drawn from public regulatory documents and can be checked there; its comparative conclusion is an indirect comparison. A pooled estimate of esketamine against placebo from a systematic review is on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023, being read by other readers in this round).

funding.funder: The author states that the work was not funded (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author states he has no financial interest in esketamine or competing treatments; he previously worked as an FDA medical officer reviewing drug applications, and is a current member of the FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, which met with the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee in February 2019 on esketamine, although he did not take part in that meeting because of the government shutdown (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Portland VA Medical Center (Behavioral Health and Neurosciences Division) and Oregon Health and Science University. The author acknowledges Peter Cary for drawing his attention to the outlier site. His standing as a former FDA reviewer and current advisory committee member is relevant to his reading of the regulatory documents. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the Comment.

what_would_settle_it: An independent re-analysis of the patient-level data of the esketamine phase 3 programme, including time to relapse in study 3003 with and without the outlier site and onset of response by a pre-specified definition; and a randomized trial comparing esketamine with an established augmentation strategy in people with more extensive treatment resistance.

domains.note: No literature search, but the source is explicit and complete for its purpose: the public regulatory record of the phase 3 programme, cited by document and page. The points chosen from it are the author's.

The Comment is itself an appraisal of the trials (definition of resistance, enrichment, dependence on one site, hierarchical testing), but it takes the comparator meta-analysis at face value and gives no methods for its own pooling and no counts for its sensitivity analysis.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The evidence is the sponsor's and the FDA's; the author cites none of his own studies.

Factual points carry page references to the FDA documents; inferences (less efficacy in more resistant patients; regulatory leniency) are marked as possibilities, but the efficacy comparison with other drugs is stated as a conclusion from an indirect comparison.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against esketamine's efficacy and approval (the case for efficacy is under-represented)
domains.note: Concerns only, by design: the sponsor's and the FDA's reasons for regarding the evidence as sufficient are reduced to two clauses.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3). The Comment is short, transparent about its sources and cites them by page, which makes its factual points checkable; its weaknesses are deliberate one-sidedness, unstated methods for its pooled effect size, a figure with labelling errors, and a conclusion drawn from an indirect comparison. It may be cited for what the FDA documents show on the points it raises (with the document page it gives) and as a critique of the approval; numbers about the trials should, where possible, be cited to the trial reports or the FDA documents themselves, and the claim that esketamine is no more effective than cheaper alternatives may not be cited as a finding.

key_findings.finding: The phase 3 trials used a regulatory definition of treatment-resistant depression (failure of any two antidepressants); of the 702 patients who entered the three short-term phase 3 trials, 22% had failed antidepressants of just one class, 60% of two classes and 18% of three or four classes; failure of psychotherapy was not required.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column), citing FDA briefing document p. 15 and Janssen briefing document p. 67

key_findings.finding: Two of the three short-term phase 3 trials were not significant; one of them (study 3005, NCT02422186) enrolled people aged 65 or older (p = 0.06) and was unpublished at the time.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: In the only positive short-term phase 3 trial (3002), the mean MADRS decrease from baseline was 20.8 with esketamine and 16.8 with placebo (FDA slide 24); the author calculates that 81% of the response to esketamine was also seen with placebo.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Horowitz and Moncrieff (horowitz_2021, p. 2 of its online-first PDF), citing the FDA review, give 19.8 and 15.8 for the same trial; both give a 4-point difference. The trial report or the FDA documents should decide which pair is right.

key_findings.finding: Turner states that the randomized withdrawal trial (3003) admitted only patients previously randomized to esketamine (not placebo) in a short-term trial who reached stable remission (FDA slides 20 and 29), giving an enriched population statistically more likely to respond to the drug.
key_findings.locator: 5th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Recorded as Turner's statement; the Comment gives no enrolment figures. The trial report (Daly et al., 2019, SUSTAIN-1) describes patients entering directly as well as by transfer from the short-term trials, so enrolment in trial 3003 should be cited to it, not to this Comment; the enrichment point (every randomized patient had remitted on esketamine) is not affected.

key_findings.finding: The FDA briefing document (p. 25) noted that one site in Poland, where every placebo patient relapsed, drove the overall result of trial 3003; the FDA told its committee, after a member's question, that its inspection found no reason to question data integrity. The author's re-analysis of the relapse proportions: significant with all sites (Fisher's exact p = 0.012), p = 0.0001 within the outlier site (esketamine n = 9, placebo n = 16), not significant without that site (p = 0.48).
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph (right column); Figure
key_findings.note: The figure's labels are partly wrong; see reporting issue 1. Time to relapse and the hazard ratio could not be recalculated without patient-level data, as the author states.

key_findings.finding: The author's pooling of the primary outcomes of the three short-term trials (FDA slide 24) gives a standardized mean difference of 0.28 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.44), which he compares with 0.26 (0.04 to 0.45) for olanzapine-fluoxetine and 0.35 (0.23 to 0.48) for aripiprazole and 0.40 (0.26 to 0.53) for quetiapine as adjunctive treatments, from a published meta-analysis.
key_findings.locator: 7th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: No methods are given for the pooling; the comparison is across different trials and populations, not head to head.

key_findings.finding: Rapid onset was not formally demonstrated: in trial 3001 the onset of clinical response could not be formally tested for the 56 mg and 84 mg doses because earlier endpoints in the testing hierarchy were not significant (Janssen briefing document p. 234); about 10% of patients given esketamine had a rapid clinical response; in trial 3002 it was 8% against 5% with placebo (Fisher's exact p = 0.32); for trial 3005 the mean changes with esketamine and placebo were essentially superimposable until day 22 (FDA slide 37).
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The definition of rapid clinical response is not given in the Comment; it is in the cited briefing documents.

key_findings.finding: The author asks whether esketamine's novel mechanism encouraged leniency regarding these concerns and concludes that clinicians and patients might wish to temper their expectations.
key_findings.locator: 9th (last) paragraph (left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The figure's labels for trial 3003 do not fit its own bars and p values. The bar for esketamine at all sites is drawn at about 27% but labelled 22%, and the 'excluding outlier' bars are labelled esketamine n = 70 and placebo n = 81. Editors' calculation: the all-site and outlier-site totals (90 minus 9; 86 minus 16) give 81 for esketamine and 70 for placebo; the printed p values (0.012, 0.0001 and 0.48) are reproduced exactly by relapse in 24 of 90 (27%) against 39 of 86 overall, 2 of 9 against 16 of 16 at the outlier site, and 22 of 81 (27%) against 23 of 70 (33%) elsewhere; with 22% (20 of 90) the overall p would be about 0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: The esketamine relapse proportion in 3003 should not be quoted from this figure as 22%: the trial report (Daly et al., 2019, p. E1) gives 24 of 90 (26.7%) against 39 of 86 (45.3%), the counts that reproduce the printed p values.

reporting_issues.issue: The opening paragraph says the FDA documents reveal concerns regarding the safety of esketamine, whereas the title and all seven concerns are about efficacy and the approval decision.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Comment should not be cited for safety concerns.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled standardized mean difference (0.28) is presented without methods (arms included, model, source of standard deviations). The sensitivity analysis of trial 3003 names its test (Fisher's exact test of relapse proportions, with and without the outlier site, from FBD p 25) but prints no counts; its p values are reproduced exactly by the counts implied by the figure (reporting issue 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the standardized mean difference as the author's own calculation, which cannot be reproduced from the Comment; the Fisher tests are reproducible but compare relapse proportions, not time to relapse, which the author could not re-analyse.
